This movie is poorly conceived, poorly acted, and poorly written.

Jon Heder is terribly annoying, and cannot escape the same Napolean Dynamite routine. Self-obsessed and ignorant.

Furthermore, Diane Keaton plays the same manish, overly obsessed mother, who cares too much and yet not nearly enough about the lives of her children (see Because I Said So).

Anna Faris, though i generally like her, plays a vapid idiot in this film as well.

Jeff Daniels is passable but nothing special.

Please, skip this film if you want to keep your soul.

"All the world's a stage and its people actors in it"--or something like that. Who the hell said that theatre stopped at the orchestra pit--or even at the theatre door? Why is not the audience participants in the theatrical experience, including the story itself?

This film was a grand experiment that said: "Hey! the story is you and it needs more than your attention, it needs your active participation". "Sometimes we bring the story to you, sometimes you have to go to the story."

Alas no one listened, but that does not mean it should not have been said.

I had a lot of expectations from this movie and more so since it was a Yashraj Film.

Jimmy operates a call centre and one day he is invited by Pooja Singh to teach her boss, Lakhan Singh, English. The two fall in love and decide to run away but Pooja tells Jimmy that she can't do this as she owes a debt to Lakhan Singh, who is also known as Bhaiyyaji. But they decide and steal money from him and its only then that Jimmy finds out that Bhaiyyaji / Lakhan Singh is a Don. In the meantime, Bhaiyyaji hires a man, Bachchan Pandey, to track down Jimmy and Pooja.

Starring Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor and Akshaye Kumar, the movie is directed by first time director Viay Krishna Acharya and is produced by both Aditya Chopra and Yash Chopra.

"Tashan" has to be one of the worse films that I have ever watched. Yes! The scenery is good and Kareena Kapoor (and her much publicised weight loss) looks good. But plot is extremely thin on story and at times makes no sense from one scene to the other - hence why I have

(No spoilers, just plot details) I can't understand such hatred for this episode. You want to watch a bad episode of Smallville? Watch Subterranean - now there's a sack of crap. Tom Welling gives a good performance (I don't say that very often), and Michael Rosenbaum is great, but he is most of the time. The alternate universe scenario seems eerily realistic. The Martian Manhunter, who previously appeared in "Static", returns and tells Clark that the doctor that is the head of the insane asylum where they are being held at is actually a phantom from the phantom zone, and if Clark wants to return to his universe, he must kill him. An overall great episode, with good acting and a decent pace.

This is far more than the charming story of middle-aged man discovering the pleasures of ballroom dancing (although it IS that as well). It's the tale of one person learning to love life again, pushing past all the pressures of work and money to discover joy once more. The bonus in this film is a fascinating insight into the slowly changing attitudes of modern Japan toward everything from ballroom dancing to physical contact. There are scenes that will make you laugh out loud ... a few where you'll want to get up and tango ... and many others where you'll just feel good.

This is a great introduction to contemporary Japanese filmmaking for those who might be under the impression that all Japanese movies are "heavy" and inaccessible.

Believe it or not, at 12 minutes, this film (for 1912) is a full-length film. Very, very few films were longer than that back then, but that is definitely NOT what sets this odd little film apart from the rest! No, what's different is that all the actors (with the exception of one frog) are bugs...yes, bugs! This simple little domestic comedy could have looked much like productions starring the likes of Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy or Max Linder but instead this Russian production uses bugs (or, I think, models that looked just like bugs). Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy were yet to be discovered and I assume Linder was busy, so perhaps that's why they used bugs! Using stop-motion, the bugs moved and danced and fought amazingly well--and a heck of a lot more realistically than King Kong 21 years later!

The film starts with Mr. Beetle sneaking off for a good time. He goes to a bawdy club while his wife supposedly waits at home. But, unfortunately for Mr. Beetle, he is caught on camera by a local film buff. Plus, he doesn't know it but Mrs. Beetle is also carrying on with a bohemian grasshopper

I honestly can't believe what passes for entertainment now. Death (and making fun of death), violence, sexual innuendo, adults threatening children, crudeness, alcohol abuse by minors, drug theft, dysfunctional parents, babysitter from hell, stereotypical jokes about African Americans, police and fat people, and kids sneaking out of the house in the middle of the night - yup, sure sounds like a kids movie to me - NOT!!! Add to that the dark and scary elements - a dead woman possessing and turning into a house and keeping her loving husband a prisoner inside for over 20 years, and also terrorizing an entire neighborhood - how sweet for kids. PARENTS - is this really what you want your kids to be watching - is this what you want to teach them about life?!

This movie is too scary for young kids, and i'm afraid that teens today may be living some of this movie scenario - so why rub it in their faces? As for an adult audience - you won't find it scary or amusing - just boring, contrived and predictable. And the characters are just wrong - clueless parents, ignorant police, stupid and annoying friends, nasty and manipulative

Melissa Joan Hart shines! This show is amazing!! There is no match. Except for maybe Melissa in Clarissa Explains it All. She was marvelous in that, too. This is SO much better than Buffy, the Vampire Slayer. This show is WONDERFUL!

I saw this many years after the television series and, initially, I didn't care for it. Then, as my memory of the series receded with the passage of time, I watched again, and found it absolutely hilarious. Based on the stage play by Neil Simon, it has not been 'opened out' much for the big screen, and that's one of its strengths. Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon are brilliant as Oscar and Felix, and the supporting cast are wonderful, particularly John Fielder as 'Vinnie'. Even now, certain moments can reduce me to tears of laughter - Felix interrupting Oscar in the middle of a ball game with a dinner request, Oscar cracking up and chasing Felix around the apartment, the giggling 'Pigeon Sisters' brought low by Felix's sob stories, and of course, the legendary cafeteria scene ( later ripped off by Nora Ephron's 'When Harry Met Sally' ). Razor-sharp dialogue too. When the boys think Felix has taken an overdose, Oscar says: "They could be vitamins! He could be the healthiest one in the room!". Fantastic!

I simply cannot believe the number of people comparing this favourably with the first film. It moved me to leave this comment! This is just an obvious attempt to cash-in on the success of the first film. The dialogue is appalling and nothing like as authentic or compelling as the original film.

The storyline is ridiculous, the portrayal of the French police laughable and the characterisation of Doyle a mile away from the first film.

How many drug bosses do you think go down to the docks in person to see a shipment come in? The ease at which Doyle finds his guy is just pathetic. Like all the French Police were just drinking coffee until Doyle turns up from America and does some REAL police work. What a joke. Try going to a foreign city and unearthing the biggest crims in the place with a travel map and some tourist pamphlets. Pathetic.

A truly awful sequel, anyone who thinks otherwise is crazy.

"After World War I, an expedition representing the Allied countries is sent to Cambodia to stop the efforts of Count Mazovia in creating a zombie like army of soldiers and laborers. Hoping to prevent a possible outbreak of war due to Mazovia's actions, the group presses through the jungle to Angkor Wat in spite of the perils. The group includes Armand who has his own agenda contrary to the group's wishes," according to the DVD sleeve's synopsis.

Heads up! the zombie make-up department revolted before the cameras started to roll.

Also, this "Revolt of the Zombies" has little to do with its supposed predecessor "White Zombie" (1932) *****, which starred Bela Lugosi. If that film's zombies didn't thrill you, this one's certainly won't. A younger-than-usual Dean Jagger (as Armand Louque) stars as a man obsessive with blonde Dorothy Stone (as Claire Duval). A couple supporting performances are good: devilish Roy D'Arcy (as Mazovia) and subservient Teru Shimada (as Buna); however, neither are given enough material to really pull this one out of the dumps.

** Revolt of the Zombies (1936) Victor Halperin ~ Dean Jagger, Dorothy Stone, Roy D'Arcy

The Fluffer may have strong elements of porn industry truth to it - but that doesn't make up for the fact that it's pretty shabbily directed and acted - and with a very mediocre script.

B grade from start to the exceedingly drawn out finish.

It would be embarassing to think of the general public being offered this piece as an example of state of the art gay film making.

Hopefully it has a limited life in the gay film festival circuit and is allowed to die a natural death on video.

This film will open the Queer Film Weekend in Brisbane on April 10, 2002. I think its success there will be strongly influenced by the amount of alcohol consumed in the preceding cocktail party - they're gonna need it.

It looks like the brilliant team of Shonda Rhimes outsourced the writing of this one somewhere offshore, maybe to the MediocreLand? "PP" reminds me any one of the many tedious, promising at first but predictable within 1 season David Kelly flicks (Picket Fences, Ally McBeal, and now Boston Legal). The crazy cases they get are so outlandish, they barely evoke sympathy or sadness. And that's what actually makes good medical dramas tick - dramatic situations you are afraid of, "This could be me" sentiment. They are not funny either.

The actors are quite good, but the plot lines are dead and cannot be brought back to live. I'm a therapist, and let me tell you - Amy Brennan plays the most unbelievably incompetent, unethical, untrained therapist. Whoever writes her stuff flunked the ethics and the transference/counter-transference courses in Stanford. Somebody should give them a Code of Ethics to read (the episode with the nose-bleeding wife and the therapist's involvement in it). No therapists are that bad.

Women yearning for men who have moved on - had been done to death, we've all graduated "Sex and the City". Addison in her youthful aggression towards the guy she likes -

Diane and I saw this fabulous film today in Fremantle and we both agreed that of the pastiche movies it was head and shoulders above the rest. I say that because we were entranced by the brief, five to ten minute segments that composed the film and the fact that this film had a theme around which each piece was composed and of course that theme was love in its many forms.

Ostensibly the film took place in the various Parisian arrondisments thus giving a particular flavour to each segment. Having only been in Paris several times, I was not knowledgeable enough to readily recognize the locations but I am sure Europeans and particularly French people could easily recognize the city's locations. In any event, the viewer is immediately pulled into each story because of their production excellence so these city locations fade into in-consequence.

The film moves quickly and the viewer is left absorbing one scenario while the new one is on the screen. The stories themselves are not graphic like some pulp Hollywood nonsense, they are subtle and thought provoking and gentle as with most of life without the media swath that buries so much of

Brian Yuzna is often frowned upon as a director for his trashy gore-fests, but the truth is that his films actually aren't bad at all. The Re-Animator sequels aren't as great as the original, but are still worthy as far as horror sequels are concerned. Return of the Living Dead 3 is the best of the series; and Society isn't a world away from being a surrealist horror masterpiece. This thriller certainly isn't a masterpiece; but it shows Yuzna's eye for horror excellently, and the plot moves in a way that is always thrilling and engaging. I'm really surprised that a horror movie about dentistry didn't turn up until 1996, as going to the dentist is almost a primal fear - it's running away from a tiger for the modern world. Dentistry doesn't frighten me, but surprisingly; I would appear to be in the minority. The plot follows perfectionist dentist Dr Feinstone. He has a nice house, a successful career and a beautiful wife - pretty much everything most people want. However, his life takes a turn for the worse when he discovers his wife's affair with the pool cleaner. And his life isn't the only one; as it's his

I rented this film in DVD form without knowing anything at all about it, part of a winter marathon of watching a film every night. After several awful American action adventure films (Ballistic, Daredevil, Cradle of Life) Zhu Warriors struck me as brilliantly original filmmaking. The story is complete nonsense, but I found the film's sincerity, good- heartedness and complete lack of irony refreshing, and the film looks spectacular. Sure, the special effects are not technically as flawless as those produced by Hollywood, but the filmmakers wisely are more interested in color, composition and movement than realism and so many of the shots are breathtaking. In one shot, two of the superhuman characters stand on craggy spires of rock, a huge moon rising before them, the image perfectly balanced by the three elements. In another, a princess-warrior spires through the heavens behind her glowing sword like a heat-seeking missile. And the colors explode from shot to shot, used to express emotion rather than to represent reality.

The characters have the same simplicity and directness of comic book characters, offering no great depth in themselves but referring to archtypes that resonate more deeply. Physically, several of the actors are astonishingly

I've been going through the AFI's list of the top 100 comedies, and I must say that this is truly one of the worst. Not just of the 90 movies on the list I've seen, but of any movie I've ever seen. Drunks are funny sometimes, Dudley isn't. Liza almost made it worthwhile, but alas... just go watch Arrested Development if you want to see her in something good. Seriously, Dudley laughing and drinking is supposed to be funny? I would highly recommend almost ANY other movie on the AFI's top 100 comedies for more laughs than this. If you want to see a funnier "drunk", try The Thin Man. Funnier movie in general, any Marx Brothers movie will kill (especially if you're as drunk as Arthur).

I just saw this film @ TIFF (Toronto International Film Festival). Fans of Hal Hartley will not be disappointed!! And if you are not familiar with this director's oeuvre ... doesn't matter. Claustrophobic environments are the ones which Polanski is best at creating, and this has to be the most suffocating and confined picture he ever created. The emphasis on side walls and distant vanishing points is greater than ever, and even in the small number of exterior scenes the sky is rarely glimpsed. But The Tenant is not just confined spatially, but also in the intensity with which it focuses on its protagonist. Trelkovsky, played by Polanski himself is not only in every scene, he is in virtually every shot. When he is not on screen more often than not the camera becomes Trelkovsky's point of view. And of course almost everywhere he looks he sees his own reflection staring back at him in a mirror.

Shelley Winters plays a woman of questionable virtue who is headed for a ranch with a man (Charles Drake) she may marry. She ends up falling for Stewart, but not before she is passed around a bit. Winters is the most complex character in a film filled with unusual characters. Watch for a young Dan Dureyea as a nutty killer and Tony Curtis in a very small role. A woefully miscast Will Geer plays Wyatt Earp.

Hope that it isn't too late to save people from the terrible things that go on in so many lives. Gangland violence is real, right? Is it right, no! This movie carries an important social message which the cynics may dislike but which nonetheless is to be praised, rather than denigrated. I have watched this movie with great enjoyment at least eight times, each time with equal enjoyment and each time with the feeling that maybe the world could be made better and is not beyond saving (well not until 2008 anyway). 9 out of 10 from me for this one. It's very nearly perfect in my view. JMV

The opening flourishes left me purring with delight at their inventiveness - the altered version of the Archers' logo, the introductory disclaimer, the way the camera pans over the cosmos. It's strange to think that `It's a Wonderful Life' came out in the same year. No great coincidence: the 1940s was awash with heaven-and-earth films; but the glowing cotton wool nebulas and cutesy angels of the competition look tattered, something best passed over in silence, when placed next to Alfred Junge's vision.

It continues to look great all the way through, as more and more striking ideas are sprung upon us. I'm not a great fan of mixing colour with black and white in general. One of the two visual schemes almost always looks ugly when placed next to the other. Not so here. Powell dissolves colour into monochrome and monochrome into colour as if it's the most natural thing in the world, a mere change of palettes. Both the colour photography and the black and white could stand on their own.

As for the story ... this may be Pressburger's best script, or at least it would have been had the conclusion been a more logical outcome

Errol Flynn plays Gay Nineties-era boxer James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett--a man who became world boxing champ in 1892. The film goes from his rather humble beginnings and follows his through his career through him winning the title match against John L. Sullivan. However, while it could have focused mostly on the matches, most are rather brief in the film (except for the final title match) and the emphasis is on Corbett's brash personality as well as his relationship with the lady played by Alexis Smith. Throughout the film, there is excellent supporting work done by a cast of wonderful supporting actors (such as the perennial supporting actor in Flynn films, Alan Hale) and the writing really helped bring these people alive.

"The Muppets Take Manhattan" is different in a lot of ways to every other Muppet Movie made so far. For one, it remains the only Muppet film not owned by Disney. As of 2008, the film still belongs to 20th Century Fox (CBS Fox at the time of its release) even though Disney owns the rights to the Muppets. Also, this film has a story line that's very non-linear, and events that are otherwise unpredictable.

Of course, it's very hard to beat the original "Muppet Movie" from 1979, especially since that movie had more memorable songs than "Manhattan" does. However, one way in which "The Muppets Take Manhattan" is better than "The Muppet Movie" is perhaps the surprisingly realistic scenarios. In the first movie, all the Muppets really have to do is go to Hollywood, walk into an agent's office, and they are immediately given a "Rich & Famous" contract. In this movie, the Muppets learn that they actually have to work for their desired success, and it's a lot harder to do that, especially in the entertainment business, than they initially thought. That's an important and often times overlooked message, provided one is willing to suspend the disbelief

For anyone who wishes to get an impression of the Soviet view of modern Russian history this monumental film is a treasure. The story starts at the turn of the century (1900) in the yellowish sepia colours of old photographs which improves to black and white during the middle of the century and to full colour when the story approaches modern times (i.e. the 1960s).

The story focuses on a boy in a remote Siberian village, who is marked by the arrival and arrest of an anarchist during the czarist era. He later joins the Bolsheviks after the revolution and brings soviet communism to his village. His son, by the local beauty, fights the Germans during the Second World War. When he returns to the village, the oil industry takes off and we are treated to some Soviet economic idealism.

This film is long and slow, but utterly logic and very well made. It can be seen in three parts.

It is a shame that so many people can see only offence in what is, and was always intended to be, a light hearted piece of entertainment that in no way sought to denigrate black people. If anything it is a tribute to the infectious humour and musicality of the black race. I have not been able to view this confection for many years as the 'race commissars' in England have deemed it too offensive to be shown in multi racial Britain. If anyone knows where I can obtain a copy I would dearly love to view this masterpiece again. I think those who routinely look for messages and intent that were never intended in these cartoons, which are, after all, sixty years old, should try to lighten up and remember that the world is a very different place today, but that does not mean that anyone has the right to censor what is viewable from the past.

I used this film in a religion class I was teaching. The golden fish is swimming happily in his bowl in an upper floor apartment. A young boy and his mother are away from home. The boy has been given money to buy milk. On the way home, he stops at carnival to play a game. Next to him stands a man in a black suit looking a little scary. The boy drops the bottle of milk. It breaks. The man in the black suit gives him money to replace the milk. This scene alternates with what is happening at home. A black cat climbs the fire escape and enters the apartment. He(?) discovers the fish bowl and watches it. The fish swims energetically and flips out of the bowl. By now, a bunch of teenagers in my class and I have fallen in love with the fish. The cat takes the fish in his mouth and we all hold our breath. The cat drops the fish into the bowl. The double story line includes the suspicious man in black and the suspicious black cat. Both inspire prejudice. Both are innocent. It was a great discussion starter in my class.

Prix de Beauté was made on the cusp of the changeover from silence to sound, which came a little later in Europe than in Hollywood. Originally conceived as a silent, it was released with a dubbed soundtrack in France, with a French actress speaking Louise Brooks' lines, but was released as a silent in Italy and other parts of Europe. I was lucky enough to see the Cineteca di Bologna's flawless new restoration of an Italian silent print at the Tribeca Film Festival. I haven't seen the talkie version yet, but I think it's safe to assume the silent version is much more satisfying, since by all reports the dubbing is poorly done (Louise Brooks is clearly speaking English, so there's no way her lips could be matched.) Also, the film is made entirely in the silent style, with few titles and little need for dialogue. Prix de Beauté tells its story visually, with exciting, imaginative camera-work. The opening is instantly kinetic, with rapidly-cut scenes of urban life and swimmers splashing at a public beach. I saw "Brother's Shadow" at the Tribeca Film Festival and found myself still thinking about it two days later. The story of a prodigal son (Scott Cohen) returning to his family's custom furniture business after a stint in jail, it offers all the necessary qualities of a solid drama--memorable characters; sharp, observant dialog; sensitive use of the camera by a filmmaker who thinks visually.

But more than that, it presents something that is all too rare at the multiplex these days: the uncompromising vision of a mature sensibility. The talent of director-screenwriter Todd S. Yellin seems to emerge full-blown, but we get the sense he (like his protagonist) has paid his dues. He knows how real people struggle in this world, and he knows how we yearn to see--or at least, to experience vicariously--success. Yet Yellin respects his audience too much to blow happy smoke up our rear ends. In the end, we see that Jake's triumph doesn't lie in commissions, or even in the esteem of his family, but in "the work" he couldn't abandon if he tried.

It's an essential theme in a world (and especially a movie industry) that can't rise above "the bottom line".

He was, in fact, so successful and well thought of that people came from all over to hear his lectures and be taken on his wilderness treks--even though he was not a mixed blood Indian and all his knowledge was from books or faked! Billy decides to play along by saying that "he eats worms all the time". Joe and his friends don't believe him but Billy assures them and bets Joe that he can eat ten worms in one day otherwise he will come to school with worms in his pants.

The boys take Billy up on his bet, leaving the weak stomached child with a mission to gain respect from his classmates by eating worms cooked, fried, or alive.

Really an amazing pile of pap!

A predictable, slow moving, soul destroying, mind numbing movie to which, slitting your own wrists with a rusty bread knife seems... well, almost necessary.

The acting is over done for the thin dialogue, every scene is at least twice as long as it needs to be, the intricate details of how this career is collapsing or that career is rising is just far too dreary and mundane for words. The music would be good if you didn't have to sit through the movie, but really, three good songs is not enough reward for the effort required to watch the movie.

Watching this film I prayed to God for narcolepsy or for someone to shoot me.

Never, ever, ever again.

The US State Dept. would not like us to see this movie, because they have a beef with the Iranian govt. However, it shows us just how civilized Iran really is, despite the content of the film, which centers on the struggle of women there for equal rights in the simplest of terms: the ability to watch a soccer game at the stadium, which is strictly limited to male audiences alone. The film is hilariously funny, and in and of itself is proof of freedom of speech and expression in Iran. I enjoyed this movie intensely. Five girls try to penetrate the police border at the ticket gates to a soccer match between Iran and Bahrain. The ensuing comedy is too funny to describe, from the bus trip to the stadium, to the interceding of the police and subsequent detention of the girls, to the resulting end. Don't miss this classic film. Its a MUST see. One of the best foreign films I've seen in years.

I have to admit I have always found it difficult to watch an Antonioni film from start to finish at the first try, and even for this one, I ended up watching it in three parts on repeated occasions. In the end, I realised perhaps it was better that way, because it forced me to stop thinking in the usual terms of plot and just enjoy the scenes one by one.

The first part seems a lot more fragmentary, which is not a bad thing, it just requires more of an effort to follow. When it gets to the desert scenes, all efforts are repaid in full. The stunning cinematography is only a part of it, what really makes it all unforgettable is how the landscape is made into an overwhelming presence, the silence and vastness of it, the sense of sadness and freedom, the way it fuses and contrasts with the two young characters. The desert is dead, but at the same time it feels less distant and alien than the urban scenes in the first part. Fortier and Profiler have almost nothing in common, aside from both being police dramas centered around violent crimes. Profiler has a sleek, modern feel, while Fortier carries a more classic aesthetic. The storylines in Profiler are relatively straightforward, whereas Fortier weaves far more intricate plots—if comparisons must be made, it bears a stronger resemblance to Prime Suspect. The protagonist is flawed and eccentric yet possesses an almost clairvoyant intuition.  

People love to compare, critique, and rank things—but why not just enjoy them? It’s amusing how some claim Fortier feels "American," then in the same breath insist they prefer American series. Perhaps it’s the language or the tone, but to me, this show feels distinctly more British than American. And let’s not overlook the actors—they deliver performances that are both brilliant and unexpectedly humorous, with a depth that never feels shallow.

This film is fantastic, staying remarkably faithful to Mark Twain’s classic novel. It opens with Hank, played by Bing Crosby, leading a group of children in the cheerful tune "When You Stub Your Toe on the Moon"—a number reminiscent of Sinatra’s "High Hopes," brimming with fun and uplifting energy. The soundtrack shines from start to finish, but my personal favorite is the lively performance by the King, Hank, and Sir Sagamore.  

Perfect for family nights or even a cozy date, this is a movie you’ll want to revisit time and again. Rhonda Fleming dazzles as the radiant princess, adding to the film’s charm. If you enjoyed Danny Kaye in *The Court Jester*, you’re sure to love this delightful adventure. A timeless classic!

George P. Cosmatos’ *Rambo: First Blood Part II* indulges in pure fantasy—rewriting the painful reality of the Vietnam War. The U.S. didn’t win the conflict; instead, it inflicted unimaginable devastation on Vietnam, yet the film perpetuates the myth of America’s virtuous soldiers. According to this narrative, the only villains were the leaders who orchestrated the war, not the men who fought it.  

Rambo himself embodies this contradiction—fervently patriotic, resentful of a nation that failed to glorify its soldiers, yet deeply cynical toward the officers and politicians who sent them to die. Like other pro-war films (such as *We Were Soldiers*), it sidesteps any meaningful justification for U.S. involvement in Southeast Asia—or why any soldier should have been there in the first place. Instead, Rambo becomes an avenger, channeling national trauma into cathartic violence.  

But vengeance isn’t healing. Rather than grappling with the past, the film buries it beneath explosions and heroics. “Do we get to win this time?” Rambo asks. The answer: In fiction, yes. In history, no. The real reckoning never comes.

The film attempts to generate audience sympathy for Jake Roedel (Tobey Maguire) by distorting history, unfairly vilifying the Union and the Jayhawkers. Missouri remained loyal to the Union, meaning federal troops weren’t invaders there. The Confederacy's fight for "states' rights" was a hollow justification—those rights included upholding slavery, corrupt governance, and a patronage system. There’s no nobility in such a cause. If Missourians truly supported the Confederacy, they could have simply joined its army in the East.  

The story’s supposed moral ambiguity rings false. When Jake abandons the Bushwhackers, it isn’t out of ideological awakening—he never embraces abolition or acknowledges the righteousness of the Union's cause.

Yeah, I get it—you’re practically buzzing with anticipation. Well, *The Secret Lives of Dentists* won’t rock your world: it’s competently crafted but utterly unadventurous, honest to a fault yet painfully monotonous. The film follows a married couple, both dentists, who run a practice together (a surefire setup for disaster—if we didn’t have separate workspaces, most of us would ditch our partners out of sheer exasperation). Campbell Scott, whose mustache and overall vibe evoke less of an Everyman and more of a Ned Flanders from *The Simpsons*, plays the excessively patient, über-dad husband, while Hope Davis is the stifled housewife who pours her discontent into amateur opera. One evening, while Scott and their daughters attend one of her performances, he stumbles upon proof that his wife’s frustrations go beyond singing—she’s caught in a heated, flirtatious embrace with the opera director. (A subtle, effective detail: the director’s face remains unseen.) Rather than diving into the messy, lawyer-enriching chaos of separation and custody battles, Scott opts for willful ignorance, burying the truth to preserve the fragile status quo.  

By now, the more discerning viewers are stifling a yawn: here we go again, another tale of the pitiful, spineless cuckold. But—

While this film's approach may lack the subtle realism a sound version might have offered, it remains a remarkable piece of cinema. In its time, it was even regarded as outstanding—earning a nomination for the inaugural Best Picture Oscar (though it lost to *Wings*). Personally, I still hold *Wings* in higher esteem, but this movie shines despite some slight overacting by its lead, Emil Jannings.  

Jannings plays a Czarist Russian general scraping by in 1920s Hollywood as an extra. His fortunes seem to shift when he lands a role—playing an Imperial Russian general battling the Communists during the revolution. The part requires little acting stretch, but it stirs up old memories of his past and the revolution’s upheaval.  

I won’t spoil what unfolds next, but the film delivers, especially in its powerful finale. Keep an eye out for William Powell as the Russian director—despite being made in 1928, the makeup leaves him looking nearly identical to his later roles.

I’d rate this movie a 7/10. The villains delivered compelling performances, and the mystery around Batwoman adds an engaging "whodunit" element. That said, I wish there had been more screen time for Robin—he only showed up briefly at the start and sporadically after. The newer animated series never gave him or Nightwing the spotlight they deserved, and this film unfortunately follows that trend.  

While Bruce Wayne’s romantic subplot could have worked, it felt unconvincing and took up too much focus. Still, if you’re a Batman fan, it’s worth watching despite its flaws.

Absolutely dreadful... The lead actor was decent, but everything else—plot, direction—was pure garbage. This mess was so inaccurate it might as well have been a random sequel with no connection to *Carlito's Way* whatsoever. Fans of the original should steer clear at all costs.  

None of the key elements from the first film were even acknowledged—no Gail, no Kleinfeld, no explanation of how Carlito got arrested or ended up in prison. They tried mimicking the original’s flashback style, but the execution was abysmal. I wanted to give it a zero, but had to settle for slightly higher.  

This is a shameless cash grab preying on one of the greatest films of the '90s. A total waste of £6 and two hours—slow, boring, and painfully predictable. *Carlito’s Way* fans, do yourselves a favor and skip this disaster.

My God, words can't fully capture how painfully terrible this movie is. Let me be clear—I didn't go in with high expectations. A PG-13 slasher film is practically guaranteed to lack, well, the actual *slashing*, so the absence of gore shouldn’t shock anyone. What truly stunned me was the sheer level of ineptitude and tired clichés plaguing every other element of this disaster.  

Take the protagonist—utterly inept to the point where you actually hope the killer wins. And here’s the kicker: SHE NEVER GROWS. That’s right, the movie breaks storytelling’s most basic rule—character development. If you’re waiting for her to finally snap and fight back by the end, don’t hold your breath.  

And then there’s the villain—quite possibly the dullest (and least frightening) killer to ever disgrace the genre. I’m not exaggerating when I say *Dora the Explorer* has more intimidating antagonists than this joke of a film.  

To top it all off, any hope of tension or shock is utterly gutted by the filmmakers’ incompetence.

*Spoilers* *Home Room* explores the aftermath of a Columbine-style high school shooting, shifting focus from the event itself to the emotional fallout experienced by the survivors. The film delves into their trauma, guilt, and denial, crafting a poignant narrative around resilience and human connection.  

The shooting is presented as a grim certainty, with no explicit depiction of the violence—only the haunting reaction of a young SWAT officer after neutralizing the gunman. The story unfolds through three central figures: a detective grappling with an investigation that lacks anyone left to hold accountable, and two teenage girls, played brilliantly by a young Erika Christensen and Busy Philipps, who survive the tragedy.  

Though the girls share little in common beyond the tragedy, it forces them together, sparking an uneasy but compelling dynamic.  

Erika Christensen, only 24 at the time, already had a reputation for delivering steady, compelling performances. In contrast, Busy Philipps—three years older and then relatively unknown—commands the screen with astonishing emotional depth and raw intensity, proving herself the standout of the film.  

*Home Room* succeeds through its intimate portrayal of the fragile yet evolving bond between two shattered lives. The film’s quiet power lies in its refusal to sensationalize, instead drawing viewers into the quiet, aching process of healing.

A wager unfolds between Edgar Allen Poe and a journalist—Poe bets the man cannot endure a full night in a foreboding castle. While he might survive, will he emerge unchanged? That remains uncertain, especially with mysterious figures lurking where they shouldn’t be, including the chilling presence of Barbara Steele.  

The film itself is peculiar—its presentation alternates between French and English, possibly due to lost dialogue. The atmosphere is oppressive, confined to dim candlelight that barely pierces the darkness, suffused with constant dread and the sense of looming catastrophe.  

The Synapse release is uncensored, leaving me curious about what might have been cut from a 1964 film—until a topless scene answered that question. Despite its quirks, the movie stands strong, cloaked in stark black-and-white gloom. Barbara Steele, without a doubt, elevates the experience. **8/10.**

Last weekend, I grabbed this 'zombie flick' from the discount bin, expecting a cheap knockoff of *Land of the Dead*.  

Turns out, I was dead wrong.  

Whoever made this clearly blew most of their budget on the cover art—total bait-and-switch for zombie fans.  

We made it to the scene where undead women reanimate, hop into a car with some clueless yuppie babbling on his phone in the middle of nowhere. They actually *talk* to him before one snaps and kills him. But when they started driving off? That’s where I checked out—my disbelief just couldn’t take it.  

Some claim it’s "so bad it’s good." Don’t believe them. I didn’t stick around for the ending, but another review spoiled that they somehow become *cops* by the finale. Thank goodness I tapped out early.  

This makes *Zombiez* look like a masterpiece. Steer clear!

The only reason I saw this awful teen slasher in theaters was because it was a sneak preview—otherwise I'd have avoided it completely. Haven't we suffered enough of these cheap horror flicks? At least *Scream* and *Scary Movie* had the decency not to take themselves so seriously! The plot is a mess, and the acting is some of the worst I've ever witnessed. (The only film that comes close is *Godzilla*, which ties for the title of the most unbearable cinema experience.)  

The story is riddled with plot holes, and the female characters are so indistinguishable you lose track of who's been killed and who's still alive—not that it matters. The only actress I recognized was Denise, who also happened to be the least talented performer in this cinematic disaster.  

Do yourself a favor and steer clear of this one. (2/10)

When my sister insisted this movie was good, I was skeptical—but I gave it a chance and ended up laughing my way through it. The story follows an eccentric girl who travels to a small town where she’s met with hostility. All she wants is to settle her late aunt’s will and leave, but nothing goes as planned.  

This film is packed with absurd humor—expect a witch, a spellbook (that doubles as a cookbook), an oddball uncle, and a memorable dog. By the end, you’ll have a whole new appreciation for the word *freak.*  

If you’re up for a mix of laughs, shocks, and maybe even some eyebrow-raising moments, track down this cult classic. Personally, I’d rate it a... zero? Just kidding—it’s a solid 9.  

Hope you enjoy it as much as I did!  

—Dakota  
(Feel free to email me at dakota_loves_it@hotmail.com!)

This film is absolutely magnificent, profoundly moving on every human level. The love portrayed is raw and powerful—this might be Will’s finest performance yet. The direction is masterful, the editing sharp, and the score beautifully complements the storytelling. The use of flashbacks is especially effective.  

This is the kind of cinema that stays with you—a rare film with real depth that leaves a lasting impact. Hollywood needs more movies like this, where even an action-packed story carries genuine heart and meaning. Will’s performance is restrained yet powerful, filled with quiet dedication and purpose—a refreshing departure from over-the-top acting.  

I’d recommend watching this alone or with someone special, because once it begins, everything else fades away. For those two hours, the outside world disappears—a rare escape in today's chaotic times. In an era often defined by self-interest, this film offers something different: a character who thinks beyond himself. Truly exceptional.

What possessed Colin Firth to sign on for this aimless movie? Is he truly that desperate for work?  

The film can't decide what it wants to be—exploring grief? exotic locations? the supernatural? or just another excuse to trot out Mr. Darcy? It's a confusing, messy disaster.  

There’s some vague notion that Italy is inherently magical and that Italian is somehow a profound language, yet in the end, the girls just want to flee back to America.  

Pointless scenes drag on—on beaches, in churches, on crowded streets—but there's no coherent reason to care about any of it.  

Then there’s the American woman in the film. Her role was baffling, existing only to spew shallow, awkward, and overly sentimental comments at the girl. Was this meant to hint at something darker?  

All in all, a complete trainwreck. I gave it two stars instead of one only because it lacks the bizarre appeal of a truly atrocious film.

In 1985, I stumbled onto this so-called "movie" while watching cable. At the time, I was in college, hanging out with a high school friend who was drowning in teenage hormones. It didn’t take long to realize this film was a train wreck—ridiculous plot (some older men hiring younger guys to teach them how to pick up women), painfully bad acting (with a single decent performance), and unfunny gags galore.  

The nonstop female nudity kept my friend entertained... for about half an hour. And that’s saying something—this was a high school boy in the pre-internet era, when skin wasn’t just a click away! We kept watching, desperately hoping for even a shred of entertainment, but it never came. The only laugh this movie ever earned was its own marketing—ads that openly mocked how terrible it was. (One poster featured a mock review: *"This is the best movie I’ve seen this afternoon!"*)  

The lone bright spot? Grant Cramer in the lead role, the only one who showed any real talent—he actually went on to have a career. The rest? A no-budget snoozefest with nothing but mindless T&A. Do yourself a favor and skip it.

It’s easy to lose sight of the fact that *The X-Files* wasn’t always about little grey men or mind-controlling slime. Early episodes like *"GenderBender"* and *"Fearful Symmetry"* proved the show could still surprise with bizarre, unpredictable alien encounters.  

*"Fearful Symmetry"* kicks off with an "invisible elephant"—actually a creature displaced in time and space, not unlike *"The Walk"*—and ends with a pregnant gorilla being mysteriously abducted. The episode is packed with unforgettable moments. While its ethical subplot (zoos: bad, except when they're not) feels heavy-handed, the core ideas are fascinating and visually striking. It even explores an often-overlooked question: Why *would* aliens only abduct humans?  

It may not be an instant classic, but it’s undeniably unique—a strange, memorable story that few other shows would dare to tell.

*Grey Gardens* (1975) is the Maysles brothers' captivating documentary about Jackie Kennedy Onassis's eccentric aunt and cousin, who live in squalor within a dilapidated 28-room mansion in East Hampton, Long Island.  

Big Edie Bouvier Beale, 78, sharp-witted and sardonic, and her daughter, Little Edie Beale, 56—whose emotional maturity hovers around that of a teenager—are former socialites now living in near-total isolation, sharing their decaying home with a menagerie of cats and attic-dwelling raccoons. Their days are filled with petty quarrels, radio programs, and impromptu musical performances (they don’t even own a television). Their dramatic descent from high society is both astonishing and strangely compelling, drawing viewers into the lives of these two uniquely dysfunctional yet undeniably fascinating women.  

Widely regarded as one of the finest documentaries ever made, *Grey Gardens* remains a cult classic to this day.

It’s rare for me to dismiss a movie outright, but this one truly tests that stance. The film’s few redeeming qualities boil down to Cornelia Sharpe’s striking presence and its mercifully brief runtime.  

The story plods along without direction, offering nothing engaging or memorable. Even the characters feel hollow—there’s no depth to them, no reason to invest in their fates. Sean Connery’s involvement here is baffling; this was a project best avoided.  

The sole justification for watching would be completionism—if you must see every last one of Connery’s films, save this for the very end.  

If, against all odds, you still choose to watch after reading this (or any of the other scathing reviews here), I sincerely hope you find more enjoyment in it than I did. Thanks for reading.

This isn’t humorous—how could anyone compare this to Monty Python? It’s utterly absurd. There’s nothing remotely funny here. The whole thing feels exaggerated yet off-putting, strange just for the sake of being strange, and it seems like the creators were under the influence—unfortunately, not of anything that sparked genuine comedy.  

I suppose some credit could be given for effort, but even that feels questionable. Is there a laugh track? It’s hard to tell—the lack of actual laughter makes it debatable.  

Maybe I’m being unfair—maybe this is some kind of experimental exercise. If it’s meant as avant-garde art, then fine, anything goes, I suppose.  

But the exaggerated performances—men playing women with shrill voices and exaggerated mannerisms? Seriously? It just doesn’t land.  

The only true successors to Monty Python’s sharp, intellectual wit today are Stephen Colbert and, to some extent, Jon Stewart.

I rented this film mainly for the director—he’s delivered some memorable work before (*Waxork* is a wild ride if you haven’t seen it). Still, I was skeptical from the start but figured I’d give it a chance. Unfortunately, it’s bad. Really bad.  

Spoilers ahead if you care.  

First off, the cover is completely misleading. The box art features a stunning long-haired Jill with highlights, and the back has slick shots, including one in red leather. Even the synopsis makes it sound promising. Then the movie starts, and—surprise—it's inexplicably set in 1977. Jill is nothing like the woman on the cover. And while the plot isn’t as predictable as you'd expect, that's not a compliment. Characters make baffling, unmotivated decisions that are just painful to watch.  

And then, with ten minutes left...

This little-known de Sica gem truly delivers. As the saying goes, "the meek shall inherit the earth"—and this story, while appearing to explore class divisions, serves as a poignant allegory for the postwar homeless populations scattered across Europe. Though cast aside by a society too destitute and indifferent to help them, treated as doormats by opportunistic profiteers, these wanderers retain their resilience and joy. De Sica frames their journey as a modern fairy tale, a kind of Cinderella story.  

Having not read the source material, I can't say whether the deus ex machina stems from the original writer or de Sica himself. But with its opening words—"Once upon a time..."—the film establishes itself as timeless, a narrative that could unfold anywhere. Its biting satire of aristocracy cuts deep, while the whimsy of the homeless characters, especially as they begin fulfilling wishes, adds charm. The ending, Spielbergian in its sentiment, turns this bittersweet fable into a true delight.  

Abandoning strict neo-realism for a style that blends classic storytelling with his signature tenderness, de Sica crafts a film that both breaks and warms the heart. Arguably his most accessible work, it also ranks among his finest.

Wes Craven, you're making us the butt of the joke here. *Red Eye’s* plot is downright absurd. Picture this: a guy supposedly stalks a girl for eight weeks, then conveniently shows up behind her at the airport, smoothly charms his way into her good graces, and—against all odds—scores the seat right next to hers in a two-passenger row (did he bribe the check-in crew?!). The painfully slow buildup is packed with cringey niceties.  

Then, once airborne and surrounded by fellow travelers, he abruptly switches gears, threatening Rachel McAdams’ annoyingly efficient but utterly shallow character with lines like, *“We’ve got your daddy—do as I say, or he’s dead.”* Wait a second—if they already had her father hostage *before* she boarded the plane, wouldn’t it have been way simpler to just abduct *her* off the street and torture her in a secluded room? Skip the shaky hostage scheme, pull out her nails or whatever, and force her to make that oh-so-crucial phone call. Or hey—since we’re in movie land, where logic takes a backseat—why not just go full Hollywood and skip the convoluted nonsense altogether?

As someone who loves horses and appreciates hand-drawn animation, I had high hopes for DreamWorks' *Spirit: Stallion of the Cimarron*. Unfortunately, it didn’t quite meet my expectations. The animation is stunning, and the initial premise—a simple tale of a wild horse in nature—holds promise. Unlike many animated films, there are no talking animals or cutesy musical numbers, which I found refreshing.  

However, the film stumbles with unnecessary narration by Matt Damon, an overly sentimental Bryan Adams soundtrack, and action sequences that feel more suited to a Jerry Bruckheimer blockbuster. Had the filmmakers embraced simplicity, this could have been a masterpiece.  

While not a great film, it’s decent entertainment for young children. I’d still recommend it to families—it’s well-intentioned and one of the few child-friendly options available. It’s not bad, but it had the potential to be so much better. That said, the visuals are undeniably beautiful.

The first and only time I saw *Shades* was at a sneak preview—before its official premiere. Someone from the director’s team was there, though I can’t recall who. It was a Belgian film, completely unknown to us, so we had no expectations. Mickey Rourke, as always, delivered a masterful performance, outshining everyone else on screen. He plays a faded star helping to produce a movie in Belgium called *Shades*.  

From the opening scene, the excessive swearing was impossible to ignore. An occasional curse can be effective, but this was relentless. When Rourke dropped an F-bomb, it felt natural. But when the non-English speaking cast did the same, it came across as forced and needlessly aggressive.  

We stopped counting the F-words and S-words early on. By the end, the whole audience just wanted to leave. When it came time to rate the film, the scale only went from 0 to 10—but we were all searching for a -10.

I absolutely adore this film—I could watch it endlessly. The only part that bothers me is when Riff refers to herself as a "teenage lobotomy," but aside from that, it’s flawless. I’ve never been fond of PJ Soles, and learning she didn’t even know who the Ramones were before filming didn’t help. Still, I can mostly overlook her presence. Most viewers who keep coming back are die-hard Ramones fans, and honestly, that’s the main reason I’m obsessed. Watching DeeDee fumble his pizza lines or Joey repeatedly botch the teacher’s name never gets old—it’s hilarious. One of the best moments is seeing them perform "Do You Wanna Dance" in the school halls—pure brilliance. The special edition DVD includes a solid retrospective, though, unsurprisingly, PJ Soles is absent (probably busy with another project, *laughs*). Overall, it’s an incredible film, especially if you love the Ramones.

This is the finest sci-fi I’ve experienced in my 29 years as a fan. I’m certain *Dark Angel* will achieve cult status. The action is thrilling, but Jessica Alba steals the show—she’s both the most captivating and stunning actress on television right now.

It’s refreshing to see Vintage Film Buff accurately label their superb DVD release as a "musical," because that’s precisely what this film is—nothing more, nothing less. Much like its unofficial remake, *Murder at the Windmill* (1949), the murder storyline serves merely as a flimsy excuse to showcase an extravagant girlie revue, with Kitty Carlisle and Gertrude Michael heading a lineup of dazzling beauties like Ann Sheridan, Lucille Ball, Beryl Wallace, Gwenllian Gill, Gladys Young, Barbara Fritchie, Wanda Perry, and Dorothy White. Carl Brisson lends his powerful vocals to *Cocktails for Two*, the film’s signature tune, which plays no fewer than four times.  

Yet it’s Gertrude Michael who commands the spotlight, not just with her sultry performance of *Sweet Marijuana* but also through her compelling portrayal of the jilted lover. As for the rest of the cast, Jack Oakie and Victor McLaglen could have easily been cut—Oakie’s only redeeming moment is a feeble running joke with cult favorite Toby Wing. The film’s humor, unfortunately, feels labored and excessive, epitomized by the bumbling Inspector McLaglen, who somehow never manages to catch the killer, despite the obvious clues staring him in the face.

I just watched this movie, and while it wasn’t outright terrible, I can’t help feeling let down. I’m genuinely puzzled about what the filmmakers were aiming for—it was mildly enjoyable, but the whole thing felt disjointed, like the creative team couldn’t agree on a vision. One day, the writer called the shots; the next, the director took over; and at some point, even the coffee runner seemed to have a say. It’s as if they tried to cram multiple movie ideas into one, but with neither the time nor the budget to pull it off.  

Some have praised the acting, but I didn’t see it. Then again, if the actors managed to keep a straight face through some of these scenes, maybe they deserve more credit than I’m giving them.  

The DVD description promised a mystery—something reminiscent of *Law & Order* meets *National Treasure*—but the film starts off that way before veering suddenly into what feels like a subpar *Twilight Zone* knockoff. Or was it *The Outer Limits*? Whatever it was, it wasn’t good.

**Rewritten Version:**  

*Slither* is a horror-comedy that fails to deliver enough scares or laughs to fully succeed as either. While it boasts one standout scene and a handful of sharp one-liners, the film lacks genuine tension and consistent humor to keep it engaging. The script further undermines the movie by sidelining its protagonists and frequently losing its balance.  

One of the film’s biggest flaws is its abrupt shift away from its hero (Fillion) in favor of Grant Grant (Michael Rooker) as he transforms into the monster. This section drags—Rooker’s character isn’t compelling enough on his own, and his slow metamorphosis might have worked in a character study like *Grant: Portrait of a Man Turning Into a Monster*, but in an alien invasion horror-comedy, it feels tedious. Ultimately, the script is the real issue—audiences don’t need exhaustive details about the monster’s behavior or propagation. A horror-comedy should focus on trapping its heroes in a desperate, shotgun-wielding standoff.

While I deeply admire Gus Van Sant's filmmaking and consider myself a genuine fan, his adaptation of *Even Cowgirls Get the Blues* misses the sharp, cerebral brilliance of Tom Robbins' novel. Individually, both Robbins and Van Sant are visionary talents—but this particular collaboration fell short.  

It wasn’t a lack of character depth or a failure to bring the story to life on screen. The real issue lies in the power of imagination. A book like Robbins' sweeps you into its world, letting your mind amplify the highs and lows with every turn of the page. The author’s meticulous unfolding creates a gripping, emotional roller coaster—something film, by its nature, can struggle to replicate. Here, I think that magic was lost.  

So, if you’re curious—skip the movie and dive into the book instead.

This film is an absolute disaster! Who are these people raving about how brilliant it is? Sure, it’s "artistic" and "foreign," but that doesn’t make up for its glaring flaws. The story drags, feels messy and disconnected—like a poorly produced reality show without any of the polish.  

The characters are dull and completely one-dimensional, making it impossible to care about them. If they’re supposed to represent real people, then I genuinely pity those individuals.  

The violence feels over-the-top and completely unnecessary, as if the director was desperately trying to channel Tarantino—and failing miserably. (Not that I’m a fan of Tarantino to begin with.)  

And honestly? If my neighbors were anything like these characters, I’d pack my bags and move immediately.

This is a straightforward B-movie sci-fi flick, and the director doesn’t pretend otherwise. The plot revolves around a dragon resurrected by a team of scientists, packed with clichés you’ve encountered countless times before. The script lacks depth, offering forgettable characters that lean heavily on stereotypes. Instead of trying to disguise its flaws, the director leans into the formulaic nature, which gives the film a certain charm—though not enough to leave a lasting impression. It’s the kind of movie you half-watch while doing chores or zoning out during a workout—mindless entertainment with a purpose, but nothing worth discussing with friends unless you’re just passing time without expectations. While I don’t think it’s as bad as many claim, the 3.2 rating seems about right. Still, I’m baffled by those who found it extraordinary—there’s no effort here to make it stand out in any meaningful way.

I lived in Rawlins when they filmed this movie and was fortunate enough to work on it—both as an extra and alongside Eddie Surkin on special effects. It was incredible seeing the behind-the-scenes magic, from the barbed wire coming to life to the electric chair rising through the warden’s office floor. Meeting the cast, from Viggo to Tiny, was another highlight. Locals still refer to the gate cut into the prison wall for filming as the "Disney Gate." If you’re ever in Rawlins, many of the movie sets remain intact and can be explored on a self-guided tour. Working for and with R. Harlin was an amazing experience—I’d love to do it again.

The moment that best captures this film's absurdity—its utter senselessness and mind-numbing idiocy—comes at the climax. **Dr. Ted Nelson** and his bachelor friend, the Sheriff, finally trap the Melting Man on a stairwell landing inside a power plant. Remember, Nelson has spent nearly the entire movie hunting the creature, who has already slaughtered and devoured multiple victims (including Nelson’s boss). He knows full well that the MM is a deranged, flesh-craving monstrosity.  

So there they stand—the Sheriff aiming his gun at the Melting Man (and credit where it's due, Rick Baker’s design makes this thing the most horrifying, repulsive humanoid abomination ever put on screen). The Sheriff then bellows the most crucial question of all to **Dr. Ted Nelson**:  

**"WHAT DO WE DO NOW?!?!?"**  

The camera swings to Nelson, and the truth is plain: Ted has no clue. Somehow, in all his single-minded obsession with **finding** the Melting Man, it never occurred to him to bring, say, restraints—or any plan at all.

It’s almost unbelievable. How did Francis Veber—one of the finest comedy directors alive (at least when working in his native France)—deliver something so utterly unbearable? The problem isn’t just the insufferable characters or the total absence of even the faintest spark of humor. No, the real agony lies in the sheer ineptitude on display—every frame a testament to baffling writing, abysmal performances, and filmmaking so inept it strains belief that seasoned professionals were involved. The film’s long-delayed, barely-there release speaks volumes. What on earth were they thinking?

Having been mesmerized by the stunning visuals of "Hero," I eagerly anticipated this film, which was promoted as similar yet superior—especially with Ziyi Zhang, an actress I admire, in the cast. Unfortunately, it fell short on both fronts. I purchased the DVD without watching it first, and that was a regrettable decision. It didn’t live up to expectations.  

While I understand that gravity-defying martial arts films are pure fantasy, this story pushed the limits of credibility to the point of frustration. A blind woman effortlessly defeating countless opponents? That’s simply too much. Additionally, the lead male character, Jin (played by Takeshi Kaneshiro), was insufferable—his dialogue, vacant expressions, and grating laugh dragged the entire film down.  

Despite its vibrant visuals and impressive action sequences, the story lacked the depth and charm to make it worth keeping in my collection. This film is no "Hero"—not by a long shot.

This film was an absolute disaster, plain and simple. It was so awful that I created an IMDb account just to warn others about its sheer terribleness.  

As someone well-versed in campy horror, I’ve endured classics like *Redneck Zombies*, *House of the Psychotic Women*, and *Slumber Party Massacre II*. I know trash cinema—and this movie is downright unwatchable.  

For nearly the entire runtime, terrified characters dart mindlessly across the screen. When they’re not sprinting aimlessly, they spout nonsensical, lifeless dialogue with zero emotion or purpose. And on the rare occasion the acting becomes somewhat tolerable, the directing collapses entirely. The shaky, low-angle shots were so relentless I wondered if Leif Jonker was filming from his knees.  

Then there’s the infamous *"Leif Maneuver"*—repeated ad nauseam—which consists of clumsily zooming out from random objects like a high school project. The laziness reaches new heights when the crew, too sluggish to capture a sunrise, just filmed a sunset and reversed it.  

By the time the gory finale rolls around, you’ll be shocked it wasn’t filmed first—because the rest feels like an afterthought.

The movie missed the chance to delve into the animals' emotional depth, leaving me deeply unsatisfied. [Spoiler warning] Dr. D’s decision to turn down a lucrative deal for his animal companions felt unconvincing and hollow. Unlike *Babe*, which stood out by highlighting the animals' nobility in contrast to their human counterparts, this film reduced its creatures to absurd stereotypes—so grating that you might not mind seeing them turned into sausage (especially if forced to endure their meaningless chatter). Without Eddie Murphy’s wild antics, this would have been an outright disaster.

**THHE2** delivers plenty of laughs, cringe-worthy moments, and those *"oh sh*t!"* reactions—you might even catch yourself yelling *"get your face away from the damn hole, you idiots!"*—but whether it’s actually worth your time is debatable. The incompetent military characters, who seem clueless about basic combat, were endlessly frustrating.  

Sure, it ramps up the violence, gore, and body count compared to the first film, but I’m still not convinced that makes up for how absurd it all feels—and not in the fun, over-the-top way of *Dead Alive* or *Feast*. Honestly, I’d have been better off rewatching **Aja’s remake** for the fifth time.  

If you're in it for mindless laughs or gratuitous gore, you might have a decent time—just don’t expect to walk away feeling truly satisfied.

(Rating: 21 by The Film Snob.) (See our blog *What-To-See-Next* for details on our rating system.)  

This is the kind of movie that will make you want to gouge your own eyes out just to escape the relentless monotony on screen.  

You won’t merely wring your hands, roll your eyes, or sigh into your popcorn. Oh no. When faced with such staggering mediocrity, only full-blown facial self-mutilation will suffice.  

Start clawing at the lower half of your face first—trust me, you’ll need those tear ducts in the upper half fully operational for the *Truly Tear-Jerking* third act. If you haven’t already fled the theater in agony, this finale may just bring you to your knees.  

In a time when Joe Six-Pack and Hockey Moms are somehow the new benchmarks for leadership and global diplomacy, perhaps a film this tedious will be hailed as proof that *anyone* can make a movie. Watching it, however, is another matter entirely—an act of sheer endurance.  

Now, let’s get to the plot...  

Sidney Young, the London-based editor of a bottom-tier celebrity gossip rag, is on the verge of watching his magazine...

Before *The Toxic Avenger* became a cult classic, Troma Films—known for their low-camp schlock—attempted to dabble in more serious slasher fare. Watching *Splatter University*, it’s easy to imagine this was the movie that convinced them to abandon all seriousness and embrace self-aware absurdity.  

This one’s strictly for the die-hard masochists in the crowd. The film drifts aimlessly between two disjointed casts and a dizzying array of useless subplots, making it downright agonizing to sit through. Here’s the gist:  

After news breaks of a deranged killer escaping from a nearby asylum, the story shifts to a Catholic college (let’s dub it St. Splatter, in keeping with the film’s title). The students are a moody, apathetic bunch, bickering over trivialities like slackers ahead of their era. Meanwhile, the new teacher, Julie Parker, flounders spectacularly in the classroom. Between teen drama, affairs, unplanned pregnancies, and predatory priests, the kids barely have time to dodge actual coursework. Julie, for her part, juggles a sketchy boyfriend, the rigid bureaucracy of St. Splatter, and counseling pregnant students—all while facing the glazed-over stares of her uninterested class.  

Not that any of it matters in the slightest.

**Authored by a woman and helmed by another director. Get ready—could this be a feminist manifesto? Brace yourselves, because we’re diving into a world where men are villains and women are pure-hearted victims.**  

In this melodrama, Trish crosses paths with a guy at an employment agency who acts, dresses, and carries himself like a sleazy hustler. He offers her a job, clearly banking on the chance to exploit her later. In his office, he even grips her chin like some power-tripping Bond villain, right before executing his grand, sinister plan. Later, this creep stalks Trish into a women’s dressing room, harassing her and nearly assaulting her. Because, of course, all men are predators—just ask the film’s divorced women’s club, led by Janet Leigh, who sums it up with her rallying cry: *"Men are all trash."* She spends her time lamenting...

**Frailty – 8/10**  

Despite its nonsensical title and the odd "Bill Paxton Directs" headline, this is a solid, old-fashioned, rip-roaring biblical horror thriller. In the end, it might just be the Southern Gothic cousin of Kubrick’s *The Shining*—but honestly, that’s a wildly entertaining idea. It delivers a killer plot twist and leaves viewers wrestling with a morally ambiguous message. Years from now, this is the kind of film that’ll keep people up late when they stumble upon it on basic cable, terrifying them beyond belief. It’s a shame Paxton cast himself in the lead, but even so, it’s one hell of a good watch.

*The Sopranos* stands as one of television’s most celebrated shows, and even with sky-high expectations, it managed to exceed them. As a fan of mafia and crime dramas, I’m drawn to the gripping narratives these worlds offer—but *The Sopranos* transcends the genre entirely. With over 86 hours of storytelling, it delivers not just an electrifying, unpredictable mob saga but also a deeply compelling family drama, a darkly humorous comedy, a haunting character study, and a profound psychological exploration of morality. The series blends intellectual depth with surreal dream sequences and hallucinations, creating a layered masterpiece. David Chase’s ambitious vision not only redefined television but also solidified HBO as a powerhouse of cinematic-quality storytelling, setting the stage for countless groundbreaking series that followed.  

Chase masterfully balances realism with artistic experimentation, occasionally weaving in surreal "dream episodes" that deepen the narrative. Alongside a stellar writing team—including future *Mad Men* creator Matthew Weiner and Terrence Winter—he crafted a show that remains unparalleled in its ambition and execution.

This uproariously witty satire explores sex, family dynamics, and class distinctions in Beverly Hills, delivering more laughs from the famed zip code than it's seen in decades. The story follows two competitive chauffeurs who wager on which can seduce their respective employers—both stunning, recently single women (played by Jacqueline Bisset and Mary Woronov). If Manuel wins, his debt to a dangerous Asian gang will be cleared; if he fails, he must submit to his friend in a humiliating role-switch.  

Filled with raunchy banter and outrageous physical gags, the film balances its surface-level crudeness with sharp, underlying satire. Bartel steals scenes as a lustful family elder who whisks his alluring teenage niece away on a so-called "missionary trip" to Africa.  

A riotous good time from start to finish.

If you're watching this movie for the first time, it still feels fresh despite multiple remakes. With sharp dialogue and a brilliantly original climax, it doesn’t get the praise it truly deserves. One of the finest comedies in years—can't recommend it enough.

Having no particular bias toward any film genre but with a genuine respect for documentaries, I can honestly say I regretted wasting my time watching *20 Dates* in its entirety. I won’t recap the plot—you can find that in other reviews. That said, Myles Berkowitz's frantic, Woody Allen-esque narration grated on my nerves so badly I either wanted him to cut back on caffeine or down a handful of sedatives. Even Berkowitz seems to realize this film was a mistake, given the segments detailing his struggle to secure funding.  

Forgive me for masking my disdain with backhanded praise, but I’ll admit Berkowitz has a knack for talking some poor fool into bankrolling this train wreck. While I recognize what he was *trying* to do, he fails spectacularly—even by his own low standards.  

And let’s be honest: How many of these women were truly comfortable going on camera with a jittery, self-proclaimed filmmaker? That alone casts serious doubt on the film’s authenticity.  

Oh, and Myles? I think I’ve seen this movie before—when it was called… (*fill in the blank*).

As a kid, I completely adored both Bill & Ted movies. The other night, *Bogus Journey* was playing, and since it had been at least five years since I’d last watched it, I gave it another shot—AND FELL IN LOVE ALL OVER AGAIN! The humor still holds up even after all this time. While *Excellent Adventure* might edge it out slightly, this one totally rocks too. Yeah, some performances are a little campy, but honestly, that’s part of the charm—it’s gloriously cheesy in the best way. Not to mention, it has the absolute coolest portrayal of Death ever put on screen! Final verdict? A seriously non-bogus flick, my dudes. Way excellent! STATION!!!

**CRY FREEDOM** serves as a powerful introduction to the brutality of apartheid, delivering its message in just over two hours. Directed by the acclaimed Richard Attenborough (*Gandhi*), the film gains added credibility through the involvement of the real-life Woods couple, who inspired both the book and movie. The current release includes an additional 23 minutes of footage, originally added for a two-part TV miniseries, extending its runtime to more than two and a half hours. While this lengthening amplifies some minor flaws—such as inconsistent character development and broad stereotypes—one potential criticism (the focus on white protagonists over African ones) may paradoxically strengthen its impact.  

Viewed as a politically and historically educational work (which, in my opinion, takes precedence over its artistic qualities), *CRY FREEDOM* tells a story familiar to many Black Africans—though younger audiences may need the visual medium to grasp its full weight. Ultimately, the film and its source material were intended primarily for white viewers, aiming to provoke reflection and inspire action.

This film mirrors the mundane rhythm of real life—little unfolds in its roughly two-hour runtime, and the sparse, often obscured cast (thanks to the "experimental" lighting noted by critics) offers little plot or direction.  

A tedious slog. Unsurprisingly directed by Altman, whose work swings wildly in quality (yes, "Gosford Park" was brilliant, but remember "Prêt-à-Porter"? "Kansas City"? "Dr. T & the Women"? Ouch). Factor in that the source material is a John Grisham story and the wasted potential of a talented cast—visible only between yawns—and you have a true masterpiece of cinematic failure. No, it doesn’t achieve the quirky charm of "so bad it's good."  

It’s simply bad.

I've watched *Miracles Still Happen* at least four times now, and it never loses its magic. From the opening scenes, the film grips you completely. The tension builds as the plane crashes, thrusting the young protagonist into a desperate fight for survival alone in the unforgiving Amazon—the sole survivor of the disaster. The loss of her mother in the crash adds another layer of heartbreak, making her struggle even more harrowing to witness.  

What makes this film unforgettable is knowing it’s based on a true story—the sheer impossibility of enduring such a nightmare feels almost beyond belief. Imagine facing the Amazon's relentless dangers: wild animals, snakes, towering forests teeming with insects, and the constant threat of the unknown. As the story unfolds, we follow her desperate journey along the river, clinging to the hope that it will lead her to civilization, just as her father once taught her—streams flow into rivers, rivers grow wider, and eventually, they reach safety.

I don’t know if it’s available everywhere, but if anyone choosing films for video stores is reading this—please, please stock this one! (To be clear: GET THIS MOVIE ON THE SHELVES!)  

You have to see it to understand—words don’t do it justice!

About a year ago, I caught a news segment about a zombie movie being shot right here in my area. From that moment, I kept an eye on *Fido* as it wrapped production and started appearing at film festivals. Two weeks ago, it finally hit my local theater—and just yesterday, I read that while *Fido* isn’t drawing crowds in limited release elsewhere, it’s thriving here at The Paramount, even outperforming big titles like *300*. It’s no surprise—locals are eager to spot familiar places (or themselves in zombie garb) on-screen. If you’re on the fence about seeing it, trust me, you’ll recognize plenty: the school, city park, and even the forbidden zone are all here, showcasing the Okanagan Valley in an unexpectedly stunning light—who knew a zombie flick could be so scenic? But beyond the local appeal, *Fido* stands on its own as a solid film, flaws and all, easily outshining most of the other 20 movies in theaters right now.

I saw this at an early screening, and honestly—what in the world? The movie unfolds about as smoothly as Mickey Mouse reciting lines from *Scarface*. It’s so weird it defies logic, and even if you check your brain at the door, the absurdity isn’t even entertaining—just baffling.  

The story follows crocodile hunter Steve Irwin attempting to "rescue" a crocodile implanted with a CIA tracking device. When the agency comes to retrieve it, Irwin mistakes them for poachers and decides to take them down.  

That’s pretty much it—the rest is just a ham-fisted parody of Australian tropes (think endless "Crikey!" and "Didja see dat?") and awkwardly staged action scenes. At one point, Irwin leaps onto a speeding RV and engages in a knife fight with a CIA agent on the roof. Yes, you read that right. If that doesn’t sum up how ludicrous this movie is, nothing will.

This celebrity skit show is genuinely entertaining, in my view. Greg Kinnear stood out as a fantastic host—his presence was a highlight. While Hal Sparks did an adequate job, there’s something about Kinnear’s charm that makes me wish he’d stayed longer. It’s rare these days to see a host stick with a show from start to finish, but all the rotating personalities still delivered plenty of laughs with their celebrity parodies. Honestly, some of those spoofs were downright hilarious. Looking back, I really miss this series. To wrap it up, if you love sketch comedy, do yourself a favor and check this one out—you won’t be disappointed.

My enduring admiration for Italian actress Lucianna Paluzzi, whose captivating role in 1965's *Thunderball* left a lasting impression on my younger years, has guided me to some unexpected cinematic discoveries. Among them is this 1959 British oddity, *Carlton-Browne of the F.O.*, featuring Paluzzi in one of her early performances. Though she portrays a princess here, the film truly serves as a showcase for the rising talents of Terry-Thomas and Peter Sellers.  

The story revolves around the fictional island of Gaillardia—once a British colony abandoned in 1916 and promptly forgotten—until the discovery of valuable cobalt deposits thrusts it back into global intrigue. The bumbling Carlton-Browne, a Foreign Office official played with delightful restraint by Terry-Thomas, is dispatched to handle the crisis. Sellers, in his second 1959 role as a leader of a tiny nation (the other being *The Mouse That Roared*), shines as Prime Minister Amphibulos.
