Yet it’s Ian Bannen as Gaillardia’s smooth-talking king who nearly runs away with the film in this clever, often hilarious political satire.

**The Strengths:** Featuring inventive and genuinely unsettling effects that will crawl under the skin of even the most hardened horror enthusiast. Instead of relying on overused jump scares, it crafts its tension thoughtfully. Even for seasoned viewers, the film delivers a handful of jaw-dropping surprises.  

**Room for Improvement:** At times, the performances fell flat and lacked conviction. While the atmosphere mostly hits the mark, certain scenes suffer from a low-budget, almost "shot-on-video" aesthetic. The camerawork leans too heavily on unnecessary close-ups of trivial actions. Though the effects are impressively eerie, a few are overused, dulling their impact. The ending feels rushed, skimming over moments that could have packed a stronger punch. Some plot points feel unclear—not as an intentional puzzle, but due to oversight.  

Despite these flaws, this indie horror flick stands well above average and is absolutely worth a watch.

**Bloodsuckers** could have been a halfway decent film—the premise of soldiers hunting vampires in space has some cheesy potential. The idea of a universe teeming with diverse vampire species, each with unique traits that remain largely unknown to the characters, is pretty neat too. That said, the logic of an entire galaxy populated mostly by vampires raises some questions—namely, who exactly they're feeding on if nearly everyone is undead.  

The movie itself feels like a low-budget mashup of *Firefly/Serenity* and generic vampire flicks, with a sprinkle of *Aliens* thrown in. The action sequences are mediocre and unoriginal (especially cribbed from *Serenity*), but they're decently shot and deliver enough gore—including some over-the-top blood-spurting—to satisfy vampire genre fans. Unfortunately, the character drama drags, weighed down by conflicts between mostly whiny, immature personalities.

Plenty of films have lulled me to sleep, but this one stands alone in putting me under twice—forcing me to watch it in three separate attempts. The dialogue was painfully stiff, with female characters speaking unnaturally and male characters reduced to shallow stereotypes. To make matters worse, two actresses playing supposedly Japanese roles appeared visibly Chinese, bore Chinese names, and spoke with unmistakable Chinese accents. The plot didn’t help either—I still can't understand the Emmenthal men's obsession with one another. Calculating the score is a struggle: subtracting 8 1/2 from 10 leaves me torn between rating this a one or a two.  

Films have bored me before, but none have managed it multiple times—until now. I had to split this viewing into three sessions just to get through it. The writing was cringe-worthy, with awkwardly delivered lines from female actors and male roles that felt like parodies. Even worse, two women cast as Japanese characters seemed visibly Chinese—from their names to their accents. And the strange sexual tension among the Emmenthal men? Still puzzling. The math doesn’t add up in its favor: 10 minus 8 1/2 leaves me debating whether this deserves a one or a generous two.

This is clearly against the law. Predators who target children exploit material like this. How was this film even allowed to be made? One word describes this movie perfectly: disturbing. What possesses people to create or even watch such content? While viewing it, I couldn’t believe they would depict a child—who looks no older than 12—involved with an adult woman. If this spoils anything for you, I apologize, but I wish I hadn’t seen it at all. What happened to common decency? Do the filmmakers have questionable motives themselves?  

Our society is already plagued by those who prey on minors, yet movies like this only encourage such behavior. Shockingly, in the comments, someone even asked if there was an uncensored version—referring to a child. How is this acceptable? What does that say about the state of things?

I’ve always loved the comic book series, but this movie was a massive disappointment. I was hoping for something with the gritty, bloody charm of *Heavy Metal 2000*—slow pacing, rough dialogue, and plenty of violence—but this went beyond my worst expectations.  

While the plot sticks fairly close to the comic, that’s where the positives end. The characters lack the vibrant energy and personality that made the original so captivating. The film only adapts a small, dull slice of the story, wasting its potential by focusing on the least compelling moments instead of the bigger, more thrilling narrative from the comics.  

With the right creative team, this could have been incredible. Instead, it’s just another forgettable flop—destined to be ignored, collecting dust on a shelf until I finally toss it out for good.

If you love gangster films, this should be your first purchase—or at least a must-watch rental. Al Pacino delivers a powerhouse performance, and the story is a true classic. 10/10!! How is this not in the Top 250 list?!

While the 3-D animation—the show's standout feature—delivered impressively, nearly everything else fell short. It felt like the filmmakers assumed the visuals alone could carry the film, neglecting the plot and character depth. And being a children’s movie is no justification—audiences love well-developed characters (think Shrek or Marlin from *Finding Nemo*) just as much as flashy graphics. The only character with any real personality was Scooter, whose one-note gag of eating everything in sight occasionally nudged the story forward.  

But the real punchline? After enduring over an hour of a stiff, robotic cartoon version of Buzz Aldrin, the real-life legend suddenly appears at the end, calling the protagonists "contaminants" and declaring their entire adventure impossible.  

Seriously? Why not just tell the kids the Tooth Fairy’s a fraud while you’re at it?

Ariauna Albright is a talented actress, so her involvement in this poorly written project remains baffling. What had potential to be engaging quickly devolves into tedium. What sets Ariauna apart is her ability to deliver strong performances while exuding undeniable charisma—unlike her co-star Lilith Stabs, whose looks may impress but whose acting suggests she prioritized beauty treatments over honing her craft.  

This was a production that demanded more sensuality and creativity—a sharper script could have seamlessly incorporated those elements. Still, Ariauna manages to make the best of the material, preserving her credibility to some extent. Tempe Entertainment should take note: when you cast two alluring women in tight fetish cop outfits, audiences will naturally expect more provocative content. Enough said.

It’s an odd experience to watch a film where some scenes fall flat—especially when compared to others in its series—while a subplot or secondary storyline delivers unexpected depth and intensity. *Sudden Impact* is a perfect example. Clint Eastwood, as star, producer, and director, demonstrates his strengths, but also his occasional missteps, in this crime-mystery-detective entry of his iconic *Dirty Harry* saga.  

The famous *"Make my day"* line returns, though unlike the first film—where his *"Do I feel lucky"* monologue was effortlessly cool at first before turning razor-sharp by the end—here, the impact feels reversed. Once again, Harry finds himself clashing with the department when he takes his usual renegade approach to crime-fighting, whether it’s a diner robbery (could this have inspired *Pulp Fiction*?) or a chaotic high-speed chase involving a bus full of senior citizens. Ordered to *"take a vacation,"* he predictably ignores the suggestion.  

The main plot itself lacks conviction beyond its expected beats and familiar dialogue, which only heightens the frustration. But then Eastwood’s story intersects with the far more compelling subplot…

**THE SUNSHINE BOYS**, the uproarious 1975 film adaptation of Neil Simon’s play, follows a retired vaudeville duo—played by Walter Matthau and George Burns—whose partnership ended in bitterness. When they’re asked to reunite for a television special, old grudges resurface, leaving them unwilling to cooperate. Richard Benjamin stars as Matthau’s nephew, a theatrical agent tasked with the near-impossible job of bringing the feuding pair together.  

This heartfelt comedy serves as a charming tribute to the bygone era of vaudeville, succeeding thanks to Simon’s sharp script and standout performances from Matthau, Burns, and Benjamin. Burns earned the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for his role, but it’s Matthau who steals the show with his flawless comedic timing as Willy Clark. Though nominated for Best Actor, he faced stiff competition from Jack Nicholson in *ONE FLEW OVER THE CUCKOO’S NEST*—yet in another year, Matthau’s masterful performance would have been a surefire contender. He dominates every scene, delivering pitch-perfect humor without a single misstep. One unforgettable moment is his audition...

Here’s a review of *The Wizard*—not to be confused with *The Wiz* or *Mr. Wizard*. *The Wizard* is a late-'80s movie starring a stoic, barely verbal kid whose only skills are dominating video games and walking endlessly during the opening credits. *The Wiz*, on the other hand, is a lackluster remake of *The Wizard of Oz*, while *Mr. Wizard* is that science guy who once made a kid drink Tang through a ridiculously long straw contraption.  

Now that we’ve cleared up any confusion, let’s be real: there’s no good reason to watch this movie. It’s essentially a 100-minute Nintendo ad, shamelessly shilling *The Power Glove*, *The Legend of Zelda*, and *Super Mario Bros. 3*. And when I say "shamelessly," I mean it—the whole thing feels like it was slapped together in a weekend by a crew who’d never even touched a Nintendo, with direction so bland it makes my grandma’s knitting look avant-garde. If the writer and director had bothered to actually play a few games first, they might’ve realized they were about to unleash cinematic garbage and instead wisely enrolled in trade school to learn how to install car stereos.

This is easily one of the dullest slasher films ever made—if you can even call it a slasher. I wouldn’t sit through this snoozefest even if it tried to pass itself off as a low-budget porno, which honestly wouldn’t be much of a stretch. Watching a handful of middle-aged strangers wander aimlessly through the woods is pure torture. These films were meant for teenage audiences, so who exactly was this supposed to appeal to? The only redeeming quality is the cover art, which is what tricked me into watching it in the first place (blame the Suspense Classics 50 Movie Pack). And after suffering through the rest of that collection, this one definitely earns its spot among the worst. Save yourself the agony—skip this and check out *Just Before Dawn* or *The Final Terror* instead. At least those deliver actual suspense.

*Cinderella 2* and *Jungle Book 2* left me underwhelmed, but this might just be the weakest of the bunch. Right off the bat, the animation felt cheap—more like a subpar Saturday morning cartoon than a Disney sequel. A few characters stood out, like Thunderbolt and Patch, but others fell flat. Cruella, for instance, was a far cry from her deliciously wicked self in the original—her lines were forgettable, and her design oddly unpolished. As for her lackey Lars? Completely laughable. And where did Roger’s smoking habit go?  

The voice acting was solid—Barry Bostwick nailed Thunderbolt—though Jodi Benson’s accent didn’t quite land for me. There were a couple of bright spots, but the story dragged, feeling more like a bloated TV special than a worthy follow-up. For a sequel to one of Disney’s most iconic '60s classics (alongside *The Jungle Book*), it’s a major letdown. Hard to rate it above a 3/10—just not my thing. (**Bethany Cox**)

For me, this story begins with amusing jokes about Frank’s wild daydreams—whether he's traveling with a staircase or zoning out in business meetings. The issue is that after an hour, you realize the same fantasies and gags keep repeating. It becomes predictable, feeling more like a TV episode where you can dip in and out without missing much.  

Felix Herngren is great as Frank, but even in a comedy, there needs to be more variety and a deeper message for the audience. Simply being funny isn’t enough.

*Ruby in Paradise* is a poignant coming-of-age story centered around Ruby Lee Gissing, a young woman breaking free from her suffocating past to forge her own identity. While the captivating Ashley Judd delivers a remarkable performance in what may be her debut role—one to be admired—the film’s focus isn’t on chasing fame or becoming "somebody," whether a revered icon or a desperate celebrity.  

Instead, it celebrates listening to one’s intuition, reflecting on personal growth, and evolving into the truest version of oneself. A quiet, introspective film (not an action-packed thrill ride!), it occasionally features Judd’s voice-over as Ruby pens her journal entries—yes, gentlemen, this might test your patience, but stay with it. The beauty of the story lies in its simplicity, showing that fulfillment can be found in life’s most ordinary moments.  

Actor-director-writer Todd Field (*Eyes Wide Shut’s* Nick Nightingale) co-stars as Ruby’s grounding yet tender love interest, helping her unlearn the relationship patterns of her past. Yet even his character isn’t presented as Ruby’s ultimate salvation—no outside force can define her journey.

This marks at least the third remake of this film, so that sense of déjà vu while watching is no accident. Aside from shifting the setting and tweaking the storytelling, the changes are minimal—and not for the better, since the core plot was flawed from the start. It simply doesn’t work. Much like its predecessors, the acting is underwhelming.  

While the ending might shock first-time viewers, it feels out of place with the rest of the story. Cutting the film ten minutes earlier would have made it far more satisfying—maybe even worthwhile. But here’s the spoiler: crime pays in the end, as the villain walks free. That’s a message I never enjoy seeing in a movie.

While it avoids mindless violence or empty fluff, the film also lacks depth and a coherent plot. There was potential here, but the director seems to have lost focus. The narrative feels fragmented, veering into odd directions without a satisfying resolution. The portrayal of golf country club culture also feels unrealistic, suggesting little firsthand familiarity. Overall, it fails to captivate.

Wait, me? No, I’m dead serious—that’s literally the description on the video case.  

**Plot, condensed:** A beautiful woman smiles endlessly, and for some inexplicable reason, this drives every man around her to murder each other.  

*"Find Ariel... Where's Ariel... Can't find Ariel..."* Dude, she’s *right behind you.*  

Honestly, most of the critiques about this atrocious little space opera have already been exhausted.  

After the initial cast is swiftly wiped out, a new batch of painfully wooden actors—mostly playing convicts—takes their place… only to meet the same predictable fate. Every twist is telegraphed a solid fifteen minutes early. Feels like they drew straws to decide who got the most screen time (and the bigger paycheck).  

The so-called "alien virus/hologram/VR witch/glitch" is bizarrely inert—she doesn’t actually *do* anything. Why not just stay in the computer instead of pulling her repetitive "teleporting vampire" shtick? (Admittedly, she’d be more compelling as an actual vampire, or *anything* beyond just lingering in the background, staring blankly. Yet somehow, that’s enough to turn men into homicidal maniacs. Go figure.)  

Oh, and don’t be fooled—this isn’t really a space movie.

While not John Cleese's strongest television venture, *Strange Case* gives the impression of an unpolished first draft hastily greenlit before refinements could be made. The series tosses in both absurd and witty concepts, yet the overall narrative never quite coheres into something substantial.  

That said, Arthur Lowe steals scenes as a delightfully eccentric Dr. Watson—bionic enhancements and all—with his perfectly timed, baffled exclamations: *"Good Lord."*

I *adored* the original Scary Movie. Parody is my absolute favorite style of comedy—it’s often considered the most clever form of humor. The Wayans brothers brilliantly captured that in the first film but somehow lost their way with the sequel. Don’t get me wrong, the Wayans family are comedic legends—even geniuses stumble sometimes.  

The sequel starts strong. The "Exorcist" spoof, particularly the "come on out, ma" bit, delivers that sharp, classic Wayans humor. Beyond that, though, only two moments really made me laugh: first, when Tori Spelling gets haunted by a ghost, then turns clingy, gushing about marriage while he panics, insisting, "It was just a booty call!" Second, the "Save the Last Dance" bit where Cindy accidentally beats up a girl while rehearsing dance moves. But even those fleeting chuckles pale in comparison to the nonstop hilarity of the original.  

The rest? Just lazy, tasteless gross-out gags—so different from the first film’s witty, understated jokes.

What’s not to love? If the high-octane car chases and Jessica Simpson’s stunning presence didn’t thrill you, I don’t know what will. Let’s be real—this movie wasn’t trying to win Oscars. It was pure, fast-paced fun with a great sense of humor. Though I barely knew the original show, catching one episode recently made me appreciate how well the film captured that same vibe. 

The theater seats practically rumbled during the action scenes—now that’s excitement! The car sequences were sharp and never dragged, unlike some *2 Fast 2 Furious* moments that overstayed their welcome. And let’s be honest, Jessica Simpson brought serious heat—just wish she had even more screen time kicking butt. 

Bottom line? I had an absolute blast and would gladly see it again. This movie delivers exactly what it promises: a wild ride. Lighten up and enjoy it for the adrenaline rush it is—definitely DVD-worthy.

This film was terrible—emphasis on the capital "T." The opening scene had potential, but that glimmer of hope vanished the moment the plot's direction became clear.  

Then there's Morty, the wooden statue. While unsettling in the original movie, here he just looks ridiculous—like some guy stuffed into a flimsy plastic suit. (And honestly, who thought "Morty" was a scary name? It's about as terrifying as "Bobby" or "Steve." Why not call him something truly horrifying, like "Senator Bureaucrat"? *Shudder.*)  

But the real head-scratcher is the scene where the so-called "hero" attacks his father's tombstone. You'd expect a sledgehammer—maybe even a plank of wood—but no. He furiously whacks it with... a twig. And as if that weren't ridiculous enough, the tombstone then starts bleeding after they leave. Seriously?  

Then there’s the random Native American character who lives with the grandparents. His sole purpose? Morty's personal caretaker. He spreads eerie tales, scolds non-believers, and even does handyman work on Morty when an arm falls off. Riveting stuff.

**Brokedown Palace** follows two best friends, Alice and Darlene, whose impulsive vacation to Thailand takes a dark turn when they are framed for drug smuggling and imprisoned. While the film could have evolved into a gripping, emotionally charged drama akin to *Return to Paradise*, it shifts its focus away from the gravity of their circumstances and instead centers on their turbulent friendship.  

Both Claire Danes and Kate Beckinsale deliver strong performances, emphasizing the complex dynamics between their characters—mistrust, jealousy, and the ultimate test of loyalty. Rather than exploring the political or brutal realities of prison life (which are somewhat downplayed), the film prioritizes the emotional tension and sacrifices born from their bond.  

Though engaging, the story suffers from inconsistencies and moments that stretch believability. The fear and desperation of their predicament never fully resonate, and glimpses of the outside world—including Bill Pullman’s role as a purportedly shady lawyer—feel underdeveloped.

I can't believe the brilliant Alan Ball was involved in this disaster. After watching the first two episodes, it's clear this show won't make my watchlist—there's just too much working against it.  

The casting feels off across the board. Anna Paquin as Sookie is painfully miscast; I’ve seen her deliver stronger performances before, so maybe it’s the weak writing. She’s also not particularly engaging on-screen—at times, she even comes across as unflattering. The actor playing Bill fares slightly better, though mostly because his character is meant to be stiff and detached. The rest of the cast struggles with poorly written roles and forced, grating accents. Tara is unbearable to watch—Rutina Wesley’s attempt at the accent is like nails on a chalkboard. Nelsan Ellis isn’t much better; his dialogue is often incoherent, and his character...

I adore this film—Jouvet, Arletty, Blier, Carné... Nearly everything about it has been discussed, but there’s one detail worth highlighting: no actual footage of the real Hôtel du Nord (still standing—or is it? I heard rumors of demolition…) was used. The entire scene was recreated on set, primarily because halting traffic along the St. Martin canal for weeks wasn’t feasible.

"Presque rien" tells the tender story of two boys who fall in love during a summer by the sea. Rather than focus on the plot—though it remains compelling and unique—the film’s true strength lies in its breathtaking cinematography. Every frame is crafted with such beauty that it captivates completely, earning nothing less than the highest praise.  

The storytelling unfolds unconventionally, weaving a complex, non-chronological narrative that leaves certain questions unanswered. Yet this deliberate ambiguity only deepens the film’s intrigue. I highly recommend "Presque rien" to anyone who values artistry in cinema—it will not disappoint.

French director Claire Denis has cemented her place among cinema’s most distinctive and celebrated auteurs with films like *Chocolat*, *Beau Travail*, and more. Her 2004 work *The Intruder* (*L'Intrus*) further enriches her profound and enigmatic filmography. A lyrical meditation on solitude and longing, the film delves into the fractured mind of a man in physical and mental decline, journeying across the world in search of absolution and serenity—only to find both elusive.  

Loosely inspired by Jean-Luc Nancy’s memoir about undergoing a heart transplant, *The Intruder* is steeped in such deliberate ambiguity that even after multiple viewings, its meaning resists tidy explanation, demanding descriptions as fluid and impressionistic as the film itself.  

Louis Trebor (Michel Subor), a hardened yet wealthy man in his seventies, is likely succumbing to a failing heart. Much like the professor in Ingmar Bergman’s *Wild Strawberries*, he grapples with the ghosts of his past while there’s still time. Though physically robust, he carries an air of exhaustion, his face etched with quiet defeat. We witness only fragments—glimpses of a life haunted by regret and unresolved yearnings.

I’ve seen this film twice already, and I still want to watch it again. It immerses you in the director’s perspective—his personal relationships and the political tension in Israel. Every time I watch, it brings me to tears, stirring nostalgia for a beautiful past while also confronting the brutal tragedy it portrays. Absolutely worth watching.

This isn't your usual vampire tale—forget Bram Stoker or Anne Rice. This is something fresh, a truly original vampyre story. These creatures aren't your typical undead; they're genetic mutants, unfazed by sunlight and dripping with pure evil.  

The film isn’t flawless. Many of the actors are clearly newcomers, though the two leads—playing Van Helsing and the vampyre woman—deliver solid performances. Brace yourself for relentless violence, which might be too much for some viewers. It's also packed with intricate scientific details that could lose or bore audiences.  

What hooked me was the clever plot and those standout performances. Imagine what this film could achieve with a bigger budget and wider release—its potential is limitless.

At first glance, you might mistake this for a biography of Claude Monet, but it’s really an intimate exploration of friendship among three teenage girls on a French synchronized swimming team. Parents and teachers are absent from the narrative, and the world of boys is represented only by the occasional, baffled appearances of the handsome but clueless Francois.  

Pauline Aquart is the youngest of the trio, still dreaming of joining the team she idolizes. She’s unconventionally striking—lanky, all elbows and knees, with big feet and no curves to speak of. Her strong jaw and full lips give her a unique look, one that slowly grows on you until, from the right angle, she becomes mesmerizing.  

Then there’s Adele Haenel, older and more poised, cutting a glamorous figure in her swimsuit. With her effortless confidence, she flirts, flaunts her long blond hair, and seems every bit the untouchable beauty. But appearances can deceive—or can they? It’s hard to tell. The French have a way of embracing contradictions over neat resolutions. No wonder Francois keeps circling back, equally intrigued and bewildered.

Critics of this film probably carry the sting of unrequited love in their hearts. It’s a wonderful movie for anyone who truly appreciates Johnny Mathis’s music—or any classic tune from that golden era, like Bobby Darin’s "Beyond the Sea" or Stan Getz’s "The Girl From Ipanema."  

A film’s worth is measured by how often you return to it—and *Chances Are* lured me back more than once.  

The chemistry among the cast was undeniable; their performances blended seamlessly.  

Let your heart open wide and allow the film’s lighthearted charm to sweep you away.  

—Alan

You can tell this movie had a $5 budget. It’s a complete waste of time... ugh. There’s nothing even slightly good about it. I don’t know why I kept watching—the lead actress isn’t attractive, the acting is painfully bad, and honestly, anything else would be a better use of your time. Watch TV, play a trashy video game—just don’t watch this. I feel robbed—absolutely robbed—of my time.  

I’ve never written a movie review before, but I had to warn anyone considering this disaster. If you’re checking IMDb to see if it’s worth watching, take my advice: skip it.  

- No action.  
- No attractive women.  
- Zero budget.  
- Horrendous acting.  

And the cherry on top? The entire “movie” takes place in one room. Avoid at all costs.

The film defies easy categorization—maybe think of it as an avant-garde spy thriller? *Mother Night* is one of Vonnegut’s finest novels and arguably his most adaptable to the screen. The movie stays remarkably true to the source material, and its indie production style works better than a big-budget Hollywood treatment ever could. These days, a thoughtful novel like *Mother Night* would likely never get the studio backing it deserves—but in this case, that’s not such a bad thing.  

With sharp direction and a strong cast, the film holds its own. Nick Nolte, who just keeps landing better roles with age, brings his reliable everyman quality to a complex character. Sheryl Lee, radiant and brilliant as ever, remains underrated—her career deserved more than her breakout as a ill-fated character (*Twin Peaks*) with limited screen time, even if the show became a cult hit.  

All in all, this is a thoroughly engaging film—no prior reading required.

After reading through numerous comments about this film, it’s evident that science fiction audiences fall into two distinct categories. The first consists of highly literate, well-read, and intelligent viewers who understand the genre’s history and the profound heights it can achieve in the hands of a masterful storyteller. For decades, science fiction was relegated to the lowest tier of literature, dismissed by critics as little more than tales of ray guns and aliens aimed at young teens. Today's knowledgeable fans recognize this past and celebrate the contributions of visionaries like Asimov, Heinlein, Bradbury, and Ellison—writers who elevated the genre beyond pulp fiction. Their works were intellectually stimulating, challenging conventions and reimagining what it means to be human.  

These discerning viewers approach Hollywood’s offerings with justifiable skepticism, scrutinizing each film not out of cynicism but because they demand substance. Flashy effects and relentless action sequences can’t distract them—what matters is the story. They’ve seen too many shallow adaptations to be easily impressed. When the emperor has no clothes, they’re the first to call it out.

This movie was truly thought-provoking. I’ve watched it multiple times—first as a four-year-old, and it stuck with me, then again when I was 12. The director’s core message is clear: we must awaken and avoid the error of excluding God from our daily lives, or worse, deliberately dishonoring Him.  

A powerful film for both skeptics and the faithful!

A merciless tale. A drifter accepts a contract from a mobster to kill a man for cash, only to be betrayed afterward. While hiding his guilt, he seduces the victim’s grieving wife and moves in with her—until she discovers the truth. In a fit of panic, he "accidentally" kills her, then seeks vengeance against the mobsters who double-crossed him in a hollow, self-serving act of retribution.  

The core issue is morality, or the complete absence of it. By taking the contract, the drifter forfeits any claim to sympathy or redemption. With no moral anchor, he’s impossible to root for, leaving the story adrift in amorality. Even the wife—a refined woman running a homeless shelter, played with grace by Kari Wuhrer (the sheriff from *Eight Legged Freaks*)—loses credibility when she swiftly takes the drifter into her bed, despite her recent loss. And when she uncovers his crime, her reaction—trapping him in her house as if it were some impenetrable fortress—strains logic further.

Twenty years ago, a five-year-old boy named Michael Hawthorne saw his father murder his mother with an axe on a deserted road before taking his own life. Now an adult, Michael (Gordon Currie) invites his girlfriend Peg (Stacy Grant) and closest friends—Chris (Myc Agnew), Jennifer (Emmanuelle Vaugier), Lisa Ann (Kelly Benson), Ned (Brendon Beiser), Mitch Maldive (Phillip Rhys), and Trish (Rachel Hayward)—to spend Halloween at his grandparents' remote farm. He asks each of them to wear costumes symbolizing their deepest inner fears. Along with his Indigenous friend Crow (Byron Chief Moon), they plan to perform an ancient ritual using a carved wooden effigy named Morty (Jon Fedele), believing it will free them from their fears forever. Michael’s own greatest terror is becoming a killer like his father—but when the ceremony goes wrong, Morty transforms into his father’s vengeful spirit, slaughtering his friends one by one.  

*The Fear: Resurrection* squanders its intriguing premise—confronting and destroying one’s worst fears—with a muddled script packed with tired horror tropes. The performances range from wildly over-the-top (like Betsy Palmer’s) to painfully underwhelming.

There have been dark times in my life—moments of confusion and despair. Watching *Rancid Aluminium* was one of them.  

The red flags were obvious: no premiere (even the cast avoided it) and no reviews in sight. My only solace was the faint hope that I might doze off.  

Nothing in the film made sense. The dialogue was mind-numbing. At one point, I actually cheered as the lead character appeared to be shot, only to sink back into misery when he miraculously survived. Frankly, everyone involved in this disaster deserves punishment.  

The few bright spots were entirely accidental—like the bizarre scene where the protagonist, for reasons unknown, loudly instructs the stranger in the next stall to cover their ears while he... well, you can guess.  

Words can’t express my rage, so I’ll leave it at this:  

*Rancid Aluminium*—a film exclusively for sadists, fools, and anyone eager to punish themselves.

I watched this movie roughly five years ago, and it still lingers in my mind like a bad dream. I went into it fully aware of its terrible reputation—so really, I have no one to blame but myself. But like many others, I doubted the overwhelming negativity. As a fan of Sandler’s work, the idea that one of his films could truly be *that* awful seemed impossible. I assumed it was just his detractors exaggerating. Turns out, I couldn’t have been more mistaken.  

What you get is a so-called comedy that doesn’t deliver a single moment of genuine humor—an almost impressive feat. You’d think in 90 minutes, they might’ve stumbled into something, *anything*, that could crack a smile. But no. It’s just relentlessly bad. This isn’t one of those "so bad it's good" disasters—it’s purely, painfully unfunny. You don’t laugh at how terrible it is; you just sit there, hoping for even the faintest glimmer of amusement. But it never comes.  

Remember *The Ring*? The one where people die seven days after watching a cursed tape? If *this* movie were on that tape, people wouldn’t wait—they'd take matters into their own hands instantly.

Many WWII-era American war films were highly entertaining but often sacrificed realism for propaganda purposes, aiming more to boost morale on the home front than to depict events accurately. That’s not to dismiss these movies—plenty remain enjoyable to this day. Yet their frequent lack of authenticity keeps them from standing among the finest war films. Take *Air Force*, starring John Garfield, where a single B-17 practically wipes out half of Japan’s air force—pure fantasy.  

*Pride of the Marines*, however, breaks from this trend, earning praise for its faithful retelling of an astonishing true story. At first glance, the events seemed too extraordinary to be real, but research confirmed that the film stayed remarkably close to the actual exploits of two Medal of Honor recipients. Sometimes, reality truly is stranger than fiction!

I came across this film after reading the book it was adapted from. Though not a strictly factual biopic, it’s "loosely inspired" by real events. Even so, it delivers a gripping and unsettling dive into depravity and insanity, with Michel Serrault delivering a haunting portrayal of Dr. Petiot.  

The film is filled with striking visuals—Petiot moving through the night like a spectral figure, his dark cloak billowing behind him, becomes an almost mythic image. There’s also a strong touch of expressionism in scenes like his twisted shadow climbing the cellar stairs, where the mutilated remains of his victims await burning—reminiscent of eerie moments from *Nosferatu*.  

Yet what stayed with me most was the film’s soundscape. The score pulses with dread from the opening credits, underscored by ghostly, wordless cries. Petiot’s clinic is nestled in a bustling courtyard full of small shops, and throughout, you hear the constant scrape of knives being sharpened and a peddler’s dissonant saw-music. Animal sounds seep in too—the concierge’s unseen goat, yowling cats—and as the story unfolds, these unsettling noises only deepen the chilling atmosphere.

This film has no artistic merit worthy of recognition. In fact, it hardly deserves an audience at all. Ironically, it was awarded for cinematography—yet the camera work is jarring at best. Every shot feels unnecessarily cramped, as if your vision is being forcibly cropped. The storytelling is weak; I’ll admit, I couldn’t stomach watching it to the end. The lowest point? A scene of soldiers partying in their barracks, with one being pressured into drinking—an embarrassingly cliché moment that felt straight out of a Steven Seagal movie.  

Do yourself a favor and skip this disaster.

To create a film like this, one must have no understanding of Nietzsche’s writings or character, psychological methods, or Vienna’s past. Start with a famous intellectual whose work you’ve never opened, portray him as unhinged, throw in some eccentric doctors attempting to treat him, add a few moderately attractive women, cast an actor with an exaggerated mustache in the lead, have every character speak in thick accents, fill it with absurd dream sequences, randomly insert a second celebrated figure with no connection to the first (Freud), sprinkle in a handful of terms from the genius’s books, exaggerate every element—especially the soundtrack—and there you have it. Audiences, steer clear.

As the director’s nephew, I can say with authority that this film is truly one of the worst ever made—it took me years to track down a copy, and even my uncle doesn’t own one anymore (yes, I asked). I can’t wait to surprise him with a copy of his own.  

Right now, the movie sits at a dismal 1.9/10 rating. Based on that score, it should rank somewhere in the mid-30s on IMDb’s "Bottom 100," but with just 206 votes, it hasn’t officially made the list yet. It’s almost disappointing that it hasn’t even earned that dubious honor.  

For this year’s holiday gifts, I’ll be distributing copies to my unsuspecting family. Best gift? Worst gift? Either way, it’ll be unforgettable.

At first, I resisted the hype around *Lost*—until I stumbled upon that unforgettable season one episode with the polar bear. From that moment, the show completely hooked me (the series, that is, not the bear). So, pardon the rambling, but I need to gush about why this show is brilliant.  

*Lost* starts with a deceptively simple premise—a plane crash leaves survivors stranded on a mysterious island—but quickly unfolds into something far richer. Each character is meticulously crafted, their backstories peeled back layer by layer. Some are running from their past (Sawyer and Kate), others toward something deeper (Locke, Claire). The island itself becomes more than just a setting—it’s a force, a nexus of eerie connections and unseen terrors that bind them all in ways they can’t yet understand.  

And while TV acting doesn’t always shine, *Lost*’s cast is outstanding, perfectly embodying their roles with nuance and depth that keeps you riveted.

I stumbled upon this movie late Saturday night—or maybe it was already Sunday morning—while watching with my brother after a few drinks. Let me tell you, this is *the* perfect film for tearing apart. The so-called "luxury" ocean liner is just a basic roll-on, roll-off ferry, complete with cast-iron everything. And don’t even get me started on the doors marked with cheap "STAFF" stickers, only for the same door to reappear as a different location in another scene. Glorious.    

The continuity is laughably bad—it hits you in the face with its flaws. In the finale, the hero leaps off a lifeboat with the ferry way in the distance. Then, suddenly, his son and new girlfriend (who, by the way, is the ship’s PR director, a kung-fu expert, and an ex-cop fired for her maverick ways—yes, really) are speeding away from an explosion on the ferry... and *bam*, the dad is right there, hugging them. How? Magic, obviously.  

There’s not a single redeeming thing here. The "casino" is the size of a bedroom, holding exactly one table. And when running from the bad guys, guess what? There’s only one possible hiding spot. You already know where this is going.

A Texas desert town becomes the site of a string of murders. Who’s behind the killings? While the film hints at mystery and touches on racial tensions (though the latter feels out of place), it ultimately caters to slasher enthusiasts with its gruesome violence and gratuitous nudity—staples of the genre.  

Dana Kimmell, known for her role in *Friday the 13th Part 3*, plays a rebellious teen who takes on a makeshift detective role.  

**1/2 out of ****  

MPAA Rating: R for strong violence/gore, nudity, and some language.

Despite its R rating, I seriously question whether you'll actually like this film unless you're very young.  

The problem? There's no meaningful story, zero character growth, and not a single genuinely funny moment.  

What it *does* deliver—in excessive amounts—is nudity. Scene after scene features attractive women with little to no clothing, if that's what you're looking for.  

I don’t get why this even carries the *American Pie* name. It fails as both a comedy and an erotic film, landing somewhere in an awkward middle ground.  

Only watch this if you want cheap titillation but feel too embarrassed to pick up an actual adult movie.  

Final verdict? 1/10 for the two times it made me smirk, plus an extra 2/10 for the attractive cast—but that’s being generous.

Another dubious group makes its mark. This isn’t a spoiler—the real reveal happens when you dig into the people behind this drawn-out, pseudo-scientific sales pitch... Ramtha’s School of Enlightenment.  

Any belief system that relies on smoke and mirrors to hide its truth isn't worth my time. Lucky for me, I borrowed this movie from a so-called "friend" instead of wasting money on this New Age mind-numbing nonsense. Maybe if they're so convinced they can walk on water, they should test that theory—let’s see them walk, sink, or finally stop talking.  

As a film, it barely scrapes a "1" for entertainment value, if only for spawning cinema’s most insufferable character (seriously, that photographer’s roommate—ugh). If curiosity insists, save your cash and borrow it from one of their already-converted followers.

This early Adam Sandler movie feels like a reflection of his stand-up comedy days in 1989. His character’s relentless self-awareness of untapped comedic talent and irritation over weak material seems more like Sandler’s own frustrations than something written into the script. It doesn’t come close to his later hits—Big Daddy or even the silly charm of Billy Madison. At this point, Sandler hadn’t yet refined his signature humor, much like the struggling comedian he portrays.  

Most of the film’s attempts at jokes consist of Sandler arguing with himself—usually about his overlooked genius or his struggles with dating due to his looks. The whole thing is painfully awkward, not just because of the humor (or lack of it), but because it never commits to being a real movie. Sandler constantly breaks the fourth wall, calling out the low budget or the absurdity of what’s happening on screen.  

By the end, I just wanted to pretend I’d never seen it—partly out of secondhand embarrassment, partly out of fear that if too many people discovered this misfire, it might retroactively stain his career. Skip this one.

Anyone capable of sitting through this film and calling it "good" has no appreciation for quality cinema. This was painful to watch—the direction felt like a high school project, and the cinematography wasn't much better. *The Blair Witch Project* had superior camerawork, and I despise that movie! The premise had potential for a gripping, intense story, but it fell flat within the first ten minutes and never recovered. Some argue it's about a child's imagination—fine, but that's no excuse for lazy execution. Take the "Indian in the store" scene: Did the kid just glance at an idol and hallucinate an entire backstory about the Wendigo? The employee claims she's alone, hinting at something eerie... but then it's brushed aside as she haggles over the price. A wasted opportunity for real suspense.

To everyone who thinks:  
1. This was a boring telecast  
2. Halle Berry and Denzel Washington didn’t deserve their Oscars  

**STOP IT RIGHT NOW!**  

This was one of the best Academy Awards shows ever, and here’s why:  

1. It was a historic moment for a Black actress—yes, **Black**—to win Best Actress. So many talented Black actresses were snubbed by the Academy for years. Honestly, I **stopped** watching the Oscars because of the lack of diversity in winners and nominees. It felt like the same cycle of white actors congratulating each other.  

The Academy had **countless** chances to award brilliant Black actresses—Alfre Woodard, Whoopi Goldberg, Diana Ross, Mary J. Blige—but didn’t.  

2. Halle Berry **earned** that Oscar. No contest. The Academy was under pressure to finally recognize her, and rightfully so. Nicole Kidman sang beautifully in *Moulin Rouge!*, but it was **time** for Black talent to be celebrated, not overlooked.  

As for Denzel Washington? The Academy **owed** him after years of unfair snubs. Finally, justice was served.  

So if you disagree—keep it to yourself. This moment mattered.

If you enjoyed *Deep Cover*, this film is right up your alley. Many of the poetic monologues Fishburne delivers in *Deep Cover* actually come from the lyrical script of *Once In the Life*, based on a play he wrote. For fans of Larry, this movie is pure, unfiltered Fishburne—intense, magnetic, and fully realized. Yes, there’s gunplay and illegal dealings—it’s a gangster flick at heart—but the writing is exquisite, and the story hits deep, even leaning into romantic drama territory.  

A *brilliant* film—dark, provocative, electrifying, and raw. If you've ever snuck out at night or lost yourself in underground scenes, the claustrophobic sets will resonate, mirroring the suffocation of a life you can't escape. Packed with sharp foreshadowing and tangled relationships, every shot and set detail reflects the film’s emotional core. *Flawless execution.*

May 1938. Hitler arrives in Italy, paving the way for a fateful encounter with Mussolini. A charged atmosphere of ambition and insecurity lingers. A quiet town, a weary housewife, and an observant journalist collide—two worlds apart yet fatefully intertwined. A fleeting sanctuary for a woman weighed down by sorrow, a fleeting moment for an archetypal casualty. This is a tale of isolation and unspoken yearning, of hidden corners of existence where desire takes the shape of quiet defiance.  

At its heart—a book given on a spring afternoon. The film unfolds like poetry, capturing the nuances of ordinary solitude with striking artistry. It is a plea for the unspoken bond between oneself and reality, between the external world and the depths within. The images of Il Duce loom, while Antonietta's awkwardness, Gabriele's fragile restraint, and the director's exquisite balance of script and performance elevate this work to brilliance. A prelude to understated elegance, it is a profound meditation on hypocrisy and unjust judgment, on life's essence and the cruelty of tyranny.  

Loren and Mastroianni command the screen with extraordinary depth—a display of masterful, intelligent artistry. Undoubtedly, a timeless masterpiece.

I nearly skipped this movie due to the overwhelmingly bad reviews, but I'm glad I gave it a chance—it turned out to be a decent horror flick. While the acting was mediocre (aside from Alice Krige's standout performance), some of the lines—like "Just consider yourself lunch"—were genuinely funny.  

Overall, a solid Stephen King adaptation—I'd rate it a 7/10.

Somewhere in the world, there must exist a ranking of the most unbearable gay films ever created—those plagued by endless, tedious shots of actors gazing blankly into the distance or agonizingly drawn-out scenes of cats slurping spaghetti. This migraine-inducing film follows the story of two young men who live, love, swim, and occasionally find themselves trapped in grottos. One has a despondent mother, the other has none at all. They talk, wander, swim, have sex, get drunk, then inevitably break up. At one point, someone lands in the hospital for a week, only to emerge and be subjected to gratuitous fast-forwards and rewinds. The film lingers on endless shots of one of them staring vacantly or simply idling—perhaps a misguided attempt at artistic depth or just a desperate ploy to stretch what would otherwise be a 14-minute story into feature length. And let me be clear—this isn’t my first rodeo; it’s roughly the 30th gay film I’ve...

Akira Kurosawa’s only misstep in creating *Dodes’ka-den* might have been collaborating with the "four knights"—Kobayashi, Ichikawa, and Konishita. They had envisioned a blockbuster to launch their partnership, but Kurosawa, arguably the group’s leading figure, crafted an abstract, profoundly humanist art film. Set in a devastated slum, it depicted characters grappling with bleak tragedies. Had he pursued a more independent path or partnered with another studio, the outcome might have been different. This creative clash, along with financial struggles, contributed to his 1971 suicide attempt. Yet, true to his artistic vision, Kurosawa remained unwavering in his signature theme: the resilience of the human spirit amid hardship. While the film’s backdrop is more unconventional than usual, this isn’t a flaw—it’s a testament to his uncompromising approach.  

*Dodes’ka-den* captivates, but not in the way audiences typically expect from Kurosawa. Its power lies in character-driven storytelling rather than plot. The film’s substance...

As a longtime Pokémon enthusiast, I absolutely loved this film. Like every installment in the series, it showcases exciting new legendary Pokémon while deepening the bonds between its characters. That said, I wouldn’t recommend it to non-fans—especially most adult viewers. Some of the dubbed dialogue felt a bit cheesy, though that's often unavoidable in English adaptations. Visually, the animation was stunning, aside from a few rough patches. The villain may come across as clichéd, but the franchise has offered a variety of antagonists over the years, so don’t assume they’re all like this one. While I respect differing opinions, any true Pokémon fan is sure to enjoy this movie.

When a group of mercenaries, insurgents, and foreign operatives assemble their forces south of the border, Gary Busey steps up to stop them. A product of its time, *Bulletproof* leans into 1980s action tropes despite a solid supporting cast that includes L.Q. Jones and Thalmus Rasulala.

This is quintessential Lars von Trier—my absolute favorite, surpassing even *Breaking the Waves* or the more recent *Dancer in the Dark*. The film's visual poetry is breathtaking, with strikingly inventive compositions. The performances are extraordinary. An essential masterpiece.

The criticism calling the show overly cheesy feels a bit exaggerated. When someone tunes into a TV show, what are they really seeking? Entertainment—plain and simple. Unless they're professional critics or narrative analysts, most viewers just want to unwind and enjoy. *FULL HOUSE* is the perfect escape after a draining day at work or school—it delivers laughter without relying on shallow humor alone.  

Sure, the Tanner family is idealized, a flawless fictional unit. If such a family existed in reality, they’d be an aspirational model for all of us. But let’s remember—this isn’t a documentary. There’s no harm in portraying an idealized family on screen. The show’s enduring success proves audiences loved it, regardless of later nitpicking.  

One of its strongest qualities? It appeals to viewers of all ages, leaving them with heartwarming takeaways—no matter how simple. And Jesse’s...

After enduring my kids’ insistence on watching this at least ten times for the past two Christmases, I consider myself thoroughly qualified to critique this adaptation of Dr. Seuss’ beloved story—and honestly, it falls short. Trying to live up to Chuck Jones’ iconic animated special was always going to be a challenge, but this version is so bloated and heavy-handed that it becomes downright tedious. While there are a few clever moments, the film mostly feels like a cynical cash grab, despite its purported message against Christmas commercialism. Jim Carrey’s trademark over-the-top performance clashes with the essence of the Grinch, who, as voiced by Boris Karloff, was a slow, sly schemer. Carrey’s manic energy lacks purpose, and that’s just the most glaring misstep. Even gifted actors like Jeffrey Tambor and Christine Baranski are squandered in forgettable roles. What were you thinking, Universal? I get that Anthony Hopkins isn’t exactly selective with his roles (much like his fellow Brit Michael Caine), but this one deserves to be buried.

This film holds the dubious distinction of being both the most expensive Canadian production shot in BC and easily the worst—so bad it never saw release. The British director’s outsider perspective is painfully obvious, reducing Canadians to a crude collection of oversexed, drug-addled caricatures. Any genuine sense of Canadian identity is missing, which is especially baffling given the public funding behind this debacle. Unsurprisingly, the British lead comes off as the only normal character, while the rest devolve into tired sitcom tropes (think "Norm!" from *Cheers*). Visually, it veers between picturesque landscapes and dim, muddled interiors, with actors who seem restless—either mirroring the audience's boredom or reflecting the director’s misguided vision. Skip this disaster and watch something by Bruce McDonald instead. A real Canadian filmmaker with authentic stories to tell, his work won’t make you want to leave after the first 10 minutes.

This film ranks among the worst I've ever watched. I attended its SXSW premiere and left thoroughly unimpressed. The director openly admitted knowing little about John Lennon during the screening, which showed in the final product. Though marketed as a drama, audiences couldn't stop laughing at its cringe-worthy moments—never a promising reaction. The sole bright spots were Dominic Monaghan and Jason Leonard as Livien's bandmates; their comedic timing provided rare moments of levity in an otherwise overly self-serious movie. The forced insertion of Beatles lyrics felt painfully awkward. While the soundtrack stood out as the film's strongest element, it's hardly worth enduring the rest. Unless you're a die-hard Dominic Monaghan enthusiast, I'd recommend skipping this one.

*"Fear of a Black Hat" is a brilliantly made film. From the opening scene to the very end, I couldn’t stop laughing. If you get the chance, do yourself a favor and watch it—it’s hands down the funniest movie I’ve ever seen. Get your snacks ready!*

Why should you watch the breathtaking nature documentary *Earth*? How much time do I have to convince you? Don’t worry—I’ll keep it short, but make no mistake: this film is essential viewing. *Earth* takes you on an immersive journey, following three animal families along their migratory paths. Witness the struggles of a polar bear mother and her cubs as the father braves solitary hunts, follow a humpback whale and her calf on their epic journey for food, and trek across Africa with an elephant mother and her (not-so-small) calf. Directors Alastair Fothergill and Mark Linfield deliver a stellar portrayal of nature, showcasing not just these central creatures but also the survival tactics of countless other species. The cinematography—led by Richard Brooks Burton, Mike Holding, Adam Ravetch, and Andrew Shillabeer—is nothing short of extraordinary, capturing stunning landscapes and raw animal instincts. And let’s not forget those breathtaking slow-motion hunting sequences.

The film's central love story is engaging and well-executed, serving as its strongest element. However, the world surrounding this romance feels overly poetic, visually stylized, and unconvincing. The protagonist's psychology becomes increasingly bizarre and hard to follow, culminating in an equally perplexing ending. While this movie may still be worth watching if the premise intrigues you, keep your expectations moderate.

Judging by this film, it's no wonder even cowgirls get the blues. Uma Thurman's performance disappointed me—she was the only reason I endured this mess. A terrible movie with just one saving grace: the soundtrack. It's a shame zero-star ratings aren't an option—this one would earn every last one of them.

At just over two hours (2 hours, 20 minutes), this adaptation covers substantial ground from Pearl Buck's renowned novel. While occasionally veering into soap-opera territory, the film delivers several visually striking moments—most notably the breathtaking locust swarm sequence that concludes the story.  

Given that this production is nearly seventy years old, the special effects remain impressively executed. Oscar-winning actors Paul Muni and Luise Rainer deliver strong, compelling performances as expected. However, the casting of Caucasian actors in Asian roles undermines credibility—some, like Walter Connolly, appear particularly unconvincing.  

A modern remake with an all-Asian cast would enhance authenticity, not for political correctness, but for a more believable portrayal of the story.

Thomas Clay has fallen in with a bad crowd—just another example of today’s youth lacking any sense of respect.  

This film isn’t just mediocre; it’s downright unwatchable. The pacing drags painfully, crawling toward its drug-fueled finale without purpose, much like its director’s apparent lack of vision. We follow the protagonist, an awkward loner who doesn’t fit in at school or at home—relatable, perhaps, until he spirals into delinquency. Skipping school, dabbling in drugs, and then, abruptly, he’s transformed into a monstrous rapist.  

The film’s biggest flaw? Clay’s baffling blindness to the connection between violent imagery and real-life brutality. He blames war footage on television for corrupting a generation, yet has no qualms about crafting one of the most gratuitously graphic scenes of *simulated* violence. The hypocrisy is staggering—does he genuinely believe his own argument?  

If Clay has somehow missed the realities of platforms like YouTube, his naivety is almost laughable. But that doesn’t excuse what he’s done—or what viewers will inevitably do with that horrifying climax.

Emily Watson’s Natalia stands as the most tender, captivating romantic lead I’ve ever witnessed onscreen. Without question, she reigns as the queen of this film—or perhaps, by the end, she transforms into its king? The intricate dance of chess matches mirrors the families’ ruthless battles for dominance, control, and triumph, creating a breathtaking narrative tapestry. Much like the chess masters themselves, the director skillfully plays multiple mind games with the audience, each thread weaving seamlessly into grand or subtle patterns. The early 20th-century Italian lake district comes alive through impeccable period detail, costumes, and visuals—every frame is meticulously crafted, leaving no inch of the screen unused.  

Countless dazzling scenes linger in memory, far too many to list. I suggest setting aside time to watch this film twice, ideally with a week’s pause between viewings—it’s impossible to absorb all the poetic depth of its 64-square, endlessly layered world in a single sitting.  

Though I haven’t read Nabokov’s novel, my experience brings to mind another triumph of romantic poetry-as-cinema: Barry Levinson’s *The Natural*. That film boldly discarded the grim fatalism of Malamud’s original novel, embracing instead a soaring, luminous romanticism—much like the spell this story casts.

This film is a complete waste of time—utterly pointless! Rachel Griffiths must have been desperate for a paycheck. The production clearly had no budget, since the lighting was practically nonexistent. If I ever see Pete Whatever-His-Name-Is in another movie, I might just lose the will to live. Was there even a plot? A script? Who knows. My only real regret? Sitting through this garbage in the first place.

Can you really call this "all shock, no plot?" The movie was packed with missed opportunities. We got no backstory about the room—just that people died there. But *why* was it evil? What twisted it into what it became? And why did it operate on an "hour" countdown? Then there were the unexplained details, like the camera in the air vent the character pointed out—only for it to vanish when he climbed up there.  

Then consider the ghosts—why did they look digital? And why did objects disappear with a static flicker before hitting the ground? Stack all of that together, and Room 1408 starts to feel like some high-tech haunted house. Except... none of that was ever explored.  

Oh, and let's talk about the rules—or lack thereof. Electronics supposedly don’t work in 1408... except when they do. The TV functions perfectly. The cell phone has no signal, but somehow wireless internet works just fine. How many contradictions can one movie cram in?  

At its core, this was just a parade of cheap scares—nothing new. Reflections in mirrors, things lurking just out of sight, paintings that change, walls that bleed. The classic "it was all a dream—psych! No, it wasn’t." And if the room...

**My girlfriend and I stumbled upon this movie while flipping through channels.**  

We both expected a heartwarming, family-friendly Christmas film but ended up completely disappointed.  

The actor playing the soldier had zero emotional range—his expression stayed the same whether he was chopping down Christmas trees, watching the girl he likes kiss her boyfriend, or being surprised by her affection. His performance was so wooden that we couldn't help but laugh at how bad it was.  

Then there's the blonde love interest, whose remarkable skill is counting dots (and cheating on her boyfriend). What a prize! Her life's ambition? Staying with her parents and counting more dots.  

So essentially, this is the story of an emotionally blank soldier who falls for a dot-counting cheater. It’s painfully predictable and a total waste of time. The only thing you’ll get out of watching it is a few unintentional laughs from how corny it all is.  

And just to top it off—her dad proudly declares he only eats French fries. Classic.

I might be among the few who genuinely stayed loyal to this film. I caught it during its original release, and like the previous comment, I believe *Up The Academy* was way ahead of its time. The humor is pure *MAD Magazine*—raw, unapologetic, and brilliantly chaotic. It's surprising *MAD* distanced itself from the project, because the tone fits perfectly.  

Another standout feature? The soundtrack, one of the early '80s gems, packed with punk and new wave tracks from emerging L.A. bands. I still own the vinyl and play it regularly—it holds up.  

Sure, it’s no masterpiece, but let’s be real—there are far worse movies out there. While *Porky’s* gets more love, I find *Up The Academy* funnier, packed with absurd gags that land either through over-the-top stereotypes or juvenile hijinks. Nobody expected *The Maltese Falcon*—and that’s exactly why it works.

While I wouldn't call myself a die-hard John Cleese fan (though *Fawlty Towers* was sheer brilliance), I do admire his work. When I spotted this forgotten gem on a Blockbuster shelf, curiosity won me over—and what a delightful surprise it turned out to be. One of the most hilarious 50-minute watches I’ve ever experienced. The humor is classic British absurdity in the vein of *The Goon Show*—honestly, as an audio sketch, it could’ve fit right into a *Firesign Theatre* album. But thanks to flawless execution and impeccable timing, *Strange Case* becomes a masterclass in comic genius, the kind of performance that turns casual viewers into lifelong devotees of British comedy.  

The British have a rare talent for blending sharp satire with meticulous character quirks and perfectly timed delivery—both of which shine here. Cleese’s take on Holmes feels inspired by Arkin and Sellers’ *Inspector Clouseau*, but with his own unmatched flair for physical comedy, he makes the role uniquely his own. The real revelation, though, is Arthur Lowe as Watson, portraying him as a cheerfully clueless fool with such precise timing and deadpan brilliance that he steals the show.

Anyone else remember the early days of Pay-Per-View? I sure do—I can still picture dialing that number to rent a movie right on your TV. As kids, we’d always eye those Playboy listings, but actually working up the nerve to call and request one? That was a whole ordeal—only to end up watching four hours of poorly shot, uninspired softcore.  

The reason I mention this is because *this* movie also aired on PPV, and I remember nearly every scene from the promo. Over the past few years, I’ve been on a mission to track down all the best films I caught glimpses of as a kid, and this one was high on the list. Once it starts, it’s hard to turn off—an all-star cast attempting the perfect bank heist, only for everything to go hilariously wrong.  

There are plenty of great spoofs in the heist genre, and this one absolutely belongs in that category. Packed with action and laughs, it never loses steam. Give it a shot—if you’re brave enough.

Seriously? This movie does absolutely nothing to support the Australian film industry. Unless you're high with nothing better to do, I can't see the appeal. Our filmmakers should be showcasing the incredible talent we have—this certainly isn’t the way to do it. Let’s be honest, the whole thing is just cheap and tasteless.

First off... I never considered myself a critic of Uwe Boll, mainly because I hadn’t even seen one of his films—until I watched *Seed*, a shockingly inept excuse for a movie. Named after its titular serial killer, this film lacks any semblance of coherence, with a laughable plot and embarrassingly transparent attempts at shock value. Instead of gripping horror, 90% of the runtime is a slog of tedium. Here’s the breakdown:  

1. A hooded killer stares at footage of animal torture—genuine clips from pelt farms—while the film cynically opens with a hollow "message about humanity," complete with a PETA plug. Since the movie has zero moral depth and devolves into the cheapest kind of torture porn, you’ll despise it from minute one.  

2. The first kill—electrocution—is telegraphed with heavy-handed on-screen text, as if catering to an audience incapable of basic comprehension.  

3. Detectives sift through a grotesque reel of starved infants, women, and animals—senseless cruelty masquerading as disturbing "artistry."  

If that wasn’t bad enough... (cont.)

John Carpenter's *Halloween* is nothing short of a horror masterpiece. It follows the chilling tale of escaped killer Michael Myers as he returns to his hometown on Halloween night, relentlessly hunting a group of babysitters.  

Unquestionably the finest entry in the franchise, Carpenter masterfully builds tension through deliberate pacing and well-crafted characters—an uncommon approach for a horror film.  

What makes it even more remarkable is its ability to terrify without relying on excessive blood or gore, solidifying its place as the most frightening installment in the series.  

The film launched Jamie Lee Curtis' career and delivered one of Donald Pleasence's most iconic performances. A timeless classic in every sense.

Last night while watching this film, I felt a persistent sense that it would stand the test of time. Something tells me I’ll return to it repeatedly in the years ahead.  

It embodies everything you’d want in a lasting story or film—depth, resonance, enduring appeal. Though a few cultural nuances escape me as a Western viewer, its heart speaks a language anyone can understand.

Rejected by Richard C. Sarafian, this cinematic catastrophe polluted Japanese theaters before washing up on American shores, where it swiftly sank straight to video oblivion. Forgotten for years, it resurfaced only when Turner's networks desperately scraped the bottom of their programming barrel, fishing it out to occupy their graveyard shift.  

The Smithee pseudonym typically shields directors from studio butchery, but Sarafian can’t pin this mess solely on executive meddling. The cast—fresh from Overacting 101—delivers one cringe-worthy line after another. The plot tangles itself into nonsense, the effects underwhelm, and whatever isn’t unintentionally hilarious is just painfully dull.  

The source material must have held promise—why else would names like Palance, Matheson, Boyle, or Heston attach themselves to such a flop? Yet somewhere between page and screen, disaster struck. Verdict: Steer clear. It fails even as a so-bad-it’s-good novelty.

Robert Altman's *H.E.A.L.T.H.* cleverly embodies the ancient concept of the four humors—not in the modern sense of comedy, but in its original medical and philosophical meaning—and does so with sharp wit and humor. Lauren Bacall’s Esther Brill personifies Phlegm, moving slowly and cautiously, more obsessed with guarding the secrets of her age and beauty than her actual well-being. Paul Dooley’s Dr. Gil Gainey is pure Choler, flailing like a beached seal, barking orders and rallying crowds to embrace his watery fanaticism. Glenda Jackson’s Isabella Garnell drips with Melancholy, channeling Shakespeare’s brooding Hamlet—right down to the occasional soliloquy. And Henry Gibson’s Bobby Hammer, spouting lines like *“The breast that feeds the baby rules the world,”* oozes Bile. Amid this sea of exaggerated temperaments, James Garner’s Harry Wolff and Carol Burnett’s Gloria Burbank serve as the (relatively) grounded figures, struggling to maintain balance at H.E.A.L.T.H.—an organization supposedly dedicated to well-being but hilariously anything *but* healthy.

I was in France around March 5th and always love attending film festivals. I had heard of the Cinémas d’Amérique Latine de Toulouse but never had the chance to go before. This time, I decided to check it out and ended up watching *Cero y van 4*.  

The film is stunning. Though it didn’t hit me as hard as it might have for Mexican audiences—since I watched it with French subtitles—it was still deeply shocking.  

This movie is a sharp satire about urban violence, kidnapping, and street crime in Mexico. It paints a brutally raw portrait of the city, of a metropolis in chaos. *Secuestro Express*, featuring the incredible Mía Maestro, also tackled kidnapping as a satirical subject but with a darker, more serious tone—and in my opinion, there’s a certain thematic link to *Cero y van 4*. Both explore themes of redemption and ask, *How much is too much?* Then there’s *Man on Fire*, an intensely powerful film that, while not a satire, gives an unflinching look at Mexico’s violent underworld. *Cero y van 4* also reminds me of *The Brave One*—a film that jolts you with its raw impact. And much like *The Usual Suspects*, it keeps you on edge with unexpected twists that leave you reeling.

**The most misogynistic movie ever made?**  

By 1968, you’d think filmmakers would have moved past white actors in brownface playing "Indians"—but no. The real highlights? The moments when women *giggle and blush* while bikers drag them off to be gang-raped. Because, apparently, *rape is fun*! Who knew?  

Then there’s the lazy rip-off of *The Hustler* (down to the scheming fat boss shooting pool while plotting against the "rebel" lead), the atrocious acting, and the painfully obvious music cues—so unsubtle they might as well scream *"FEEL THIS NOW!"* Oh, and not a single actual Indigenous person in sight.

Jean-Paul Sartre once wrote, *"Hell is other people."* Few films illustrate this idea as brilliantly as *The Odd Couple*, where Jack Lemmon and Walter Matthau bring the phrase to life. Playing Felix Ungar and Oscar Madison, Lemmon and Matthau portray longtime friends who move in together—only to slowly unravel under the weight of their clashing habits. The comedy escalates perfectly before Felix finally walks away, leaving Oscar a cleaner, if not entirely reformed, man.  

Lemmon is exceptional as Ungar, capturing the frantic energy of a neurotic neat freak struggling to adjust to single life. Opposite him, Matthau shines as the chaotic, poker-obsessed sports writer who just wants to scrounge up enough cash for child support. Their dynamic is electric, heightened by Neil Simon’s razor-sharp script and their own effortless chemistry.  

Lemmon and Matthau are flawless in their roles, partly thanks to Simon’s writing and partly because they play off each other so effortlessly. As two men bound by failed marriages and fatherhood yet divided by every other aspect of their lives, these late, legendary actors crafted a partnership that feels irreplaceable—so perfect, in fact, that audiences couldn’t get enough.

Right from the start—let’s be clear—there’s no flirting here, not with Anthony or anyone else. These characters don’t waste time with subtlety—they go straight for it. Your endurance is put to the test within the first 15 minutes, a relentless onslaught of graphic violence and twisted sexuality. Normally, that’s not an issue—heck, most critics, myself included, can appreciate a healthy dose of depravity—but without any meaningful context, it’s just disgusting.  

Once you survive the carnage, we meet Donna, and the film shifts gears entirely—not for the better, just... different. It morphs into a soulless road trip movie, propped up by weak comedic attempts thanks to over-the-top cameos from performers like Judy Tenuta and Mink Stole (along with an assortment of hookers and drag queens). Frankly, they deserved better material.  

The cinematography is deliberately chaotic, so if you’re prone to motion sickness—or just general unease—steer clear. Actually, I’m not entirely sure who this movie is for—unless you’re a gay or bisexual S&M enthusiast with a soft spot for badly written, poorly shot indie films that clumsily attempt to reflect your lifestyle.

What a staggering downfall for Sean Ellis.  

You invite your closest friends over, all buzzing with excitement for his latest work. You’ve got a rough sense of the premise—no spoilers to ruin the thrill—and expectations are sky-high.  

It’s late. The mood is perfect for a film like this.  

Fifteen minutes in, you reassure yourself it’ll soon hit its stride. By the 25-minute mark, you’re debating whether to just turn in and try again when you’re more alert—maybe then you’ll catch those supposedly brilliant nuances that, so far, seem absent. Half an hour passes, and half your once-enthusiastic audience is already dozing off. You admit defeat and call it a night.  

Days later, with nothing else left to watch, you give it another shot—this time in broad daylight, hoping the sun will keep you engaged. Ten minutes in, you’re already skipping through painfully drawn-out transitions and filler shots. With any other film, you’d have quit by now. But this is *Cashback*’s creator—there’s legacy here. Still, even legacy has its limits.

This has to be one of the most disappointing films I’ve ever watched. Critics may praise it, but to me, it falls completely flat. The issue likely stems from Kundera’s original novel—not because it’s impossible to adapt, but because, like much of his writing, it comes across as self-indulgent and overly drawn-out. His work often feels pretentious, his characters endlessly introspective, and his narratives tinged with misogyny.  

Having read several of his books—including his painfully dull Socialist Realist poetry—I still can’t grasp the hype. The very traits that frustrate me in his writing (the excessive self-absorption, the laborious prose) are only amplified onscreen. Maybe there’s some deeper brilliance I’m missing, but I doubt it.  

And seriously, a Criterion release? There’s no way this film deserves that kind of recognition.

Reunion shows come in various forms. Some bring back veteran actors to reprise roles they haven’t played in decades—with mixed success. *Return to Mayberry* had its share of goofy moments but was enjoyable, while *Return to Green Acres* was downright terrible (Eddie Albert’s unprintable opinion of the script said it all). *Rescue from Gilligan’s Island* tied up a loose end for the castaways, though it was just as absurd as the original series. Most of these revivals suffer from weak writing, often trying too hard to be clever—something that rarely works in comedy, where self-awareness kills the humor. New characters are sometimes added, but they rarely gel with the original cast. On the whole, these reunions fall flat.  

Another type of reunion show features the cast gathering to reminisce, sharing behind-the-scenes stories while revisiting classic clips from the series. Then there are the film adaptations, which rarely live up to the original shows—and occasionally, movies about the making of the show itself (like *The Brady Bunch*).

**Rewritten Version:**  

I gave *Timecop* a perfect 10—this one barely deserves a 1.  

The story is painfully dull and barely connects to the original *Timecop*. Most of what made the first movie great was tossed out, replaced with nonsensical ideas. The plot is set in 2060 (if I recall correctly), yet somehow, time travel is now *more dangerous*—which makes zero sense.  

The action scenes are underwhelming, with only the first one being remotely decent. The rest are forgettable, and there aren’t many to begin with. At one point, the main character jumps through time multiple times in quick succession—maybe twice? It’s poorly executed either way.  

Bottom line: Skip this movie. It’s a waste of time.

This is one of those films that feels like it should be brilliant—but for me, it fell flat. It tries so desperately to be "artsy" that it loses any real substance. Sure, there are stunning visuals, and each scene on its own is impressive. But strung together, the experience becomes tedious—more of a chore than a pleasure. I gave it a chance based on the rave reviews plastered on the DVD case and my love for Shakespeare, but in the end, I found it pretentious and, frankly, dull.

After Harry Reems' young girlfriend is assaulted by Zebbedy Colt (The Night-Walker), a devastated Reems seeks solace in the company of several women. Colt, flaunting a magician’s attire and wielding a cane, continues his violent attacks. Determined to stop him, Reems sets out to bring his reign of terror to an end. Though shot on film and mildly provocative, the production feels like a run-of-the-mill 70s adult film, clumsily put together. The assault sequences are unexpectedly subdued, and the half-hearted attempt to mimic *Death Wish* falls flat. R. Bolla (*Cannibal Holocaust*) appears as a detective. Colt, typically exaggerated, has a few erratic moments, but remains oddly restrained. For a so-called roughie, it could have pushed far harder.

**Ouch! My Brain Hurts!** And no wonder—after enduring this cinematic marathon. How I resisted the urge to fast-forward is beyond me.  

Maybe it’s me! Maybe I just missed the point... or failed to grasp its supposed mystical depth. But honestly? The film has all the mystique of a stop at a fast-food joint.  

Worse yet, the characters were painfully bland—Tom and Jerry show more personality! *Ugh!* Why do I put myself through this? Why suffer such nonsense? It’s enough to make me flee to a monastery—or at least the nearest escape route! *Aaargh!* A truly dreadful film in nearly every way.  

...Other than that, it was fine.

This is a fantastic film that I’ve loved revisiting time and again. Michael Caine delivers yet another stellar performance—though he’s known for taking on varied roles, regardless of quality, he truly shines as Sidney.
