The writing is brilliant from the outset—who would have expected such sharp wit from Ira Levin, the mind behind chilling tales like *The Boys from Brazil* and *Rosemary’s Baby*? And with a powerhouse cast—Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan Cannon, Henry Jones—guided by Sidney Lumet’s direction, how could it possibly miss?  

I don’t want to say too much because spoiling anything about this movie would be a travesty. Just watch it and fall in love.

Oh my! It's rare for a horror movie to bore me—or make me laugh unintentionally—as much as this one did. Though it kicks off with an engaging premise, it quickly devolves into a shallow slasher flick, tossing in half-hearted supernatural and sexual subplots. Alice Krige, typically brilliant, is utterly wasted here, and the so-called twists border on absurd. Skip it unless you're truly out of options. Rating: 3/10.

I caught this movie during Joe Bob Briggs' Monstervision on TNT—and if even *he* couldn’t salvage it, you know it’s dire. The sole reason I suffered through to the end? I teach video production and needed firsthand proof of what *not* to do. That said, enduring it required every ounce of willpower I had. It’s as agonizing as witnessing your great-grandma shamelessly hitting on a high school freshman.  

Honestly, you’d get better entertainment by soaking the actual film reel in paint thinner and staring at the fumes.  

If you spot this abomination in a S-Mart bargain bin, treat it like a coiled rattlesnake—back away slowly. No sudden moves.

Farrelly brothers films usually aren’t my thing—in fact, I can’t remember ever seeing one. Same goes for Jimmy Fallon movies, though I’ll admit I suffered through *Taxi* once (I repented, so let’s move on). But this one had Drew Barrymore, and I have a weak spot for her. There’s something about her that just makes me grin the whole time she’s on screen—she has that rare charm. I even sat through Adam Sandler in *50 First Dates* just for her. Pathetic, right?  

This wasn’t some deep baseball drama—it wasn’t meant to be. It was a love story about a lovable underdog clinging to the one thing that never failed him… until he found something worth letting go for. Yeah, the ending was predictable, but the journey? Absolutely worth it.

**Rewritten version:**  

Shamefully, I only just watched this film for the first time—13 years after it came out. It’s a story any father or brother can understand… one sibling is the reckless type, while the other plays the responsible older brother. Craig Sheffer’s performance as the eldest is a bit too stoic, but Pitt shines, and Skerritt is ideal as the father. The Montana fishing scenes are stunning—I never knew fly fishing could look so captivating. The film stays faithful to the book, with only minor tweaks to fit the cinematic format. Unlike most book-to-movie adaptations, this one holds up beautifully. Perfect for a quiet evening when you want a deeply moving, emotionally rich story.

This is easily the funniest of all the Cheech & Chong movies. It was my first introduction to their comedy, and I thought it was fantastic. Believe it or not, my dad suggested I watch it—what a great role model, right? Even my grandma ended up buying it for me, fully aware of what it was about. What a family I’ve got!  

Overall, it's a solid film and a great pick when you're in the mood for a classic comedy. Just don’t expect nonstop, laugh-till-you-cry humor—it has its standout moments, but it’s not as relentlessly funny as something like *There’s Something About Mary*. Still, definitely worth checking out. Unless, of course, you're completely anti-drug or anything like that. In that case, maybe skip it.

This film was a complete waste of time...the director should be ashamed. I can’t understand why anyone would bother making such a pointless movie. The ending, where she died, was so ridiculous it actually made me laugh. The acting was unbearable—I had to keep switching channels out of sheer secondhand embarrassment. The actor who played Heath deserves nothing but unemployment, and the director should be banned from ever making another film. Honestly, they should refund everyone who paid to see this garbage. {0.02/10}

This movie falls flat with its dull pacing. Scattered scenes of nudity feel like a half-hearted effort to hold the audience's attention—they don't work.  

Lena Olin shines as the film's strongest element, delivering a nuanced performance, while Day-Lewis struggles to articulate his dialogue.  

Kaufman's direction lacks cohesion, awkwardly jumping between marital drama and political turmoil. Characters shift motivations abruptly, leaving the narrative feeling messy and uneven.

I went into *Still Crazy* without high expectations, assuming it would be just another rock nostalgia trip for baby boomers. While it delivers on that front, it also offers so much more. Director Brian Gibson, known for his Tina Turner biopic, brings a sharp style to the film—fittingly, this turned out to be his final project.  

The casting is spot-on. Bill Nighy shines as the band’s frontman, while Bruce Robinson (better known as a director these days) makes a memorable return as the washed-up guitarist—his first major role since the late '70s. If you're after a film that’s both heartfelt and hilarious, with a killer soundtrack to boot, this is it.  

**7.4/10**

I received the book version of *Kazaam* for my 8th birthday, and while people often claim books are better than their movie adaptations, this was the rare exception. If anything, the movie had one advantage—it was over quickly.  

The acting is painfully bad, which isn’t surprising given Shaquille O’Neal’s starring role as a magical, rapping genie who emerges from an old boombox (and honestly, there was probably a good reason he was trapped in there). The kid playing Max is insufferably whiny and delivers every line with cringe-worthy awkwardness. He gets bullied by neighborhood kids, and after watching him, it’s hard not to side with them—he’s just that annoying.  

The plot is a lazy, cliché mess: a boy with an absent, workaholic father stumbles upon a magical friend who fixes his life and eventually helps mend their strained relationship. Even as an eight-year-old, I remember thinking the premise was ridiculous.  

It’s a miracle anyone involved in this film had a career afterward. The whole thing is an embarrassment—a movie that never should’ve existed. I could go on, but honestly, why waste more words on such a disaster?

What a dreadful movie! It must have been competing with absolute trash to even score a Golden Globe nomination. They took the fascinating life of the first renowned female Renaissance painter and butchered it beyond comprehension. My issue isn’t with creative liberties—if the storytelling had been compelling, that would’ve been forgivable. But this mess is just inexplicable. By all historical accounts, the artist’s real life would’ve made a far more gripping film, so why did they settle for this insipid script? My guess? The true story didn’t have enough gratuitous nudity. The ending hastily slaps together a summary of her life—if only the rest of the film had been that concise, we’d have saved ourselves two painful hours.

In reality, it's nearly identical to the original film—and they couldn't even keep the timeline accurate. Maybe that was deliberate, whether out of laziness or sheer apathy. Regardless, this is an absolute disaster. It shouldn’t even qualify as a movie.  

I watched this so-called "second feature" on the same disc as the original *The Boogeyman*, and it nearly made my head explode. I’m warning you—if you ever stumble upon this atrocity, run in the opposite direction as fast as you can. It deserves a caution label: **"Warning—may lower your IQ on contact."**  

For me, this is a solid **0/10**—no question about it.

In my opinion, this is a pretty bizarre movie filled with humor. I wouldn’t call it very scary—more like fun, at least if you enjoy horror films. The Scarecrow character reminded me a bit of *Children of the Corn*, though not exactly. Compared to that movie, this one is far more entertaining to watch!

Alright, alright, no need to get upset—I was just joking.  

"Bustin' Out" really is the better, more fitting title anyway.  

Ralph Bakshi—our X-rated animation legend—delivers sharp satire on racism and crime dramas here, and honestly, it's some of his best work.  

The crime storyline rings true: they build their empire, defend it, then boredom and stronger enemies threaten to tear it all down. You’ll have to watch to see how it unfolds.  

Racist? I’m not so sure. With Scatman Crothers (RIP) and the loveable walrus (also RIP) as Black leads driving the story, it feels more like a critique of racism than anything. The fact that Richard Pryor endorsed it says something. And spotting a young Philip Michael Thomas (pre-"Miami Vice") was a fun little surprise.  

It’s basically a Blacksploitation flick in animated form—and that’s a good thing. Well-executed and bold. Some moments will make you uncomfortable (like the lynching scene), but sadly, those horrors are rooted in reality.  

That said, Ralph really should’ve reconsidered the original title.

Last night, I finally watched *Starlight*—and all I can say is… wow! Where do I even start? The laughably cheap special effects (those *lasers* shooting from Willie’s eyes!), the painfully stiff acting, the clunky dialogue, the jarring stock footage, or the whole thing’s painfully serious self-importance. It’s a *unique* masterpiece, that’s for sure—and honestly, the world is better for it. Move over, Ed Wood—Jonathan Kay is the new king of so-bad-it’s-gold cinema!

What else is there to say? I dismissed the critics and decided to see for myself—big mistake. The reviews were spot on. For such a high budget, it was a complete waste of cash.  

At least I redeemed the night by watching *Kill Bill* afterward.  

If you want real horror, check out *Crossroads* instead.  

Honestly? I’d take *Girl in Gold Boots* over this trash any day.

I fully support jamrom4's opinion—this was easily the worst film I've ever endured. It was absolutely atrocious. Despite being warned, I foolishly ignored the advice and suffered the consequences. Within the first agonizing 10 minutes, I'd already lost hope but forced myself to sit through the entire disaster just to say I survived it. Big mistake. The film was revolting—nothing of substance occurred, and the ending was insufferably sanctimonious. A movie this awful doesn’t deserve to exist.  

Take my advice: avoid **Fatty Drives the Bus** at all costs. I regret not listening to the warnings, and now I’m begging you to save yourself. Honestly, I suspect the few positive reviews came from people involved in its creation—and the world would be better off without them.

**This is hands down my absolute favorite movie. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve watched it—definitely over 10—and without fail, it brings me to tears every single time. My family even pleads with me not to watch it just to spare them from my emotional breakdowns! What makes it even more special is knowing it's based on a true story, written by Antwone himself. The incredible acting and perfectly cast roles elevate it to another level. Denzel Washington, one of my all-time favorite actors, delivers what I believe is his best performance yet.**  

**The story hits especially close to home for me. Years ago, I cared for a sweet little boy who, like Antwone, was born in jail. He was the most precious child I’d ever met. After a long, tough legal battle—almost two years—he was finally adopted by an amazing family who never gave up on him. I watched this movie while his future was still uncertain, and seeing him now, safe and loved, fills my heart with joy. Just like Antwone, who found his own happiness and family in the end.**  

**I’d love to hear more about Antwone’s life since reuniting with his family. This film is just unforgettable—I can’t praise it enough!**

Farrah Fawcett never impressed me… until now. Her performance in this film was extraordinary. Imagining the emotional toll of endless retakes is almost unbearable to consider.  

This was an intensely difficult watch—its subject matter is relentlessly grim, leaving you feeling powerless as you witness a woman’s suffering stretch on endlessly. The tension somewhat unraveled for me when her friends reappeared, and the ending struck me as unconvincing.  

The director relied heavily on high-angle shots and mirrored reflections—visually striking, but I wish that same precision had been applied to the pacing in the latter half. While undeniably impactful as a theatrical piece, the film, though commendable, didn’t fully deliver for me.

Don't bother wasting a single minute on this disaster – and certainly don't spend a dime renting it! I still can't fathom how this film even got made. (Not sure why I need ten lines for this review when a simple "it's terrible" would suffice, but here we go...) The performances were painfully bad – it’s like the cast skipped acting class entirely. The story was flimsy, and the ending? Just laughable. The only redeeming quality was the cinematography, which wasn’t completely awful... and I suppose the sound was passable. Still, if something this dreadful managed to get produced—and even turn a profit—then there’s hope for any aspiring screenwriter with actual talent. Take that as encouragement! Honestly, the same goes for actors—if these amateurs got paid, then you definitely can too.

**SPOILERS AHEAD**  

This film was a mess. It bills itself as a Catholic-themed supernatural thriller but rehashes the same tired tropes we've seen countless times before.  

A priest plagued by doubt. Forbidden desires within the clergy. The tangled web of faith and politics. Corruption in the Church. A shadowy conspiracy at its core. The rise of a new era of darkness. Endless, over-the-top clashes of sacred and sinister forces.  

The plot is paper-thin, propped up by two central ideas: **Absolution** (the final sacrament to cleanse a dying soul’s sins) and **Excommunication** (expulsion from the Church, stripping one of absolution). Enter the Sin Eater—I’ll spare you the rest. Toss in every predictable element already mentioned, and you’ve got *The Order*.  

The attempt at provocation falls flat—particularly the jarring inclusion of a priest’s intimate scene intercut with imagery of the Virgin Mary, which feels more tacky than transgressive. It all limps to a conclusion with Heath Ledger delivering some half-baked monologue about being a "redeemer and damner of sins," wandering moodily into the shadows. Cue eye-roll.

HA! So *this* is the movie those "Next Action Stars" were scrambling to get into? Yeah, glad I dodged that bullet—winning would've been more of an insult than an honor.  

Funny how just the first 10 seconds can tell you everything, huh? I mean, seriously—those opening titles alone were a red flag the size of a billboard. We caught part of it (if you can even call this TV-grade slog a "movie") during military service, stuck in a room with your standard-issue guys who’d happily sit through *Las Vegas* just for the eye candy. And let’s be real, their standards weren’t exactly lofty—*The Girl Next Door* was practically high art in that crowd (and we all know it wasn’t the plot keeping them glued to the screen).  

But this? Zero originality, cringe acting, a script that felt like it was written on a napkin—honestly, flipping to *Las Vegas* (or was it *CSI*? Doesn’t matter) mid-way earned zero protests. And that’s saying something.  

Save yourself. Skip it. Burn the DVD if you own it. Change the channel if it’s on. Just—*don’t*.

You’ll likely notice that most viewers rating this movie a perfect 10 are devout Christians—I’m not one of them. If you want a faith-based film, this may suit you. But if you're after a well-made movie for general audiences, I'd suggest looking elsewhere.  

The characters frustrated me with their inconsistent and irrational actions. The film’s central argument is that teaching morality without attributing its foundation to Jesus is inherently flawed. One particularly grating scene has the protagonist telling a child it’s wrong to steal—then adding that Jesus was the one who originally taught this principle. That’s absurd. Do they really believe "thou shalt not steal" originated with Jesus? Did he carve the Ten Commandments? Was theft morally acceptable before him?  

I rented this on Netflix, ignoring the red flags in the reviews. Lesson learned.

This movie is both highly entertaining, thanks to its brilliant comedic performances, and politically engaging. Produced during the final years of the Soviet Union, it cleverly satirizes the Soviet mindset from start to finish. Set in the early days of the USSR, the film challenges the cultural and practical logic of the revolution. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, many of Soviet society's strange restrictions had loosened, but the underlying ideology and mentality persisted—ripe for much-needed critique. Fortunately, all this thought-provoking commentary is delivered through a delightfully humorous and enjoyable story!  

—Jur

This movie was absolutely fantastic! As a devoted Tom Hanks admirer, I’ve always been captivated by his incredible range—from deeply emotional performances in films like *Cast Away*, *The Green Mile*, *Saving Private Ryan*, *Forrest Gump*, *Apollo 13*, and *Philadelphia* to his unforgettable comedic turns in *A League of Their Own*, *Turner and Hooch*, *Catch Me If You Can*, *The Ladykillers*, *Big*, and of course, *Toy Story*.  

But in this film, Hanks isn’t the only standout. Tyler Hoechlin, a rising star with undeniable potential, shines alongside him as his on-screen son, delivering a performance that’s nothing short of outstanding. He’s definitely an actor to keep an eye on—I have no doubt he’ll achieve incredible things in his career.  

The legendary Paul Newman, as always, lights up the screen with his brilliance, further cementing his status as an icon. And let’s not overlook the supporting cast, who played essential roles in making this film so memorable. The stunning and immensely talented Jennifer Jason Leigh—whose work in *Bastard Out of Carolina* and *Single White Female* left a lasting impression—brings elegance and depth to her role as Hanks’ wife, adding yet another layer of greatness to the story.

The movie is simply a blast—especially for those of us who grew up loving The Ramones when it first came out. I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve watched it, alone or with friends, and it never gets stale. The humor still lands, and the whole idea of obsessing over a favorite band—or just hating the monotony of school—never gets old.  

And let’s not forget the golden moments: the fear about our "permanent record" haunting us forever (spoiler: mine hasn’t shown up in decades)... the legendary "static" bit ("I'm getting some static"/"Not as much as you're about to get" right before Principal Togar storms in)... the ancient school board member who needs nurses just to stay upright... the overly enthusiastic Nazi hall monitor who lives for a good "body search"... Togar’s chilling "final solution" while torching Ramones records (yes, actual records—kids, ask your parents)... and, of course, Joey Ramone’s perfect line: "Things sure have changed since we got kicked out of high school," followed by Togar’s priceless reaction.

I absolutely loved this show—it aired as the first and only series in the UK on Channel 4. The characters were spot-on, echoing the charm of *The Simpsons* in how they captured the quirks of small-town life.  

One standout feature was the absence of a laugh track—a rarity for American sitcoms at the time, aside from *The Larry Sanders Show*. It made the cops' antics feel genuine, as if they truly were that eccentric rather than just playing for the camera.  

Overall, it was a delightfully offbeat gem that hit all the right notes for me. Though I suspect it didn’t resonate with everyone, it could’ve easily been a cult favorite in the UK with a better time slot.  

Now, my usual plea: Does anyone know where I can rewatch this? Seriously, I need to find it!

It’s almost unbelievable, but this movie was condemned as immoral from more pulpits than any other film made before the puritanical Hayes Code took effect. Believe it or not, priests warned their congregations that simply watching it would be a mortal sin.  

I’m not exaggerating. Their objections were clear:  

First, Jane openly enjoys sex. In one scene, she and Tarzan wake up in their treetop home. Stretching seductively, she teases him with a playful, "Tarzan, you’ve been a bad boy!" Not only does this imply they’ve been intimate—but suggestively so. Just a few years later, under the Hays Code, women weren’t even allowed to be portrayed taking pleasure in sex.  

Second, Jane chooses an untamed, instinctive man (Tarzan) over a refined, conventional suitor (Holt). Though she’s briefly tempted when Holt presents her with an elegant London gown, and even wavers further after Holt seemingly kills Tarzan, her loyalty never truly falters. The moment she discovers Tarzan is alive, civilization loses all appeal. And who could blame her? Tarzan’s—

**THE BRAIN THAT WOULDN'T DIE** was deemed so objectionable in 1959 that it underwent multiple edits and a three-year delay before finally hitting theaters in 1962. By today’s standards, it’s baffling that anyone ever took this film seriously—even in its time. Equal parts garish, vulgar, and absurd, it barrels along with a kind of brazen ridiculousness that’s impossible to ignore.  

The plot follows a doctor obsessed with experimental limb transplants. After his girlfriend dies in a car crash, he whisks her decapitated head to his clandestine lab. Armed with little more than phone cords, clamps, and what suspiciously resembles a baking tray, he somehow reanimates her. But does she appreciate the gesture? Not a chance. In fact, she’s furious—especially once she learns his next move: grafting her head onto a new body.  

Of course, the doctor has high standards for this replacement. He’s after a top-tier physique, sending him on a grotesque shopping spree—lurking around city streets, scouring strip clubs, crashing beauty pageants, and stalking pin-up models in pursuit of the perfect match.

That fleeting yet magical moment in life—the delicate transition between childhood's sweet innocence and adulthood's turbulent whirlwind—lies at the heart of this film.  

At the start of the story, Danni (brilliantly portrayed by Reese Witherspoon) stands precisely at that crossroads. Lost in daydreams, she swoons over Elvis, spinning his records while wistfully longing for love. Her sister Maureen, soon bound for college, effortlessly attracts boys with her effortless beauty and projected confidence—though beneath the surface, she's just as uncertain. Dating a local troublemaker with a predatory father, Maureen yearns for a decent boy to sweep her off her feet. Like most teens, Danni wishes she could be anyone but herself, blind to her own quiet beauty, convinced she’ll never measure up. She envies Maureen’s charm without realizing her own worth.  

Then comes Court Foster—the moment adulthood begins to press into Danni’s world. Recently bereaved, Court moves with his mother and two younger brothers to work their family’s old farm. Their paths cross, and suddenly, the simplicity of youth starts slipping away.

Emma remains my favorite Jane Austen novel because of its charming protagonist—flawed yet endearing, making it easy for readers to adore her. Her dynamic with Mr. Knightley is everything one could want: affectionate, familiar, and filled with playful banter that sparks that perfect romantic thrill. He embodies the ideal man, while Emma, though young, stands out as an independent, intelligent, and self-assured woman—rare for her time. Who wouldn’t wish to be in her shoes? And who could resist being gently chastised by Mr. Knightley?  

Sadly, this adaptation fails to capture what makes *Emma* so special. I couldn’t bring myself to finish it—it felt utterly lacking. The warmth and generosity that define Emma were missing: her tender patience with her father, her deep bond with Mrs. Weston, her selflessness in securing Miss Taylor’s happiness, even at her own expense. Even Mr. Woodhouse comes across as odd rather than merely eccentric, stripping away the charm of the original.

I wanted to like this show—I truly did. I even purchased the pilot episode, first on VHS and later upgraded to DVD. But no matter how hard I tried, I just couldn’t connect with it, largely because the two leads, David (Bruce Willis) and Maddie (Cybill Shepherd), seemed completely infatuated with themselves. I'll admit the series had sharp, witty dialogue—a major reason for its success—and I did enjoy much of that banter.  

At its core, the show felt like a throwback to the screwball comedies of the 1930s and '40s, with endless male-female clashes full of arguments, accusations, and shouting matches. While many clearly adored that dynamic, it just wasn’t for me—which is why I never jumped on the *Moonlighting* bandwagon.  

The only character I found genuinely entertaining was Allyce Beasley’s clueless assistant, Agnes. It’s a shame she didn’t get more screen time. Sure, Shepherd was easy on the eyes, and I imagine women felt the same about Willis—but their constant bickering ultimately pushed me away.

This movie has haunted me from the moment I first saw it.  

Back in '92, my mother caught it on TV. I still remember waking up late at night to her tearful, panicked murmurs as my father guided her upstairs.  

She kept repeating things like, *Don’t let her take me* or something along those lines. When I asked what had shaken her so badly, she said she’d just watched *The Woman in Black*.  

Naturally, I had to see it too—and even though I was only eleven, she allowed it. It terrified me beyond words. To this day, no horror film has ever chilled me quite like that one.

This feels less like a movie and more like an expensive kids' TV show. From what I gather, the antagonist is essentially a massive horde of coffee beans coated in chocolate—confirmed by subtitles labeling it "Insomnia." When they mentioned an entire civilization falling to insomnia, I briefly hoped for a dark martial arts epic, but alas. You could argue it's avant-garde cinema when the bad guy gets choked out by an old man's absurdly long white eyebrows. *Zu Warriors* remains equally baffling with or without subtitles, which speaks volumes. The effects land somewhere between Ray Harryhausen's stop-motion and *Xena: Warrior Princess*—charmingly dated at best.

I’ve long admired Woody Allen’s work and always will for much of his earlier brilliance, but even the most devoted fan must admit this film is painfully dull, pretentious, and shockingly poorly acted. It amounts to nothing more than empty self-indulgence built on shaky foundations. Casting Will Farrell as a forced Allen impersonator—delivering lines and mannerisms Allen himself might have used decades ago—was a disastrous miscalculation, resulting in pure absurdity. The so-called philosophical dialogue, meant to provoke deep thought, instead becomes an unintentional parody of intellectual musings, completely oblivious to its own absurdity. What a disappointment.

This obscure film is a slow-burning, deliberately paced giallo that strays from genre conventions, opting for a more relaxed narrative style. The story follows a woman desperately seeking her vanished lover—a psychiatrist who disappeared without explanation—leading her to a villa inhabited by peculiar characters. As expected in giallo fashion, violence lurks just beneath the surface.  

The cast delivers strong performances, featuring Adolfo Celi (known from *Thunderball*), Alida Valli (of *Suspiria* fame), Horst Frank (from *Cat o’ Nine Tails*), and a young Sybil Danning, who later became a prominent scream queen in the 1980s. Rosemary Dexter takes on the lead role with convincing presence, anchoring the film effectively despite her relative anonymity.  

What truly sets *Eye in the Labyrinth* apart is its unconventional score. Departing from typical giallo soundtracks, Roberto Nicolosi’s jazz-rock fusion compositions evoke Miles Davis—particularly the moody elegance of *In a Silent Way*. The music elevates the film, enhancing its dreamy, unhurried tone while perfectly complementing the sun-drenched coastal setting.

An actor’s debut film is often one you can skip—it’s usually a project where everyone’s inexperience shines through, and this one is no different.  

But what makes it worse is how laughably bad it is, even by 1982 standards. Shot entirely in Chicago on a shoestring budget, the performances are painfully stiff, wooden, and overdramatic—like a mix between an awkward high school play and cringe-worthy community theater. Nearby traffic noise frequently drowns out the dialogue, which itself is painfully forced, delivered in a way that feels stilted and unnatural. The scenes are clunky and disjointed, and despite the story unfolding over years, neither the kids nor the adults show a single sign of aging.  

It’s certainly possible to make a faith-based film that appeals to a broader, secular audience, but too often, filmmakers get so caught up in pushing "The Message" (or in this case, their own personal ties to the story) that they neglect basic filmmaking craft. (I’m sure it’s—

*The Unborn* delivers an effective low-budget horror experience, tapping into the deep-seated fears surrounding pregnancy. Brooke Adams delivers yet another strong performance, alongside reliable B-movie veteran James Karen, though the rest of the cast is fairly typical for this genre. Surprisingly, the score by Gary Numan adds a distinctive and effective layer to the film. Henry Dominic’s script stands out as unusually thoughtful for a B-grade horror flick, though it carries an unsettling undercurrent of misogyny. Rodman Fender’s direction is serviceable but uninspired, relying too heavily on predictable jump scares. Still, if you're a fan of the underrated Brooke Adams—whose talent has long deserved more recognition—it's worth a watch just for her compelling performance.

*The BFG* remains one of Roald Dahl's most beloved stories, but this animated adaptation struggles to capture its magic. John Hambley’s script stays true to the original tale, so the fault doesn’t lie there—instead, it’s the uninspired animation, sluggish pacing, and flat voice performances that drain the life from the film. What should have been a joyful, lively adventure turns into a dreary, monotonous experience that even young audiences may find tedious. Children unfamiliar with the story would be far better off reading the book first—this dull retelling could easily discourage them from discovering what is, in reality, a true children’s classic.  

Young orphan Sophie (voiced by Amanda Root) endures a harsh life in an unfriendly orphanage under the watch of the cruel Mrs. Clonkers. One night, while gazing out her window, she spots a towering figure creeping through the village. Realizing it’s been seen, the giant snatches Sophie from her bed, tucking her into his enormous pocket before vanishing into the darkness. Soon, Sophie learns she’s been taken by a giant—but the wonder of the story gets lost in this lifeless portrayal.

What a travesty…  

You neglected to brush your teeth… now let’s stretch that into a half-hour spectacle, complete with a pair of rowdy kids causing a commotion before Dad steps in to scold them—because that’s his role, after all.  

Of course, Uncle Joey has to chime in with his bizarre sound effects and exaggerated expressions, while Uncle Jesse saunters in wearing that signature black leather jacket and tight jeans, just to stand around looking effortlessly cool while everyone reminisces about how Mom *would’ve* handled things… if she were still here.  

Ah yes, a whirlwind of wacky, meaningless misadventures, padded out with an unnecessarily drawn-out plot to give it the illusion of substance.  

*Full House* doesn’t just bore you to death—it accelerates aging at twenty times the normal rate.

This is one of the most iconic films of the 1970s French sexual liberation movement, featuring Gérard Depardieu and Patrick Dewaere in bitingly sarcastic roles. It stands among the many psychologically dark dramas of the '70s and '80s—like *Série Noire*, *Buffet Froid*, and *Beau Pere*—all directed by Blier.  

That said, I should clarify a point from an earlier comment about this film: the English translation of the title strays far from the original French. While the protagonists are indeed "going places," the French title would more accurately be rendered as *The Waltz Dancers*—a sly metaphor for the movement of testicles...

Mesmerizing to behold, but what would *you* do if you stumbled upon Atlantis? Dive right in and uncover its secrets! This was a rare chance to transport audiences somewhere extraordinary. Yet, Disney fell back on the same tired storytelling formula.

This was the most hilariously bad movie I’ve ever seen—and that’s exactly what made it amazing! Sci-Fi originals thrive on their ridiculousness, and this one delivered. The line *"I like my dinosaur meat well done!"* has to be the greatest thing ever uttered on screen. The whole plot feels like the result of a late-night, sleep-deprived brainstorm—picture the writers coming off a wild night of questionable decisions and Dance Dance Revolution, then scribbling down: *Space marines land on a dino-infested alien planet with medieval castles to guard scientists.* It’s pure gold. Honestly, it ticks every box for a perfect trashy sci-fi flick: guns, dinosaurs, knights, spaceships, and gloriously awful acting.  

Do yourself a favor and watch this masterpiece—just don’t waste money buying it.

The story had zero redeeming characters—the protagonist was an unbearable mix of Woody Allen, Paul Provenza, and Paul Reiser at their most irritating. The forced, predictable scenes (did anyone actually believe the rollerblading kid wouldn't wipe that guy out?) were groan-inducing and painfully bad.

The film was beautifully understated, capturing the harsh reality of gender segregation with a delicate yet bittersweet touch. Its subtle humor carried an edge, reflecting the deeper societal struggles. The use of non-professional actors added authenticity, giving the movie a raw, almost documentary-like quality. Some of the most powerful moments came when the girls, forbidden from watching, eagerly listened to the soldier broadcasting the game—the passion in their quiet rebellion was palpable. For Iranians, the scenes of cheering and dancing in the streets after a victory will stir national pride, but even without that cultural connection, the film’s charm is undeniable.

Over the centuries, Christmas traditions—both sacred and secular—have transformed, yet the season remains a time when people are expected to treat one another with greater kindness. This sentiment, however, never reached Ebenezer Scrooge, a 19th-century London merchant and moneylender.  

His nephew observes that Scrooge dismisses Christmas entirely, dismissing it as mere nonsense. Long stripped of compassion, Scrooge is a hardened man, not unlike his 20th-century counterpart, Mr. Potter of Bedford Falls, New York.  

Yet as Charles Dickens’ story unfolds, redemption proves possible for even the most callous soul. Through the haunting visit of a solitary ghost and three spirits, Scrooge is offered a glimpse of his own humanity—and the chance to change.  

*The Christmas Carol* stands as such an enduring holiday favorite that we often overlook its sharp social critique of 19th-century Britain, much like *Oliver Twist*. The characters in this tale belong to the struggling middle and working classes. The Cratchits, though a step above the destitute in *Oliver Twist*, fight desperately to hold onto their fragile foothold. Still, their resilience shines through.

This film is masterfully crafted! Every element shines flawlessly—from the set design and lighting to the sound and storyline. The script unfolds like an intricate puzzle, drawing viewers into a deceptively simple mission.  

Paxton delivers a career-defining performance, with impeccable mannerisms and pitch-perfect vocal inflections. Every frame is meticulously composed! As the story unfolds past the first hour, surprises unfold in quick succession. While it may not claim the title of best picture of the year, it’s a brilliantly polished gem—one that demands a keen mind to fully appreciate.

Growing up, my babysitter was a fan, so I caught a lot of the classic episodes. I’ve never been big on Scooby-Doo, so I’m not sure why I kept the TV on when this new show first aired—but to my surprise, I actually enjoyed it. For me, Shaggy and Scooby were always the only interesting characters (*ducks flying tomatoes from fans of the rest*), so I appreciate that the focus stays on them. That said, it might not sit well with die-hard fans of the original.  

The voice acting is great, especially Dr. Phineas Phibes—I loved his voice even before realizing it was Jeff Bennett. And Jim Meskimen as Robi? He sounds like he’s having a blast with the role. Plus, I get a kick out of the techies with their mildly autistic quirks and their obsession with fantasy RPGs and sci-fi reenactments (though they’re obviously not called by those names in the show).

*Rewritten version:*  

"The Crush" works well as a lighthearted, forty-something romantic comedy for its first two acts, playing like a British take on "Sex and the City."  

I especially liked the subversion of the typical trophy-boy role—though the young hunk’s character isn’t deeply developed (and, come to think of it, we don’t see much of Kenny Doughty’s physical presence either, which is a shame).  

The film makes a much bigger fuss over the young man/older woman dynamic than older versions of "Sabrina" ever did (neither of which I particularly liked), or even real-life pairings like Douglas/Zeta-Jones or Dion/Svengali.  

Andie MacDowell, playing an ex-pat, is surrounded by a strong supporting cast of familiar British actors, including the sharp-witted Anna Chancellor.  

The final act’s plot twists feel forced, like a hasty fix. But it wasn’t until the credits rolled that I realized what might be off—similar to "Sex and the City," the writer/director here is a man, first-timer John McKay, who may have actually wanted to tell a story about three gay men, possibly about coming out.

I originally caught this film on MST3K. While the riffing had me in stitches, I didn’t actually find the movie itself terrible. Yes, it’s undeniably low-budget and a bit confusing at times, but it carries a plot with real Hitchcockian flair. After watching the untouched version, I was surprisingly engaged—it held my attention. Honestly, this story deserves a high-quality remake.  

(Note: Let me know if you'd like any further refinements to the tone or structure!)

*Redline* is a cheap imitation of *Fast & Furious*, missing everything that makes those films entertaining. It doesn’t need an intricate plot full of twists, but it needs *something* worthwhile. This movie is like a poorly made adult film—just a flimsy excuse for action, with minimal setup and zero payoff. Only here, you don’t even get the satisfaction of getting what you paid for. The racing sequences are laughably unrealistic, the pacing is painfully dull, and the stunning cars featured might as well have been ruined by association with this mess. Yes, the lead actress is attractive, but is that really enough to justify sitting through this trainwreck? It feels like the director randomly picked plot points and lines of dialogue out of a hat, then switched scenes on a whim. Anyone with even basic knowledge of racing would cringe at the absurdity of these races. Save yourself the agony—this one’s not worth your time.

Kirstie Alley appears slightly thinner, though not by much, stuck in this chaotic mess alongside a bleach-blond man who could pass for a MacGyver double. The film’s premise revolves around an older woman—gasp, 50!—facing age discrimination in Hollywood, so she enlists her nephew to pose as the screenwriter. It’s an unoriginal concept executed poorly, plagued by terrible acting, cringe-worthy dialogue, and an absurd plot. Even more baffling is a subplot involving a lovestruck writer obsessed with Kirstie’s character—completely pointless. To make matters worse, the actor playing her brother delivers such a stiff, unconvincing performance that every scene with him is painful. In short? Skip this disaster.

This is hands down the most terrible film I've ever endured. Once again, I fell for the trap of purchasing based on an intriguing synopsis and slick cover art (after this disaster and the equally awful "Malevolence" - which I also reviewed - I've finally learned my lesson). 

I typically enjoy horror movies with rural settings - woods, deserts, farms - but this alleged "Texas woods" thriller looked like it was shot in someone's suburban backyard. The production quality might be the worst I've encountered in my life. The acting? Unbearably bad. The actual plot bore no resemblance to the description on the case. 

I even attempted to offload this disaster at F.Y.E. and several local used DVD shops - none would take it off my hands. That's how fundamentally unwatchable this cinematic catastrophe is. While I've suffered through some bad movies before ("Troll 2" comes to mind), this one sets a new standard for awful. I never thought anything could surpass "Troll 2" in sheer terribleness - how naive I was! 

Unless someone literally pays you to take this movie, do not - under any circumstances - waste your money on it. Even then...

This visually refined game of perception unfolds as a story within a story. The narrative follows Bart Klever, a screenwriter wrestling relentlessly with his latest script—the very film we’re observing. Within the movie’s frame, Bart portrays a writer crafting the screenplay, turning his creative struggle into a central motif alongside the claustrophobic intimacy of his apartment, where he balances work with caring for his young daughter.  

This confined space becomes a playground for illusion, where light, color, and shifting perspectives intertwine—heightened by the mischievous presence of two cats. The seemingly simple domestic setting grows increasingly layered as the screenplay on Bart’s computer screen morphs with the filmmaker’s interruptions, mirroring the room’s own fluid reality.  

Shifting vantage points blur the boundaries between truth and artifice, raising critical questions: Which world holds authority—the written or the lived? What serves as our anchor in this ever-shifting narrative landscape?

Visually tacky and painfully dull, this film failed to hold even the children's attention—aside from a single, mildly funny bathroom gag. Christopher Lloyd feels painfully miscast, dragging through his role with a tired performance made worse by the weak script's pitiful attempts at humor. Elizabeth Hurley's awkward, unconvincing turn in what should have been a comedic role borders on cringe-worthy. Only Jeff Daniels and Darryl Hannah manage to escape unscathed. The entire project feels pointless, particularly when compared to Robin Williams' razor-sharp, spontaneous genius in *Mork & Mindy*.

This version had none of the original's strengths—energy, flair, or bold performances. Even the writing fell flat here. So much didn’t add up: If Farrah wasn’t truly pursuing an acting career, why bother with a manager (and why would he invest time in her)? If Kate and Barney considered themselves artists, why join what amounted to a blatant display of superficial appeal (a bit like Robert Reed’s Shakespeare-loving dad stuck in the "Brady Bunch" movie)? They weren’t A-listers, but they weren’t desperate either. Some historical details were accurate—Farrah’s poster predated the show—but fabrications like Silverman shooting down "Funniest Home Videos" and "American Idol," or Spelling vowing to craft a series for baby Tori, were pure fiction.  

What really grated was the misrepresentation of Spelling’s involvement. He’s portrayed as the driving creative force behind the show, which simply wasn’t the case. His sudden "lightbulb moment" for the series? Absurd.  

And let’s talk logistics: How could Spelling and Goldberg legally bind Farrah to an oral agreement when the rest of the cast had signed contracts? Why didn’t Farrah or Bernstein speak up about this?

Released in 1999, this film boasts solid production quality with a cast that's both attractive and skilled. The action avoids clichés—there's no endless shootouts where bullets never seem to find their mark or over-the-top car chases that senselessly wreck expensive vehicles.  

The sets reflect contemporary design, and the props hold up well—except for that high-tech computer room, which seems stocked with relics from a 1950s electronics lab. The makeup on the corpses, though, was unintentionally amusing. Instead of traditional pancake makeup, it looked like dried batter smeared on their skin, supposedly illustrating their calcification. How a virus could cause such a transformation is left to the viewer’s imagination.  

And then there's the absurd premise. I wish I could say this wasn’t the weakest sci-fi horror concept I’ve encountered, but a computer virus transmitted through a TV or monitor that mutates into a deadly biological pathogen? Give me a break. Warp drives may be...

This film captivates for three compelling reasons. Its visual splendor is breathtaking – a vibrant color palette flows through every frame, enhanced by stunning costumes and meticulously designed sets. The cinematography achieves a lavish appearance that likely defied its budget.  

I’ve always been drawn to stories of misfits and loners forging unlikely bonds, though many veer into predictability—this one avoids those traps entirely. The ensemble cast brings flawed yet deeply endearing characters to life, with Alan Larkin standing out brilliantly (his presence, the van, and the road-trip vibe irresistibly reminded me of *Little Miss Sunshine*, my favorite film from last year). Fabrizio Bentivoglio was a revelation, while Til Schweiger’s performance occasionally grated.  

The humor shines in moments of botched magic tricks, particularly the opening scene, balanced perfectly with emotional depth. The ending resonates beautifully, and of course, the central theme of illusion—how a magician directs the audience’s gaze to craft deception—ties it all together.

The title says everything. I saw this film with my father when it was first released, and as a Korean War veteran, he held immense respect for the general. The only letdown is that the movie focuses solely on a brief chapter of his life—when in reality, his full story would have made such a sweeping biographical epic that the scale of production is almost unimaginable.  

A few comments here highlight the man’s flaws, which feels like low-effort criticism. The film’s core message—"Duty, Honor, Country"—isn’t just empty rhetoric from a decorated officer; it’s the profound reflection of one man’s unwavering dedication to his nation.  

It’s ironic that Peck, despite his liberal views, captured the essence of the general so well. His portrayal masterfully balances the fearless leader with the compassionate man beneath the uniform.

This clever film explores love across different eras, with Keaton chasing romance in the Stone Age, ancient Rome, and the 1920s present day. In each timeline, the lovably awkward Buster faces off against Wallace Beery to win his lady’s heart. Though all three settings deliver classic fun, the Roman segment stands out—despite being delightfully cheesy. Highlights include a hilariously unconvincing lion costume and an absurd snowy chariot race, but Keaton’s incredible stunts steal the show. While not his greatest work, this film remains an entertaining and remarkable ride—definitely worth watching!

When I first joined the discussion for this movie, I fully expected to see people mocking it. I was genuinely surprised to find viewers older than seven actually enjoyed it. Personally, I had fun watching it—but only because my 10-year-old sister and I spent the entire time cracking jokes.

Let me be honest, Jordan—the acting was rough. A weak lead performance usually spells disaster, and unfortunately, the shaky script and flimsy plot didn’t help salvage it. Pamela’s character was especially weak, almost cringe-worthy at times.

That said, a few performances stood out—Spencer, Hollywood, and Ronnie brought some charm to the screen. But their efforts weren’t enough to save the film.  

Two things still bug me:  

1) The idea of Spencer’s character falling for her. I checked the real-life ages, and while the gap is only about four years, in *Go Figure*, it felt way more noticeable. Jordan is lovely, but in this movie, she came across as...

I probably overrate this a bit because it was Halloween season—I’d just come back from Knott’s Scary Farm and was in the perfect mood for a gloriously cheesy horror flick.  

Oh, and I only paid a buck for it.  

Normally, I’d fast-forward through something like this to skip to "the good parts," but for some reason, I didn’t. Right from the start, it was clearly not a "real" movie—not even a B-movie. It fits more in line with those ultra-low-budget DeCoteau "horror" films, like *The Brotherhood*, shot on film-look video for pennies (honestly, I halfway expected one of his shirtless college jocks to stumble into frame at any moment, rubbing himself in his underwear). The production lacked cutaway shots (multiple setups are pricey) and had flat lighting, but… it’s hard to explain. There’s something oddly satisfying about watching a director stretch no budget into something halfway watchable. The fact that it even works a little is impressive, and this movie does have its strengths—the acting isn’t awful, the cinematography is decent (if too bright to be scary), and…

Sidney Franklin’s *The Good Earth* has earned its place as a classic, thanks to its enduring story and masterful performances—most notably from Luis Rainer, who took home an Oscar for her role as O-Lan. Rainer’s transformation is so profound that she becomes nearly unrecognizable, embodying the character with remarkable authenticity. With minimal dialogue in this lengthy film, she conveys O-Lan’s depth through subtle yet powerful expressions and body language. Her portrayal is so convincing that viewers unfamiliar with her work might easily believe she is Chinese.  

The film’s relevance persists because it delves into the timeless rags-to-riches journey and the universal struggles that accompany it. After enduring years of famine and hardship, Wang Lung and O-Lan finally attain wealth—only to discover that material abundance brings emptiness rather than happiness. It is not until they reconnect with the land, battling a devastating locust plague (brought to life with stunning, still-impressive special effects), that they rediscover true fulfillment.  

Told through the lens of a Chinese family—a rare perspective for 1937—*The Good Earth* elevates a familiar narrative into something extraordinary. Its message resonates deeply: wealth means nothing without the bonds of family and community, a truth the film delivers with lasting impact.

Claims that this is a poor film couldn't be more wrong. In truth, it's the greatest movie I've ever watched - with a brilliant storyline and truly outstanding performances. Every actor delivered flawlessly, leaving no room for critique. This film stands unparalleled, and its greatness will remain unchallenged.

Busy Phillips delivered an outstanding performance, balancing comedy and drama perfectly. While Erika Christensen was strong, Busy completely stole the spotlight. This was a refreshing follow-up to *The Smokers*, a less impressive film also featuring Busy. If she doesn’t earn at least a nomination for *Home Room*, it would be a huge oversight. Skip *Mona Lisa Smile*—*Home Room* is the one to watch.

I despise Hollywood yet adore cinema, which forces me to endure these mediocre films in theaters. I went into *Vanilla Sky* hoping it would be great—either a faithful remake of *Open Your Eyes* or a bold reimagining. Instead, it awkwardly straddled both approaches and failed miserably.  

It began well—Radiohead’s haunting soundtrack was a highlight. I wish there had been more of that. Yet by the climax, we’re subjected to *Good Vibrations* by The Beach Boys. The soundtrack swung wildly between decent and unbearable. A couple of tracks in the club scenes worked, but blasting *Good Vibrations* over the film’s pivotal moment? It wasn’t just baffling; it was downright irritating, especially since the song had zero connection to the story. At least Radiohead’s *Kid A* carried thematic weight.  

The club scene was undeniably stylish—one of the film’s few strengths. Beyond that, *Vanilla Sky* reeked of arrogance, assuming audiences would grasp its convoluted plot. Truth is, those who could appreciate its depth would’ve just watched the original with subtitles, while everyone else was left bewildered.

When the U.S. joined World War I, Hollywood was pressured to produce propaganda films, and *The Little American* stands out among them—largely thanks to Mary Pickford’s starring role.  

Pickford portrays a woman caught between two suitors: Jack Holt, playing a German, and Raymond Hatton as a Frenchman. The war interrupts her choice when both men enlist. After her ship is torpedoed by the Germans (reminiscent of the *Lusitania* incident) for carrying arms, Pickford delivers a powerful moment, defiantly shouting at the German commander from a lifeboat. Later, she encounters both Holt and Hatton when she's taken prisoner at a château.  

Director Cecil B. DeMille crafts one striking scene as Pickford and Holt walk through a devastated village. Amid the ruins, only a single church wall remains, bearing a large crucifix. As they watch, the wall crumbles—yet the figure of Christ hangs suspended in midair. This surreal, haunting image contrasts sharply with the film’s otherwise straightforward style.  

As always, Pickford shines...

I watched this movie on DVD last night and looked up reviews this morning. It appears *I, Robot* has sharply divided critics on IMDb—sparking quite a bit of heated arguing in the process.  

Honestly, I’m a little surprised by the extreme reactions. The film isn’t great (or even particularly good), but it’s far from terrible (or even truly bad). More than anything, it’s just... disheartening. Disheartening that audiences seem eager to embrace bland, recycled ideas and praise them as groundbreaking. This movie screams "been there, done that," from its muddled storyline (a shaky blend of Asimov and generic action tropes) to Will Smith’s character (yet another quick-witted, tough-as-nails skeptic) and even the effects (borrowing heavily from *The Matrix* and others).  

Sadly, *I, Robot* might just be the ideal action flick for modern tastes: a shallow plot, painfully clichéd dialogue, and nonstop, over-the-top thrills. Smith’s performance is mediocre—no surprise there (Hollywood keeps trying, and failing, to position him as the next Bruce Willis). The story is riddled with plot holes, big and small, but I doubt...

In Bridgeport, deranged high school teacher Richard Fenton (Johnathon Schaech) becomes dangerously obsessed with his student Donna Keppel (Brittany Snow). After she witnesses him murder her family in a twisted attempt to keep her close, Richard is sentenced to life in prison.  

Three years later, Donna, still recovering from the trauma, is in therapy and on medication. Hoping for a fresh start, she attends her senior prom with her boyfriend Bobby (Scott Porter) and two other couples at the Pacific Grand Hotel. But their night turns deadly when Richard escapes prison and stalks Donna, slaughtering hotel staff and her friends who stand in his way.  

*Prom Night* is a forgettable slasher riddled with clichés and devoid of originality. The flimsy, uninspired plot is matched by Johnathon Schaech’s unconvincing performance as the deranged killer. The predictable script telegraphs every move, draining any suspense. A mediocre entry in the genre.  

My rating: 3/10  

**Brazilian title:** *A Morte Convida Para Dançar* ("Death Invites You to Dance")

This might be one of the most disappointing films I've watched recently.  

I don’t see the appeal of Heath Ledger’s character—his look didn't work for me. Had I known he and Naomi Watts were together off-screen, maybe I wouldn't have spent two agonizing hours questioning her attraction to him.  

As for Orlando Bloom being a heartthrob? The messy beard and dazed expression didn’t do him any favors.  

Rachel Griffiths delivered her usual strong performance, but Geoffrey Rush seemed completely detached—like he couldn’t wait to leave.  

Am I really expected to sympathize with criminals? This film falls painfully short compared to classics like *Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid*, which succeeded in being engaging. Instead, this was predictable, full of tired tropes, and dull. We kept watching, hoping it would improve—it never did.  

The final act was almost comical. Heath’s gang barricaded in a hotel, causing innocent casualties, wasn’t amusing—but their absurd armored exit? All I could think of was the Black Knight from *Monty Python*.

This movie left me completely disconnected. It didn’t resonate with me on any level—intellectually, emotionally, or visually. The dialogue felt heavy and hard to engage with, and I struggled to feel invested in any of the characters. Honestly, it’s difficult to think of much to praise about it.  

I’ve heard that a deep understanding of Catholic theology is necessary to fully appreciate the film. As someone who isn’t religious, I might lack that background, but I’ve seen other films with religious themes that still moved me because they spoke to universal human experiences—without requiring niche knowledge or faith.

*The Bourne Ultimatum* erupts onto the screen in a frenetic chase, never letting up as Jason Bourne (Matt Damon, brilliant as ever) races to uncover the architects of the CIA black-ops program that forged him into a lethal weapon—all in a desperate bid to reclaim his lost identity. David Strathairn delivers a chilling performance as the shadowy puppet master, joining returning stars Joan Allen (excellent) and Julia Stiles (barely present).  

Much like its predecessor, the film’s relentless handheld camerawork—courtesy of Paul Greengrass—can be exhausting, begging for a moment of stillness. Yet this chaotic style heightens the intensity of the brutal close-quarters combat and electrifying rooftop and foot chases, punctuated by the occasional explosive car wreck. A key allure of the Bourne saga is its breakneck global pacing and near-mythical tech wizardry, bending the limits of realism with surveillance hacks and impossibly precise coordination. The films thrive in a heightened, hyper-kinetic world where technology borders on sorcery—even if logic strains to explain how everyone converges at just the right moment.

This unusual cartoon carried surprising emotional depth compared to typical animated films. It follows a lonely, insecure girl at summer camp with only two equally unhappy siblings as companions. At her lowest moment, she enters into a literal pact with a devilish creature. What makes this story resonate is its authenticity—just when all seems hopeless, the girl recognizes her mistake, regrets her actions, and transforms. Through her redemption, she unexpectedly teaches the dark magical being about human compassion. The twin siblings also grow by helping little bears, discovering their own self-worth in the process. While undeniably quirky in places, the film delivers a powerful positive message for young viewers that remains impactful. Stephen Bishop's heartfelt soundtrack (known for his work in *Tootsie*) elevates the entire experience, making this strange but meaningful movie genuinely enjoyable.

This is the perfect movie to unwind with—pour yourself a glass of wine, get cozy by the fire, and kick back. It's lighthearted and easy to follow, ideal after a draining day. Don't expect realism—if you're looking for something serious, skip it—but it's downright hilarious. The idea that a businessman would not only agree to live in a slum but actually thrive there is absurd in the best way. Highly recommended for a good laugh!

There’s no question that Ealing comedies are excellent, but this film shines as one of their finest.  

The story follows a small section of London’s Pimlico, which is unexpectedly declared part of Burgundy rather than the UK. The residents must defend their newfound independence—particularly the treasure uncovered after a bomb blast—while fending off black marketeers eager to exploit their exemption from British rationing laws. When the government seals their borders, trapping them in their own neighborhood, they rally together to resist the system.  

Their fight for justice leads them to ration water and food, leaving them even worse off than before—until they reach a breaking point. Just as they prepare to surrender, Londoners rally behind them, flooding their streets with supplies. Their solidarity reignites the community’s spirit, proving that unity triumphs over adversity.  

Every note of this film rings true, with brilliant performances that bring its wit and heart to life.

I’ll never forget being five years old when my parents put on what they assumed was just a harmless cartoon—until bras and bullets started flying across the screen. There’s no denying this film was designed to offend just about everyone, and it absolutely succeeds… but beneath the shock value lies something sharp, hilarious, and surprisingly profound. If cult classics are your thing, this one’s a must-watch.  

And while you're at it, check out *Fritz the Cat* and *The Nine Lives of Fritz the Cat*—both (if I’m remembering right) also directed by Ralph Bakshi. They follow the misadventures of a streetwise cat grappling with family struggles, shady jobs, and urban chaos. Once I was old enough, I hunted down all of Bakshi’s films, including *Coonskin* (which was controversially rebranded as *Street Fighter* due to its title).  

Speaking of Bakshi, don’t miss *Cool World*, featuring a fresh-faced Brad Pitt, or *Heavy Traffic*, a raw, animated dive into a young man’s struggle with inner-city life. His films don’t hold back—and that’s what makes them unforgettable.

Patronizing "world music" drivel—droning synths, clichéd ethnic drums, kids chorusing on cue. This is a tourist reel at its worst, and what sinks it completely is the jarring lack of coherence. One moment India, then suddenly Egypt, South America, Africa—no logic, no narrative thread, just a lazy parade of stock "exotic" imagery. Endless scenes of people walking with baskets on their heads, as if sheer repetition could conjure profundity. If the goal was a third-world music video, they could’ve spared the globe-trotting and just filmed in Mexico, a stone's throw from where Koyaanisqatsi’s strongest sequences were shot. That, at least, might’ve offered something authentic about "life in transformation."  

Instead, we get a garbled travelogue drowning in overcranked, over-filtered visuals. The sole redeeming quality? It’s marginally less insufferable than *Naqoyqatsi*.  

—RstJ

Let me begin by saying that I generally appreciate Renny Harlin’s directing style, and the cinematography deserves praise for several standout shots. However, unlike Harlin’s films *Elm Street 4* and *Die Hard 2*, both of which I thoroughly enjoyed, this movie feels like it’s missing something crucial. That missing piece, my friends, is a decent script. While bad dialogue is common in films of this genre, this one takes stupidity to new heights. The lines are so cringe-worthy, I’d rather forget them entirely. Worse yet, the delivery feels painfully awkward—more suited to a cheap adult film than an action-adventure. It’s as if Harlin believed slowing down the actors’ speech could somehow salvage the script. Spoiler alert: it doesn’t.  

What truly disappoints is seeing talented actors wasted on poorly written roles. Stallone has never been at the top of my list, but when he outacts Lithgow, Turner, and especially Rooker—who delivers the weakest performance—there’s clearly a problem. Lithgow, who was brilliant as a villain in *Ricochet*, falls flat here.

**Lessons from *The List*:**  

A skilled cinematographer, a talented and attractive lead actress, and even Malcolm McDowell couldn’t save this disaster.  

Blockbuster has a no-refund policy—consider this a warning.  

Malcolm McDowell commits to his role, even when the script makes him groan aloud.  

Chuck Carrington’s performance is proof that acting classes exist for a reason.  

Next time, invest in a writer.  

Divine punishment comes in many forms—mine was spending $5.50 on this film.  

Who needs a coherent ending? Just leave everything vague, dull, and mind-numbing so the audience dozes off first. Revolutionary.  

Turns out, any landlord can resurrect the dead with a window-drawn cross. Networking pays off.  

A maid’s lullaby can literally revive the deceased.  

(Reminder: Chuck Carrington *still* needs acting classes.)  

Bring this movie home, and your roommate will mock you relentlessly.  

And no, sorry won’t fix it.

Cheesy '70s horror flicks...you can't help but adore them. Unlike today's stale slasher films, these low-budget gems deliver genuine scares without relying on worn-out tropes.  

This B-movie centers on the disastrous production of another B-movie. Faith Domergue (*This Island Earth*) plays a faded scream queen filming a movie based on a real-life family's gruesome murder. Her controlling director boyfriend—who channels Gordon Jump with a chip on his shoulder—is racing to finish the shoot on location. The film’s bland leading man stumbles upon a book of Tibetan chants, which they foolishly incorporate into the script for "authenticity." Too bad they got more than they bargained for.  

John Carradine, long past his mad scientist days (*The Unearthly*), now scrapes by as the estate’s creepy caretaker. He goes about his duties but keeps clashing with the egotistical director.  

The terror creeps in slowly—a dead cat here, Carradine lurking near a grave there—before exploding into a full-blown bloodbath. Seven murders, to be exact. (At least the title doesn’t lie.) Too bad the killer didn’t get the memo.

Can anyone tell me what model pickup truck John T drove? It appears to be a mid-to-late 1970s Ford. This film holds a special place in my heart—it’s mine and my wife’s favorite. It was the first memorable movie we watched together as a married couple. The truck caught my attention because it’s similar to the first one I ever drove, and I recently found one just like it. I’d love to restore mine to match the one from the movie.  

The soundtrack was incredible, and the performances were outstanding. Does anyone know where the actress who played John’s aunt is now, or what she’s been in since? Was there a stunt double for John during the tower scene where he nearly fell?  

Also, what year Mustang did Debra W drive? It looked like a 1960s model. Thanks for any details!

This Three Stooges comedy ranks just as high as my other favorite, *Disorder in the Court*. It’s a riotous laugh fest that any Stooges fan will love.  

The boys work as janitors in a recording studio when they overhear Christine McIntyre delivering a stunning performance of *Voices of Spring*. Though she's about to land a record deal, she’s afraid to confess to her father that she’s pursuing a singing career instead of his expectations. After she and the studio crew leave, the Stooges can’t resist some mischief—they play her record and disguise Curly as Christine. A talent scout, impressed by the recording, mistakes Curly for the singer and invites "her" to perform at a high-society party.  

Of course, chaos ensues when they cross paths with a vengeful musician whose own performance they ruin—leading to hilarious revenge schemes.  

A must-watch for Stooges fans—pure comedy gold!  

10/10

**The College Girl Murders** is packed with intrigue. A deranged scientist develops a nearly undetectable poison gas, but before he can profit from his creation, a hooded monk wielding a whip murders him. When a college student is killed by the same gas in a church, Scotland Yard steps in—yet the deaths don’t stop. Who can halt this elusive killer, able to move unnoticed through the campus at will?  

### **What Works:**  

- **The Killer** – A figure clad in a stark red KKK-style robe, complete with red gloves, is undeniably striking. The contrast of the white whip against the vibrant crimson gown makes for a visually chilling effect. While the idea of a hooded assassin stalking a girls' school may seem outlandish, the costume itself is one of the most unsettling I’ve seen.  

- **Groovy ‘60s Music** – The film’s title track is a standout, with its jazzy, upbeat ‘60s vibe—I’d love to find out what it’s called.  

- **Bizarre Touches** – Beyond the killer’s eerie presence...

What stood out most was the compelling central theme of "intruders"—the Others embedded within the fragile Self, operating on subconscious and sometimes allegorical levels. These invasive presences pervade the entire film: along the Swiss-French border where the protagonist isolates himself, in his recurring dreams and nightmares, even within his own failing body after a heart transplant. By the latter half, he becomes the intruder, journeying back to an old French colony in a futile attempt to confront his past.  

The mood leans toward bitterness rather than sorrow, steeped in regret, guilt, and an overwhelming sense of futility. It paints a stark portrait of aging—outwardly self-sufficient but hollow and profoundly lonely beneath the surface. The director crafts images to evoke fleeting sensations of unease and longing rather than clear-cut messages. Some scenes are hauntingly hypnotic, laced with an absurdist wit that feels like the fragmented vision of a sleepwalker.

**(Major Spoilers)** Having only seen one other Takashi Miike film—the deeply unsettling and violent *Audition*, which dissects Japanese femininity—I was prepared for another provocative experience. *Visitor Q* (a title I interpret as "Visitor Question") delivers just that, delving into the family unit with grotesque absurdity. Miike’s portrayal of dysfunction borders on Lynchian in its chaotic storytelling, though it lacks the finesse and depth of Lynch’s work.  

The film throws the audience into bizarre scenarios from the start: a father (played compellingly by Kenichi Endo) soliciting sex from his estranged daughter (Fujiko), only to return home and be ambushed by the titular "Visitor" (Kazushi Watanabe), who fractures his skull with a rock. Somehow, they both wind up back in the fractured household. The mother (Shungiku Uchida) endures abuse from her son (Jun Muto), who, in turn, suffers beatings from classmates. The Visitor’s arrival marks a sinister shift as he weaves himself into the family’s toxic dynamic. Gradually, under his unsettling influence, their bonds begin to mend—through breast milk, murder, and preservation.

I’m always stunned—and sickened—by the sheer cruelty committed throughout history in the name of religion. Even with the lessons of the past and the progress of modern times, the Catholic Church’s actions in 20th-century Ireland stand out as some of the most egregious.  

*A Love Divided* tells the true story of a family torn apart by blind bigotry, all justified by the cold rigidity of Church doctrine. The film opens with a glimpse of idyllic village life in Ireland, where Sheila and Sean Cloney live happily with their two young children. Sean is Catholic, Sheila is Protestant, and she has no objection to raising their children in the Catholic faith. The village itself seems free of religious tension—until Sheila wants their eldest child to attend the Protestant school. What follows is a devastating chain of events, as the local priest condemns this decision as a "sin" and turns Sean, along with the entire Catholic community, against her. The love and peace they once knew shatter under the weight of dogma and control.

This is a classic case of directors with exceptional technical skills in music videos and commercials attempting their first feature-length film. On one hand, the visuals—camera work, lighting, CGI, and even sound—are meticulously crafted, radiating a distinctly high-budget aesthetic. Even the acting shows glimpses of promise—up until the point where no performance, no matter how strong, could salvage a weak story.  

Here, it’s not just a weak story—there’s almost no story at all.  

Half the dialogue consists of variations of *"What the hell was that?"*—repeated endlessly without ever offering the characters (or the audience) the slightest explanation. The remaining conversations feel completely improvised, as if the actors were left to invent lines on the spot with no script or coherent direction.  

The lone standout is Skye Bennet’s performance—largely because her role as an autistic girl spared her from the painfully awkward dialogue forced upon the rest of the cast.

Do you love unraveling mysteries? Are you drawn to intricate storytelling? This film is made for you. A brilliant and sharp masterpiece by Francis Leclerc—son of the legendary French-Canadian singer Félix Leclerc. Stunning cinematography and masterful editing define Leclerc’s style, elevated by Roy Dupuis’s electrifying lead performance.  

The story follows Alexandre Tourneur, a veterinarian in his 40s who awakens from a coma after someone mysteriously unplugs his life support. Struggling to recall who attacked him while he was euthanizing an injured deer on the road, Tourneur’s behavior grows increasingly erratic—as if something has taken hold of him.  

Though not outright terrifying, it’s deeply mysterious and superbly acted. I have my own theory about the ending (I suspect the Indigenous man caused the accident), but it remains open to interpretation.  

A must-watch—9.5/10.

This film is a bright spot in an otherwise gloomy time, radiating warmth through its simple celebration of kindness. Morgan Freeman slips into a role that mirrors his own persona—a seasoned actor nearing 70. His character visits a modest, slightly rundown grocery store, scouting for inspiration to play a manager in an upcoming role. Before long, he charms everyone around him, especially the spirited but somewhat irritable young woman (Paz Vega) running the "10 items or less" checkout line.  

*10 Items or Less* doesn’t aim for grand themes or heavy messages. Instead, it focuses on the effortless bond that forms between Freeman and Vega as they spend the day together. Freeman’s character, stranded when his studio ride forgets him—and unable to recall his own phone number—leans on Vega for a lift home. In return, he offers her bits of wisdom. On a dull, overcast Sunday in New York, this little movie was just the remedy for my low spirits.

Don’t be deceived by the "A Stanley Kubrick Film" label. This is a terrible movie, yet it’s been wrongly praised as one of the most terrifying horror films ever made. A true horror film should instill such fear that it haunts viewers long after, leaving them trembling at night. *The Shining*, however, fails to deliver any real horror—instead, it offers a clumsy, shallow attempt at creating dread.  

What works in the film? Only the visuals—the icy landscape and the grand hotel set. As for the acting, Jack Nicholson wanders through his role like a confused, lethargic man with no clear direction. The other performances, including a bald, dark-skinned actor mostly preoccupied with babysitting a child actor, are equally forgettable.  

And don’t blame the harsh weather for the film’s flaws—it's simply poorly made, and Kubrick, unfortunately, isn’t around to fix it.

It's hard to believe this film was released as late as 1984—the acting is painfully bad, and the storyline might just be one of the most ridiculous ever. Who in their right mind would send a heavyset Texas sheriff like Joe Don Baker to transport an Italian man he unlawfully arrested in Mexico back to Italy? Even the title is utterly meaningless, probably the most generic name they could slap on this failed attempt at an action-cop flick.  

Thankfully, I only experienced this through *MST3K*, with Mike and the bots as my buffer. They crack jokes about the female lead's uncanny resemblance to Elaine from *Seinfeld* ("Not one of them is spongeworthy") and never let up mocking Baker's size. While this movie might not sink as low as *Mitchell*, Baker’s infamy clearly precedes him—when his name flashes on screen at the start, Tom quips, *"I wish I was illiterate so I wouldn't have to read that."*

The film boasts a brilliantly crafted story within its genre. It includes all the classic *Columbo* trademarks: the way Lieutenant Columbo interacts with and connects to his suspect, how the mystery unfolds for him, appearances by Columbo’s dog, the gripping cat-and-mouse dynamic—which is particularly strong here—and, fortunately, some well-placed humor, mostly tied to Columbo himself. The writing shines, even though the premise isn’t entirely original. The idea of Columbo pursuing a mystery novelist had been explored in earlier *Columbo* films.  

Direction by James Frawley is outstanding. After this film, he went on to helm five more *Columbo* movies in the '70s and '80s, bringing a distinct style and several unforgettable scenes to this installment.  

While one of the slower-paced entries in the series, the movie doesn’t overstay its welcome. This deliberate pacing doesn’t always suit *Columbo*, but here it works effectively—likely due in large part to the strong performances.  

Most *Columbo* films featured either a major star or a veteran actor from Hollywood’s golden age.

I’ll confess—Al Pacino is a guilty pleasure for me. He was a brilliant actor up until *Scent of a Woman*, after which it seemed he became a parody of himself, never quite recovering. When I stumbled upon *City Hall*, a film I’d barely heard of before, I hoped it would be an underrated gem—a sharp, ahead-of-its-time political thriller simmering with intelligence. Instead, it disappoints.  

The movie drowns its own story in a flood of characters, names, and "gritty" urban dilemmas, giving the illusion of a sprawling, intricate conspiracy that will ultimately leave you stunned. The reality? Its tangled subplots only lead to tired clichés—power-hungry politicians, backroom deals, mobsters with badges—all familiar tropes of city-based dramas.  

In theory, this web of deceit should create tension, the kind where no one is safe and anything could happen. But it doesn’t. The twists feel inevitable, culminating in a series of underwhelming monologues that preach about the murky morals of politics—more of a dull sermon than a gripping tale.

Let’s start with Christopher Cross’s unforgettable theme song, *"If You Get Caught Between the Moon and New York City."* Even after all this time, the track remains timeless—a perfect musical ode to New York itself.
