The film stars the brilliant Dudley Moore CBE as Arthur, a spoiled, drunken millionaire engaged to Jill Eikenberry’s character (who would later rise to fame on *L.A. Law*). Assisting him is the impeccable Sir John Gielgud OM, whose performance as Arthur’s dry-witted butler earned him an Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor.  

Arthur’s life takes a turn when he falls for Liza Minnelli’s character, who shines just as brightly here as she did in her Oscar-winning role in *Cabaret*—though this time, she’s not singing but playing a down-to-earth diner waitress. Geraldine Fitzgerald is equally magnetic as the formidable Bach family matriarch, controlling the family fortune with steely elegance; she absolutely deserved a Best Supporting Actress nomination. And let’s not forget Barney Martin (best known as Jerry’s dad on *Seinfeld*), who brings warmth and humor as Liza’s father.  

With sharp writing, outstanding performances, and a pitch-perfect delivery, *Arthur* remains a classic.

Robert Duvall delivers his weakest performance here, adopting an unconvincing William Buckley-like accent that never lets up. His over-the-top, melodramatic delivery drowns out any real dramatic tension—whether intentional scene-stealing or accidental, it's the only memorable element in an otherwise bland film. This movie belongs in acting workshops as a textbook example of what to avoid. Fortunately, Duvall moved past this phase, ditching the forced sophistication for more substantial roles. He’s a solid character actor, but that's his limit. By contrast, Klaus shines with subtle, compelling work that actually leaves an impression.

This captivating film tells the remarkable true story of Grey Owl, a man whose life unfolded against the backdrop of 1930s Canada. With the emotional depth of classics like *Rudy* and *Awakenings*, it focuses on the pivotal, turbulent chapter of Grey Owl's later years.  

The story follows a Canadian Indigenous trapper who transforms into an unexpected advocate for wildlife, particularly the endangered beaver. His warnings about vanishing wilderness and humanity's reckless exploitation of natural resources were bold for their time—yet astonishingly, they resonated with audiences. As his voice grows stronger, he emerges as a prominent speaker whose message finds eager listeners.  

Pierce Brosnan's casting may seem unconventional at first glance, but his nuanced portrayal quickly dispels any doubts. He delivers a compelling performance, matched by Annie Galipeau's strong, natural presence on screen. Their chemistry feels effortless, a welcome contrast to the often-forced pairings in modern blockbusters.  

I highly recommend this film to anyone who appreciates powerful drama, breathtaking landscapes, or environmental themes. While suitable for families, younger children (under 10, depending on maturity) may struggle to fully grasp its layered narrative.

I honestly can’t recall who suggested this, but they called it one of their all-time favorite movies—and it’s undeniably bizarre, like gawking at a car wreck you can’t look away from.  

They say truth is stranger than fiction, and this documentary proves it. I don’t know how a fictionalized version set for release this year could possibly compare. Imagine Jackie Kennedy’s aunt and cousin abandoning New York high society, retreating to the Hamptons, and transforming into reclusive "crazy cat ladies." Their squalid existence might have remained hidden forever if the city hadn’t threatened to condemn the property—until Jackie stepped in.  

This film captures the aftermath of that rescue, leaving you wondering: *How much worse was it before?* It’s a chilling, mesmerizing glimpse into the shadowy side of wealth and privilege.

I was really excited to see this movie when it was first announced, but it ended up being a huge disappointment. It didn’t capture the magic of Dr. Seuss’s whimsical world—instead, it felt crude and tasteless, something I doubt he would have endorsed.  

*How the Grinch Stole Christmas* was far better. Sure, it had a few subtle adult jokes, but they went over my kids' heads. *The Cat in the Hat*, on the other hand, was packed with so much vulgarity that my children picked up on much more than I would have preferred.  

As someone who grew up loving Dr. Seuss, it was painful to see such a beloved classic butchered on screen. Here’s hoping *Horton Hears a Who!* does justice to his legacy.

Are you kidding me? This film is downright insulting to anyone with half a brain. Honestly, who would believe three kids could take on an army of 30 or 40 trained ninjas—and win? And let’s not even get started on the painfully unfunny jokes stuffed into every scene. This movie is painfully, painfully awful. It feels like a warning sign—the only value it has is as a mindless way to waste time or as a source of unintentional comedy.

**Rewritten Version:**  

A theater troupe is thrown into panic when a mysterious murderer dubbed "The Fiend" begins hunting them down. Two journalists, along with their bumbling photographer, take on the case—only to become targets themselves. Just as the trio believes they’ve uncovered the truth, an unexpected twist leaves the killer’s identity in question, as described on the DVD sleeve.  

Producer Sam Katzman brings *The Hunchback of Notre Dame* to Hollywood in *A Face in the Fog*, where the absence of elaborate studio sets adds an intriguing rawness, particularly in scenes featuring 1930s street traffic. The film could benefit from stronger direction—some shots, like the awkwardly angled fight sequence, fall flat. Despite its modest budget, the cast—many transitioning from silent films to talkies—delivers a likable performance.  

**A Face in the Fog (2/1/36) Robert F. Hill ~ Lloyd Hughes, June Collyer, Al St. John**

"…for Paris is a moveable feast." —Ernest Hemingway  

Countless great talents have enshrined Paris in paintings, novels, songs, poetry, fleeting yet unforgettable quotes—and, of course, films. The renowned director Max Ophüls once remarked on the city:  

"It offered gleaming wet boulevards under streetlights, breakfast in Montmartre with cognac in your cup, coffee and lukewarm brioche, gigolos and prostitutes at night. Everyone in the world has two homelands: their own and Paris."  

Paris is forever linked to love and romance, and *Paris, Je T'Aime*—subtitled *Petites romances*—captures this essence through a mosaic of short films by 18 acclaimed directors from around the globe. Each vignette invites us into one of the City of Light’s 20 arrondissements, where Parisians of every age, gender, color, and background navigate love in all its forms and phases. Some of these "little romances" reveal unexpected encounters between strangers—sparks of instant connection that may blossom into something more, as with Podalydès and Florence Muller on a Montmartre street in the opening scene, or for Cyril...

For ages, I’ve been eager to watch this—James Merendino is an incredible director. *SLC Punk* remains one of my all-time favorites, and the opening ten minutes of this film felt like a strong follow-up. But then, it started to lose momentum. The acting and direction were outstanding, and the pacing worked—except for the script. At points, the only reason I stayed engaged was because of Claire Forlani, the most stunning woman alive, in the cast. It’s a decent film, but I’d hoped for more.  

*P.S. Keep an eye out for fantastic cameos by Chi McBride and Chris McDonald.*

Hands down, this is the funniest movie I’ve ever watched. From the very start—when four troublemakers get shipped off to Wienberg Military Academy by their fed-up fathers—the film establishes a ridiculous, over-the-top tone that never falters.  

Trying to explain this movie is a challenge because its humor is so perfectly executed. At first glance, it might seem like just another dumb 80s teen comedy, but it’s far smarter than it appears. Crafted by the twisted geniuses behind *MAD Magazine*, *Up the Academy* delivers a brand of comedy that Hollywood hasn’t even come close to replicating since. Packed with gloriously juvenile gags, you’d swear it was written by a couple of snickering teenagers. If you love unapologetically silly humor, don’t miss this one. A true cult classic. *****

I’ll be honest—the sole reason I picked up this movie was my love for Gackt and my *massive* admiration for Hyde. I went in expecting eye candy for the ladies with a bit of a silly plot, given how outlandish the synopsis sounded. But after just finishing it, I’m blown away and have to shout its brilliance from the rooftops! Both Hyde and Gackt delivered performances that shattered my heart, and my eyes are still stinging from sobbing through the entire second half. The story pulls you in completely, making you deeply invested in the characters by the end. The vampire theme—something I adore but often goes overboard or derails a story—is woven in so naturally that it feels exotic yet organic, never forced or out of place. At first, I rated it a 9/10… until I stopped to ask myself why I was holding back that final point. I couldn’t find a reason.

This film is truly outstanding. If you get the opportunity to watch it, don’t hesitate—run to see it. While it bears little resemblance to the 1932 original, Al Pacino delivers a phenomenal performance as Tony Montana, making the role entirely his own.  

Pacino has a unique ability to deliver any line with such intensity and charisma that it simply captivates. If you enjoyed the sharp, gritty dialogue in *Pulp Fiction* (assuming you’ve seen it), then *Scarface* offers another masterclass in how an actor can wield profanity with raw power—it’s downright mesmerizing.  

Though the movie is packed with relentless action and moves at a breakneck pace, jumping through time without strict adherence to real-time chronology, it remains remarkably easy to follow. That said, you’ll need to stay fully engaged to catch every detail. Personally, I find that the three-hour runtime flies by effortlessly—it’s just that compelling.  

This is one of those rare films where the acting and direction are so flawless that you completely forget it was made in...

By sheer chance, I discovered Act-I over a decade ago—though the tape's cover didn’t even hint at what was inside. I was amazed. Intimidated. Shocked. Eventually, I forgot about it until, nearly ten years later, the memory resurfaced. I tracked down and bought both acts, and they surpassed my first impression.  

My only gripe is with the Tank Police’s constant insistence that they’re at war with crime, justifying their tanks and heavy firepower. Yet, they never seem to face much real resistance—either they’re struggling off-screen, or it’s all a farce, since they mostly appear relaxed. If their “war” is propaganda, the show never makes that clear.  

I doubt the original Japanese version could match the Americanized one’s charm, though some story depth was inevitably lost in translation. Still, it’s easy to overlook.

Chris Rock takes the lead in this fresh take on Warren Beatty’s *Heaven Can Wait* (which itself was a reimagining of the 1941 classic *Here Comes Mr. Jordan*). The comedy follows a man who meets an untimely end before fulfilling his aspirations, only to embark on wild misadventures in a borrowed body. While Beatty’s version centered on a backup quarterback for the Los Angeles Rams, Rock puts a modern spin on the story, portraying a struggling—and painfully unfunny—stand-up comic.  

Watching the usually razor-sharp Rock play a terrible comedian is pure comedy gold, akin to seeing Tom Hanks awkwardly flounder as a bad actor. His character, Lance Barton, fantasizes about headlining Harlem’s iconic Apollo Theater—outside of amateur night, of course. But every time he steps onstage, his cringe-worthy jokes and painful delivery earn him thunderous boos, eventually branding him with the humiliating nickname “Booie.” In short, Lance is the polar opposite of the real Chris Rock.  

When he isn’t bombing onstage, Lance works as a bike messenger, pedaling through the city while rehearsing new material—until **BAM!** A truck sends him flying. Maybe he was yanked from his body a split-second too soon...

I received the original *Bill and Ted* movie as a Christmas gift and immediately bought the sequel when I spotted it in a store. This one was just as hilarious as the first, though with an even weirder plot. I loved their twisted version of a personal hell and the ridiculous showdown against Death himself—especially how they challenged him to silly games like *Clue*. The only tweak I’d make is keeping Station and Death out of the band, but otherwise, it was fantastic!

Whoever greenlit this film must have been out of their mind—or seriously pulling a prank.  

First off, there's no way this was actually made in 1993. The fashion and soundtrack scream 1980s, so my best guess is that this disaster sat collecting dust for years before some deranged distributor dug it up and unleashed it on an unsuspecting world.  

There’s something resembling a plot—barely. A socially inept weirdo crosses paths with a random bearded man who claims that meditating while singing his favorite song will let him shapeshift into anyone he wants. And what’s this loner’s favorite song? *London Bridge Is Falling Down.* Why? Because he’s an utter moron. We’re barely a minute in, and the film has already achieved staggering levels of idiocy. And it only gets dumber.  

Our "hero" is the notorious nose-picker—at least, I assume so, given the two (!) scenes dedicated to him excavating his nostrils. Hence the title, I guess. His grand plan? Transforming into a woman to infiltrate some girl’s life. Because of course.

Powell and Pressburger have crafted a mesmerizing film that left me eager to dive deeper into their filmography. It delves into the blurred line between perception and reality, exploring how challenging it can be to tell them apart. The cinematography is stunning, the performances are superb—though David Niven's portrayal of a 27-year-old stretches believability. A delightful surprise was spotting a young Richard Attenborough. Thought-provoking long after the credits rolled, this movie lingered in my mind.

If you're looking to grasp the fundamentals of quantum mechanics, save your money by picking up a secondhand textbook instead of watching this film. I’m honestly concerned my ticket purchase might be funding a bulk Kool-Aid order bound for Guyana.  

The directors seemed to throw a handful of vague ideas at the wall without fully committing to any: 1) Science can decode all human behavior, proving life is predetermined; 2) Science falls short of explaining our choices, suggesting free will exists; 3) Science is, like, totally rad, man; 4) We're basically divine; 5) Reality is just a mental construct; 6) Sarah Norman set a high bar; and 7) Here, toss this little paper on your tongue and brace for a wild trip.

This is the type of film that unsettles me the most. Cocky and reckless, it delivers such a shallow, offensive portrayal of Colombia’s conflict that it borders on disrespect toward its people. The acting is painfully bad—Grisales' cringe-inducing nude scene, Bejarano’s wooden performance, Fanny Mickey’s bizarre, Burton-esque presence, and Díaz’s valiant but doomed attempt to salvage a flat, poorly written role defined solely by a mustache. Then there’s the gratuitous finale, an over-the-top bloodbath so laughably tacky even Ed Wood would wince. Every aspect fails miserably—cinematography, art direction, costumes, makeup, editing, and especially direction. Jorge Alí Triana has never been a great filmmaker, but at least his past work had some decency. There’s nothing redeeming about this embarrassing waste of resources, except maybe as a cautionary tale for Colombian cinema on the importance of honesty, integrity, and responsibility—lessons this cynical disaster sorely ignores.

Let me share how I discovered this film. It was the winter of 1990 in Alaska, when an Australian friend was crashing at my tiny apartment with my girlfriend. Alaskan winters can be harsh, trapping people indoors with nothing but liquor and whatever's on TV. I stumbled upon this movie buried in a snowbank outside a thrift store—immediately recognizing it as a rare find.  

This might just be the greatest terrible movie ever made. For two straight weeks, we drowned ourselves in drinks and played it on repeat. We loved it so much that we’d flip the TV sideways or upside down just to spice things up. A genuine masterpiece. The laughs never stop, and the memories stick with you forever. If you ever spot this movie in a rental shop—take it. No regrets.

I expected *The Sentinel* to be just another average film, but it turned out to be a pleasant surprise. While it’s not a masterpiece, the movie is highly entertaining, with expertly executed action sequences. It has the same gripping energy as TV shows like *24* or *Alias*, and it also brought to mind Wolfgang Petersen’s thriller *In the Line of Fire*. Don’t go in hoping for one of the most groundbreaking thrillers ever—you’ll likely be let down. But if you keep your expectations modest, *The Sentinel* delivers solid enjoyment.  

**Rating: 7/10**

You were hoping to watch *THE Gamers* by Dead Gentlemen Productions—this isn't that movie. Don't waste your time; there's no humor here.  

The positive reviews feel suspiciously fake, like poorly masked attempts by the filmmakers to drum up artificial hype.  

This isn't a clever mockumentary. Comparing it to *Spinal Tap* or Christopher Guest’s work is downright laughable.  

The film is so bitter and spiteful that anyone with real familiarity of its subject matter would struggle to find it funny. Self-deprecation works, but this? You’d have to despise yourself to find amusement in its mockery.  

The offense isn’t in bold satire or daring taboo-breaking—it’s in the relentless, dreary shallowness of every joke. A complete misfire.

This film ranks among my absolute favorites. The clever, punchy dialogue packed with witty wordplay, the brilliant performances from the cast, and the refreshingly unique storyline make it unforgettable.  

Don't just take my recommendation—experience it for yourself and savor every moment.

**The House of Spirits** boasts a stellar cast capable of lighting up the heavens, yet the final product leaves much to be desired. The film’s intentions are undeniably noble—advocating liberal democracy over violent fascism, openness over racism, and so on—messages few would dispute. The problem lies in their execution, delivered with all the subtlety of a sledgehammer.  

What unfolds is a simplistic battle between paragons of virtue and irredeemable villains, lacking nuance or depth. The tension feels as predictable as a poorly staged wrestling match, robbing the story of real stakes.  

Jeremy Irons brings complexity to his role as the conflicted patriarch, while Meryl Streep shines as his talented wife, and Glenn Close captivates as her sister-in-law. When the film lingers on these performances, it thrives, offering moments of genuine engagement. But **The House of Spirits** drowns in a sea of subplots, introducing characters only to discard them like targets in a shooting gallery. With no time to invest in them, their fates leave us indifferent—and worse, bored.  

Director and screenwriter Bille August, adapting Isabel Allende’s novel, struggles to balance the sprawling narrative, leaving the film feeling overstuffed and underdeveloped.

This first regularly filmed *Columbo* movie episode actually aired second, following Steven Spielberg’s *Murder by the Book*. Yet, it remains one of the series' strongest entries!  

Bernard L. Kowalski was a brilliantly creative director—so much so that he was invited back to helm three more *Columbo* films. His work here is packed with inventive shot compositions, and the entire production radiates style, passion, and meticulous attention to detail. Every frame serves a purpose, elevating this well above the average made-for-TV movie. Without a doubt, it's one of the best-directed installments in the series.  

What makes this *Columbo* entry stand out? For one, the murder itself is more accidental than premeditated—an impulsive act that leaves the killer no time to craft a foolproof plan. Instead of meticulously covering his tracks in advance, he scrambles to erase evidence and dispose of the body. This time, the story frames the culprit not just as the perpetrator but as someone desperately trying to clean up his mess after the fact.

Sandra Bernhard is a true original – one of the wittiest, most razor-sharp women alive. She first made waves in the 1970s as a stand-up comic, but her breakthrough arrived in 1983 with Scorsese’s overlooked gem *The King of Comedy*, where she shared the screen with Robert De Niro and Jerry Lewis. While her film career never quite skyrocketed, she starred in a handful of delightfully offbeat movies like *Dallas Doll* (1994) and *Dinner Rush* (2000). Still, her most brilliant performances have always been the ones she crafted for herself.  

The crowning achievement of her career is *Without You I’m Nothing*, a bold, dazzling adaptation of her hit off-Broadway show that catapulted her to stardom—and briefly made her Madonna’s closest confidante. Across ten brilliantly staged vignettes, Bernhard transforms from Nina Simone to Diana Ross, spinning tales of her upbringing, Andy Warhol, and San Francisco while delivering unforgettable covers of songs by Burt Bacharach, Prince, and Sylvester. Director John Boskovich captures her in a 90-minute tour de force—equal parts seductive, hilarious, and utterly singular. For any Bernhard devotee, this film is essential—an electrifying tribute to her striking (if unconventional) beauty and her wildly original genius.

Snagged this for just 50 cents at the flea market—what a steal!  

At first, it grabbed my attention for about 15 minutes, but then it started feeling repetitive and boring.  

There’s something cool about watching Mick and the band in their prime, though I wish the heavy overdubbing didn’t drown out their real voices and music.  

The sketches haven’t aged well—they’re politically outdated, painfully naive, and come off like a clumsy, psychedelic knockoff of Monty Python. Honestly, I found myself more interested in the late-'60s British scenery than the actual skits.  

This film is a solid reminder of how fast times shift—what once seemed cutting-edge now comes across as downright goofy. The soundtrack’s great, but after this DVD, I’ve heard that song enough for a lifetime.

I just bought the restored edition of a film I loved as a child, and it made for a strangely fascinating afternoon of viewing. *Bedknobs and Broomsticks* feels more coherent in its complete form—the deleted scenes (especially those featuring Roddy McDowall) tie the story together much better.  

That said, the remastering is a bit odd. It’s clear the original audio for these scenes was either lost or unusable, so Disney had the bright idea to record new dialogue. Not a bad solution—except many of the original cast weren’t available (for various reasons), and the result feels cheap. The lip-syncing is off in places, and David Tomlinson’s lines are dubbed by someone who sounds nothing like him (there’s even a slight German accent in there, I think).  

Still, hearing the complete versions of all the songs is a treat (though *Step in the Right Direction* is still missing), and the magic of the film holds up. And good luck keeping a straight face when little Paul stares so sweetly at Angela Lansbury and coos.

This film clearly wasn’t made with me in mind. As a man close to 50, I only recently wandered into the realm of independent cinema—completely by accident. It started late one night when I caught a movie called *Clerks* on TV. Right away, two things stood out: it was 1) technically rough around the edges, and 2) brilliantly written. After reading an interview with this film’s director in the local paper, where he cited *Clerks* as an influence, my interest grew. Then he mentioned *The Station Agent*—a movie I’d watched on DVD just a week earlier—as his main inspiration, and I knew I had to see it.  

The result reminded me of *Clerks* in one key way: both films rise above their technical flaws through sharp, compelling writing. But that’s where the similarities end. *Clerks* follows a day in the life of a man stuck in emptiness, too afraid to confront his own reality, while *Less Like Me* centers on a man who fills every moment with relentless motion—always running, never pausing.

I walked into this film expecting a dark drama about a man with supernatural abilities, transformed into a monster by society. What I got was completely different—but in the best way. My friend and I both found it surprisingly romantic (helped by the male lead’s undeniable charm), with plenty of plot twists, action, and even humor (the audience couldn’t stop laughing when it took them until the third act to learn each other’s names). It kept us hooked from start to finish. In short: not what I anticipated, but a delightful surprise. I’ll absolutely be buying the DVD when it releases.

passes for everyone), but the lack of fresh ideas, wit, and the spark that once made these iconic characters so engaging.  

After languishing in development for years, this much-anticipated TV reunion of two of television’s most cherished sitcom characters began on a sour note—and only grew worse from there. Mary Richards (Mary Tyler Moore) and her dear friend Rhoda Morgenstern (Valerie Harper) reconnect in New York after years apart, but their long-awaited catch-up reveals little of substance. Neither has anything particularly compelling to share—hardly enough to justify a reunion special, let alone a full film. Instead, the script leans on tired, recycled storylines (many fixated on older women navigating the workforce), utterly missing the sharp wit and clever charm that made the original series a classic. The supporting cast fades into obscurity, the humor falls flat, and the once-electric dynamic between Moore and Harper is nowhere to be found. Moore reportedly delayed this project for years, holding out for "the perfect script." If this was the best of the bunch, one can only imagine how dismal the rejected drafts must have been. The failure doesn’t lie in the characters’ age—time spares no one—but in the absence of creativity, clever writing, and the magic that once brought them to life.

This might just be the most hilarious film I’ve ever watched. Robert Harling’s script is practically flawless—just take a look at the "quotes" section, though honestly, you should rent the DVD instead, because the performances bring those lines to life in a way words alone can’t.  

Sally Field delivers a wildly over-the-top comedic turn unlike anything she’s done before, while Kevin Kline makes hilarity look effortless. Robert Downey, Jr. is, as usual, outstanding, and Kathy Najimy steals her brief scenes as the frazzled costume designer. I never considered myself an Elisabeth Shue fan, but she shines here as the only grounded character amid the exaggerated personalities on the set of *The Sun Also Sets*—that faint rumbling you hear is either Hemingway spinning in his grave or laughing hysterically.  

Five stars. Hilarious from start to finish.

Here’s your rewritten version:  

After *The Baron*, Monty Berman and Dennis Spooner created this imaginative series about a trio of superhuman spies—predating *The Six Million Dollar Man*. It was a childhood favorite of mine, and even now, I still love revisiting it. Stuart Damon and William Gaunt shared fantastic on-screen chemistry as Craig Stirling and Richard Barrett, while the effortlessly glamorous Alexandra Bastedo played Sharron Macready with perfect poise. The late Anthony Nicholls brought a beautifully gruff presence to his role as Tremayne. The standout episodes were penned by Tony Williamson, Terry Nation, and Brian Clemens, though Spooner’s own *The Interrogation* held its own against *The Prisoner*. It’s a shame the show never got a second season—so many possibilities remained unexplored. Would Craig and Richard have vied for Sharron’s attention? What if Tremayne had discovered the Champions’ true powers? Did they have other abilities beyond what we saw? Sadly, we’ll never know.

This film presents a peculiar love story that stands out in its own way. While it may not leave a lasting impression, Nicole Kidman shines in her role, single-handedly carrying the film—most of the cast fades into the background, though Ben Chaplin delivers a solid performance. The setting, with its scenes of St Albans and Hemel Hempstead town centre, authentically captures the charm of Hertfordshire life.  

At first glance, it feels like an episode of the beloved British TV series *Heartbeat*, but it unexpectedly shifts into a raw, fast-paced gangster escape thriller. Though nothing groundbreaking happens in this modest, small-scale film, it offers pleasant weekend entertainment. If you’re drawn to lonely thirty-something heroes, you might even find something relatable in the protagonist’s journey. A worthwhile watch.

We all face moments when we need to prove ourselves again—and that’s exactly what Jack Dundee (Robin Williams), the humiliated small-town resident in *The Best of Times*, sets out to do. Fresh off his energetic radio antics in *Good Morning, Vietnam*, Williams trades the mic for a football helmet, determined to rewrite history by replaying the infamous game that cost his high school a championship. But his former teammate, Reno Hightower (Kurt Russell), isn’t exactly eager to relive the past.  

Admittedly, this isn’t either actor’s strongest film, but Williams and Russell make a surprisingly great comedic duo. And if the quirky character names alone don’t make you laugh, the banter between them will. Give it a watch—you might be pleasantly surprised.
Steer clear of this film—it's hands down the worst I've ever watched. Even bad movies usually have some merit, but this one offers absolutely nothing. A complete waste of time!

That summer unleashed other cinematic abominations like *Snakes on a Plane* and *The Da Vinci Code*, so calling this out takes some nerve. But I’ll say it anyway: *Superman Returns*, much like *King Kong* six months earlier, is bloated, self-indulgent, and drowning in CGI. Honestly, it’s exhausting.  

Richard Donner understood the power of restraint in his two films, grounding the spectacle with tangible effects that felt real. Bryan Singer, on the other hand, bombards us with relentless CGI, constantly yanking us out of the story and reminding us we’re watching a desperate, overpriced spectacle—one that foolishly believes throwing $250 million at flashy visuals will make up for its lack of substance. By now, CGI has shown us everything it can do, yet here it adds nothing but hollow spectacle. There’s no depth, no immersion. When a film is 95% empty digital noise, you do the math.  

I’ve seen countless fanboy reviews gushing about the film’s supposed "soul" or emotional weight—

I was barely thirteen when I first discovered this series, and now, more than thirty years later, I’m revisiting it on DVD. The opening credits alone left an indelible impression on me—they shaped how I see the world and its people. My parents watched it with me back then, and we always discussed each episode afterward. The show ignited my passion for history, and I even earned top marks in my school exams because of it.  

Sir Laurence Olivier’s narration is flawless—timeless in its power. Watching it, you sense that those who lived through the war would recognize it as their own story. I could never tire of revisiting this masterpiece. It makes me wonder if a similar series about the Cold War could ever be made—though finding someone to match Sir Laurence’s gravitas seems impossible.  

Don’t hesitate—buy it now.

Mario Lewis from the Competitive Enterprise Institute has produced a thorough 120-page rebuttal dismantling the deceptive film—aptly deserving the label *A Convenient Lie*. His detailed critique, titled *A Skeptic's Guide to An Inconvenient Truth*, is available at [www.cei.org](http://www.cei.org), with a condensed 10-page summary at [www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf](http://www.cei.org/pdf/5539.pdf).  

After reviewing this meticulous takedown, it becomes clear that so-called "global warming" holds as much legitimacy and threat as the Y2K hysteria of 1999—another alarmist narrative championed by Gore, much like his endorsement of the scientifically baseless film *The Day After Tomorrow*. That movie, ironically, drew inspiration from a book by Whitley Strieber, a self-proclaimed UFO abductee.  

Mario Lewis exposes Gore’s film and the broader "global warming" fraud with the same precision that James Randi applies to debunking psychics, Philip Klass to UFO myths, and Gerald Posner to dismantling JFK conspiracy absurdities. The truth, meticulously laid out, speaks for itself.

Scott Henderson (played by Alan Curtis) is wrongly convicted of murdering his cheating wife. On the night of her death, he was with an enigmatic woman who wouldn’t reveal her identity. When the police investigate his alibi, witnesses only recall seeing him alone. Sentenced to death, his devoted secretary (Ella Raines), who harbors feelings for him, takes it upon herself to track down the real killer.  

Produced as a low-budget B-movie by Universal, the film features a cast of character actors and a fading star, Franchot Tone. Despite its modest resources, it stands as one of the finest film noirs of the 1940s. Directed masterfully by Curt Siodmak, the sharp script is adapted from William Irish’s gripping novel (a pseudonym for Cornell Woolrich). The film is briskly paced, visually striking, and includes an electrifying jam session between Raines and Elisha Cook Jr., charged with raw, sensual intensity—surprisingly untouched by censors.  

A handful of flaws keep it from perfection, most notably Tone’s lackluster performance.

The critics who praised this film clearly haven’t seen enough cinema.  

A hopeless protagonist spends the runtime documenting his dysfunctional family with a camera. The film is packed with grating characters and even features an awkward "teabagging" scene—that should tell you everything.  

Save yourself the time. No matter how much you hope it improves, it never does.

I was so looking forward to this movie – I genuinely hoped Australia had finally produced a great film. Unfortunately, I was mistaken.  

This has to be the weakest slasher movie I’ve ever seen. Poor Molly Ringwald—traveling all the way to Australia just to be part of such a disaster.  

The acting was cringe-worthy (particularly the Australian actor butchering an American accent), and the storyline wasn’t any better.  

From the start, I thought the title was ridiculous—sounding like a cheap knockoff of *Stab* from *Scream 2*—but I was willing to overlook it if the film delivered.  

**MAJOR SPOILER ALERT!**  

The worst part? The ending. Instead of a clever killer reveal, we get... a non-human antagonist, turning what could’ve been a gritty slasher into a ridiculous horror mess.  

Save your time—this movie is a letdown.

Among the three remakes of this story, I enjoy each one. I own all three on VHS and also have a DVD copy of this version. The subtle differences in the scripts keep all three engaging and worth revisiting. Can any other film boast three remakes, each featuring such stellar casts? While the lead actors here are outstanding, the supporting cast shines just as brightly—William Tracy as Pepi is a particular favorite of mine. He stole every scene, prompting me to seek out his other films, though many remain hard to find. Like others have said, don’t hesitate—add this one to your collection.

With a reported $20 million budget, I can't help but wonder where all that money disappeared to. The CGI effects in this train wreck are so laughably awful they look like they were slapped together by an untrained chimp. Honestly, the machines and Martians would've fit right into a mid-90s PlayStation 1 game—though that might actually have been an improvement.  

What baffles me is how Pendragon Films botched this so spectacularly. For the same budget, they could've crafted something worthwhile with practical effects—like the model-and-miniature techniques George Lucas mastered in the late '70s and early '80s. And maybe, just maybe, they could’ve cast actors who didn’t look like they were being held hostage on set.  

This isn’t just bad; it’s a strong contender for the absolute worst movie ever made. I’d rather endure *Ishtar* on a 24-hour loop than subject myself to this mess again. At least films like *Plan 9* or *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians* have a certain so-bad-it’s-good charm. This? It’s just plain painful.

Eddie Murphy's *Delirious* is his groundbreaking first stand-up special, released in 1983. At the time, Murphy was already a rising star from films like *48 Hrs.* and *Trading Places*, as well as his legendary run on *Saturday Night Live*. He went on to film two iconic stand-up specials—*Delirious* and *Raw*. While *Raw* remains my personal favorite due to its edgier humor, *Delirious* is equally hilarious, featuring Murphy’s sharp takes on his childhood, along with playful jabs at celebrities like Mr. T and Michael Jackson. A must-watch for any stand-up comedy fan.  

*(Note: Though officially Rated NR, it would likely earn an R for pervasive strong language and crude sexual humor. Québec's rating: 16+—though 13+ would be more fitting. Canadian Home Video Rating: 18A.)*

I settled in to watch a documentary on Puerto Rico, but it turned out to focus on Nuyoricans instead. Whenever I visit Puerto Rico, I don’t encounter the 50% living in poverty—when I do see people struggling, they’re often Haitians, Dominicans, or Cubans who’ve recently arrived. Spanglish? It doesn’t exist. You either speak Spanish or you don’t... and from what I can tell, you don’t. To me, Pedro Albizu Campos is no MLK—King was a great man, while Campos is only revered by the 1% pushing for independence. To everyone else, he’s as extreme as Osama bin Laden. Those Puerto Ricans advocating for independence are misguided. Just look at Cuba, Haiti, the Dominican Republic, the Bahamas, all of South and Central America, and Mexico—independence has been a disaster for them. This film wasn’t about Puerto Rico; it was about Nuyoricans and their struggles.  

To the viewer who complained about a lack of African representation—this was supposed to be about Puerto Rico, not Africa. Maybe Denzel will cover that next.

I adore early Technicolor films—who knew 1940s fashion wasn’t entirely monochrome?  

Margaret Rutherford utterly steals the show. Her so-called "eccentric" wardrobe is surprisingly stylish, and yes, that hourglass silhouette is stunning. But I think she was given too much free rein. This character was likely honed over countless performances, yet it seems nobody ever advised her, "If it gets an easy laugh, cut it." She leans too far into exaggerated antics when her role calls for grounded pragmatism. The humor in Madame Arcati lies in the contradiction—while mediums were typically depicted as ethereal women in flowing robes, Arcati carries herself like a no-nonsense former schoolmistress ("We’ll really put our backs into it!"). Sadly, the contrast between her brisk, ordinary demeanor and her outlandish spiritualism isn’t fully explored.  

Just because the cast is mostly British (aside from Cummings), American critics trot out the same tired clichés—"Brit," "stiff upper lip," and all that. Enough already! The three leads are constantly losing their tempers and tossing around cheeky innuendo (*"Did he make love to you?" "Yes, but very discreetly—he was in the cavalry!"*).

what makes *The League of Gentlemen* so extraordinary—a phenomenal blend of dark, twisted humor that stands head and shoulders above its forgettable successors like *Little Britain*. This show wasn’t just comedy; it was a masterclass in originality during a time when British comedy needed a jolt of fresh, unsettling brilliance.  

Before *The League of Gentlemen*, nothing quite like it had existed. What seemed like a simple sketch show at first glance quickly revealed itself to be a richly layered, macabre, and riotously funny world teeming with unforgettable characters. Unlike other sketch shows that relied on repetitive, interchangeable segments, this one wove continuous narratives for its bizarre residents. Each appearance by a character brought something unexpected, ensuring no two encounters ever felt the same.  

Over three series and a Christmas special, the eerie town of Royston Vasey grew into a grotesque yet uproarious microcosm. The show’s genius lay in its ability to balance the absurd with the unsettling, crafting a comedy unlike any other—one that remains criminally underrated yet undeniably legendary.

As many have pointed out, the film completely falls apart in its final half-hour. Before that, it struggles with predictable storytelling and a painfully flat performance by Kate Capshaw—who never seems to grasp her character, dragging down every scene she’s in. While Connery and Fishburne deliver solid performances, most scenes feel artificially constructed for cheap thrills rather than emotional honesty, leaving the whole film feeling hollow. And then there’s the ending—which is just plain baffling.  

It’s clear the filmmakers realized they had a mess on their hands, so they tried desperately to compensate by drowning everything in an over-the-top, melodramatic score. Every minor moment gets swamped by deafening orchestral swells, turning what should be suspense into outright comedy. If you're looking for a masterclass in terrible filmmaking, this one’s a prime example—otherwise, steer clear.

Ettore Scola stands among Italy’s greatest filmmakers. One summer evening, my parents and I watched *C'eravamo tanto amati*—we liked it, though not as much as *A Special Day*, which we adored. I think Scola is often overlooked, perhaps because his later works didn’t quite meet expectations.  

So last night, my mother and I settled on the couch to revisit this masterpiece. The writing, direction, cinematography, score, and production design were subtle and precise, but what truly captivated me was the electric chemistry between Loren and Mastroianni. Both deliver outstanding performances as Antonietta and Gabriele.  

Antonietta, a housewife married to a zealous Fascist, already has six children—yet her husband pressures her for another to claim a prize for large families. Gabriele, on the other hand, is an anti-Fascist. Their paths cross on that singular day in 1938 when Hitler visited Mussolini in Rome. I won’t say more—seek out this film and experience it for yourself!

captures her charm in a uniquely captivating way—blending innocence with a knowing sophistication. One admirer described the experience as "that electrifying mix of pleasure and guilt, like a reckless youthful dalliance teetering between fascination and fear, or the peak of clashing emotions." This was their reaction to *LOVE AT THE TOP*, the misleadingly retitled version of Michel Deville's stylish *LE MOUTON ENRAGÉ*.  

Vincent Canby offered a different perspective in *The New York Times* following the film's 1974 premiere: "*LOVE AT THE TOP*, which opened yesterday at the 68th Street Playhouse, is a 1973 French comedy that faintly echoes 1950s English tales about ruthlessly ambitious young men—driven and consumed by their own hunger for success." However, he noted one crucial distinction: unlike those British stories, *LOVE AT THE TOP* sidesteps any obsession with the English class system... (January 27, 1975)  

While individual opinions vary, time has been the fairest judge. Decades later, what remains undeniable is how rare a film like *LE MOUTON ENRAGÉ* truly is—where decadence feels oddly pure, affairs pulse with youthful fervor, and emotions are wielded like cunning instruments.  

For devotees of Romy Schneider, there’s little need to explain why this performance stands apart...

A mediocre TV movie that aired on TBS, following Antonio and Janine as they hunt down a dangerous computer virus—and not much else. Fun fact for trivia fans: it premiered the same weekend the real-life "Melissa" virus began wreaking havoc in inboxes worldwide.

Some films are so hilariously bad they become enjoyable. This wasn’t one of them. Claiming to be "based on a true story," it was about as authentic as Pinocchio’s wooden nose. The acting was cringe-worthy, the directing was sloppy, and the pacing raced along as if the director had a dinner reservation to catch.  

Melissa Joan Hart never convinced me of her acting chops, though to be fair, she mostly starred in bargain-bin productions. As usual, she butchered her role—overacting, rushing her lines as though velocity equaled intensity, and making it painfully obvious she was performing for a camera rather than inhabiting a character. She single-handedly dragged down whatever feeble credibility the film might have scraped together.  

The one redeeming moment? Watching her downfall in the finale—though even that failed to deliver any real satisfaction.

This film is an utter disaster—the epitome of terrible filmmaking. It holds zero appeal, not even for dedicated B-movie enthusiasts. Avoid at all costs—I insist, do **not** sacrifice a single minute of your life on this abysmal mess. The acting is atrocious, the direction is inept, and the script is downright painful—not a shred of actual entertainment exists here. I picked up the DVD for just $3, and even then, I'd have paid someone to rid me of it. Destroying it wouldn't be enough retribution for the agony it caused. I'm no stranger to campy films—killer dolls, mutated sea creatures—but this? It’s not so bad it’s funny. It’s just pitiful. Pure, unfiltered mediocrity.

I stumbled upon this movie around 1990 on VHS, completely unaware of what awaited me. Many horror fans might have skipped it, mistaking it for just another prison flick—and those who did watch it were dissatisfied because it wasn’t what they expected. These reasons likely explain its low rating, but if you love the genre, disregard that and give it a shot.  

The film excels in every aspect—tight scripting, gripping atmosphere, solid performances, and a hauntingly immersive prison setting.  

A true hidden gem, one I still keep on VHS to this day. Don’t miss it.

*52 Pick-Up* never received the recognition it truly deserved. A multi-layered film with a complex yet coherent plot, it showcases some of the strongest performances from its brilliant cast. Ann-Margret, Roy Scheider, and John Glover are impeccably cast, delivering nuanced and compelling portrayals. Standouts also include Vanity, whose surprising dramatic talent deserved a lasting acting career beyond this role, and Kelly Preston, whose haunting performance lingers long after the credits roll. Fans of hard-hitting action paired with a gritty, intricate narrative will find this film deeply rewarding.

At first, I couldn’t tell whether this was a documentary, propaganda piece, or a dramatic film. Given when it was made, it seemed to blend all three.  

The storyline was fairly predictable, but as it progressed, it offered glimpses of compelling moments. The training sequences and equipment had an air of authenticity that stood out.  

What really pulled me in were the later scenes—they carried a rawness I’ve rarely seen. You could almost feel the tension of the young soldiers, stepping into their perspective. That said, the portrayal of Japanese troops had its limitations—unsurprising, given the era and likely shortage of Japanese actors.  

Beyond the drama, the film serves as a fascinating snapshot of America’s wartime attitude in 1943. One notable moment even throws shade at Japan, referencing past U.S. aid—an interesting layer of historical context.

I rarely criticize films harshly—I usually look for their strengths rather than dwell on flaws—but this one offers almost nothing redeeming. Frankly, if a project turns out this poorly, what was the point in making it?  

Half the film lingers on prolonged shots of Anne’s face as she breathes heavily, underscored with violin music. The rest is plagued by stiff, unconvincing performances. Rupert Penry-Jones delivers his lines with almost no emotion, while Jennifer Higham portrays Anne’s sister with jarringly modern mannerisms. Anne herself is written as timid and self-effacing—fine for an initial character trait, but she never grows, leaving no plausible reason for Captain Wentworth to fall in love with her.  

Worse still, the production utterly fails to capture the period’s authenticity. The blunders are impossible to ignore: characters sprinting out of concerts, kissing publicly in the streets, or wandering hatless (why include such a scene at all? The book’s original moment was among literature’s most romantic).  

In short, this was a dismal adaptation—deeply unsatisfying.

Al Pacino's gripping delivery of the eulogy over the child's coffin deserves every ounce of praise—Shakespeare's Mark Antony himself would pale in comparison!  

Credit for the film's sharp, intelligent dialogue must go to either Paul Schrader or Ken Lipper—whoever crafted these lines deserves recognition. If well-written scripts are your preference, this one won’t disappoint. The narrative unfolds smoothly, holding attention all the way through to the final voice-over.  

Beyond these strengths, the film offers little else worth noting. Even John Cusack, though capable, has taken on more compelling roles. Strangely enough, the story is dominated by its male characters—the women feeling like afterthoughts rather than fully realized figures.

If you're a kid, this is a solid 7—maybe a 6 if you insist on being an adult. This spinoff from *The Lion King* shifts the spotlight to fan-favorite sidekicks Timon and Pumbaa, revisiting the original story through their eyes while revealing how their friendship began. True to Disney’s legacy, direct-to-video sequels and TV series often expand on secondary characters—and while cynics might scoff, younger viewers and die-hard fans won’t mind. Packed with humor, catchy tunes, and enough fresh twists, it manages to stand out as one of the rare sequels that actually holds up.  

The charm lies in its beloved leads, brisk storytelling, and playful nods to the first film, with a few winks thrown in for older audiences. The animation retains its polish, if slightly toned down from the original’s grandeur—but then again, the whole vibe here leans into relaxed, *Hakuna Matata* energy.  

Timon and Pumbaa essentially host a rewatch of the first movie, pausing to crack jokes and riff on scenes like a pair of rowdy theatergoers. Along the way, we learn how Timon—once a misfit on the fringes of his meerkat colony—finally found his place.

This summer has been packed with blockbusters and long-awaited comebacks—some triumphant, others disappointing—leaving me desperate for a film I could simply relax and enjoy.  

If you'd rather skip ahead (don't worry, no spoilers), here's the gist: It’s more mature than *Ella Enchanted* (with some surprisingly violent moments, several deaths, and a bit of blood—definitely not for young kids), but it never veers into forced corniness or overplays its hand. Imagine *The Princess Bride* with a touch more seriousness and magic, and you're on the right track.  

----------------------------------------  

I’m not the most frequent moviegoer—maybe once or twice a month when I’m feeling motivated. But as a dedicated sci-fi and fantasy fan, I’ve grown weary of recycled plots and style-over-substance spectacles. This film? It’s the rare gem that stands apart.  

By late August, after one too many letdowns from hyped releases, I couldn’t even bring myself to watch *Bourne*.

Michael Stearns portrays Mike, a sexually repressed man with a warped sense of morality regarding intimacy. While he freely objectifies nude dancers, the moment women engage in actual sexual activity, he snaps. To him, the act of sex strips women of their supposed "innocence" and "beauty." Driven by this twisted mindset, he prowls the Hollywood Hills, spying on couples through a rifle scope before mercilessly gunning down the men.  

The film's main purpose seems to be an endless parade of sexual encounters, with the plot feeling like a flimsy excuse to string them together. This will likely satisfy heterosexual male viewers, as it bombards them with prolonged nude scenes and explicit acts—many of the women are undeniably attractive without clothing. However, the voyeuristic angle adds a deeply unsettling layer, with Mike obsessively watching through his rifle scope for extended periods before killing. The intrusive, moody soundtrack only amplifies the discomfort, reinforcing his disturbing fixation.

This film is a chaotic 80-minute mess with no real storyline—just a parade of obnoxious characters alternating between heavy drinking and painfully unfunny jokes. The soundtrack is grating, the humor falls flat, and the female roles are reduced to either hypersexualized fools or awkward outcasts. It feels like it was penned by a teenage boy who idolizes crude party culture, views women as mere accessories, and dismisses anyone who disagrees as a loser. Despite borrowing a few names and featuring Mr. Levenstein in a minor role, it has zero connection to the original *American Pie* films. The only redeeming quality? Some of the actresses are attractive. Skip this trainwreck—ignore the inflated 5.4 rating, as it’s barely worth a 2 at best.

The film's trailers might display moments of violence or unconventional sexuality, but these fleeting glimpses are merely attention-grabbing snippets. What they do reveal, however, is the film’s core truth:  

It’s about those who endure relentless humiliation in their daily lives, only to wield whatever power they have elsewhere to mercilessly crush others—most often, women at the bottom of this oppressive chain.  

A film like *Hundstage*, which portrays this reality with raw brutality, is undeniably hard to watch. Yet living such a life is infinitely harder.  

Technically, the movie resembles *Short Cuts*—structured as stark, documentary-like vignettes featuring everyday people, utterly unadorned. There’s no glamour, and most unsettling of all, no hope. Its realism is what makes it so unsettling; it forces you to acknowledge that these people exist, in numbers we’d rather ignore while clinging to society’s polished facade.  

Pornography thrives in unseen corners. Domestic violence festers behind closed doors. Dreams are routinely shattered. I’ve known such people—they’re real.  

If you’re looking for a film without...

Bogmeister and others have summarized it perfectly. *Shore Leave* stands as TOS’s first foray into lighthearted sci-fi—a tone they would later master with the beloved classic *The Trouble with Tribbles*. It provided a much-needed break, both for the *Enterprise* crew and the audience, from the high-stakes, galaxy-endangering tension of episodes like *The Corbomite Maneuver*.  

Searching for a peaceful retreat, the *Enterprise* stumbles upon an apparently tranquil M-class planet and dispatches a landing party to investigate. Before long, absurd and surreal events unfold—some appearing dangerous, others just bizarre—creating a strange mix of extreme human emotions. The episode blends whimsical fantasy (McCoy’s journey through the looking glass), psychological tension (Kirk being relentlessly pursued by a figure from his past), and romantic comedy (enough said).  

Compared to later entries in the *Trek* franchise, TOS was notably episodic, making it easy to overlook how many first-season installments leaned into intense, high-stakes drama. Unlike later series writers, the TOS team wasn’t afraid to boldly venture into uncharted storytelling territory—truly going where no TV show had gone before.

Did HeidiJean actually watch this film? A fantastic holiday flick? Far from it. Boring, forgettable, and utterly devoid of creativity or emotion. I kept asking myself who thought Carly Pope could carry this movie—her performance was painfully wooden, with zero presence. Baransky, as always, shined, bringing the only spark of life to this dull affair. Honestly, her participation might have been the sole reason this project got approved. Maybe my standards are too high for a Lifetime movie airing two weeks before Christmas, but with better direction and a more compelling lead—someone who could actually evoke empathy—this could've been a charming little story.

The film opens with a voiceover explaining the setting and introducing the characters—and that’s when I began to lose interest. Given the endless creative tools at a director’s disposal, resorting to a voiceover to spell out the situation feels lazy and uninspired. To me, narration like this is a betrayal of true filmmaking.  

There’s nothing more frustrating than hearing a disembodied voice announce where we are, what date it is, or—worst of all—what the characters are thinking and feeling. A skilled director should convey emotion and thought visually, letting the audience discover these layers rather than being told outright.  

Thankfully, after this disappointing start, the film finds its footing and remains compelling for quite some time. It portrays the lives of a middle-class family with striking realism, each member depicted in meticulous detail. The director has a clear gift for capturing authentic moments—like a father forced to take private calls in the bathroom, a seemingly odd choice that, in reality, mirrors life’s unpredictable demands.

I had no idea a film could be this terrible. The description made it sound so promising, but with a cast of 20 people, you'd think at least one could act. My wife gave up after 20 minutes and went to bed—clearly the smarter choice.

The movie excels in its storytelling, seamlessly blending flashbacks of childhood and the experience of growing up with an eccentric father alongside the darker threads of serial murder. This gripping combination ensures the audience remains captivated throughout. The core plot—rich in both substance and intrigue—is inherently engaging. Director Bill Paxton maximizes its potential, crafting a narrative that feels fully realized and compelling.  

From start to finish, the film maintains a heightened sense of anticipation, keeping viewers guessing about its direction. The creativity driving the story is exceptional, making it one of those rare cinematic treasures devoid of dull moments. The pacing is sharp, with each scene transitioning smoothly and purposefully into the next.  

Beyond its entertainment value, the film delves into unsettling truths about human extremes—how individuals, consumed by delusion in the name of faith, can commit unspeakable acts against their own loved ones. It’s a chilling exploration of morality and fanaticism, executed with striking intensity.

I get the humor—it’s just not funny. The show is awful, and the fact that I understand it makes it even worse. The only decent character they ever had was that one hobo in a single episode, but then I watched more and realized how terrible the rest of it is. It’s not clever, not amusing—just painfully unfunny.  

I hate when fans say, "Only smart people get it." If they were so smart, why insult strangers by claiming they just don’t "get" it? That’s like insisting the sky is red without ever looking up. Either way, this is hands down the worst show I’ve ever seen. The jokes are lazy—yes, you can follow them, but they’re still awful. The edgy humor tries too hard, the gross-out gags are cringe, and the acting makes it even worse.  

I don’t know what these so-called "intellectual" fans see in it, but looking down on people you know nothing about? That’s not smart—that’s just obnoxious.

While there are countless new sitcom styles these days, the classic formula—shot indoors with a live audience—still works best. *That 70’s Show* is a perfect example. When it first aired, Kurtwood Smith and Debra Jo Rupp weren’t household names, and neither were the young stars like Topher Grace and Ashton Kutcher (both leaving the show this year to chase other projects). I really wish Topher would stay—after all, the show revolved around his character, Eric, and his tight-knit group of friends. As for Ashton, he’s already this generation’s John Travolta—just picture his high-profile romance with Demi Moore like Travolta's *Eight Is Enough* days with Diana Hyland.  

One of the show’s strengths was its relatively unknown cast—big-name stars can sometimes overshadow the dynamic. I still miss Mo Gaffney as Joanne, Don’s girlfriend, and Lisa Robin Kelly as the original Laurie. Her replacement never quite captured the same magic. Tommy Chong was brilliant as the lovable, perpetually stoned father figure to Steven Hyde, and seeing Tanya Roberts post-*Charlie’s Angels* was a treat.

This gets a 2/10 from me.  

My expectations were completely let down.  

The plot felt rushed and underdeveloped—scenes were too short, making the overall message unclear. While Brenda Song delivered a decent performance, Shin Koyamada struggled with his role. The attempt to blend Western elements was noticeable, but it lacked necessary Chinese cultural touches, especially with the villain, who looked more robotic than traditionally menacing. The biggest issue? The historical inaccuracies scattered throughout.  

Some might argue it's "just a kids' show," lowering the bar. But Disney has done better—take *Mulan*, for example, with its stronger storytelling and execution.  

Ultimately, Disney needs to invest more effort in research and planning. Flashy fight scenes alone don’t make a great film.

Anyone who considers this film dull clearly lacks the patience for thoughtful cinema—perhaps they’d be better suited to mindless action flicks or predictable rom-coms. This movie is utterly engrossing, with not a single wasted moment. Why? Because it thrives on sharp, intelligent dialogue between fully realized characters facing a dire situation, capturing their struggle to endure. Yes—*intelligent dialogue*! That’s the hallmark of nearly every Rohmer film, and it’s precisely why some dismiss his work. They crave spectacle. Fine, let them gorge on endless explosions while the rest of us, with discerning taste, savor films like this.  

Rohmer is often labeled "talky"—and rightly so. But to me, that’s praise, not condemnation. Shakespeare was talky too—when was the last time you saw a wordier play than *Hamlet*? When art grapples with ideas and moral dilemmas, it demands discussion—debate, even. This film embodies that entirely. It pits aristocracy and inherited privilege against the ideals of equality, while probing loyalties strained to the breaking point when old friends are tested.

I hate to be the bearer of bad news, but Brad Sykes is behind two of the most uninspired and formulaic films I’ve ever endured—this being one, and *Camp Blood* the other.  

The performances are painfully bad, the production quality is dismal, and the entire film feels like a dare to see if you could make something worse. Maybe it's an open invitation to flood YouTube with our own half-baked zombie nonsense.  

I only paid £1 for this, but let’s be honest—you can't get back 71 minutes of your life. Even at rock-bottom prices, this one isn’t worth your time. Steer clear.

Ever been told to cherish each moment as if it were your final one? Well, whether it’s your last day or not, I urge you—don’t waste a single second on this film. Nichole Hiltz offers brief visual appeal (though frustratingly underused), while David DeLuise proves he’s better suited for TV spots or pet food ads. With its flimsy, implausible storyline and cringe-worthy writing, *The Art of Revenge* falls painfully short of artistry.

I had the chance to catch an early screening of this film, and here's my take. While I've never been particularly drawn to either Dane Cook or Steve Carell's work, I went in with an open mind—and surprisingly, I really liked it.  

*Dan in Real Life* follows a widowed father of three who visits his family for a weekend getaway. During a quick bookstore trip, he meets someone who seems perfect—only to discover she’s his brother's girlfriend.  

The film is well-crafted, with excellent music, strong visuals, and standout performances (Carell especially shines). My only criticism is that some characters—mainly Cook's—could have used more depth. A deeper exploration of the brothers' relationship would have made Dan’s emotional conflict over his feelings for his brother’s girlfriend even more compelling.  

That said, *Dan in Real Life* is a charming, heartfelt movie—a refreshing change from the usual horror and action releases we’ve seen lately.

This movie has one redeeming quality: Lola Glaudini’s performance—specifically her undeniable screen presence. It’s a shame the film didn’t capitalize on her talent with more depth. There’s a brief, underwhelming attempt at risqué content, but it pales in comparison. As for Armand Assante, age has clearly taken its toll, leaving his performance feeling strained.  

*Consequence* falls short of its potential. The plot had promise, but poor execution drags it down. The cinematography feels amateurish, the direction lacks vision, and the end result is a forgettable thriller with predictable twists and a tired cast. Even Glaudini’s magnetic, albeit campy, portrayal can’t salvage this lackluster effort. In the end, it’s not even entertainingly bad—just flat-out dull.

I read Chris_m_grant's comment from the United States.  

He wrote: *"A fantastic documentary about 1924. This early 20th-century geography of today's Iraq was powerful."*  

I’d like to thank Chris and everyone interested in the Bakhtiari Nomads of Iran, the Zagros Mountains, and the landscapes featured in the film *Grass: A Nation's Battle for Life*. The traditions you saw have lasted for centuries and will continue as long as life endures. I am from this very region in Iran—I am Bakhtiari myself.  

Chris, my apologies for correcting, but the Bakhtiari region of Zardkuh is in Iran, not Iraq, as you mentioned. Iran and Iraq are two distinct countries. Mistaking an Iranian for an Iraqi is almost like confusing an American for a Mexican.  

Thanks,  
Ziba

Seriously, Shaq should stick to basketball—because this movie was a complete disaster, not even fun in a so-bad-it’s-good way. The whole premise is laughable: a genie living in a boom box instead of a lamp? That’s the best they could come up with? Shaq’s character is supposed to mentor a kid played by the equally irritating Francis Capra, but the plot is flimsier than *Waterworld*, and the acting is downright painful. Honestly, anyone who admits to enjoying this mess must have incredibly low standards—or be too embarrassed to admit the truth.

May and her husband visit their children and grandchildren, but the gathering feels strained—there’s a noticeable distance, an absence of the warmth that should bind them together. After dinner, May’s husband complains of feeling unwell, blaming their daughter’s cooking before abruptly insisting they leave. That night, he dies.  

Now a widow, May drifts through grief. Her marriage hadn’t been passionate or particularly fulfilling, but it gave her purpose. For years, she had someone to care for, even as her own needs faded into the background. Without him, she feels unmoored—directionless and numb.  

She moves in with her daughter, Paula, who soon unleashes years of pent-up frustration. Paula accuses May of emotional absence, of never truly giving of herself. May is taken aback, even wounded, but she lacks the will—or perhaps the ability—to mend what’s broken. A hollow “I’m your mother and I love you” feels empty, meaningless. What does that even mean, after all?

I didn’t particularly care for the first *Cube* film. The concept was solid, but the grating performances and unlikable characters always held me back from fully enjoying it. I had little interest in watching the sequel, so when I heard about a third installment—one that served as a prequel to the original—I was curious. Maybe this time, they’d address some of the first film’s flaws and deliver a more compelling group of characters. Turns out, I was wrong.  

*Cube Zero* opens promisingly by introducing us to two men tasked with monitoring and maintaining the deadly, ever-shifting maze of traps inside the Cube. The filmmakers effectively build an air of mystery around the pair’s mundane routine, raising questions about why people are sent there and who truly controls the operation—all left deliberately unanswered for the audience to ponder. The acting wasn’t stellar, but the first half of the film moved along well enough.  

Then, as the story progresses, one of the two "watchers" starts to—

I didn’t catch the start of this movie, and that might explain why I hated it so much. Then again, I’ve spent years studying the fall of the Roman Republic, so the story wasn’t new to me. Though that knowledge might have actually made me dislike it even more.  

This film has more historical mistakes than background actors. It’s so wildly inaccurate that I doubt they even tried to get things right—which, in a way, makes it forgivable. The strange part is how they occasionally strain for accuracy, only to make everything more confusing. Take Antony’s marriage to Octavia, for example—it’s briefly mentioned, then forgotten two scenes later. Why include it at all if it adds nothing to the story and Octavia never even appears? Or the inconsistency with names—sometimes he’s Marcus Antonius, other times he’s Mark Antony.  

But even putting the historical errors aside, the movie could have been entertaining—if not for the lead actress. She carries herself with zero dignity, all hysterics and melodrama, completely unable to control herself. Instead—

Hey there. Paul Raddick here—better known as Panic Attack from WTAF, Channel 29 in Philly. Today, let’s talk about the train wreck of a movie that somehow kickstarted Adam Sandler’s career before disappearing into digital oblivion.  

*Going Overboard* stars a young Sandler as a struggling comic who lands a gig on a cruise ship... and basically bombs. Or so I thought. Along the way, he meets some babes who weirdly adore *History of the World: Part 1* and *Rebound*. Supposedly engaged, they meet a grisly fate at the hands of Sawtooth, the nastiest cannibal to ever hit the screen.  

Let’s be real—Sandler tanked in *Going Overboard*, but thank goodness he bounced back with *Big Daddy*, *Billy Madison*, and Jen Leone’s beloved *50 First Dates*. (Side note: Drew Barrymore was *fire* in that one.) *Spanglish*? Solid gold. *Going Overboard*? Not even close.  

End of story.

This movie immerses you in a family’s extraordinary journey, letting you experience each moment of their struggle. With stunning performances and breathtaking cinematography, it captures raw, heartbreaking truth. The final line lingers with a poignant hope, leaving an unforgettable impact.

Skip this movie—it's not worth your time! The plot is weak, the acting falls flat, and there's nothing redeeming about it. I'd rather do anything else than sit through this mess again. Save yourself the frustration and avoid it altogether.

This movie has been my lifelong favorite. The groundbreaking special effects were award-winning for their time. Every line of dialogue feels fresh in my memory, as if I just heard them yesterday. It's a truly magnificent, enduring adventure. The legendary Miklos Rozsa composed its unforgettable score. Sabu shines as the Thief while Conrad Veidt delivers a masterful villainous performance. My personal copy sits ready for whenever nostalgia calls. Wait—Rex Ingram's genie is bursting free from his bottle!  

*(Note: Rewritten with more vivid language while preserving the enthusiastic tone and key details - film references, nostalgia, and excitement about specific elements. The exclamation at the end maintains the playful energy.)*

**ELVIRA, MISTRESS OF THE DARK (1988)**  

**Directed by:** James Signorelli  

**Starring:** Cassandra Peterson, W. Morgan Sheppard, Daniel Greene, and Edie McClurg  

**Plot:** After quitting her TV show, Elvira (Cassandra Peterson) travels to the conservative Christian town of Fallwell, Massachusetts, to claim her late aunt's inheritance—hoping to fund a lavish Las Vegas act. Instead of striking it rich, she inherits a run-down house, a poodle, and a mysterious magic cookbook. While navigating small-town life, Elvira hustles to earn cash, shakes up the bored local teens, woos a handsome mechanic (Daniel Greene), dodges witch-hunters, and fights to keep the occult recipe book away from her sinister uncle (W. Morgan Sheppard), who plans to use it to bring about the apocalypse.  

**My Thoughts:** Cassandra Peterson and her iconic persona, Elvira, are irresistible—brimming with wit, beauty, and unapologetic camp. As the Mistress of the Dark, she’s equal parts seductive and clueless, delivering morbid humor with a dazzling charm (and yes, those legendary curves). This film showcases her magnetic presence perfectly.  

The fish-out-of-water premise shines as Elvira—decked in her signature vampy wardrobe—clashes with Fallwell’s prim morality.

This poorly shot, clumsily scripted, and awkwardly paced sequel to Joe Dante's 1981 classic is a letdown in every way. *The Howling* remains one of the few truly great werewolf films ever made, only to be tarnished by a string of unbearable follow-ups like this one. If there's any silver lining, *Stirba* is a sequel in name alone—there's zero connection to the original's characters or events.  

The plot centers on a savage Transylvanian werewolf cult, mostly female, led by Stirba—played by Sybil Danning. She morphs from an elderly woman into a voluptuous blonde (with a notably striking bosom) in seconds, growing hairy when aroused. Opposing her is Christopher Lee, looking thoroughly exhausted as Stefan Crosscoe, an occult investigator who journeys to Stirba's domain with an American couple seeking answers about their lost friend.  

If mindless gore and shameless nudity are all you're after, this is your movie. Even minor deaths are lingered on with gruesome detail, featuring exploding eyeballs and the repulsive sight of an impaled dwarf.

Assessing this or similar films from the early sound era requires a different lens than conventional film criticism. At moments, a sense of urgency emerges as silent-era stars grapple with the new medium, anxious about fading into obscurity—a fate that befell some, unlike Rin-Tin-Tin, who adapted effortlessly. In this patchwork of disjointed scenes, a few shine brightly, like John Barrymore’s poignant soliloquy from *Richard II*, a standout worth remembering. Generally, actors with prior stage experience carried themselves with assurance. Despite its unevenness, the film remains engaging and essential for cinephiles, particularly those fascinated by the transition from silent to sound cinema.

I planned to catch this film in theaters, but it was completely sold out. Instead, I ended up watching *Solaris*, which turned out to be the absolute worst movie of 2002.  

Victor Rosa (John Leguizamo), a hardened street dealer, panics after witnessing a child get shot and decides to go straight. He pours all his money into a shady investment with Jack (Peter Sarsgaard). Everything appears smooth—until Jack vanishes with his girlfriend Trish (Denise Richards). This twist comes late in the story, and had the trailers not spoiled it, it might have had some impact. But they did, so it doesn’t.  

Honestly, there’s nothing compelling about this movie—every major moment is revealed in the previews. If you’ve seen even one trailer, you’ve essentially watched the whole thing. Save yourself the rental fee: just replay the trailer in your head and imagine the rest. The only real shock is how painfully bad the soundtrack is.  

Whoever was responsible for the music should—

*The Cobweb* is one of many films that boast strong—even exceptional—performances and moments of brilliance, only to be undone by a convoluted plot and a lack of compelling material to hold the audience’s attention. Richard Widmark stars as a psychiatrist at a mental institution, his life upended by personal struggles and an absurdly overwrought conflict that ultimately feels trivial.  

The premise is ludicrous. The story hinges on the institution’s need for new library drapes—an elderly woman insists on using her own, while the patients rally to create their own designs. This baffling, almost juvenile dispute escalates to the point of endangering lives and tearing families apart. It reads more like a petty squabble among schoolchildren than a gripping dramatic conflict.  

The plot’s sheer implausibility raises so many questions that only someone detached from reality could accept it at face value. That said, the acting is not the issue—Widmark leads a talented supporting cast, all delivering solid performances.

The movie *Kazaam* starred Shaq as a goofy genie with weak rhymes and cringe-worthy lines. The plot? A kid moping over his deadbeat dad. The acting? Terrible. The casting? Questionable. The effects? Cheap. This flop probably barely made $20 at the box office.  

Instead of a magic lamp, this genie lives in a boombox—because why not? The whole thing feels as pointless as a soggy food stamp.  

Bottom line? It’s one of those "so bad it’s funny" trainwrecks. Grab some friends, turn off your brain, and laugh at the absurdity. Just don’t expect anything close to good.

Dr. Alan Feinstone (Corbin Bernsen) and his wife Brooke (Linda Hoffman) appear to have it all—a luxurious Los Angeles home, a thriving dental practice, and a seemingly perfect marriage. But beneath the polished surface, their life is unraveling. On their wedding anniversary morning, Alan learns of Brooke’s affair with Matt (Michael Stadvec), their pool cleaner. The humiliation worsens when he discovers Matt is also involved with Paula Roberts (Lise Simms), their neighbor. As if that weren’t enough, Alan faces relentless pressure from the IRS over a crushing debt.  

The revelations push Alan over the edge. Consumed by rage and paranoia, he becomes obsessed with decay—seeing rot and corruption everywhere, much like the teeth he treats. At his office, he begins violently lashing out at his patients: he brutally harms a young boy, Jody (Brian McLaughlin), sexually assaults April Reign (Christa Sauls) in a twisted hallucination where she becomes Brooke, and sadistically performs unnecessary, agonizing procedures. His descent into madness accelerates as he seeks to "fix" the world the only way he knows how—through pain.

*How the Grinch Stole Christmas* captured my heart immediately, securing its place as my all-time favorite film after just one viewing. Even after watching it eight times, its magic remains as powerful as that first unforgettable experience.  

Screenwriters Jeffrey Price and Peter S. Seaman, known for *Who Framed Roger Rabbit*, deliver a brilliant adaptation, seamlessly translating the beloved tale to the screen. Under Ron Howard's direction, the story comes alive with vibrant energy, while Jim Carrey's electrifying performance as the Grinch dominates every scene.
