Some critics argue the film strays from the spirit of Dr. Seuss’ original story, but as someone familiar with the book, I strongly disagree. The movie not only preserves the core message about the true meaning of Christmas but also deepens the emotional resonance by exploring the Grinch's backstory—revealing how and why he became the bitter outcast we know.  

*MILD SPOILERS* (These likely won’t ruin the film for you, but if you prefer going in completely blind, skip ahead!)

I’d like to praise the series as a remarkable effort. The storyline, though needing some refinement, was quite solid, particularly in Season 1. However, Season 2 leaned more toward a spectacle, losing the original essence that made *Dark Angel* special. Season 1 had a compelling balance—the lighter moments at Jam Pony contrasted with the intense chase of the X-series by Manticore.  

Even now, I'm still eagerly waiting for new seasons. I hope the folks at FOX and the *Dark Angel* production team recognize that many fans are still holding out hope for its return. Even after two years since its cancellation, *Dark Angel* has the potential for a major comeback if handled right—and a visionary like James Cameron should take on this challenge.

*Collusion Course* sinks even lower than your run-of-the-mill "evil white male corporate capitalist" flick. This film is more painful than a nagging toothache.  

Jay Leno can actually act—his surprisingly solid debut in *The Silverbears* proved he could deliver a performance tailored to his role. But here, the movie is so abysmal that even Leno’s insufferable, self-righteous clown feels tolerable next to Morita’s equally grating, holier-than-thou idiot.

A brilliant chemist invents an indestructible fabric that resists stains and never deteriorates, only to find his creation perceived as a menace to entire industries. In this charming Ealing Studios gem, Guinness delivers a masterful performance as the unassuming yet tenacious scientist. Greenwood, with her alluring voice, portrays his romantic counterpart, while Parker adds humor as her flustered father. Thesiger shines as the witty head of the textile trade. Balancing an entertaining narrative with thought-provoking themes about science, commerce, and power, the film is deftly helmed by Mackendrick—who would later craft *The Ladykillers* and the exquisite *Sweet Smell of Success* in the following decade.

How far will some stoop in their desperate attempt to relive past triumphs? *Star Trek: [REDACTED]* is ready to demonstrate.  

If you appreciate what once defined great *Star Trek*, avoid this at all costs.  

The writing is a jumbled mess, the actors’ performances lack conviction, and worst of all, the production design is shockingly amateurish.  

Expect strong leadership? Look elsewhere. Respect for Starfleet’s ideals? Not here. Instead, ensigns stroll around with *spiked hair*, mocking decades of tradition.  

Within moments of the opening credits, we’re treated to an embarrassing attempt at shipboard romance—initiated by "Ensign Spike," no less. From there, it only spirals downward. Uniforms are a disgrace—ill-fitting, mismatched from different eras, with collars sagging absurdly low. Gone is the discipline, the professionalism, the essence of Starfleet.  

The sole redeeming feature? Visual effects—marginally better each season. Though honestly, even that’s a stretch.

If Todd Sheets ever admitted this movie was meant to parody zombie films, I'd bump my rating up to an eight. Picture a film where every line, scene, and even the tiniest acting choices were crafted as one big joke. Honestly, I could vomit alphabet soup, shuffle the leftover letters, and still end up with a better script. Two moments in particular stand out—**SPOILER ALERT!**  

First, there’s the scene where Mike’s dad and another guy casually *walk* down a narrow staircase packed with zombies. They brush right past flailing undead arms, completely unharmed. At the bottom, the ex-marine turns around, quips, *"God, you’re a horny bastard,"* and kills exactly *one* zombie.  

Then, in the military complex, a girl stabs a zombie with a machete and is instantly encircled. The camera lingers for a full forty seconds as zombies hover inches away—doing nothing—before she nonchalantly strolls free. **SPOILER OVER!**  

These scenes *have* to be...

Robert Wuhl leads a film class for students at New York University in Manhattan, blending entertainment with little-known historical truths. His engaging teaching style combines storytelling with tangible examples to challenge common misconceptions—like revealing that Paul Revere wasn’t actually the one who completed his famed midnight ride, a detail altered by Longfellow for poetic effect.  

As a longtime fan of Wuhl’s work—from his stand-up roots to *Arli$$*—I’ve always admired his wit, but here he shines as an educator. This series is both insightful and unexpectedly fun. If you enjoy history reframed with humor, don’t miss it. Every minute spent watching is rewarding.

**A Lackluster Film**  

The story introduces Chrissy, a supposedly "young," moody character who drifts through life with little purpose. Surprisingly, she does almost nothing to drive the plot forward, which made the sudden shift in focus to her relatives feel inevitable—though disappointing, since Chrissy had potential to be a far more engaging protagonist.  

The narrative was formulaic and entirely predictable, raising the question: when will we finally see filmmakers like Campion, Jackson, and Tamahori deliver bold, visually striking stories that inspire, rather than just killing time for two hours?  

On a technical level, the film was poorly shot—bluntly put, it looked terrible.

A mysterious figure—or perhaps something more sinister—is leaving puncture wounds on victims' necks, draining them of blood until they perish. Detective Karl Brettschneider (played by Melvyn Douglas before he moved beyond B-movie horror to bigger roles) is baffled by the string of gruesome killings. As panic grips the village, Karl turns to the brilliant but enigmatic Dr. Otto von Niemann (Lionel Atwill, delivering another compelling mad scientist performance) for insight into the baffling deaths. Complicating matters, Karl fears for the safety of his beloved Ruth (the radiant Fay Wray, reuniting with Atwill after *Doctor X* and *The Mystery of the Wax Museum*), who serves as Niemann’s assistant.  

Dwight Frye shines as the unhinged village eccentric, obsessed with collecting bats and exuding an unsettling aura—making him an obvious target for suspicion as fear spirals out of control. Meanwhile, Maude Eburne provides comic relief as a gullible patient of von Niemann’s, convinced she suffers from every ailment she reads about in medical books. Easily swayed and endlessly paranoid, she becomes an amusing distraction for the doctor, who indulges her endless list of imagined illnesses.

I haven't seen the first movie, and if it's anything like this one, I have zero interest in watching it.  

Watching it just a few hours ago, I can barely recall a single thing about it—which says everything.  

From what little I remember, the plot revolves around a group of intensely irritating people staying in a house with that creepy old woman from *Friday the 13th*, while being stalked by what might as well be a sentient slab of wood.  

Some characters die (no loss), the movie finally ends, and I’m considering legal action against whoever convinced me to buy it—I want reparations for the wasted hours of my life.  

I’d offer you £1 to take it off my hands... except I already "gifted" it to a so-called friend.

...and even then, some may choose never to watch it. To call this a film would be generous—its sole appeal lies with bondage enthusiasts. Devotees of Bettie Page will find no fresh insights here (truly, *none*), nor will they revisit the comfort of beloved or familiar moments.  

Nevermind the painfully dull script, the stiff, amateur-hour performances, the nonexistent direction, the dismal lighting, or any of the other cut-rate production flaws. This reeks of backyard filmmaking at its most amateurish—the sort where you're just relieved they figured out how to turn the camera on. But none of that even scratches the surface of why this mess feels so deeply *off.*  

What truly sinks it is the miscast lead—a heavyset actress whose sole connection to Bettie Page is dark hair and those signature bangs. Beyond an eagerness to endure bondage scenes, she brings nothing to the role. While that might have furthered her career before and after this disaster, it does nothing to salvage this dumpster fire.

I recently rented this film expecting just another clichéd story about a girl out to prove something, but Diane’s journey into boxing felt genuinely personal—she fought because she wanted to, not just to make a statement. Honestly, I was impressed. Solid 8/10—that’s how much I enjoyed it. And let’s be real, any movie with Michelle Rodriguez is worth watching, even if she’s only been in a handful.

This is a prime example of a growing issue in modern films. Why are background noise and soundtracks overwhelmingly louder than the dialogue? What’s the logic behind that? This movie isn’t an exception—most films today suffer from the same problem. For two years, I thought it might just be my TV acting up, but even with a new one, the issue persists. It was even more frustrating in this film because, at least in the English version, the female lead constantly mumbles. I kept wishing Jean Reno would cut in with, "Excuse me, could you speak up or clear your throat?" If you’re watching the DVD and know even basic French, I’d recommend switching to the original French audio with subtitles.  

I’m giving it a 4 because Reno was brilliant in *Leon*. Some people praise the scenery, but having seen it on TV and lived in the Rockies myself, I wasn’t overly impressed—just "meh."

The movie opens at a leisurely pace, introducing Wallace Napalm—a quiet employee at a photo-service drop-off counter. His wife, confined to their home with an ankle monitor due to an arson conviction, adds to his subdued existence. Wallace himself is a dedicated volunteer firefighter, taking his role with solemn seriousness.  

Just as the monotony of Wallace’s routine settles in, disruption arrives in the form of a traveling carnival. Among its performers is Wilder Napalm, Wallace’s estranged brother—a clown with a startling secret.  

Both brothers share an extraordinary and dangerous gift: pyrokinetic abilities, allowing them to summon flames with their minds. Wallace conceals his power, living cautiously, while Wilder flaunts his, embracing the spectacle.  

A dark childhood incident—where their powers accidentally led to a stranger’s death—still divides them. Wallace suppresses his ability, fearing its consequences; Wilder craves the spotlight, eager to demonstrate his talent on national television.  

Tensions escalate when Wilder reignites an old rivalry over Wallace’s wife, a woman they both once loved. Her presence becomes the spark that ignites a fiery showdown between the brothers.  

While engaging, the film doesn’t—

Let me clarify—though I wasn’t raised in the South, I’m as American as they come. Country music isn’t my favorite, but I can tolerate it. You won’t catch me in a cowboy hat, though I do wear them. Trailer parks aren’t my backdrop, but I’ve eaten my share of tuna salad and pay a mortgage. Why does any of this matter? Because it challenges the assumption that only "country folks" connect with this film.  

At its core, this is a story about love found and lost—simple, raw, and achingly real. Directed by James Bridges, it stands out in an age of spectacle and oversharing, offering something rare: honesty.  

Bud, on the cusp of adulthood, steps into independence with his aunt and uncle’s support, trading small-town life for the city. The local honky-tonk becomes his refuge, the kind of escape a working man understands. There, he crosses paths with Sissy, another soul shaped by hardship. What follows is a romance as turbulent as it is tender—proof that heartache knows no zip code.

*Satan's Little Helper* stands out as one of the stronger B-horror films I’ve come across—not in terms of polish, but because of its story. The movie breaks away from tired horror tropes, offering something genuinely fresh and unpredictable. That said, it also leaves you scratching your head at times, raising bizarre questions that linger long after the credits roll.  

I first stumbled upon it while browsing the horror section at HMV, exhausted by the endless parade of overhyped Hollywood "terror" flicks. The cover art alone was enough to pull me in—it's unsettling in the best way. Sure, I knew it was a straight-to-DVD release, but after sitting through *Boogey Man* the night before, I figured it couldn’t possibly be worse.  

In the end, I walked away with mixed feelings. The premise hooked me—the idea of a killer manipulating a young boy, believing they’d become some twisted crime duo, was chilling in its own disturbing way.

Branagh stands out for his rare grasp of the distinction between cinema and theater. His *Hamlet* remains one of the most accurate Shakespearean film adaptations while still delivering gripping intensity—at times resembling a fast-paced thriller. The haunting encounter between Hamlet and his father’s ghost lingers long after viewing.

*Xizao* is a rare gem among films—unassuming yet profoundly moving, effortlessly simple yet rich in warmth and joy. Its narrative is straightforward, and the clash between tradition and modernity is beautifully established in the opening scenes. This central theme drives the story, but it’s the extraordinary characters and the actors behind them that give it life.  

Master Liu, the aging patriarch, embodies a fading era—China before rapid modernization took hold. He tends to a bathhouse in an old neighborhood, and every scene set within its walls fills us, stressed and discontented viewers, with quiet envy. Even the most hardened cynics would struggle to fault the film’s immersive and deeply comforting atmosphere.  

The second compelling force in the story is Master Liu’s mentally disabled son, Er Ming, alongside his brother, who represents the relentless pace of contemporary life. The interactions among these three, as well as their exchanges with the bathhouse’s patrons, are exquisitely nuanced and sincere. Some scenes brim with such raw emotion that they surpass nearly anything else captured on screen.  

A film with its quietly critical undertones, *Xizao* faced not only censorship but also inexplicably limited exposure. Whether by coincidence or not, when a movie...

This is easily the worst movie I've ever watched—yet somehow it's still entertaining and surprisingly amusing. Clearly, the filmmakers weren't aiming for polished Hollywood production value. Instead, it's a ridiculous story about a serial killer splashed with toxic waste, which reacts with the winter snow and transforms him into a murderous snowman. The premise alone is laughable.  

Yes, the film is absurd, but that's what makes it so funny. The kills are downright comical. I wouldn’t recommend rushing out to buy it (I fell for the cool cover art), but if you stumble across it on TV late one night and just want a mindless laugh, give it a shot.

Hilarious! Not a terrible way to kick things off. At first glance, I assumed this was something fresh—until I realized it’s a total rip-off of the 1976 *King Kong* remake. I didn’t catch *King Kong* until I was 15, but this gem hit my radar at nine. And let’s talk about that funky, brain-melting disco soundtrack—good luck getting it out of your head! Then there’s the Yetians’ bizarre theme song. The creature effects? Hands down the cheesiest I’ve ever witnessed. Yet, weirdly enough, this movie is practically a sacred relic among B-movie fanatics.  

Unforgettable lines like *"Take a tranquilizer and go to bed"* and *"Put the Yeti in your tank and you have Yeti power"* still crack me up. I first stumbled on this during an *Movie Macrabe* airing hosted by the legendary Elvira. One scene flipped the *King Kong* script—instead of climbing up a building to snatch the girl, this beast *climbs down* to catch her mid-fall! Around the same time, another *Kong* knockoff, *Mighty Peking Man* (1977), slithered out of Hong Kong.  

Between the laughable traveling matte shots and the clunky motorized limbs, this flick is pure comedy gold. Just like I said—nothing more than another shameless…

Let me start by saying it's disappointing how few viewers truly value imagination today. The brilliance of this show lies in its heightened reality. Questions like why Ned can resurrect the dead—but only for sixty seconds—miss the point entirely. Whatever happened to childlike wonder, the kind we found in magical stories like *A Wrinkle in Time*?  

What sets it apart is its defiance of conventional TV storytelling, where everything is spoon-fed, leaving no room for mystery or daydreaming.  

A little escapism on screen is a welcome change.  

The show’s surreal charm is what captivates me most—the nostalgic 1950s aesthetic, the endearingly odd characters, and the deliberately exaggerated world that never pretends to be real.  

While most shows fixate on death’s darkness, this one disguises its grimness with whimsy. Though entertaining, other series pale in comparison. It reignites something long missing from television: curiosity, magic, and pure delight.  

*Pushing Daisies* instantly became my favorite.

I first watched this movie years ago as a 12-year-old and remembered being impressed by it. But after revisiting it recently, I regret those wasted hours. It’s just not good.  

The cast includes some solid talent—Lee Majors, Chris Makepeace (check out *My Bodyguard* (1980) for one of his better roles, or *Meatballs* for a fun Bill Murray comedy), and the great Burgess Meredith. Unfortunately, this film did nothing to showcase their abilities or advance their careers.  

The plot follows Franklyn Hart (Majors), a retired race car driver who plans to drive his old car—stored away for years—cross-country to California. The catch? The government has banned all private transportation. While the premise isn’t the worst I’ve heard, the execution falls completely flat.

This film is a perfect case study in how even the best jokes can fall flat. The trailer had me in stitches, raising my expectations—only for the movie to disappoint halfway through.  

Oddly enough, some moments actually land well, like the spoofs on the smoking ban and *"Jo Bole..."*—genuinely clever humor. But the bigger mystery is where exactly things went wrong. The main culprits?  

1. The cast—neither the actors nor actresses brought the laughs (and not in a good way).  
2. The director’s questionable choices.  
3. Whoever decided this was the right team for the job.  

If you're *truly* desperate for entertainment (and I mean *truly*), give it a watch. Otherwise, just binge the teasers and ads—they pack more laughs than the entire film.  

P.S. The only redeeming feature? Mahesh Manjrekar and the hilarious *Chappu Bhai*.

A genuinely revolting movie. Rick Baker's visual effects are undeniably skilled—though thoroughly nauseating—but that's the only positive aspect. Much like numerous films from the 70s, it leaves you desperate for a scalding shower, desperate to wash away the lingering grime. Every character is utterly unlikeable, and the storyline is completely incoherent.

**SPOILERS** In *Omen IV*, the sinister legacy of the late Antichrist Damien Thorn returns through his offspring—spreading terror like a malevolent force. The dark seed takes the form of a girl named Delia York, also known as Asia Vieila. Given to a "deserving" couple, Karen and Gene York (played by Fay Grant and Michael Woods), by the Catholic Church's St. Francis Orphanage, she quickly begins her reign of terror.  

Little Delia wastes no time asserting her dominance—first lashing out at her mother with a vicious scratch during a house party. Later, she narrowly escapes death from a runaway truck, only to be mysteriously saved by a demonic guardian known as Ryder, the "Devil Dog." At school, she humiliates the class bully, forcing him to wet himself in front of everyone. And when her father threatens legal action against the Yorks, she orchestrates a gruesome "accident," leaving him decapitated. Crossing Delia is a fatal mistake—one you’ll regret if you value your life.  

Meanwhile, Delia’s adoptive father, Gene, rises to political prominence, believing his success is his own doing. Elected to Congress as an environmental champion, he remains oblivious to the dark forces truly pulling the strings.

The story lacked any trace of originality, cobbling together themes from *The Ninth Gate*, *In the Mouth of Madness* (yet another Carpenter flick), and *The Ring*. It even shamelessly recycled the same glowing circle from *The Ring*, making it the film’s defining symbol. Cody Carpenter’s score might as well have been stolen straight from *Suspiria*. And before anyone tries to defend it by shouting "HOMAGE," spare me—yes, I noticed *Deep Red* playing in the theater. Calling this an homage would be a pathetic excuse. This was scraping the bottom of the barrel. Dumping gore and "shocking" visuals into the mix doesn’t magically create good horror. Carpenter once understood that. Now? He should either vanish into obscurity or find a way to turn back time.

I saw this film during a Sundance Film Festival screening and was utterly overwhelmed by its raw emotional force. It delves deep into the psychological toll on service members who enlist with noble intentions—to defend their country with honor and trust they'll be cared for in return. The film meticulously traces the mental transformation soldiers undergo in boot camp, where they're molded into combat-ready fighters, then follows them through deployment and the harrowing aftermath of coming home. It also explores the profound impact of taking human life on the psyche. Rather than condemning the soldiers—as some films do—it honors their sacrifice while sharply critiquing a system that fails to fully address veterans' physical and mental health needs.  

Powerful, haunting, and deeply affecting, this movie is more than just a story—it's a rallying cry. It challenges us to move beyond superficial support like bumper stickers and parades, urging real action: listening to veterans' struggles and advocating for better care and systemic change.

Director Vincenzo Natali brought a distinct visual flair to this film, employing creative camera angles and impactful close-ups. Jeremy Northam and Lucy Liu delivered compelling performances in their leading roles, showcasing their versatility as actors. The movie also featured one of the most inventive escape sequences seen in contemporary cinema. The collaboration between director and cast resulted in a gripping thriller.  

While the plot was intricate, the narrative remained coherent as it peeled back layers of corporate corruption and deceit.  

George Orwell’s 1949 novel *1984* famously envisioned a dystopian future dominated by an oppressive state that stifled freedom. This film, however, presented an intriguing twist—rather than the government, it was ruthless corporate power that manipulated and exploited the individual.

You should absolutely make time for this film—especially if you love horror or cult classics.  

Trust me, I did!  

It’s phenomenal: dripping with eerie atmosphere, deeply unsettling, and genuinely frightening.  

What’s astounding is how they crafted such a masterpiece with what was essentially *no* budget.  

Here’s the premise (from their site): *“One morning, an old man wanders into the woods searching for his missing cat. Instead, he finds an abandoned child—and a murder with no body.”*  

While IMDb doesn’t have a trailer, you *can* watch one on the film's official site—and trust me, it’s chilling. Don’t miss it:  

[www.softfordigging.com](www.softfordigging.com)

The Geico commercials were mildly amusing the first few dozen times—I even appreciated their dry humor. But honestly? *This* is the pinnacle of creativity they landed on?! The show is painfully dull, like a caveman-themed knockoff of *The Office* (yes, I know that comparison will offend some people, but *The Office* never clicked for me).  

Let’s break it down: you’ve got the unlucky everyman just trying to survive, his miserable boss who despises him, the self-proclaimed genius who barely has two brain cells to rub together, and the bumbling oaf desperate for approval. Big deal. I’ve dealt with these types in real life—why would I want to waste even a fraction of my week watching them on screen? And if, after some reflection, you genuinely think this counts as entertainment? Call your parents. Ask if they accidentally dropped you as a child.

It was immediately clear to me that this film took significant liberties with Dodie Smith’s original story. Still, I thought it was charming how Pongo and Perdita’s son now had a litter of his own. The most adorable of the Dalmatians was undoubtedly little Snowball, who remained spotless right up until the film’s final moments.  

I’ll admit, I was caught off guard when Cruella de Vil appeared to have undergone a complete change of heart. While I’ve occasionally wondered if she could ever truly turn over a new leaf, her abrupt return to her villainous ways—declaring herself "Cruella" again—left me genuinely concerned for Chloe’s Dalmatians.  

Surprisingly, my favorite moment was when the puppies watched *Lady and the Tramp* during Chloe and Kevin’s dinner—it was far more entertaining than I’d anticipated. The parrot pretending to be a dog was another delightful touch, and I was amazed by how many tricks the dogs had mastered for the film.  

Naturally, I was relieved when the Dalmatians were saved in the end, though I still found myself curious about what would happen to them next.

Before I begin my review, I have to say—this movie is criminally underrated.  

Sharon Stone delivers a brilliant performance as Catherine Tramell, matching the intensity of her iconic role in the original. David Morrissey also shines as Dr. Glass, the analyst assigned to evaluate her after a sports star's mysterious death. She pulls him into a dangerous mind game, weaving a seductive web of manipulation.  

The acting is strong overall—with one glaring exception. Stone is flawless, just as sharp, provocative, and captivating as she was in the first film. She owns the role completely (much like she did in *Casino*). Morrissey holds his own, bringing the necessary vulnerability to his character. Unfortunately, David Thewlis falls flat—his performance feels exaggerated and out of place, dragging down every scene he’s in.  

While this sequel doesn’t quite reach the heights of the original, Stone makes it worth watching. Just do yourself a favor and tune out Thewlis.

First, it's clear the A-list actors needed a paycheck... The medical scenes were downright ridiculous—anyone with basic medical knowledge would find them completely unbelievable.  

Anesthesiologists don’t walk out in the middle of a heart transplant, nor is the procedure done in a cramped room with no equipment, no heart-lung machine, and zero sterile precautions. The whole thing was a farce. The absurd surgery scenes were so distracting that the plot became impossible to follow—no blood, no staff, and then the "hero doctor" swoops in to take over. This isn’t a movie for anyone with half a brain.  

The production values were clearly lacking—street scenes were passable, but whoever consulted on the medical details should be fired. It feels like the director had no clue what they were doing. Save your money—skip the theater, and don’t even bother renting it later.

Halloween follows the chilling tale of Michael Myers, a deeply disturbed man shaped by childhood trauma. His violent tendencies first emerge when he murders his older sister—an act that foreshadows the darkness yet to come.  

Donald Pleasence delivers a gripping performance as Dr. Loomis, the psychiatrist who has spent years studying Myers. He recognizes an unnatural evil within him, an unstoppable force that defies explanation. When Myers escapes confinement, he begins stalking his younger sister, driven by an unknown compulsion to finish what he started.  

Though others stand in his way, Myers eliminates them one by one, relentlessly pursuing his target. This film laid the groundwork for countless slasher movies, setting the standard for masked killers and suspenseful horror. Long before Freddy or Jason became icons, Halloween introduced the terrifying archetype of the silent, unstoppable murderer.

For those who adore the stage production of *A CHORUS LINE*, the film adaptation is a disappointing letdown. Key songs are missing, pointless plot twists are inserted, and the new dance sequences feel out of place. And frankly, Richard Attenborough’s direction fails to capture the energy and precision of the dancers.  

Onstage, *A CHORUS LINE* was unmistakably Michael Bennett’s masterpiece—his vision, choreography, and direction all came together in a raw, gripping portrayal that made you truly care about these dancers. The movie, by contrast, feels shallow and artificial. The actors come across as if they’re performing *A CHORUS LINE* rather than living it—every line, every movement too polished, too deliberate. Michael Douglas’s portrayal of Zach is particularly unconvincing; he’s too restrained to sell the character’s notorious harshness, and even his outbursts feel calculated. And the fact that he doesn’t dance? It’s a glaring omission—especially when you consider that Kevin Kline, who also couldn’t dance, once auditioned for the role on Broadway and lost it for that very reason.

This movie is mine—not by choice, but it is. Out of sheer boredom, the box caught my eye, so I slid it into my trusty VCR and wasted the next 90 minutes screaming, *"Why, God, why?"* The plot wasn’t *terrible*—as a gamer, I could vibe with bits of it. If you dig painfully nerdy, cheesy romance scenes, you *might* enjoy this trainwreck. *"I always thought of myself as a Vulcan, you know, like Dr. Spock... unable to love."*  

Let’s be real—there’s very little to praise here. It’s genuinely *bad*. But if you thrive on cinematic disasters, this one’s a goldmine. The *real* story behind it, though? Now *that’s* interesting.  

If I had to describe this film in one word?  

**LAME.**

This silent action drama captured my heart. Only Kurt Russell could have delivered such a powerful performance. Raised from childhood to understand nothing but combat, Todd (Kurt Russell) is discarded on a desolate planet after being replaced by genetically enhanced soldiers.  

The stage was set—and another legendary action hero was born: **SOLDIER**. Not Rambo, Schwarzenegger, Bruce Willis, Mel Gibson, or Jason Statham—this role belongs solely to Kurt Russell. He made it original, bold, and profoundly human. It’s a shame sequels never followed.  

10/10  

—LD

I went into this film with low expectations—it came in a bargain bin bundle of five movies, each terrible in their own way, so what could I really hope for? Turns out, my instincts were right. This one barely manages a couple of half-interesting moments (and even that feels generous). The scattered camcorder shots add a slight touch of authenticity, and the drummer nails the "annoying drummer" stereotype. Beyond that? Nothing worth praising.  

The biggest issue? It’s *dull*. What I assume was meant to build tension instead drags on forever—scenes crawl by with nothing happening, and when something finally does, it’s painfully tedious. I hovered over the fast-forward button for most of it but held out just to give it a fair shot. And can we talk about how often they harp on the lead singer’s looks? Supposedly, he’s some heartthrob, but honestly? I thought he resembled a meerkat.  

Oh, and the killer? Don’t even get me started—it’s not worth the breath. To sum it up: Skip this one. It’s just not worth your time.

I watched this movie for one reason—Al Adamson. He’s easily one of the worst directors ever, standing shoulder-to-shoulder with legends of bad filmmaking like Ed Wood, Jr. and Ray Dennis Steckler. But I was a little let down—while the movie was definitely terrible, it didn’t quite reach the staggering depths of his earlier trashy films. Because of that, it lacked the ridiculous charm that makes bad movies so entertaining for fans like me.  

Going in, I had reservations about “Naughty Stewardesses”—the title made it sound like a cheap porno, something I wouldn’t typically review on IMDb. And for the first 10 minutes, it sure seemed that way. But the script must have gone through endless rewrites, because most of the movie lacks any real titillation. Then, out of nowhere, an absurdly violent plot twist kicks in near the end—definitely not sexy! The whole thing is just a mess of contradictions.  

Even worse, none of the individual elements work. As a skin flick, it barely delivers, and what little it does makes no sense—why would anyone cast a 71-year-old...?

This independent film was the standout of the Tall Grass Film Festival for me—one of the best I’ve ever seen there. I adored it, with so many outstanding elements working together perfectly. Above all, the cast and crew I met were phenomenal.  

Avi delivered a fantastic performance in his role, and Ricky Ullman completely embodied his character. For a Disney actor, his ability to transition seamlessly from lighthearted teen comedy to such a mature, compelling role was remarkable. The entire ensemble was incredibly talented, and the cinematography was stunning. If you're looking for a must-see indie film, this is it.  

I believe Mr. Gruver would have been proud to have such an exceptional entry in his festival. When it won the Audience Favorite award, his parents loved it so much they went back for a second viewing. This film truly had everything—dark humor, sadness, raw emotion—and it was simply extraordinary. Honestly, I’m still buzzing with excitement over it, and I can’t—

**A Delight for All Ages, This Film Delivers Laughs and Thrills**  

Packed with everything from slapstick comedy like car chases and pie fights to clever, understated jokes for grown-ups, this movie is a blast for audiences of all ages.  

Glenn Close shines as the wickedly fabulous Cruella De Vil ("please, call me Ella"), delivering her most devilishly entertaining performance yet.  

After spending three years in Dr. Pavlov’s Behavior Modification Clinic, she’s finally cured of her obsession with fur—even the puppy-skin coats she once craved. In a dramatic move, she locks away her entire fur collection in the depths of her lavish castle’s dungeon.  

But what’s a *Dalmatians* film without Cruella’s scheming? It’s only a matter of time before something unravels her progress. This time, she needs just one more puppy (bringing the total to *102 Dalmatians*) to pull off her latest sinister plan.  

Ioan Gruffudd charms as the film’s heroic lead, running a "Second Chance" dog shelter. Though he appeared in *Titanic* and last year’s TV adaptation of *Great Expectations* as Pip, he’s almost unrecognizable here—then again, he played the relatively minor role of Fifth Officer Lowe in *Titanic*, and I missed *Great Expectations*, so maybe that’s not so surprising.  

Gerard Depardieu brings his signature charisma to the mix, rounding out an already stellar cast.

At a time when Hollywood profits by amplifying our flaws—despair, crime, addiction, and conflict—this film stands apart, reigniting the idea of the "Indomitable Spirit." If life has weighed you down, this story will lift your mind and send it soaring. We all face hardships, but sometimes we need a reminder that grit and bravery will carry us forward. That’s the gift this movie gave me—and I hope it does the same for you.

I still have those fuzzy, late-night recordings of this show—transferred onto cheap VHS tapes from way back when, complete with grainy late-night commercials. I’d stay up until whatever ungodly hour they decided to air it just to hit record.  

The series wasn’t really *about* Freddy Krueger—aside from the first few episodes, he mostly just lurked in the shadows like a Rod Serling wannabe, introducing the nightmares. Instead, each episode tackled its own twisted tale, playing on classic horror themes: childhood terrors, cannibalism, money, death… and, of course, *dating*. So much dating.  

There was the episode where a teenage boy accidentally whispered *"I’ll love you forever"* to the wrong girl and wound up literally fused to her (at least temporarily). Or the one about a flight attendant who followed a mysterious man home, only to discover his cabin had a “trophy room” full of other stewardesses. And then there was the hazy memory of an episode comparing blind dates to hockey—complete with penalties and injuries. Clearly, romance was the real nightmare fuel here.  

One episode even featured Jeffrey Combs (*Re-Animator*, etc.) as an *extremely* driven pizza delivery guy…

A delightfully romantic comedy with elegantly woven subplots and razor-sharp performances, where actors trade lines with flawless comedic precision—a joy to witness. When Cher's meek fiancé begs her to reconcile with his brooding, estranged younger brother, the ensuing chaos defies expectations. A mix of operatic grandeur, whispered confessions, love-fueled passion, and snow-kissed nights—*Moonstruck* remains effortlessly timeless. Though the film takes a few scenes to find its rhythm (the opening cemetery sequence with the grandfather and his dogs feels uneven, followed by a cryptic exchange between Cosmo and an old man at the gate), its intricate storytelling quickly falls into place. With its quirky charm and unpredictably endearing tone, the movie casts an irresistible spell. ***½ out of ****.

John Boorman’s *Deliverance* follows four suburban men from Atlanta as they embark on a canoe trip down the raging Cahulawassee River. The river—soon to be submerged by a dam—offers one final chance to navigate the last untamed wilderness.  

Each of the four friends represents a distinct archetype: a rugged, risk-taking outdoorsman who scoffs at insurance (Burt Reynolds); a devoted family man and skilled guitarist (Ronny Cox); a heavyset, bachelor insurance salesman (Ned Beatty); and a reserved, introspective father who enjoys his pipe (Jon Voight).  

Their journey swiftly descends into a harrowing struggle against nature’s brutality, testing their limits and exposing the fragile boundary between civilization and savagery.  

Expertly filmed, this gripping adult thriller delivers intense, unforgettable moments.

Adding to the previous point, *Fear of a Black Hat* doesn’t feature the storyline about the criminal whose image is copied by the band—that’s from *CB4*. The two movies are often mixed up because of their similarities, but *Black Hat* is clearly the better film... no question.

How can anyone take her gritty, high-octane bounty hunter tale seriously with *that* ridiculous accent? It’s laughable. On top of that, the director’s flashy visual style is more nauseating than stylish—just cheap gimmicks masking a hollow, tedious rehash of gangster tropes. The plot is a tangled mess, stuffed with shallow characters dumped in at random, and the acting is painfully wooden.  

The storytelling is a chaotic jumble, bouncing between disjointed flashbacks just to keep the audience disoriented. Worse still, the film casually shows scenes that "never happened," only to backtrack later—like the entirely fabricated assassination of the (phony) 'first ladies.' What was the point of wasting our time with fake sequences?  

Between the miscast lead, the incoherent narrative, and the migraine-inducing direction, this film is a disaster. 1/5.

First saw this decades ago on a grainy black-and-white TV in a remote Samoan village and remember laughing until my sides hurt. Watching it again now, after so many years, I didn’t laugh—not because the film isn’t funny, but because life has a way of sanding down that kind of joy. Even so, this remains a sharp, breezy comedy that never drags, and I still found every minute delightful.  

Set in 1945, Fred MacMurray plays a 4F civilian desperate to enlist. After rubbing an old lamp in the scrapyard he oversees, out pops a genie ready to grant his wishes. (Yes, it sounds tired, but stick with it—the setup may be plain, the fantasies that follow are anything but.) MacMurray’s first wish? To join the army. In a flash, he’s marching alongside George Washington’s troops straight into a suspiciously cozy USO, where June Haver and Joan Leslie lounge in frilly lace and absurd lavender wigs. Soon, Washington dispatches him to spy on the enemy—German-accented Hessians in red coats, not Brits. Crammed into a raucous beer hall, the soldiers belt out a drunken anthem glorifying the Vaterland—"where the...

This is a fantastic B-movie, especially if you love campy, low-budget flicks. It’s a throwback to the classic 80s slasher genre, complete with a single cheesy song looping endlessly on the soundtrack. Sure, it’s objectively terrible—but that’s what makes it so entertaining. Perfect for a laugh-filled viewing with friends, watching over-the-top moments like elderly men lunging from closets with knives. Honestly, it’s hilarious in the best way possible.

This film is uplifting for anyone who's ever faced tough times, whether struggling with money or emotions. Get ready to laugh—it’s the perfect remedy! :) After losing her husband and her financial security, Grace turns to an unconventional—and slightly illegal—way to make ends meet, leading to hilarious moments. Even my boyfriend enjoyed it, so don’t assume it’s just a chick flick!

Two houses. A single street. A lonely phone booth. One car. A girl next door. A boy next door. And a zombie. With ingredients like these, you'd expect a solid horror flick—just add moody blue lighting, eerie background music, and voilà! But in the hands of Dutch director van Rouveroy? Think again.  

I’m a fan of hosting "bad movie nights"—gather some drinks, invite fellow film enthusiasts, and dive into the glorious depths of cinematic disaster. And let me tell you, this gem of a train wreck is perfect for the occasion. Guaranteed laughter!  

The strangest part? Van Rouveroy still stands by this monstrosity as if it were a masterpiece. For proof, just listen to her DVD commentary. Prepare to be baffled—and entertained—all over again!

I generally avoid TV movies since you can often tell they’re TV movies within the first few seconds. But this one caught my eye with its intriguing title and the somber, meticulously crafted atmosphere from the opening scene. Though the constant rain gave away its questionable setting—supposedly California but clearly filmed in the stormy landscapes of Vancouver, B.C.—it created a dark, brooding backdrop that perfectly highlighted Edward James Olmos’ outstanding performance.

**Warning: Spoilers ahead...**  

I’ve watched this film three times, and each viewing reaffirms how brilliantly made it is. Though an HBO TV movie, it’s crafted with the same excellence typical of their productions—had it been released theatrically, the performances alone would have deserved Oscar recognition.  

As many reviews here note, the film centers on the infamous serial killer Andrei Chikatilo, who murdered 56 people over eight years in the former Soviet Union. (With three victims' remains never found, he was ultimately convicted of 52 out of 53 killings.) However, the story primarily follows forensic analyst Victor Burakov, portrayed flawlessly by Stephen Rea—a man consumed by obsession and anguish as he hunts the killer, battling both the case’s horrors and bureaucratic resistance.  

A particularly poignant moment near the film’s end highlights how American investigators are typically rotated off serial killer cases after 18 months to protect their mental health—a stark contrast to Burakov’s relentless, tormented pursuit.  
(According to...)

As a longtime fan of James Spader, I had high hopes this film would at least be watchable. Sadly, it fell far short. Within the first thirty minutes, I found myself keeping the remote handy for frequent fast-forwarding. The plot is painfully predictable—every scene unfolds exactly as you'd expect, down to the clichéd dialogue. It’s the kind of film that leaves you wondering how it ever got greenlit. If I had to find a silver lining, the special effects were somewhat decent. But honestly, if you’ve seen even a handful of sci-fi films or you're older than nine, save yourself the time and skip this one.

Alan Alda portrays real-life *Sports Illustrated* journalist George Plimpton, who was granted the unconventional opportunity to join the Detroit Lions football team as an honorary member. Despite its potential, the film falls flat as a lackluster drama, oddly infused with elements of fantasy. Director Alex March approaches the material with a unique blend of quasi-documentary realism—complete with rugged, macho narration—and a hint of Capra-esque charm. However, by emphasizing cinematic flair, he muddles the central storyline. Alda's performance, unfortunately, comes across as self-satisfied and lacking magnetism, though the supporting cast shines with genuine pro-athletes (and the electrifying Lauren Hutton as Alda’s love interest—talk about wish fulfillment). *1/2 out of ****.

Here’s the rewritten version:

---

**Brief Summary**  

The story begins with soldiers discharged from their unit. One relentlessly follows another with an unusual plan that is repeatedly rejected. Eventually, both become trapped in an office building during the Christmas holidays while attempting to crack a safe. What starts as hostility shifts into playful rivalry, then spirals into a desperate struggle for survival—made all the more dire after they lose access to drinking water. With their bare, muscular bodies gleaming, they force their way through a wall to escape—only to discover they were manipulated and betrayed by women. One is captured while the other remains free, protected by his companion’s silence. A final meeting, a shared flame for a cigarette, and a parting farewell: *adieu l’ami*, goodbye, friend.  

The dynamic between the two leads—played by classic tough-guy icons Alain Delon and Charles Bronson—hints at deeply repressed desire. Their clear mutual attraction contrasts with their callous, disdainful treatment of women. The narrative carries a potent symbolic weight, reminiscent of *Deliverance* in its subtext.  

---  

I refined the phrasing for conciseness and clarity while preserving the original tone and key details.

I caught this a few nights ago with low expectations, and unsurprisingly, it fell flat. The premise—a team of vampire hunters (V-San, short for vampire sanitation) patrolling space in their ship, eliminating space vampires and rescuing victims—had real potential. With better execution, this could have been something great. Instead, after a promising start, any semblance of quality quickly evaporates, leaving behind a movie that’s mindlessly watchable but undeniably ridiculous.  

I don’t expect much from these Sci-Fi Channel flicks, and at least this wasn’t another creature feature with laughably bad CGI monsters lumbering around. Still, it was pretty awful, thanks to the weak script and stiff performances—though the truly unforgivable offense was the cringe-worthy soundtrack. When the film stuck to eerie sci-fi soundscapes, it was passable. But all too often, painfully dated soft rock would blare in, turning scenes into unintentional comedy. The cheesy acting and writing might have been tolerable if not for the music’s relentless assault on good taste.

For most of my life, I haven’t watched many online films, but if I had to choose one, it would be *Spatula Madness*. A brilliant parody of franchises like *Star Trooper* (among others), this short film combines clever camerawork, razor-sharp wit, and the creative genius of Jason Steele. He transforms ordinary images into vibrant paintings, weaving them together through meticulous frame-by-frame animation to craft a surreal world ruled by spatulas.  

The storytelling is unconventional—starting in the middle, looping back to the beginning, and bending structure in ways that would delight any director. When I first saw it, I braced for a pixelated, low-budget mess, but Jason—like me—has an eye for aesthetics, pushing every detail to its limit.  

Fair warning: it’s not for kids, and I doubt many would appreciate it as much as I do. Still, I urge you to look it up (it’s a short film—search *Film Cow* online). Its style echoes *South Park* but with far less violence.  

Visuals? A perfect 10. Humor? A solid 6. Story? Another 6. Yet somehow, it all adds up to a flawless 10/10.  

Jason Steele—I’m eagerly waiting for your next film.

Hey there. So this film is... um... decent. Just kidding—IT'S INCREDIBLE! It might not be some massive box office sensation, and that's not what it's going for. But in my book—and my sister's too—it's a total win. We're die-hard rock 'n' rollers. GO RAMONES!!! This movie? Absolutely amazing... for ME!

Let me start by admitting I have a serious fear of dentists—which makes this movie especially unsettling for me. That slow-building dread and skin-crawling discomfort are exactly why I love it, though I’ll admit the pacing drags in places, costing it three stars.  

**Spoiler Alert**  

The story follows Dr. Alan Feinstone, a man unraveling after discovering his wife’s infidelity. His descent into madness is brutal: hallucinations, patient mutilations, murdered colleagues, and the gruesome demise of both his wife and her lover.  

**End Spoiler**  

Visceral, graphic, and unflinchingly violent, this isn’t one for the squeamish—but if you enjoy gore, it delivers.  

Final verdict? A solid 7/10. Dr. Alan Feinstone is anything but your average dentist.

*Rewritten Version:*  

An independent feature can now be regarded as both a cinematic work of art and a creative video résumé. Enter *Broken*—a boldly marketed, twenty-minute short brimming with style and relentless energy. But does it succeed as a film, or does it merely function as a demo reel? Ah, therein lies the question.  

*Broken* follows Bonnie Clayton, who is kidnapped after waking from a recurring nightmare by a sadistic stranger and his eccentric crew (as the video box describes). As she’s held hostage, it becomes clear her captors know unsettling secrets about her—secrets even she doesn’t realize. The tension escalates when a black-clad soldier storms their hideout in a brutal rescue attempt, unleashing chaos.  

Director Alex Ferrari, thankfully, appears to know his craft—or at least excels at selling the illusion. *Broken* showcases impressive visual polish, particularly commendable given its budget and the crew’s novice status. Where it falters is in its writing, which feels thin and somewhat unoriginal—imagine *The Long Kiss Goodnight* colliding with *The Matrix*, hastily scribbled after a *Fight Club* binge.

*Deliverance* is a gripping thriller, delivering all the heart-pounding tension a great thriller should while also being deeply unsettling. Though not a horror film, it is every bit as horrifying as the genre’s most chilling classics. Imagine being an ordinary man on an adventure getaway, far from civilization, only to fall victim to brutal backwoods assailants—this scenario is the stuff of nightmares for nearly anyone. The film could have easily veered into exploitative shock value, but director John Boorman resists that urge, crafting a story that examines and deconstructs traditional masculinity.  

Unlike most films that leave you longing to embody the hero—saving the day and winning admiration—*Deliverance* leaves you grateful you’ll never endure what its protagonists suffer.  

The story follows four urban men—Ed (Jon Voight), Lewis (Burt Reynolds), Drew (Ronny Cox), and Bobby (Ned Beatty)—as they embark on a wilderness canoe trip, expecting a simple escape from city life. Instead, their journey descends into a harrowing fight for survival.

I’m shocked critics praised this film. The story is incoherent, the characters are stiff and lifeless, and Michael Bowen’s role mostly involves creeping around, misreading everyone. None of them have depth or intrigue. This isn’t daring, creative, or witty—it’s just dull. Skipping theaters was no loss, and airing it on "This Network" drags down their reputation. If you stumble on it during late-night TV, switch to a PBS rerun—even a bland documentary would be better. If it’s on daytime, step outside instead. Breathing smog beats wasting time on this slog. Life’s too short, and this movie feels endless.

I absolutely loved this movie—it was adorable! While I had a great time watching it, if you didn’t enjoy it, that’s on you. Emma Roberts made a fantastic Nancy Drew, even if she wasn’t exactly like the book version. The vintage-inspired outfits felt a bit out of place in a modern setting, but she totally pulled them off.  

Honestly, the rich girls' wardrobes didn’t scream "wealthy" to me—it looked like they blindly grabbed mismatched pieces from a thrift store and went with it. Most of the outfits were pretty tacky, especially those clunky penny loafers paired with everyday clothes.  

Don’t get me wrong, though—the movie itself was far from bad! It’s worth seeing in theaters, and I promise you’ll have fun watching it!

**"People I Know" is a flat, uninvolving film with no compelling characters to latch onto—despite a skilled cast giving it their all.**  

Al Pacino delivers his trademark intensity as Eli Wurman, a washed-up publicist eroded by years of moral decay. Yet unlike his iconic Michael Corleone, Eli inspires no emotional connection—his struggles and ultimate fate feel distant and irrelevant.  

The story follows Eli as he organizes a fundraiser for a left-wing political cause while juggling the latest scandal involving one of his clients (a thinly written role played capably by Ryan O’Neal). Tea Leoni injects charisma into her underdeveloped part as a troubled TV actress, while Kim Basinger manages to be quietly moving as Eli’s sister-in-law, despite the contrived plot surrounding her.  

This film will only appeal to die-hard Pacino fans eager to see him command the screen. Sadly, with its weak script and clumsy direction, *People I Know* feels like a misfire from start to finish—hence its swift exit from theaters and quick shift to home video. Consider this fair warning.

It’s no surprise this film earned an Oscar nomination for Best Live Action Short—its craftsmanship is exceptional. Even if Blues music isn’t your preferred genre (though the soundtrack leans more toward jazz, in my opinion), the film’s artistry is undeniable. The direction is so skillful that it’s baffling why Gjon Mili never helmed another project after this. Despite the film’s acclaim, his career failed to take off—a puzzling outcome.  

As for the Black performers, their lack of career momentum post-film is sadly unsurprising, given the widespread indifference—or outright prejudice—from white audiences toward both Black artists and the genre itself.  

A word of advice for viewers: if the opening segment feels slow, jump ahead to around the 5:50 mark, where the energy shifts dramatically. The moment the vocalist steps back and the instrumentalists take over with improvisation, the film truly comes alive.

This film clearly resonates deeply with a particular audience—though I don't count myself among them. I walked into the preview without any expectations, only to leave feeling underwhelmed. The story follows a deeply troubled, often disturbingly twisted Hungarian Jewish family, which simply wasn’t for me. An epic of this scale should leave its audience with something profound, yet this one fell short. Films like this are meant to explore the human experience, but this one offered little fresh insight into its most significant dimensions.

Rap and ghetto culture don’t appeal to me—I’m a white guy who prefers classic rock. But that didn’t stop me from loving this brilliant comedy. It’s basically a sequel to *This Is Spinal Tap*, following the same mockumentary style but swapping rock for rap—and it’s hilarious. While not every joke lands, the majority hit hard, and the characters are both absurd and oddly believable. I stumbled on it at 3 a.m. and couldn’t stop laughing—any film that can pull that off deserves a watch.  

What makes it work so well is its sharp take on rap culture. Unlike today's overproduced, shallow trends, this movie reflects an era when rappers actually had to earn their stripes. It skewers music industry clichés while tackling race, sex, and culture with equal irreverence. If you loved *Spinal Tap*, you’ll recognize the same wit—just transplanted into hip-hop’s world. Same jokes, different scene, and somehow, they’re just as funny. Highly recommended.

It's debatable whether Rob Schmidt truly deserves the title of "Master" in the horror genre, given that his only prior horror film, *Wrong Turn*, was just slightly above average. However, he undeniably delivered one of the most chilling and standout episodes of *Masters of Horror* Season 2 with *Right to Die*. A similar case occurred in Season 1, when William Malone—despite his underwhelming films *Fear Dot Com* and *House on Haunted Hill*—crafted one of the best episodes, *The Fair Haired Child*.  

*Right to Die* smartly taps into the timely debate around euthanasia while weaving in classic horror elements: vengeful spirits, deadly schemes, macabre humor, and over-the-top comic book violence. The story follows the Addison couple, whose late-night drive turns tragic when they crash after an argument about Cliff’s infidelity. Cliff escapes unharmed, but Abby suffers severe burns, leaving her on life support. As Cliff and his unethical lawyer (played by Corbin Bernsen of *The Dentist* infamy) push to end her suffering—or so they claim—the twisted horror unfolds.

I’ll be honest—I didn’t give this movie much of a shot. Almost immediately, I decided it just wasn’t for me.  

Visually, it’s stunning. The cinematography perfectly captures early '70s Manhattan, and the black-and-white aesthetic is so sharp it almost feels timeless. The lead actress looks fantastic, too. But then the filmmakers throw in jarring, disruptive editing—very much a product of the late '60s, straddling surrealism and New Wave experimentation—and that timeless vibe falls apart. The story itself feels locked in that era, caught between free-spirited idealism and artsy self-indulgence.  

The plot follows a young woman wandering the city in search of a man she had anonymous phone sex with. Along the way, she meets a parade of eccentric characters, trading quirks and oddities. It bills itself as a quirky, irreverent comedy but leans hard into avant-garde territory. If you’re a fan of Andy Warhol’s films, discovering *The Telephone Book* would probably feel like unearthing buried treasure.  

That said, my issues with it...

Opinions on "The Aristocrats" were sharply divided—some adored it, while others walked out mid-show. Reactions to Eddie Izzard are unlikely to be as extreme, provided you're comfortable with a transvestite comedian (who jokes about his preference for women) and a vocabulary that leans heavily on the kind of language that would turn his act into one long bleep on network TV. Many of Izzard’s fans adore him so fiercely they refuse to acknowledge any flaws in his performances. Personally, I found this show uneven—sometimes as flat as Izzard’s chest, but more often than not funny, with moments of pure brilliance. His cleverness lies in weaving early references into later routines. He isn’t a traditional storyteller or joke-teller, nor does he channel Robin Williams’ frenetic energy. Instead, he toys with ideas—some landing brilliantly, others (like the San Francisco cable car and Alcatraz bit) falling completely flat. Yet he navigates seamlessly past the misses, shining even brighter when a joke clicks. I’d rate this performance a solid 7, maybe even...

11 Oscar nominations and not a single win—still baffling! It’s not like the cast went on to outperform their roles in *The Color Purple* later, yet others snagged awards for far lesser performances (looking at you, Halle Berry and Denzel). Whoopi, Oprah, Margaret Avery, Danny Glover—all delivered powerhouse performances. I'd love to see the Oscar deliberations from that year—bet they belong in the "shoulda-woulda-coulda" hall of shame.  

The book is incredible, though Alice Walker’s signature style sometimes makes her characters feel larger-than-life. Honestly, the film adaptation wisely trimmed some of that excess.  

Visually stunning, but the Africa scenes? A letdown. In the book, it’s set in Liberia—West Africa—but Spielberg apparently assumed audiences only know Africa through safari clichés. Of course, we *had* to see zebras and wildlife, even though they had no place in the story. Classic Hollywood ignorance.

I’ve read the book several times, and this movie doesn’t stay entirely true to it. Normally, I’d overlook that—it’s just a film. But what really bothers me is how inaccurate the setting is. Nobody seems to point out that both the movie and the book are based on real events that took place in Nebraska. As someone who grew up in the town this story is meant to depict, I can’t ignore the glaring errors.  

First, the so-called "small town" setting is actually Nebraska’s third-largest city, with roughly 50,000 residents. Grand Island isn’t some tiny place—it’s the biggest city between Lincoln and Denver. Second, the scenery is completely off. Grand Island sits in the Platte River Valley, which is mostly flat with very few trees. The movie’s landscape doesn’t match reality at all.  

I tried giving it a chance, but seeing my hometown portrayed so carelessly just made me angry. This wasn’t just fiction—it was a real disaster that devastated huge parts of the city. The book even mentions biking from Mormon Island to Fonner Park, which would be a 15-mile trek—not exactly a casual ride.

This film packs a punch. At first, the thick Scottish accents threw me off, making it hard to follow and spoiling the experience. I set it aside—until I got the DVD. With English subtitles filling in the gaps, I fully appreciated just how incredible it is. Absolutely outstanding.  

The sweeping widescreen cinematography showcases breathtaking rugged landscapes, immersing you in the story—a gripping battle of good versus evil that echoes *Braveheart*. Liam Neeson embodies the noble hero, while Tim Roth plays a villain so loathsome you’ll want to reach through the screen and wipe that smug smirk off his face. (Critics adore his revolting character precisely because he’s so detestable.) Neeson’s rugged, commanding presence rivals Mel Gibson’s in *Braveheart*, and Jessica Lange delivers a powerhouse performance as the female lead.  

This movie grips you from start to finish, pulling you deep into its emotional intensity. Buckle up—it’s a visceral ride.

Why do films about Cleopatra, the last pharaoh, bring out the worst in cinema? Whatever allure she held for Rome's greatest leaders—Julius Caesar and Mark Antony—fails to translate onscreen, coming across instead like the melodramatic antics of overeager teenagers. Despite opulent sets and costumes, this movie sinks to the same level as Italy’s cheap 1950s "sandals and toga" spectacles. While grand historical epics belong on the big screen, as *Gladiator* proved, that film succeeded without drowning in romance-novel clichés.  

Miss Varela's acting is as unconvincing as Elizabeth Taylor's was, though Timothy Dalton’s talent shines. It’s a shame none of it rubbed off on the rest of the cast.

Whenever someone asks about the most terrifying film I've ever watched, my answer is always "Black Noon"—yet no one seems to recognize the title.  

I first saw it alone around 30 years ago at the impressionable age of 13 while my parents were out for the evening. As far as I know, it only aired once in the UK, and it’s never been released on DVD or VHS.  

If anyone manages to track down a copy, I’d love to hear about it.  

Watching it now would likely ruin the eerie mystique, but that unsettling little film has haunted my memory ever since.

I had high hopes for this movie given its trailers and media buzz, but it turned out to be a massive letdown. *Slums* is painfully humorless, blending the unsettling realism of a Todd Solondz family drama without any of his signature wit. The plot plods forward, with each scene more tedious than the last. Perhaps I didn’t grasp its message, but if this is what every girl endures growing up, I’m grateful to be a man.

Here’s a rewritten version of your text:  

---  

When you consider *Captivity*, several words spring to mind: dull, tedious, predictable, bland, baffling, and unbearable.  

I used to despise those late-'90s *Scream* knockoffs, but these newer *Saw* clones are somehow making them seem like masterpieces. They still target the same audience—young teens craving shock value—but now they crank up the depravity to make their impressionable viewers feel edgy and cool.  

This movie is a tedious mess! What happened to Larry Cohen? He hasn’t been involved in anything decent since 1993. Even so, I never expected him to sink this low. And let’s talk about that "twist"—was anyone actually surprised when the love interest turned out to be the killer? If you didn’t see it coming from the first scene, you must have never watched a thriller before.

This version maintains your strong opinions while refining the structure and flow. Let me know if you'd like any further adjustments!

This episode stands out for its playful simplicity—the storyline feels more like a vehicle for sheer enjoyment than anything else. Yet, there’s charm in its carefree tone, making it one of the most purely entertaining installments. Picture this: the crew crosses paths with Wonderland’s White Rabbit and Alice, a Bengal tiger, a samurai warrior, and even a knight on horseback who fatally strikes McCoy—all before the chaos finally clicks into place. Though peril lurks throughout, the absurdity keeps things lighthearted, creating a delightfully surreal experience. It may not be deep, but as pure escapism, it’s fantastic.

Horror movies usually don’t frighten me, but this one was different. Somehow, it got under my skin! Despite its simplicity, the film is incredibly effective—full of tense atmosphere that builds to truly shocking moments. The scene with the girl’s father coming down the hill was especially chilling, and the family photo moment caught me completely off guard—I nearly leaped out of my seat! I’d highly recommend watching this movie, ideally in the dark—it’ll haunt you long after the credits roll.

The concept might appear silly at first glance, but since Murphy's character plays it with a light touch, it smoothly blends mystical elements with a gritty contemporary kidnapping story. The stellar cast, especially Charles Dance and Charlotte Lewis, shines, while Murphy delivers one of his finest 80s comedy-action performances. Standout practical effects, a bizarre dream sequence, and a refreshingly unique storyline round out the film. Though often overshadowed by Murphy’s bigger hits, this hidden gem deserves attention.

**SPOILER ALERT**  
If you haven’t watched the film yet, skip this comment.  

I haven't seen every movie out there, but *The Hamiltons* was a complete letdown. It failed to entertain on every level—from the mediocre acting and absurd plot to the ridiculous twist at the end. Absolutely terrible!  

The movie tries to sell us on this family that consumes people, but here’s the problem: what *are* they? Cannibals? Inbred freaks? Some kind of inhuman *things* experimenting with human flesh? The film never bothers to clarify, making the whole premise feel lazy and half-baked.  

And let’s be honest—this movie was just plain bad. If you somehow thought *The Hamiltons* was good, I have to ask... *how?* There was nothing redeeming about it. A total waste of time.  

Skip this mess and check out *The Gravedancers*, *Tooth & Nail*, or *Borderland* instead—those actually deliver real entertainment. *The Hamiltons*? A big, loud **BOOOOOOO** from me.

"Return of the Jedi" often gets criticized for its flaws rather than celebrated for its strengths, which is unfortunate—because the final chapter of the original Star Wars trilogy delivers a spectacular and emotional conclusion to the saga. It masterfully ties together every thread from the preceding films, crafting a finale that feels both satisfying and earned.  

Yes, the Ewoks can be divisive—adorable yet undeniably aimed at broadening the series' appeal—and the pacing lags a little in the middle. But the film’s final act stands as one of the greatest sequences in all of Star Wars, culminating in Luke’s climactic confrontation with Darth Vader, cinema’s most iconic antagonist.  

What "Return of the Jedi" achieves deserves far more recognition: a brilliant resolution to Vader’s arc (elevating the once-debatable twist from "Empire" into something profound), a thrilling Jabba’s Palace opening, Ian McDiarmid’s chilling portrayal of the Emperor, Luke’s full transformation into a Jedi, the heartfelt payoff of Han and Leia’s romance, and the unforgettable, emotionally charged finale on the forest moon of Endor.

The United States seems to be directing the UK police force, with officers patrolling heavily armed—and did you know that CID detectives switch into uniform after their shifts to hit the pub? This has to be one of the most absurd portrayals of "real" British policing ever dumped on an unwitting audience.  

I get that Wesley Snipes might’ve needed a paycheck to sort out his tax troubles, but why a talent like Charles Dance signed on is beyond me.  

It’s even more painful than the cheesiest 1950s B-movie. Ninety minutes of pure agony—time I’ll never recover.  

Steer clear of this one like your life depends on it.

I rarely take the time to leave reviews, but I felt compelled to warn anyone expecting real comedy—this isn’t even close. The core premise (a forced change of color/gender/etc.) is weak and overdone, but the execution here is dismal. The so-called “transformation” of two Black men into white women is among the most unconvincing ever filmed.  

Even if the script only demanded a generic swap, it would still be bad—but no, the Wayans brothers had to mimic two specific women. Unsurprisingly, they fail spectacularly. I’ve seen drag queens with no makeup look more naturally feminine than these two do, despite Hollywood’s best efforts at prosthetics and effects. It’s painful to watch.  

Throw in a basketball player built like a skyscraper, cringe-worthy dialogue, and more plot holes than a sieve, and this movie sinks to a new low—and I *enjoy* bad films. Steer clear at all costs.

This thought-provoking period drama—partially rooted in historical events—is too often carelessly grouped with the shallow "nunsploitation" flicks that dominated 1970s Euro trash cinema, ignoring the righteous fury at its core. Notably, this was also Gianfranco Mingozzi’s sole venture into narrative filmmaking, stepping away from his acclaimed documentary work.  

Set against a carefully rendered historical backdrop, *Flavia* follows the mounting defiance of a 15th-century Italian nun (Florinda Bolkan in a career-defining performance, eclipsing even her haunting role in Lucio Fulci’s *Don’t Torture a Duckling*). Confined to a convent by her dishonorable noble father in a bid to suppress her awakening sensuality, she begins questioning why women are condemned to subservience in both life and scripture. As she witnesses the destructive consequences of male domination, her rebellion is stoked by the ravings of Sister Agatha (a unforgettable turn by Maria Casarès of *Les Enfants du Paradis* fame) and—more meaningfully—by the arrival of Muslim invaders. Allying with the oppressors, and possibly wielding unseen influence over them, Flavia fully embraces the outsider status she has long felt.

Despite its title, *The Sword Bearer*, and the DVD cover depicting heroic action poses, this isn’t a typical superhero film.  

*(Minor Spoilers)* The story follows Sasha, the Sword Bearer, cursed with a retractable blade embedded in his forearm. At first glance, it might sound thrilling—until reality sets in. Imagine having such a power as a child: could you control it when confronted by a violent madman or your mother’s abusive boyfriend? And if you couldn’t, how would you cope with being a two-time killer by the age of twelve?  

This is Sasha’s life when we first meet him—adrift after yet another killing, reminiscent of *À Bout de Souffle*. Then he crosses paths with Katya, and their instant love gives him a reason to live and change his ways. But his past won’t let go, personified by two relentless police officers.  

That’s the core of the story—one with almost no on-screen action, though much is implied.  

What sets this film apart is its depth. Unlike many Hollywood superhero tales, it avoids excessive backstory or flashy battles, choosing instead to explore the weight of power and consequence. A refreshing departure from the usual spectacle.

It’s odd that this film never had a theatrical release in Denmark, so I had to wait for it to come out on video. My expectations were sky-high, and they were absolutely met. As with any Ang Lee film, the performances are outstanding, the plot is smart and gripping—keeping you guessing until the very end—and the cinematography is exceptional. Alongside *Unforgiven*, this stands as one of the two finest Westerns of the '90s.  

If you're expecting something like Mel Gibson in *The Patriot* (overly sentimental) or *Braveheart* (decent but formulaic), you’ll be sorely let down. But for anyone who values the qualities mentioned above, this movie is a must-watch. 9/10.

Before continuing, I should confess that I'm a massive Bon Jovi fan—it’s honestly what first caught my eye about this DVD. Given my love for horror and my enjoyment of the original *Vampires* film, I likely would have bought it anyway.  

That said, this sequel doesn’t come close to measuring up. Not even Jon’s presence could redeem it for me. My biggest issue? It just isn’t scary. Aside from his character, Derek Bliss, none of the others leave any impression, making their fates utterly inconsequential—especially the grating vampire/drug addict woman. The female vampire herself fails to be either terrifying or alluring; instead, she comes across like a malnourished teenager, which might explain her desperate thirst for blood.  

Another major flaw is the overly bright cinematography. There’s no atmosphere, no creeping sense of dread. While the first *Vampires*—set in New Mexico—wasn’t exactly a masterpiece of gothic horror, it still knew when to plunge into darkness and menace. This film, in contrast, lacks that kind of tension entirely.  

The plot, at its core, is essentially…

William Powell’s final performance as Philo Vance takes place in *The Kennel Murder Case*, where the death of a prized show dog spirals into two additional murders and an attempted killing—all human, of course. The mystery lies in piecing together the *how* to uncover the *who* and *why*.  

The Philo Vance novels by S.S. Van Dine were immensely popular, and the shrewd Van Dine devised a way to auction his books individually to the highest-bidding studio. That’s why so many actors played Vance across various studios. Had Powell not achieved even greater fame as Nick Charles in MGM’s *Thin Man* series, he would have been remembered as the definitive Philo Vance.  

In the film, Powell’s own terrier, Captain, was competing in the same dog show where the initial victim—a champion canine—was killed. Soon after, a rival owner becomes the first human victim. As always, Powell outshines Eugene Palette’s Sergeant Heath, whose most notable contribution is using his considerable size to break down a door—locked from the inside—at the first murder scene.

This story takes place a year after the events of *Stargate*, following the Abydos mission. It fills in many details the film overlooked, such as how the Stargate was activated without a human computer, the origins of the Goa'uld (Ra’s species), and just how many of them exist.  

The first episode reunites viewers with Jack O’Neill (spelled with two Ls), who is pulled out of retirement by General George Hammond after Apophis—a formidable Goa’uld—launches an attack through the supposedly inactive Stargate, killing four soldiers and abducting one woman. Enter Samantha Carter, a brilliant astrophysicist who insists she should have been part of the original mission and is now determined to go through the Gate. Meanwhile, we learn that Daniel Jackson has married on Abydos and that there are hundreds of potential Stargate addresses to explore. The stakes rise when Apophis kidnaps Daniel’s wife, making her his queen.  

The second episode sees General Hammond officially establishing the Stargate Command (SGC), assembling nine teams—including SG-1, led by Jack, with Samantha and Daniel as key members. Their first mission takes them to Chulak, a Goa'uld stronghold, in a desperate attempt to rescue Daniel’s wife.

I’ve seen so many negative reviews for *Stay Away, Joe* that I can’t stay silent any longer—this movie deserves a fair shake. Let me share a different perspective.  

Elvis Presley’s films are my ultimate comfort watch for one simple reason: they’re effortless. There’s no intricate plot to keep up with, so I can just kick back, pop open a beer, turn off my brain, and soak up the ridiculous charm and infectious rock 'n' roll vibes from the grooviest decade ever.  

*Stay Away, Joe* absolutely belongs in the "so bad it's good" hall of fame. If you, like me, have a soft spot for cinematic absurdity, this is peak 1960s camp at its finest. It’s gloriously terrible in ways that border on surreal—just when you think it can’t get any more ridiculous, it cranks it up another notch. By the end, you’re left in awe of its sheer audacity, torn between laughter and stunned disbelief.

This film has an impressive cast, but a thriller needs more than big names and endless dialogue. The first act dragged with nothing but conversation—mostly women venting their frustrations at one another.  

With the top five billed actors all female, it’s clear this leans more toward a "chick flick" than a gripping thriller. It feels like something tailor-made for Lifetime.  

After a brief murder scene, the talking resumed, and by the halfway mark, I was completely checked out.  

On a side note, Sally Field looked decades younger than her age here.

I always believed the French were incapable of making a truly bad film—yet here we are, proven undeniably wrong. This movie takes Artemisia Gentileschi’s name in vain, treating her as little more than a loose inspiration rather than honoring her real life or legacy.  

The script is insufferable—pretentious, wooden, and utterly hollow. Its flagrant disregard for historical truth feels especially egregious, even in a genre notorious for twisting facts beyond recognition.
