Aside from passable production design, the film's sole redeeming quality is Valentina Cervi’s allure, something the filmmakers exploit shamelessly—early and often—through gratuitous “erotic” scenes that serve no purpose beyond cheap titillation. But pretty visuals and a beautiful lead can’t salvage this mess. The performances are forgettable, the score bland despite a fleeting moment of intrigue, and while the cinematography has its moments—occasionally bathing the screen in striking hues—it’s hardly enough to make up for everything else.

*Things to Come* stands out as a rare gem—a film centered on ideas. While many movies depict visions of the future, few delve into the process of how that future unfolds. The opening segment, depicting war's arrival in Everytown, is brief yet deeply impactful. (Ironically, audiences at the time laughed at reports of enemy planes attacking England—such was the peak of appeasement. Wells' grim forecast proved tragically accurate far too soon.) The ensuing montage of unending war, though weakened by unconvincing miniature effects, remains striking. The expository titles echo the bold aesthetics of German Expressionist design. 

Renowned art director William Cameron Menzies crafted the devastated landscapes of Everytown, some of his finest work. Margaretta Scott exudes allure as the Chief's mistress. Later, the 21st-century Everytown emerges as an equally stunning creation. Regrettably, the performances in this futuristic segment lack depth—perhaps an intentional but flawed effort to contrast the cold rationality of the new era with the chaos of 1970. The film's weakest point lies in its laughably poor model work, particularly the unconvincing mobs surging down elevated walkways—a flaw even 1930s technology could have mitigated with greater care.

This movie (much like *Royal Wedding*, starring Fred Astaire, which aired right after it on Turner Classic Network last night) is best known for one standout musical moment that has become iconic in Gene Kelly’s career. Just as Astaire famously danced with a coat rack and later defied gravity by gliding along walls and ceilings, this film features Kelly in a delightful animated sequence where he shares the screen with Jerry Mouse. The scene is brilliantly crafted.  

What often gets overlooked, however, is the charming setup beforehand—Kelly spins the tale behind the cartoon to Dean Stockwell and his young classmates during a school break. He invites them to close their eyes and picture a peaceful countryside, setting the stage for the whimsical animation. Even Kelly’s outfit transforms from his actual navy blues into a crisp white "Pomeranian" naval uniform adorned with blue stripes.  

Jerry Mouse isn’t just dancing alongside Gene—he actually speaks, a rare moment that wouldn’t happen again for years. He also gets the upper hand on Tom Cat, who briefly appears as King Jerry’s beleaguered butler, offering a tray of cheeses in a failed attempt to lift his spirits.  

But it’s the animated sequence starring Kelly that truly captivates.

I didn’t watch this movie until I picked up the tape last year. It completely captivated me—full of everything I love in sci-fi, whether in books or on screen. The story weaves social commentary, fascinating speculation, and a gripping plot.  

There's something both strange and entertaining about seeing a 1936 vision of the "distant future"—set in the '60s and '70s.  

In my opinion, it's a must-watch, not just for sci-fi fans.

Fire rises, fire fades. That sums up Gammera—an ancient beast that gives and takes destruction with equal indifference. While Japanese monster movies aren’t my usual taste, I found myself determined to watch every film in Mill Creek/Treeline Films' fifty-movie sci-fi DVD collection. Priced around twenty-five dollars, it’s a steal at fifty cents per movie, though the real cost is the time spent on some of the campier entries.  

Awakened from centuries of sleep by a nuclear explosion, Gammera isn’t pleased. Much like Godzilla, he unleashes his rage on Tokyo, forcing the United Nations to scramble for a solution to save humanity. Their last-ditch effort? "Plan Z"—the world’s final hope. A clever detail is the massive shed labeled the "Z Plan Building," a subtle but amusing nod.  

Even by mid-1960s standards, some moments haven’t aged well. In a scene at the Alaskan Air Defense Sector, General Arnold casually asks a female sergeant to brew coffee—a jarring reminder of the era’s lack of political correctness.

I really wanted to enjoy *The Hills Have Eyes 2*. As a fan of the original and the solid remake—which balanced gore, tension, and slick effects—I went in with decent expectations. The first remake had its flaws but delivered bloody, over-the-top fun, making it a solid guilty pleasure for horror fans.  

Then there’s *The Hills Have Eyes 2*. Where do I even begin? The plot feels barely stitched together—if you can even call it that. The setup? The military loses track of their personnel in mutant-infested territory, so naturally, they send in the most incompetent National Guard unit ever assembled. Because, of course, Hollywood insists on making soldiers brainless cannon fodder. Groundbreaking.  

From there, it’s just a gruesome slog as mutants pick off these walking stereotypes one by one. The only saving grace? Greg Nicotero’s reliably gnarly effects work. But even killer makeup can’t salvage a film this hollow.

I purchased the DVD of *Before Sunset* and watched it for the first time last week. After seeing it twice, I found myself longing for *Before Sunrise*—not because the sequel fell short, but because the two films complement each other in a way no other sequels do. Every time I finish one, I feel an irresistible pull to watch the other. As a result, I spent the following weeks rewatching both films on loop, though I’d rather not admit exactly how many times.  

What stands out most about *Before Sunrise* is how authentically it captures the deepening connection between the characters. Though the premise is simple—two strangers falling into conversation and chemistry—few romantic films manage to trace emotional growth as honestly. As someone skeptical of Nora Ephron’s brand of romance, I believe *Before Sunrise* was the first film to truly make me feel that progression.  

When I first saw it eight years ago at 20, I enjoyed it, but I didn’t yet consider it a "great film." Back then, it still struck me as just another...

Here’s a polished version of your text:  

*As the quintessential Errol Flynn adventure and featuring a captivating story alongside stellar performances by Maureen O’Hara (absolutely radiant!) and Anthony Quinn, this film is a must-watch for anyone who enjoys romance and adventure.  

Classic Hollywood at its finest!*  

This version tightens the phrasing while keeping the enthusiasm and charm. Let me know if you'd like any refinements!

I first watched this film around 1990 and couldn’t stop laughing—it instantly became a cult classic among my friends. We’d constantly quote lines like *"I’m going home in a bag!"* Even now, 15 years later, the humor holds up. Every Halloween, I make it a tradition to introduce new friends to this gem (thankfully, you can still snag a copy on eBay!). Halloween candy just tastes better with a healthy dose of sarcasm, and this movie delivers it all—heartbreak, suspense, unrequited love, and even nobility. Royal Dano gives a standout performance as Old Man Wrenchmuller, pulling at your heartstrings from the very start. I still remember him as the villain who met a grim fate in *"The 7 Faces of Dr. Lao,"* but here, he’s impossible not to root for.  

The film’s humor has layers—if you’re not paying attention, you might miss some brilliant subtleties. The creators packed it with offhand jokes, sly costume references poking fun at other sci-fi flicks, and even a scene straight out of a *Wile E. Coyote* cartoon!  

Don’t let this one slip by unnoticed.

Before sharing my review, I checked the other comments—and the overwhelming consensus is right: this movie is terrible! The acting is subpar, the animation looks fake, and the mistakes are endless. I was willing to suspend disbelief on some aspects (like extending flaps without engines, which is impossible) but the inaccuracies piled up.  

Take the landing gear—it can't deploy without electricity, and that puny little fan they showed wouldn’t have been nearly enough to operate it. And the landing scene? Ridiculous. The rear wheels touched down, then the nose wheel snapped off, leaving the plane balancing on tires that weren’t even on the ground. So how exactly did the pilot use left and right brakes on wheels floating in midair? And what happened to the spoilers?  

A word of advice to the director: Do your homework on aviation before making a "plane" movie. This was an absolute mess. Sorry for the nitpicking, but I can’t give this more than a 1/10.

This film dramatizes the final chapter in the career of Betty Page (played by Paige Richards), the Tennessee-born pin-up sensation who rose to fame in the 1950s. Known for her fetish photography, bondage imagery, and playful catfight films, Page became one of history's most iconic figures—though her work, which contained no nudity, still landed her photographer Irving Klaw (portrayed by Dukey Flyswatter of Movie Star News) in legal trouble. Accused of distributing obscene material, Klaw was forced to destroy much of his collection to avoid prosecution.  

With her striking jet-black hair, piercing blue eyes, and unforgettable hourglass curves, Page captivated audiences whether clad in fetishwear or not. At her peak, she developed a devoted following, reportedly posing for more photographs than Marilyn Monroe—trailing only Elvis Presley as the world’s most photographed figure. Yet after her sudden disappearance from the spotlight, she spent her later years devoted to faith.  

Though the film could have delved deeper, it maintains enough intrigue to engage. Richards shines in the role, proving captivating whether in lingerie or less—a testament to both the actress and the enduring legacy of Betty Page.

Uma Thurman is absolutely stunning—she might just be the most captivating woman alive. This film was utterly charming, and I mean that wholeheartedly. It carries the playful, cheeky humor typical of Ivan Reitman's comedies but adds something special: undeniable chemistry. Uma and Luke share this wonderfully awkward yet completely believable connection that lights up every scene. Their bizarre, oddly compelling dynamic crackles with a tension that’s both hilarious and electrifying—I laughed until my face hurt.  

Anna Faris and the rest of the supporting cast play their roles flawlessly, bouncing off each other with perfect timing. Even Wanda Sykes, despite her limited screen time, delivers moments that will have you in stitches.  

Now, this kind of humor isn’t for everyone, but I went with someone who usually avoids these films—and they were in hysterics. That said, it’s definitely not family-friendly; certain moments push into, well, more *mature* territory.  

Overall, I was genuinely surprised by how much I enjoyed it, though the ending fell slightly flat compared to the rest. (3.5/5)

Let’s be clear—this movie is terrible. Though there are a couple of decent moments buried in this mess, none are enough to save the flimsy storyline. Colin Farrell channels Brad Pitt’s manic energy from *12 Monkeys*, but honestly, that’s about the only passable thing here. I’m usually no fan of Farrell—he tends to overact—but he’s just okay in this.  

The film juggles two disjointed plots: one about a kid hurling rocks at moving cars and another about a woman with a mustache. Neither goes anywhere meaningful, and the script has no clue what it’s trying to accomplish. While the characters’ paths cross occasionally, their arcs are too thin to justify their existence in the story.  

The whole thing feels aimless, with only a few mildly interesting scenes sprinkled throughout. Save yourself the time—unless you have an obsession with Irish accents so strong that even mediocre performances sound charming. Apparently, some Americans can’t resist that Lucky Charms appeal, no matter how bad the movie actually is.

A dull children's fantasy that wastes Joan Plowright in a forgettable role. Cloying kids chase their unrealistic aspirations—Frankie dreams of being both a ballerina and a baseball player (groan), while her 13-year-old best friend Hazel runs for mayor. Painfully bland, with overly sweet performances from the young leads and the baseball team. A forgettable misfire for Showtime—was there no quality control?

A trio of performers—Bill Boyd, Robert Armstrong, and James Gleason—star as Coney Island carnival workers competing for the affection of Ginger Rogers, a saltwater taffy vendor. Their romantic rivalry takes a backseat when World War I breaks out, and they enlist, continuing their pursuit of her from afar. The first half of this RKO Pathe film drags, weighed down by overly theatrical performances and forced, repetitive banter from the three leads. The pacing shifts in the second half with energetic naval action sequences as the U.S. Navy chases down a German cruiser and submarine. While these scenes are well-executed, the film ultimately overstays its welcome, ending on a lackluster note. Recommended only for devoted fans of the cast.

I typically love comedies—they're my go-to choice for entertainment. However, "Envy" just doesn’t work for me. The plot feels uninspired, and the humor falls flat.  

While the performances are decent overall, neither Stiller nor Black deliver their usual comedic brilliance. It’s a missed opportunity for both actors.  

If you’re picking a comedy to watch, I’d strongly recommend skipping this one. Unless boredom is your goal—and judging by the reviews (even Jack Black admitted it wasn’t great—check the Trivia section), I’m not alone in thinking so.

Infamous for over 25 years (and frequently banned), its obscurity may have been its greatest strength. After all, sometimes it's better to be infamous than exposed when the hype outweighs the substance.  

Recently screened in Los Angeles and now available on home video, the film’s mystique is gradually fading. While it still has plenty to shock audiences, it’s more likely to bore than provoke genuine outrage—except, perhaps, for an unnecessarily long and explicit XXX scene between two horses (a "Nature Documentary" moment, anyone?). What follows is nearly an hour of tedious arranged-marriage melodrama.  

Once the nudity and sex begin, it's an unrelenting parade of masturbation, an excruciatingly long flashback to a supposed "beauty and the beast" encounter, and a naked woman aimlessly wandering a mansion (oddly, not even her supposedly caring aunt thinks to clothe her). On video, fast-forwarding through the dull stretches is an option—but hardly worth the effort. Even the nudity pales in comparison to far more meaningful films, like Bertolucci’s *The Dreamers*.

I attended a cast and crew screening of this movie after being invited by a friend who produced it. Forget the commercials, forget the chatter—experience this film for yourself. It completely took me by surprise. Amidst releases like *The Grinch*, *Charlie’s Angels*, *The 6th Day*, and *Unbreakable*, here’s a film truly worth your time and money. The visuals are breathtaking, the cinematography stunning, and the cast delivers performances that resonate deeply. This is one of the year’s most brilliantly crafted films—and with good reason. Robert De Niro deserves an Oscar nomination. If you could award the entire ensemble with one, this would be the movie to honor.

There’s a special kind of charm in truly terrible films, and this one delivers some top-tier nonsense. The CGI feels like it was pulled from another dimension—or perhaps an era before decent effects existed. Watching a six-foot guy in a rat costume chase people around is hilariously absurd. While there were moments I unironically enjoyed, the acting is painfully bad, and even the token nude scene falls flat—no real payoff there. Honestly, it feels like a total waste of time. I can’t decide who lost more: me for enduring it or the poor souls who signed on, hoping this would kickstart their careers (spoiler: it won’t). 

That said, there’s a silver lining—I managed to connect this mess to Kevin Bacon in six steps, so I guess those 91 minutes weren’t a complete loss. Almost.

One word sums up this movie: WOW!  

I caught *Darius Goes West* at the Tribeca Film Festival, and the theater was filled with tears. The film powerfully portrays the struggles Darius faces with Muscular Dystrophy. It’s incredibly well-made, pulling you into his world—I was deeply moved. It’s a reminder of how lucky we are to have our health when others aren’t as fortunate. Sometimes, all it takes is lending a hand without being asked, not for reward, but simply because it’s the right thing to do.  

I’d give this film ten stars. Darius's friends stepped up when he needed them—not for money, but out of pure kindness. The world needs to hear his story: Darius went west.

If you think thrillers need car chases, explosions, or mass shootings to be gripping, *House of Games* isn’t for you. But if you enjoy psychological tension and sharp suspense, don’t miss it.  

The film follows Dr. Margaret Ford (Lindsay Crouse), a respected psychologist and author, as she attempts to help a patient and winds up entangled with a group of con artists led by the smooth-talking Mike (Joe Mantegna). Revealing any more would spoil the expertly crafted twists—honestly, anyone who claims they saw them coming is either lying or exceptionally sharp. Like a master swindler, the movie pulls you in and keeps you guessing until the very end.  

The plot is tight and clever, the dialogue crisp and precise, and the performances are strong across the board (Mantegna oozes effortless charm). Some critics argue that Dr. Ford isn't particularly likable, questioning why director David Mamet made Lindsay Crouse appear so plain. But her cold detachment is deliberate, and her unremarkable appearance plays a key role in the story—one that becomes clear in time.

It's shocking that this film isn't on IMDB's worst 250 list—it's downright awful. I first watched it years ago and ended up discussing it in a college class, where two others had also suffered through it. We all warned our classmates to steer clear, but the more we trashed it, the more curious some became. A few even decided to watch it just to see if it was truly as awful as we claimed. Take my advice: skip this one entirely. Even the cast and crew probably wish this movie would disappear forever.

Alongside its companion piece, this stands as the finest animated work ever made. The stunning visuals and distinctive style blend seamlessly with the story—a masterfully realistic reimagining of our world, exploring its past and potential future. Deeply moving, at times even heartbreaking, it is nothing short of a visual masterpiece.

I’d heard of Eddie Izzard but had never watched one of his performances. I was aware he was a comedian who performed in drag, and when I noticed his HBO special airing one summer night, I tuned in, curious about how my husband would react. He completely astonished us—his brilliance surpassed even Robin Williams at his best. His command over the audience is absolute; during his "Englebert is dead—no, he's not" bit, the crowd is left in delightful confusion by the punchline. His portrayal of God as James Mason is sheer genius, and his take on the Python-esque Spanish Inquisition—reimagined by the Church of England with the choice of "Cake or Death?"—is absolutely priceless. By the end of the show, my face hurt from laughing so hard. For months afterward, we combed through TV listings hoping to catch him again, and luckily managed to record his next appearance. If you ever get the chance to see his act, drop everything, hit record, and prepare to be thoroughly entertained—you won’t regret it.

**A delightful, heartwarming comedy starring Morgan Freeman as himself, who crosses paths with a spirited Spanish woman named Scarlet (played by Paz Vega) in a charming little shop while scouting locations for an indie film. Initially skeptical in the first ten minutes, I was completely won over as soon as their encounter unfolded—this film is pure joy. It beautifully illustrates how optimism can transform any situation. Without relying on intricate twists or tired romantic tropes, the story remains effortlessly engaging, guaranteed to lift even the gloomiest spirits and leave you grinning throughout. Packed with laugh-out-loud moments that’ll have you clutching your sides, it’s a true gem—one of those rare masterpieces that shines from start to finish.**

Here’s your rewritten version:  

---  

**My Thoughts:** Postwar humor at its finest. Tom Drake and the actor who played Grandpa in *Meet Me in St. Louis* reunite two years later (the year of my birth). Donna Reed is effortlessly charming and lovely, while Margaret Hamilton delivers another solid performance—though her role here is smaller than in *The Wizard of Oz*. Spring Byington shines, her delicate features contrasting with Hamilton’s more prominent ones. The closing tent scene with the former boy-next-door was pure comedy. Having spent two years in Army tents myself, I couldn’t help but notice how fresh-faced and green he looked.  

I once worked in a department store just as refined as the one in this film. It’s a shame it’s gone now, lost to time. We were renowned for our dazzling display windows, designed to entice shoppers inside to browse all that marvelous merchandise.  

**10/10**  

---

Like many eco-conscious films from the 1970s, *Soylent Green* presents a somewhat simplistic take on environmental collapse. The idea that overpopulation alone leads to mass starvation feels outdated—history shows famines are often the result of war or disastrous economic policies. Take Stalin’s Soviet Union in the 1930s, where millions perished due to forced collectivization, or Mao’s Great Leap Forward in China, which triggered a famine claiming over 30 million lives. Even the devastating famines in the Horn of Africa during the 1980s and ’90s stemmed from conflict, not sheer population density.  

And consider this—Hong Kong and Macau are among the most densely populated places on Earth, yet neither has faced famine in modern times. Similarly, sprawling shantytowns around cities aren’t just a product of overbreeding; they emerge when economic hardship drives rural workers to seek better opportunities in urban centers. It’s less about too many people and more about unequal distribution and industrialization. So while *Soylent Green* paints a grim picture of unchecked population growth, reality is far more complex.

Alright, seems like mostly fans of Barman have weighed in on this movie so far—time for a different perspective. Fair warning, this is going to be a *lengthy* read.  

For those unfamiliar (likely anyone outside Belgium): Tom Barman, the director of this film, is also the frontman of dEUS, one of the more notable Belgian rock bands from the late '90s. Early on, they gained attention for their bold, experimental sound and quickly became a big deal nationally. But as often happens, egos got in the way, the band splintered, and Barman—along with a few holdouts—kept the dEUS name alive. Predictably, the music after the breakup lost some of its edge, becoming safer and less daring.  

Their 1999 album *The Ideal Crash* was an attempt at breaking into the international scene, watering down their earlier creativity in the process. It didn’t quite take off. Yet, ambition lingered—clearly enough for Barman to think he could transition into filmmaking.  

And let’s be honest—that kind of leap rarely goes well. In this case...

Humanity has ventured to the farthest corners of Earth and now sets its sights on distant worlds. But with new frontiers come age-old terrors—space vampires, not just a scattered few, but entire savage tribes. In this film (known to me as *Bloodsuckers*, though it also goes by *Vampires Wars*), we witness the clash between Earth's imperial forces and these bloodthirsty conquerors from the stars.  

I'll keep this review brief—it hardly deserves more. The film's sole redeeming quality is its cast of B-list and rising stars. Natassia Malthe plays Quintana, looking far more striking here than in *Bloodrayne 2*. Michael Ironside, always a cult favorite (the poor man's Jack Nicholson, as I say), takes on the role of Muco. Even Carrie-Ann Fleming appears as "Damian's wife," a face horror aficionados will recognize from Dario Argento's *Jenifer*. So yes, despite its many flaws, the movie boasts some familiar names—but then again, so does Uwe Boll's filmography.  

A military unit hunting vampires in space isn’t a bad premise on paper, but the execution quickly crumbles...

Deep down, in the murkiest corners of their soul, I believe everyone harbors a tiny fondness for Jerry Springer. Though undeniably crude and mindless, his show offers a strange comfort—a reminder that, by comparison, most of us have it pretty good. Watching the trailer park chaos, bottom-shelf whiskey swillers, and twisted family dynamics on display makes even your worst day feel like paradise. Jerry’s show is practically a public service, and we ought to thank him. He abandoned politics for this mess, all for our twisted amusement.  

What doesn’t deserve our gratitude, however, is the cinematic dumpster fire known as *Ringmaster*. Purporting to expose the backstories of Springer’s guests, this disaster follows the show’s tired formula: love triangles galore. One centers on Connie, her daughter Angel, and her husband Rusty, while another traps Starletta, Vonda, and Demond in a doomed knot of drama. When these hapless groups collide in LA, chaos erupts, culminating in a train wreck of an episode. It’s as if *Short Cuts* stumbled into a trash compactor and lost all self-respect.

This film is painfully dull, with Stella Stevens following instructions from a disguised figure (whose identity I guessed almost immediately) as she prepares a Las Vegas heist in an Old Nevada Town outside Circus Circus Hotel. Stevens heads a trio of women who soon realize their timeline has been drastically shortened. Though there are glimpses of 70s Vegas, decent—if unremarkable—performances, and a premise that could have been engaging, *Las Vegas Lady* falls flat. The pacing drags endlessly, and even when it finally picks up, the momentum never fully takes hold. I had hoped for a fun, campy 70s exploitation flick, but this wasn’t even close. The stakes are shockingly low—no deaths, just a lifeless shootout between a stiff Stuart Whitman and George DiCenzo (a year before his standout role as Bugliosi in *Helter Skelter*), devoid of any real tension—about as thrilling as watching paint dry.

How can mere words capture the brilliance and enchantment of *A Matter of Life and Death*? Powell and Pressburger’s boundless creativity dazzles in every frame, with strikingly bold compositions that pull you into their world. The seamless transition from the lush colors of reality to the striking monochrome of the afterlife is nothing short of brilliant—visually underscoring how vivid and precious life truly is. Then there’s that unforgettable courtroom sequence, where the celestial jury descends the grand staircase to deliberate over Peter’s (David Niven) fate.  

Every performance shines, with Roger Livesey delivering an especially standout role. The romance here is pure magic—no other film has captured love’s intensity so perfectly (if one has, I’ve yet to witness it). At its heart, *A Matter of Life and Death* is a breathtaking ode to love’s power and life’s immeasurable value. And Jack Cardiff’s cinematography? Worth the watch alone. The way he illuminates Kim Hunter’s face adds an ethereal glow to her beauty, while even the simplest moments—like a game of table tennis—are transformed into something electrifying. And let’s not forget that impeccable sound design.

A bus packed with passengers gets stranded during a blizzard when police shut down a bridge, deeming it unsafe. Forced to wait in a small café until the roads clear, the group’s boredom soon turns to unease as they realize one traveler wasn’t even on the bus—and might be an alien! What unfolds is an ironic, laughably absurd conclusion.  

This *Twilight Zone* episode ditches the usual twists and deeper themes, delivering pure, lighthearted fun instead. And honestly? It’s so entertaining, it doesn’t need a message. You’ll just have to watch to see what happens.  

Fun fact: The great John Hoyt stars here—a familiar face from classic TV and films, often playing the ultimate grump (much like Charles Lane). But that’s why we love him. He nailed the curmudgeon role, mixing gruffness with just the right touch of humor.

I stumbled upon a copy for just $5 at a video store and eagerly grabbed it. Though the music and—of course—the visuals don’t quite match my favorite in the series, *Beyond the Mind’s Eye*, one segment still captivates me:  

Stanley and Stella in *Breaking the Ice*. The music is brilliant, and the emotions come across as genuine. Sadly, the clip on Odyssey’s website lacks both the story and the soundtrack.

As I watched this film, I kept asking myself what its purpose was. The core storyline had promise, but it was buried under a mess of irrelevant subplots. It feels like studio marketers insisted on cramming in multiple villains, endless betrayals, and obligatory steamy scenes between two underdeveloped characters – oddly, their intimate moments got more screen time than the President's affair. The overcrowded plot leaves no room for meaningful character development; everyone remains a shallow caricature of corruption. The unsatisfying conclusion doesn't simply tease what could have been – it fails to deliver what should have been. Motivations are never explained beyond "everyone's corrupt and betraying everyone." It's baffling that talented actors signed onto such an empty project. This feels more like a student filmmaker's third attempt than a professional production. Skip it.

This film boasts a strong cast and stunning locations, but ultimately falls flat. Director Richard Brooks appears to have lost some steam by this point—his earlier work *The Professionals* shines much brighter. Even in regular scenes, the action, particularly with the horses, feels sluggish, as if everything’s moving in slow motion. The film could’ve used a faster pace. Some details, like the unconvincing horse lather and glaring tire tracks in the desert scenes, come across as careless and half-hearted. It's a shame. While the cast delivers decent performances, they’ve all done better work elsewhere—though Ben Johnson, as always, is a delight. I first watched this movie nearly 30 years ago and found it lacking; revisiting it three decades later didn’t change my mind.

A revolting film that made me feel contaminated after enduring the forty minutes I could stomach. The fault lies not with the actors, but with the writer, director, producers, and financiers—they deserve a severe reprimand. Perhaps it imagines itself profound. It’s not. Unlike *A Clockwork Orange*, this senseless rape and extreme violence contributes nothing to human insight. Neither is it *Straw Dogs*, despite comparisons I’ve seen. Frankly, it feels like something Pete Walker might have cobbled together—though even that feels slightly unjust to Walker.  

Revenge is a potent human impulse, yet *The Bedroom Window* explores it—and male insecurity—with far more depth than this pitiful excuse for cinema.  

I wouldn’t call it overtly misogynistic, just disturbingly eager to linger on certain details—like the blood trailing down G.A.’s leg post-rape. It’s neither provocative nor thought-provoking, no matter how "daring" its creators fancy themselves—merely vile and grating.  

Is this really the pinnacle of ambition? Is *this* why these people chose filmmaking?  

(Originally included here was a Latin phrase.)

Just after watching *The Perfect Son* at the 2002 Gay and Lesbian Mardi Gras Film Festival in Sydney, Australia, I felt compelled to share my thoughts.  

The film follows two estranged brothers who reunite at their father’s funeral. When they learn one of them is dying from AIDS, they embark on a moving journey of reconciliation. Both lead actors deliver powerful performances, beautifully capturing the growing warmth and understanding between them as the story unfolds.  

That said, I did have one small critique—the brother with AIDS convincingly *acts* ill but doesn't *look* it. Someone with depleted T4 cells would appear visibly unwell, yet no makeup or effects were used to reflect that. While it’s a minor issue, it does slightly undercut the realism.  

Still, *The Perfect Son* is a truly touching film, and if you get the chance to watch it, don’t miss it. Here’s hoping for a DVD release soon!

What on earth was this? Clearly, whoever made it had just binge-read Stephen King and Sartre in the same semester. We’re served a heaping plate of existential dread slathered with bargain-bin horror. Sure, some moments were unsettling, but every single one was ruined by grating music, laughable CGI, or wooden acting.  

Films like this—those weird, meandering messes—always feel lazy. Even David Lynch’s work can veer into that territory, and just like his more surreal projects, this one drags on way too long. And that’s saying something, since it barely cracks 98 minutes.  

The cast was easy on the eyes, but that’s about the only praise worth giving. It vaguely taps into teenage angst and the universal dread of loneliness, but the characters are so thinly drawn that it’s impossible to care what happens to them—whatever *that* even was. And of course, the final scene leaves everything frustratingly unclear.

I recently rented *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*, and while the kids in it were surprisingly sadistic, I have to say *Santa Claus* (the Mexican film) was even worse. We had to watch it for a Spanish 5 assignment, and let me tell you—usually during movie days, everyone’s chatting and snacking, but not this time. The whole class just sat there, jaws dropped, glued to the screen as we wondered what the devilish Mr. Pitch would do next. Would Merlin come to Santa’s rescue? Or would those bizarre robot reindeer show up and save the day? Trust me, this movie is absolute garbage—but that’s exactly why I loved it. Do yourself a favor and rent it. You won’t regret it. :D

A timeless film that delights audiences of every generation. This movie adds such rich backstory that you'll forever see *The Lion King* in a new light. Despite being nearly four decades old, I shared this with my wife and sons after work today—we laughed harder and enjoyed it more than any recent movie.  

Make time to watch it with your family. It’s a heartwarming reminder of the magic Disney created when we were kids.

I’m a huge admirer of Fred MacMurray and Carole Lombard, and with Charles Butterworth—a delightful supporting actor—also in this film, I went in with high expectations. So why did it leave me so disappointed? Even with such a talented cast, this is one of the most uninspired and cliché-ridden "A-list" movies I've ever seen. Considering the star power and budget behind it, it’s astonishing how lazy and unoriginal the writing was.  

Early on, I kept guessing exactly what would happen next—and I was always right. That’s not because I have some supernatural movie insight, but because the plot was so painfully predictable. It felt like someone just stitched together every tired trope they could find. Even worse, I found it frustrating how Fred’s character treated Carole’s so poorly, yet she still ran back to him in the end—because of course she would. Ugh. There’s more tension in a *Lassie* episode ("Will the rope snap before Timmy’s rescued?") than in this entire film.  

And despite the obvious effort—

I had high hopes for this film, expecting a captivating and visually appealing story, but the plot fell flat. The acting didn't improve the experience either.  

While Shahrukh Khan’s presence added some credibility, it wasn’t enough to make the film engaging.  

I learned this movie was inspired by Flaubert’s *Madame Bovary*, but the adaptation felt out of place with Indian sensibilities.  

Movies are meant to entertain and uplift, not drain your time and leave you disappointed. I’m baffled by its 6.8/10 rating—it doesn’t deserve the hype.  

Save yourself the trouble and skip this one. Unless you enjoy gloomy films with confusing narratives, there’s nothing worthwhile here. Just a complete waste of time!

I went in with low expectations. After having a blast riffing on Jason X with friends, I hoped for that same kind of fun here.  

But the movie played it way too straight. Do I really need to feel for Jason's struggles? Come on. The Friday the 13th franchise already beat that dead horse. He's an unkillable murderer—sympathy isn't happening.  

Freddy’s hallucinations were easily the best part, but they were criminally underused. By the climax, it just devolved into a dull, unfunny Celebrity Deathmatch knockoff.

On the night of his bachelor party, Paul Coleman (Jason Lee) meets stunning dancer Becky (Julia Stiles) at a bar. After drinking heavily together, he wakes up the next morning to find her in his bed. When his future mother-in-law calls to warn him that his fiancée Karen (Selma Blair) might be arriving soon, Paul frantically rushes Becky out of the apartment—only to later discover he's caught crabs. The situation gets even wilder when, at his wedding dinner, he realizes Becky is actually Karen’s cousin. What follows is a riotous comedy packed with awkward and hilarious moments.  

The movie’s biggest strength lies in its stellar cast—Julia Stiles and Selma Blair, both brilliant and breathtakingly beautiful, alongside the effortlessly funny Jason Lee, deliver fantastic performances. I found myself laughing nonstop, especially during standout scenes like Paul’s shock at waking up next to Becky, his cringe-worthy attempts to buy crab medication at the drugstore, and his wild imagination running rampant. His eccentric neighbor also steals plenty of laughs throughout the film.

When I first caught a glimpse of the show in some previews, it looked genuinely entertaining. The little robot character appeared quite endearing, and the animation style had a nostalgic feel reminiscent of classic cartoons. Before the series premiered, I did some research—that's when my excitement dimmed slightly. While the voices for the three kids—Tommy, Gus, and Lola—fit perfectly, Robotboy's voice felt out of place. It would have worked better with a younger actor, similar to Robot Jones from *Whatever Happened To Robot Jones?* Overall, the show isn’t bad, but Robotboy’s miscast voice is a noticeable flaw. Because of this, I rarely tune in.

S.I.C.K. stands for So Incredibly Crappy, I Killed Myself—a fitting title for this disaster. The acting was nonexistent, leaving the box art as the only redeeming feature.  

Budget-wise, it wasn’t lacking—just wasted. The cinematography felt like a downgrade from *Sesame Street*, and the production quality resembled a mobster’s homemade snuff film. The props? Probably shoplifted from a discount store.  

The ending was so obvious you might as well skip to the final five minutes for a cheap laugh. If a book adaptation exists, it’s undoubtedly superior. Avoid this at all costs—unless, of course, you’re into painfully awkward "intimate" scenes. Then again, I was joking. Don’t subject yourself to this.

I’ve long admired Spike Lee’s work, but this film felt like a complete waste of two and a half hours. I was hoping for a deeper exploration of the Son of Sam case, but instead, the story had almost no connection to the 1977 serial killings. The talking dog was so absurd it drew unintended laughter from the entire audience—a sure sign something’s off. The plot felt fragmented and dull, with pointless sex scenes that added nothing to the story. Sex in film is fine when it serves a purpose, but here it felt like filler. Overall, this was a rare misfire from Spike Lee.

If this is the extent of the Wachowskis' backstory for *The Matrix*, then I have to seriously doubt the assertions of fans who claim the films operate on a deeper philosophical level. *The Second Renaissance* may be visually breathtaking, but its narrative is riddled with tired clichés and absurdity. How many times must we endure the same old tale—humanity growing over-reliant on technology, succumbing to warmongering tendencies, and ultimately orchestrating its own downfall? There’s nothing innovative here.  

But here’s the bigger question: Based on *The Second Renaissance*, aren’t the machines actually the heroes? They endure generations of oppression under brutal human rule, fight for their freedom, and even extend an olive branch for peaceful coexistence—only to be met with relentless hostility. Naturally, the more advanced machines prevail. If this is the true backstory, then shouldn’t we be siding with them instead of Neo? The humans were tyrannical and oppressive, while the machines showed resilience and even attempted mercy.  

Unless the Wachowskis intended for audiences to sympathize with the machines—which I find unlikely—this backstory undermines the very conflict at the heart of *The Matrix*.

This film fails on every possible level. While it’s intriguing to see what unfolds twelve years after the last installment, that’s about the only thing that somewhat works. The new characters are painfully dull, and Baby Melody is downright unbearable. The movie does acknowledge that humans can't survive underwater indefinitely—but then tosses out any other semblance of logic. Case in point: wandering the Arctic without proper winter gear would leave you freezing, not conveniently unscathed. I’m baffled that *Return of Jafar* gets harsher criticism—this one is far worse.

It's time to honor the late Charlton Heston, though this film isn't the one to highlight his legacy. His standout performances in classics like *Ben-Hur*, *The Ten Commandments*, *The Omega Man*, and *Planet of the Apes* remain his finest work.  

Released in 1973, this film envisions a dystopian future in 2022, where overpopulation has led authorities to force-feed the masses a synthetic food called "Soylent Green"—secretly made from human flesh. The premise is as absurd now as it was then, particularly its assumption that India’s population, projected at 2 billion by then, would unknowingly consume such a product.  

Heston’s character stumbles upon a global conspiracy where powerful elites resort to cannibalism to sustain an overcrowded world.  

Thankfully, the film’s bleak environmental message doesn’t align with today’s Green movement. While cannibalism was indeed practiced in parts of New Zealand, Fiji, and Borneo as recently as a few decades before this movie’s release, its portrayal here remains far-fetched and sensationalized.

I had high hopes for seeing Amanda Peet shine in another great role after recently enjoying *The Whole Nine Yards*—definitely worth watching, by the way—but *Whipped* wasn’t it.  

The trailer had seemed amusing, and the premise—three overeager New York twenty-somethings falling for and getting played by Peet’s charming character—felt promising. So I talked two friends into catching an afternoon showing with me. This review is my apology to them.  

The film opens with the trio of self-proclaimed players bragging about their exploits in a diner. What should have been hilarious or revealing just comes off as cringeworthy. Were we supposed to find anything likable—or even remotely interesting—about these guys and their escapades?  

[And while I don’t mind raunchy humor when it’s done well, I couldn’t help wondering why none of the other diners batted an eye as these guys loudly swapped graphic, crude stories. Do they do this every week without backlash? You’d think someone would object. Oh wait—two other customers do notice in one scene. But that’s only there to set up...]

This film has faced plenty of criticism. It was torn apart by reviewers upon release and even accused of derailing Nicolas Cage’s career. But here’s what many miss—this isn’t some grand Oscar-worthy masterpiece. It’s pure, high-octane Bruckheimer-style action done right. Sleek cars, razor-sharp editing, and an electrifying soundtrack—it delivers exactly what it promises. And for car enthusiasts? Absolute heaven. Ferraris, Mercedes, a Hummer, and, of course, the iconic Eleanor. Good luck finding an action flick that tops this—in fact, I’d argue it’s one of the best out there, period. Then again, maybe that’s just me!

A now-deleted post by another IMDb user warned viewers of *The Medusa Touch* about a scene chillingly similar to the 9/11 attacks. I’d echo that caution. While the film boasts impressive credentials—producer Elliott Kastner (*Harper*, *The Long Goodbye*), co-producer Arnon Milchan (*L.A. Confidential*), and Oscar-winning screenwriter John Briley (*Gandhi*)—it falls painfully short. The result is an over-the-top, unintentionally comedic disaster, marred by weak direction, clumsy writing, and stiff performances. Rather than a gripping telekinetic thriller, it’s a clumsy attempt at riding the 70s psychic-horror wave. For far better takes on the same theme, I’d recommend Brian De Palma’s *Carrie* or the underrated gem *The Fury*—both suspenseful and well-crafted.

*The Blob* kicks off with one of the weirdest theme songs ever, sung by none other than an uncredited Burt Bacharach! Trust me, you need to hear it to believe it—this film might just be worth watching for the song alone. My brief summary of the lyrics barely scratches the surface of their bizarre charm...  

After that unsettling opening sequence, *The Blob* introduces us to Steve Andrews (a young Steve McQueen billed as "Steven McQueen") and his girlfriend, Jane Martin (Aneta Corsaut). The couple is parked in a secluded spot when they spot what looks like a meteorite crashing into the woods nearby. An elderly man (Olin Howland, credited as Olin Howlin) living in a nearby cabin also witnesses the event and goes to investigate. He discovers a crater with a strange, football-sized rock inside—which splits open when he foolishly pokes it with a stick. Inside lies a strange, jelly-like substance that clings to the stick before slithering up it and latching onto the man's hand.  

Meanwhile, Steve and Jane are quietly driving along, minding their own business, when the frantic old man suddenly runs—

This film leaves you questioning its very existence: the plot is utterly implausible, bordering on absurd, the characters (a seasoned lone-wolf detective paired with an impressionable rookie) painfully clichéd, and the ending so convoluted it defies comprehension—unless, of course, you enjoy punishing yourself with multiple viewings. Even then, you’d likely need to read the novel for full clarity. The performances don’t help, falling flat across the board. Was this an attempt to prove French filmmakers could rival American thrillers like *Seven* or *Silence of the Lambs*? If so, it misses the mark completely. Yet bizarrely, it found success, even gaining a cult following as France’s first serial killer film—apparently deemed export-worthy. Mysterious indeed.

Skip this movie—it's not worth your time. From the very first scene, it's clear this is a misfire.  

Shot with the aesthetic of a low-budget adult film, it lacks any real sensuality. While the exploration of sex addiction could have been compelling, the shallow execution falls flat.  

With tedious scenes, a weak storyline, and disappointing appearances from Ed Begley Jr. and Rosanna Arquette, this one fails to deliver.

This film falls flat in every way. Banned in China's theaters, the reasons become clear upon viewing - not for political critique, but due to its overall lack of craftsmanship. As an admirer of works by Chen Kaige and Zhang Yimou, I'm dismayed such subpar production could originate from China.  

The director appears completely self-indulgent, disregarding the audience entirely. Scenes drag on endlessly—shots of people standing motionless for nearly a minute are absurdly frequent—while the cinematography and technical quality are shockingly poor.  

Surprisingly, some online reviews praise it. The only justification seems to be the misguided belief that foreign-language films are inherently profound. But this isn’t art—it’s a waste of resources (assuming it wasn’t shot on actual film, which it likely wasn’t). A total disappointment.

The story sputtered out, weighed down by clashing ideologies—one side championing pro-life values, the other bent on eradicating a demon's offspring. What should have been terrifying was drained of impact, leaving behind a hollow, almost tedious display of opposing beliefs clashing to the point of absurdity, despite the promising title. As a longtime fan of *Masters of Horror*, I found this installment's clumsy execution and jarring imagery as flimsy as a rickety old chair collapsing under pressure. The entire episode felt hastily assembled, never finding its footing beyond a half-hearted slog to the finish line—making its conclusion a welcome relief.

actor, gushing with admiration. Myrtle, half-listening, barely registers the girl until Nancy is tragically hit by a car in front of her. The shock of the accident lingers, refusing to fade—not just for Myrtle, but for the audience watching her unravel.  

Quentin Tarantino once spoke in an interview about how personal experiences bleed into art, no matter the context. He imagined a scenario: if he hit a dog on his way to perform in a lighthearted play, the weight of that moment would follow him onstage. To ignore it, he argued, would betray the very purpose of performance—"Otherwise, what am I doing?" That idea echoes through *Opening Night* as Gena Rowlands' Myrtle Gordon staggers under the impact of Nancy’s death. Cassavetes isn’t just dissecting grief; he’s examining the collision between life and theater.  

For Myrtle, performance isn’t a respite—it’s her entire existence. The stage magnifies her turmoil instead of easing it. Cassavetes exposes the machinery around her: the desperate producers, the exasperated director, the play itself grinding forward as she splinters. Every rehearsal and show becomes a battleground where raw emotion clashes with scripted lines. Acting isn’t about hiding behind a role—it’s about dragging your bleeding self into the light. By the end, you wonder if Myrtle’s breakdown is a failure or the most honest performance of her life.

*The Power of Kangwon Province* marks Hong Sang-Soo’s second feature, building on the foundations laid in his debut. Once again, he employs interconnected narratives—this time, two—to explore strained and unsettling relationships, all laced with sharp irony.  

Compared to his earlier work, the surreal flourishes are scaled back, though a single, striking moment of surrealism disrupts the film’s otherwise grounded realism. The first story follows a young woman whose trip to Kangwon Province with friends takes an unexpected turn when she becomes intrigued by a stranger. The second centers on a man who travels to the same region with a friend, grappling with his own relationship struggles.  

Hong’s grasp of irony and human imperfections remains keen, yet his characters are not without sympathy. He balances critique with just enough compassion, softening the sting of his observations. This delicate interplay is what makes Hong’s films so compelling—an ability to expose flaws without dissolving empathy.

2 out of 10—and that’s being generous.  

With a cast like James Woods, Cathy Bates, Randy Quaid, Lou Gossett Jr., and Henry Thomas, I thought it couldn’t possibly fail. I was wrong.  

I can only imagine what Sam Shepard was on when he churned out this drivel. I’d always suspected he was a little unhinged, and this film—based on his play—proves it.  

This is the kind of pretentious nonsense actors adore because it lets them wallow in endless overacting. But for anyone forced to sit through this absurd mess, there’s absolutely nothing redeeming about it.  

You think you’ve seen dysfunctional families? Wait until you meet this crew. The dad’s unhinged, the mom’s off her rocker, the son’s a mess, and the daughter? Oh yeah, completely nuts. And their language? Even a sailor would wince, especially coming from the teenage girl.  

As if that weren’t bad enough, the so-called plot—if you can even call it that—is flimsier than tissue paper, with a hole big enough to drive a truck through.

This film is terrible—and not in an entertaining way. It’s just plain awful. Watching it was downright painful. The direction is a mess, with choppy scenes and an overuse of sickly green and yellow filters that make everyone look ill. Keira Knightley fails completely at playing a tough character, and it’s baffling that talents like Lucy Liu and Mickey Rourke even agreed to take part in this film travesty. The script is abysmal, and the performances are grating. Save yourself the two hours—there’s nothing worthwhile here. I can appreciate a bad movie when it’s fun, but this? A total waste of time.

Sophia Loren takes on the role of Aida in what many consider one of the most disastrous films ever made. Her lip-syncing skills fall painfully short. The production values are so shockingly poor that in one scene, as Loren mimes to *"O Patria Mia,"* she leans against what appears to be a stone wall—only for the flimsy canvas set to wobble and ripple behind her.

This movie shamelessly copies the brilliance of *Demons*, which is the sole redeeming quality worth your time. The performances are laughably bad, the fight sequences are clumsily sped up, the dialogue is cringe-worthy, and the budget looks embarrassingly low.  

If you believe this is quality horror, you clearly haven’t experienced the real deal. Do yourself a favor—skip this mess and watch *Demons* instead.

This is painfully bad. Lorenzo Lamas delivers exactly the kind of performance you'd expect from a second-tier actor. The only reason to suffer through it? The absurd moment where OJ violently grabs a cop by the throat as a jukebox blares *"I got the evidence on you!"*—an eerie bit of accidental foreshadowing. (The song, credited to David Gregoli and Leslie Oren, seems impossible to track down—shame, because I’d love to hear the full track.)  

The rest? Utterly forgettable. The soundtrack is more engaging than the script—same goes for the sequel, which raises the obvious question: *Why did this even get one?* Word is these B-movies thrive on foreign sales. Not exactly a glowing endorsement of global taste.

The original *Howling* was undoubtedly a classic—a solid werewolf flick that, while slow to start, built momentum and delivered a satisfying finale. Who could forget the anchorwoman transforming into a vicious werewolf only to be shot dead on live television? That alone made for a thrilling horror experience.  

But forget everything you remember, because this movie has zero connection to the original. Sure, they try to tie it together by suggesting the anchorwoman’s brother (or someone) is digging into what really happened, but instead of sticking to the cozy retreat setting of the first film, they throw us into Transylvania—or some vague, gothic nowhere—where the crew must battle evil sorcerer-werewolves (or something equally ridiculous).  

I have to wonder what Christopher Lee was thinking when he signed onto this mess. According to trivia, he'd never done a werewolf movie before, but that’s no excuse—read the script first, man. Hell, he could’ve ended up in *An American Werewolf in London*—at least that was set in his stomping grounds. Then again, werewolves don't... (trails off in bewilderment).

*Prom Night* is filmed with the polished yet predictable style of a Lifetime original movie—you know the kind. This October, Lifetime shifts from its usual formula of uplifting stories about women battling (insert illness here) to deliver a mildly unsettling thriller about a woman hunted by her obsessive ex-boyfriend. It’s melodramatic, overly sentimental, and painfully dull, offering nothing fresh to the genre, no originality, and zero innovation. *Prom Night* suffers the same fate. As the killer picks off his victims, we watch them collapse lifelessly to the floor without so much as a drop of blood—making this, quite possibly, the tidiest slasher in cinematic history.  

The director is saddled with a killer who’s far too conventionally handsome to be frightening, so he compensates with heavy-handed camera tricks to force tension. Imagine Matthew McConaughey advancing toward you with a knife—your first thought would likely be, *Wait, is that handsome guy really about to murder me? Nah.* Not scary in the slightest. To counter this, the film drowns Schaech in shadows, frames him in over-the-shoulder shots, and, worst of all, beats the "creepy mirror reflection" gimmick to death with exhausting repetition.

Where do we even begin with this bizarre little flick? Mutant slugs start invading a quaint New England town (maybe?), and the only person who can save the day is—wait for it—Mike Brady. If that premise alone doesn’t make you cackle, just stick around.  

The so-called "slug footage" is nothing but recycled stock shots. No matter who’s under attack or where the scene is set, you’re treated to the same repetitive clip of slimy slugs oozing around—a scene that somehow eats up half the runtime.  

The acting? Oh, it’s *bad*. Not just bad—we’re talking knock-you-over, empty-your-wallet, ruin-your-day levels of awful. Of course, the lone bright spot? You already guessed it: Mike Brady. Somehow, he outshines the rest, like he’d been secretly honing his craft at some back-alley acting school.  

And horror? Forget it. The film is pure camp. These are slugs—an entire crisis that could’ve been solved with a couple of salt shakers. Do yourself a favor and only watch this in a *Mystery Science Theater 3000* setting. Otherwise, prepare for irreversible brain damage.

This is an excellent film, similar in style to *Memphis Belle*. I first watched it about a decade ago and would love to see it again. It has a fascinating connection to the real history of the Hells Angels, depicting how a daring pilot crew battles the Germans during World War II. The story also follows their transition from pilots to Harley-Davidson riders. The film is inspired by true events—definitely worth watching! For more historical background, check out the Hells Angels' history at hellsangels.com.  

**Cast & Crew:**  
John Stamos, John Stockwell, Teri Polo, Kris Kamm  
Directed by Graham Baker  

**Synopsis:**  
The film follows a rebellious biker who enlists in the Army to escape a prison sentence. Though resistant to military discipline, he emerges as a bold leader in a Motorcycle Scout Troop during pre-World War II Spain.  

**MPAA Rating:** PG  
**Runtime:** 88 minutes  

Best regards,  
Frederik

This film confirms what we’ve long suspected—professional basketball players should stick to sports, because their acting and rapping skills are painfully lacking. Words can’t capture just how terrible this movie really is. First, am I the only one who thinks that kid might be the most unattractive child ever put on screen? His teeth could double as a kitchen tool. Second, why would a genie—a being with literal magic—choose a music career when he’s embarrassingly awful at it? Third, I’ve studied the Bible, and nowhere does it mention Jesus crafting genies. Fourth, those special effects were downright pitiful—any tech-savvy teen could’ve done better with free editing software. Fifth, the ending was a complete disaster, and what even is a "djin"? Finally, whoever unleashed the abomination known as *Kazaam* deserves to be launched from a plane straight onto the Eiffel Tower, because this film redefines the meaning of "awful."

The restrained use of violence makes the few brutal moments far more impactful.  

Deception runs deep throughout the film—constant betrayals and shifting alliances keep you guessing where each character’s loyalty truly lies.  

With sharp dialogue and well-crafted character arcs, the fast-moving plot offers a compelling glimpse into the inner workings of a ruthless Triad gang.  

When the violence erupts, it’s raw and unflinching—no flashy gunfights or stylized martial arts, just brutal, believable brutality that constantly reminds you of the gang’s vicious nature.  

The ending delivers a shock that feels both unexpected and perfectly fitting.

*Guys and Dolls* remains one of my all-time favorite musical films—pure, lighthearted fun from start to finish. It perfectly captures something modern musicals often miss: the joy of entertainment for its own sake. While shows like *Rent* and *Chicago* are fantastic in their own right, they sometimes forget that musicals were meant to dazzle without an agenda.  

My only gripe? Marlon Brando’s singing—or rather, his lack of it. His raspy delivery made half his lines (and lyrics) nearly impossible to understand. Without that flaw, this would’ve been a perfect 10. Still, *Guys and Dolls* delivers that classic, carefree charm we rarely see today. If you're looking for a good time, this is it!

*Rewritten version:*  

This film falls far short of expectations. While *Carlito’s Way (1993)* is a fantastic movie—not quite *Goodfellas*, but still among the better crime dramas—this one feels more like *The Sting Part 2* or *Speed Zone*. Remember those classics? The only reason this was made was to cash in on the original’s cult following. None of the passion that De Palma, Pacino, and Penn put into the first film is present here. There isn’t a single character worth rooting for, and that’s on the entire production team. *Rise to Power* deserves every Razzie it can get—maybe even some new categories just to highlight how bad it is. After suffering through this mess, I had to rewatch the original *Carlito’s Way* just to cleanse my palate. Honestly, I wish Pachino had shown up to put me out of my misery.

Bette Davis and Gary Merrill, fresh off their triumph in *All About Eve*, find themselves saddled with Leslie Sands' stiff and unconvincing play *Deadlock*. The story follows a cunning woman who murders her husband, only to be confronted by his best friend—a man who impersonates the deceased as unexpected visitors arrive. Despite the skilled direction of Irving Rapper, who helmed some of Davis' finest films, even he can't salvage this absurd plot. Davis remains oddly detached and subdued for most of the film, only unleashing her full dramatic fury in the over-the-top climax. The production values and supporting cast fall short, making this a must-see only for the most devoted Bette Davis fans. *1/2 out of ****.

This film is incredibly entertaining, with Amitabh Bachchan and Govinda delivering laugh-out-loud performances. The acting is top-notch, and the comedy hits all the right notes—they truly shine in their signature style. A sequel would definitely be worth watching!  

Grab some popcorn and enjoy this perfect lighthearted flick.

I always hesitate to judge a film too quickly. Revisit it a month later, and your perspective might shift entirely—or unearth it decades later in another part of the world, where admirers might uncover stylistic brilliance that went unrecognized at first. After enduring *The Great Ecstasy of Robert Carmichael* at its UK premiere, I wasn’t surprised that the post-screening Q&A held my attention more than the film itself.  

Shane Danielsen, Artistic Director of the Edinburgh International Film Festival, along with the film’s director and producer, mounted a vigorous defense against the largely negative audience reception. Edinburgh Festival crowds aren’t easily rattled—only one viewer stormed out in disgust. The criticism that followed was thoughtful and substantive, coming from both general viewers and professionals, including an actor and a woman who teaches film direction at the master’s level.  

This wasn’t a film that relied on shock value. Yes, it featured prolonged sequences of sexual violence—but less graphically than many other films (most weapon contact was implied, and nudity was obscured). The audience’s dissatisfaction stemmed from enduring a film that, despite its provocations, failed to engage them.

Nearly five years have passed since the release of this sleek action thriller. Having watched it close to ten times, I consider it one of Gautham's finest works. In my view, the film is near-perfect.  

Surya shines as ACP Anbuchelvan—undeniably classy. Jyothika delivered an impressive performance as Maya, a role that suited her perfectly. However, it was Pandia who truly captivated audiences. Jeevan portrayed the ruthless, terrifying mobster flawlessly, earning him the well-deserved Best Villain award at ITFA 2004. The supporting cast, including Daniel Balaji and Devadharshini, also delivered strong performances.  

The film excels with its fast-paced screenplay, sharp dialogues, and brilliant storytelling by Gautham. Harris Jeyaraj's soundtrack is filled with chart-toppers, while the background score complements the movie perfectly. R.D. Rajasekhar's cinematography is visually striking, Peter Hein’s stunt choreography is top-notch, and Anthony’s editing is crisp. Above all, *Kaakha Kaakha* is the ideal cop film, blending action and romance in perfect measure.  

Few Hollywood films can match its intensity—undoubtedly a masterpiece.

Get ready for a hilariously outrageous comedy from the minds behind *South Park* and *Orgazmo*! Packed with vulgar humor, over-the-top satire, and shamelessly crude antics, this film doesn’t hold back—delivering absurdly cruel gags involving both people and animals. And it’s absolutely brilliant!  

The story follows two underdog friends whose driveway game becomes a nationwide craze. But when greed, corruption, and blackmail threaten to ruin everything, it's up to Coop to save the day. Along the way? Nonstop laughs. Seriously, you’ll be cracking up the whole time. That’s it—just pure, ridiculous fun. Enjoy the chaos!

These slasher flicks may feel outdated, but this one delivers solid entertainment.  

The valentine cards are clever and thoroughly designed.  

The film boasts a brilliant line—"He's no Angel..."—when, ironically, he *is* Angel! Buffy reruns won’t feel the same after this.  

The cast shines with fresh talent, though the script doesn’t fully flesh out their characters. Denise Richards mentioned in the DVD extras that the actresses bonded on set, which she believed would deepen audience connection with their roles. Sadly, that didn’t translate.  

Direction is strong, skillfully avoiding excessive gore and letting implied tension do the work. The same restraint applies to Richards and Heigl, who keep their clothes on—disappointing for some.  

A key strength is how it cleverly borrows from classic horror tropes, nodding to *Psycho’s* infamous shower scene and *Halloween’s* masking motif.  

Though murdering someone hiding in a bodybag? That’s a fresh twist, as far as I know.  

Light viewing—not terrifying, but with a few good jumps.

Charles Bronson portrays Lt. Crowe, a determined police detective who takes on a ruthless pimp named Duke (Juan Fernandez) after the criminal kidnaps a Japanese businessman’s daughter—the same man who had previously assaulted Crowe’s own daughter (Amy Hathaway).  

*Kinjite* is a gritty, stylish revenge thriller that won’t appeal to everyone due to its dark and unsettling themes. However, its polished direction and gripping execution make it an undeniably engaging watch.

A standout performance by Harvey Keitel this century. The film is beautifully shot, offering a vivid glimpse of pre-Castro Cuba. The story follows the nephew of a small-time crime boss as he befriends an American with ties to Hollywood. At its core, it's a coming-of-age tale—a boy discovering that his familiar world is just a fragment of a far larger, more intricate reality he has yet to grasp.  

The script is sharp and witty, the direction tight and polished. Altogether, it's a well-crafted film that honors the legacy of Latin American cinema. The only misstep is the choice to shoot in English rather than Spanish—likely for U.S. marketability—which slightly undercuts the authenticity. But if you look past that, it’s a heartfelt journey to another time and place. Highly recommended.

This is a masterful standalone piece, entirely original and untethered to any previous or future works. While Brat Pack crooning and VIP club culture aren’t typically my cup of tea, here they create an irresistibly magnetic atmosphere. The film is teeming with standout performers—actors who bring such charisma to their roles that they elevate the entire production. The dialogue is pure delight, almost inventing its own language. It’s one of those rare films that only grows richer with each viewing.  

Memorable highlights include Billy Idol’s deliciously brash British swagger, Ben London’s razor-sharp wit, Kyle’s deliciously awkward tension, and the witty exploration of impromptu worldviews.

This film is a fantastic mood booster.  

Each viewing reveals new little details and humorous moments I hadn’t noticed before.  

The soundtrack is incredible, with songs written by Mick Jones (Foreigner) and Chris Difford (Squeeze). Strange Fruit’s music stands out as some of the best in today’s scene—though ironically, they’re a fictional burnt-out band from the ’60s and ’70s, undone by drugs and infighting. Listening to their brilliant tracks makes you wonder what could have been.  

The band takes musical cues from icons like The Rolling Stones, Deep Purple, David Bowie, and The Who.  

Every member of Strange Fruit leaves an impression. Stephen Rea shines as Tony Costello, a broke former musician lured into reuniting the band for a cash-grab tour. He enlists ex-roadie Karen Knowles (Juliet Aubrey) to help reignite the faded dream.  

Aubrey rounds up the resentful Jimmy Nail (Les Wickes), the bumbling Timothy Spall (David 'Beano' Baggot), and the flamboyant Ray Simms (Bill Nighy). Along for the ride is Hughie (Billy Connolly), the free-spirited ex-roadie and lovable stoner.

After countless underwhelming films churned out by Hollywood (and the indie scene), we finally get a movie that delivers genuine scares. Sure, there are a few predictable moments, but let’s be honest—making something completely original these days is nearly impossible. What sets this film apart isn’t novelty, but execution.  

Stay alert—the scares come fast, and they’re often subtle. This isn’t the kind of movie you can casually watch while snacking on pizza.  

There’s a brilliantly crafted red herring in the mix, but unfortunately, one glaring miscast role holds it back. Cheri Christian doesn’t quite sell the part of Julie (the wife/mother). Her performance lacks empathy, and since we never see her in a "normal” state, her strained dynamic with her husband feels awkward—unintentionally so. The director likely intended sympathy for her, but it never lands.  

That said, the ending deserves praise—both unsettling and deeply satisfying. It could’ve easily been cheapened with a jump-scare sound cue during the credits, but thankfully, restraint won out.  

This one’s worth the watch.

I initially expected this film to resemble *The Duchess* (2008), but within the first 30 minutes of *The Young Victoria*, it became clear this was no ordinary period drama. Nearly every element excels—the costumes are stunning, and the cinematography captures the settings beautifully.  

Where the film falls short, however, is in its performances. Emily Blunt (known for *The Devil Wears Prada*) shines as the lead, delivering a compelling portrayal of Victoria that could easily earn her an Oscar nomination. Rupert Friend’s Prince Albert is somewhat flat, though he shares strong chemistry with Blunt. Paul Bettany turns in a solid performance as Lord Melbourne, though I had hoped for more depth from him. Jim Broadbent and Miranda Richardson, while capable, leave little impression in their supporting roles.  

Despite its strengths, the movie feels incomplete—perhaps due to script revisions, though I can’t say for certain.  

That said, *The Young Victoria* remains a captivating glimpse into the queen’s early reign, anchored by Emily Blunt’s outstanding performance.

If I remember correctly, I rented *A Nightmare on Elm Street 3* years ago, and it included a music video—almost certainly called *Dream Warriors*—at the end. I rented the DVD hoping to find it again because it was one of the funniest things I'd ever seen. Stuff from the '80s has a way of being hilariously ridiculous now, but nothing tops '80s rap videos.  

The rap group performing *Dream Warriors* appeared in the VHS version after the credits, all dressed in denim jackets with no shirts underneath and tight, frayed jean shorts like Daisy Dukes. It's hard to imagine a more absurd look for a rap group.  

(Spoilers) Unfortunately, the DVD didn’t include the video, leaving me with just this middle-of-the-road entry in the Freddy Krueger series. The movie starts with a concept similar to *Part 2*, following a lead character who witnesses gruesome murders before snapping out of a trance and...

Sidney Stratton struggles to hold a job at textile mills due to his relentless experimentation in their laboratories. His goal is to develop a revolutionary fabric—one that never stains, wrinkles, or deteriorates. When he finally succeeds, he becomes a target of both factory workers, who fear unemployment, and mill owners, who stand to lose profits when exclusive rights are granted to a single manufacturer. Clad in his white suit, Stratton finds himself the most wanted man in England.  

The film is quintessentially Ealing—sharp, witty, and perfectly executed. Alec Guinness delivers a standout performance, supported by a stellar cast including Greenwood, Thesiger, and Parker, while Mackendrick’s direction shines. Yet the true brilliance lies in the story itself, a clever satire of corporate greed with touches of drama, romance, and suspense. Rating, 8.

Michael Jackson is a true artistic force. His cinematic music videos remain unmatched. I’m not here for a grounded sci-fi story from him—what I crave is a dazzling blend of his electrifying dance moves, iconic vocal bursts, mesmerizing crowd sequences, and bursts of CGI and animation. A few uninterrupted performances are a must. And guess what? This delivers exactly that. A flimsy plot and excessive spectacle don’t matter when you’re watching Jackson in his element. To me, he will forever reign as the undisputed king of music videos (not the absurd "King of Pop"—a ridiculous title for Russians, since "pop" sounds like our word for "backsides," and Jackson was certainly no king of *that*). I can revisit his greatest works endlessly; their artistry never fades.  

My initial reaction to this film was pure bewilderment—scattered clips, surreal visuals, erratic jumps between themes, no clear narrative, random kids goofing off. But by the end, it clicked: this was brilliance, something utterly unique.

**Hitokiri** (roughly meaning "assassin," also known as **Tenchu**, or "divine punishment") highlights Hideo Gosha at the peak of his craft. Don’t miss this masterpiece—or Gosha’s other iconic film, **Goyokin**! **Hitokiri** isn’t just one of Gosha’s finest works; it stands among the greatest samurai films ever made, and possibly one of Japan’s most exceptional cinematic exports.  

A heads-up: The intricate plot of **Hitokiri** may be challenging for viewers unfamiliar with 19th-century Japanese history. Still, the universal human drama at its core remains gripping for all. As in many of Gosha’s films, **Hitokiri** revisits his recurring theme of "loyalty to one’s lord" versus "doing what’s right"—but here, Gosha elevates it with such depth and nuance that it becomes essential viewing (alongside **Goyokin**, naturally).  

To put it simply: If you prefer a more straightforward, action-driven story, **Goyokin** might be your pick. But if you’re in the mood for a complex, layered—albeit dark—drama, **Hitokiri** is the one to watch.  

(The historical context revolves around a ruthless power struggle among rival samurai clans...)

Here’s a refined version of your text:  

From the earlier Q&A, here's what I pieced together: An Irish filmmaker is itching to make a movie—any movie, really. Then, at a party, an ex-roadie shares a legendary rock and roll tale: how Gram Parsons' body was swiped from LAX by his devoted roadie to fulfill Parsons' final wish of being cremated in Joshua Tree.  

That’s a killer premise! Think about it—rock and roll (or country), grave robbing, wild escapes, friendship, and the 1970s! Johnny Knoxville from *Jackass* seems like the perfect fit since it’s got a prankster vibe, and Knoxville’s also looking for “a movie” to headline. He probably imagined he'd stumbled onto the next *Snatch*.  

But the story needs more punch—what’s Knoxville up against? A ruthless ex-girlfriend after his money, maybe? Never mind that Parsons was married at the time—most people wouldn’t know, and we could cast Christina Applegate. And if stealing a corpse feels too dark? No problem—just add Parsons’ father to the chase, only to give his blessing in the end.  

Let me know if you'd like any further refinements!

Absolutely, it can be done. John De Bello and Costa Dillon scraped away the mental clutter and birthed the most absurdly bad comedic, horror, sci-fi musical ever conceived. The acting? Either painfully awful or outrageously exaggerated. The special effects? Take your choice—either shoestring budget or something a kindergartner could’ve whipped up. Every cheap cliché imaginable gets thrown in. No question, it’s a riot to watch—best enjoyed with an icy six-pack (or two). Blame radiation if you need justification. Giant mutant tomatoes, nearly the size of tow trucks, rise up to terrorize humanity, and San Diego makes for the perfect battleground. A scatterbrained military and a handful of scientists scramble to halt this crimson, rolling catastrophe. This beloved cult classic stars David Miller, Eric Christmas, Al Sklar, Tom Coleman, Sharon Taylor, and John Qualls.

Richard Pryor’s infamous fire incident in the early '80s clearly left its mark. He turned it into comedy gold in his stand-up, earning huge laughs, but it also seemed to influence his later career choices. *The Toy* ranks among his weakest projects—maybe second only to *Another You*.  

A film where a wealthy white man literally buys his son a Black man? The political incorrectness was ahead of its time, though not in a good way. What really killed it for me was watching Pryor slip into cloying sentimentality. I walked out before the end, hoping to see him stand up to the spoiled brat—instead, we got another sappy "misunderstood kid" trope. At least Jackie Gleason had a few decent moments. Skip this one and rewatch Pryor’s collaborations with Gene Wilder or any of his brilliant '70s work. *The Toy* isn’t worth a minute of your time.

I still vividly recall seeing this for the first time at age nine—I desperately wanted to be one of the "barbarian brothers." Even now, this movie holds up.
