A unique touch was how brief the fight scenes were, suggesting the brothers dispatched their foes with effortless skill! You get thrilling chases, an intense cage match, a fearsome dragon, and of course, a classic bar brawl.  

Sure, the acting isn't great, which keeps it from a perfect score, and the plot has drawn plenty of criticism. But I find it refreshingly original—few films in this genre boast such creative storytelling or vibrant dialogue.  

Without a doubt, it’s worth watching.

MINOR SPOILER  

This underrated Stephen King gem delivers solid chills despite its flaws. While far from perfect—Dale Midkiff and Denise Crosby’s performances fall flat, and the film struggles to balance mystical elements like the Micmac burial ground, Rachel’s ailing sister, and the ghostly Victor Pascow—its sheer audacity makes up for the messy execution.  

Few horror films nail true discomfort like *Pet Sematary*. With its unapologetically grim twists, from the undead toddler to Zelda’s grotesque portrayal, it revels in bad taste and shocks that stick. It’s brutal, over-the-top, and politically incorrect—yet it digs under the skin in ways tamer horrors can’t.  

Fred Gwynne’s standout performance and Mary Lambert’s sharp direction elevate it further, even with the campy finale. A must for horror lovers craving something genuinely unsettling. **7.5/10**

Deliverance is a gripping, unsettling, and often disturbing story by James Dickey, masterfully adapted into film by John Boorman. The narrative follows four businessmen, fueled by bravado and machismo, as they embark on a weekend canoe trip deep in the remote mountains. There, they confront the darkest aspects of humanity—brutality, depravity, and violence—in an environment stripped of civilization.  

What begins as a quest for adventure quickly spirals into a harrowing journey through a savage wilderness, where every turn brings new horrors. The film stands as one of the most visceral and nightmarish experiences ever put to screen—each ordeal the men endure is something you pray never to face yourself.  

Beyond its raw intensity, *Deliverance* remains a landmark in cinema. John Boorman’s finest work (rivaled only by *Zardoz* and *Excalibur*), the film’s influence is undeniable, with iconic scenes endlessly referenced and imitated. From the haunting brilliance of the "Dueling Banjos" soundtrack to the infamous "squeal like a pig" assault sequence, every moment lingers in the mind. The performances are electrifying, ensuring this film’s place as a timeless classic.

Skip this movie if you enjoy genuine entertainment or compelling storytelling. If you're looking for heroic wartime drama, sophisticated performances, or a well-crafted script—steer clear. But if clichéd Hollywood war glorification, shallow patriotism, and formulaic action are your thing, then by all means, watch it.  

War films, when done right, expose the futility and contradictions of battle. This one, however, is just mindless chaos—predictable dialogue, absurd heroics, and the same violent tactics used by the oppressors being glorified as justice. It’s an insult to cinema and a poor reflection of American values. Imagine audiences worldwide seeing this and thinking it represents who we truly are—no wonder the world resents us. Save yourself the disappointment.

I wouldn’t call myself a fairy tale movie enthusiast, but *Stardust* caught my attention—largely because of Michelle Pfeiffer’s role as a villain in the trailers (especially since I’d just seen her as the domineering Velma Von Tussle in *Hairspray*). And wow, does she deliver as a witch—chillingly evil, especially with the aging makeup that makes her grotesque early on and at the end. Robert De Niro is also fantastic as the flamboyant pirate captain who conceals his true self to safeguard his "reputation."  

The entire cast shines—Claire Danes, Rupert Everett, Ricky Gervais, Peter O’Toole, and more. Danes and Pfeiffer bring classic beauty to the screen, but Sienna Miller, Olivia Grant (who plays Girl Bernard), and Kate Magowan also leave a striking impression, particularly in their first appearances. Charlie Cox, a newcomer at the time, holds his own as the lead, Tristan. His resemblance to his on-screen father, Dunstan, was so strong that I initially mistook young Dunstan (played by Ben Barnes) for Cox in early scenes.  

Many have compared *Stardust* to *The Princess Bride*, and while there are similarities, the key difference is tone: *The Princess Bride* always feels like a whimsical fantasy, while *Stardust* has its own distinct magic.

I'm a true film enthusiast. Feeling under the couch, I decided to watch this movie—and from the very first scene to the final moments, I was completely captivated. The performances were outstanding, delivered by actors I'd never seen before, yet they spoke with such authenticity. The cinematography was stunning, and the entire experience was exactly what I needed. Amidst any negative reviews, I hope my appreciation shines through—this director pours heart into every frame, working in perfect harmony with the cast.  

Thank you for creating something so special. The characters were beautifully complex—awkward yet endearing, flawed yet graceful. It's rare to find storytelling this rich. I didn’t want it to end. More than anything, I hope for future projects from this director, these actors, and the brilliant mind behind the script. Simply extraordinary.

**Jet Li stands among the greatest hand-to-hand combat fighters in the world, a title he has held for over two decades, surpassing others in the genre with unparalleled skill. Though a massive star in Asia, he remains relatively under the radar in the U.S.**  

*Black Mask* was expected to be his breakthrough film, but it falls far short. For starters, the dubbed dialogue—while perhaps amusingly bad—feels out of sync and emotionally flat, making it difficult for general audiences to take seriously. Beyond that, director Daniel Lee’s execution is lackluster. The editing is frantic, with scenes cut so quickly that the action becomes confusing rather than exhilarating. At times, shaky and unstable camerawork further muddles the action, robbing viewers of the crisp, fluid fight sequences that define Jet Li’s appeal.  

The pacing is equally jarring—some moments are abruptly truncated (such as Li cutting through a jeep floor, only for him and his love interest to suddenly be underneath it seconds later), while others stretch believability to absurd extremes. Instead of showcasing Li’s martial arts brilliance, the film’s choppy direction leaves fans struggling to follow the action, let alone appreciate its artistry.

The French films I’ve watched—and loved—tend to be dialogue-heavy rather than action-packed, but that's part of their charm. I’ve always found them engaging, beautifully shot, and full of fascinating performances. (At one point, I even wondered if Gérard Depardieu starred in every French movie ever made—it certainly felt that way!)  

This film shares that same visual appeal and starts strong. But then it gets lost in endless conversation—fine for a drama, but underwhelming for a murder mystery. Before long, I was struggling to stay awake.  

It plays more like a stage production, with nearly every scene confined to a single room. If you love theater, you might enjoy it. But for a murder story, I was hoping for more excitement.

The writing is clumsy and uninspired, drowning in tired clichés and lifeless conversations. Every scene falls flat. The actors fight against a mind-numbingly tedious script that offers zero surprises, tension, or meaningful conflict. Within minutes, you can predict exactly where it’s headed.  

Despite being set in New York, the film has no sense of place. Plenty of low-budget indies capture the city's magic, but this one feels like a generic stand-in—Canada, maybe?  

Natasha Henstridge is wasted in frumpy sweaters, while Michael Vartan looks inexplicably dull. Where’s the spark? The whole thing could pass for a sanitized, preachier-than-thou TV movie—sexless and stiff.  

Steven Feder's only achievement? Somehow getting this bland, forgettable mess made.

A twisted spectacle of bondage, humiliation, and sadomasochism—little more. The storyline is hollow, serving mainly as a flimsy excuse for its provocatively staged sequences. The show’s host, a ridiculous figure babbling nonsense while flaunting garish costumes, proved just as irritating as the film’s pretentious editing. The dreamy conclusion felt hastily stitched on. At least Aya Sugimoto delivered a compelling performance as the tormented protagonist. While *Flower and Snake* draws comparisons to *Eyes Wide Shut*, Kubrick’s work remains superior—richer in depth, artistry, and mood.

I’ve never seen acting this bad in a movie before. The casting choices are baffling—the female lead has a distracting nasal appearance that makes it hard to focus on anything else. Honestly, you’d have better luck finding a more convincing and visually appealing leading lady at any grocery store on a Sunday afternoon. I rented this purely because the DVD cover looked interesting—big mistake. The production quality feels like a student film from a community college media class. I would’ve rather spent this time watching low-budget public access TV—at least the effects are marginally better, and the people are far more engaging than anyone in this movie.

This film is hands down the worst I've ever watched - and I've suffered through some terrible ones. The amateurish production makes it seem like a group of friends randomly decided to make a movie without any experience. Every aspect is painfully bad - from the unconvincing no-name actors to the completely nonsensical plot that feels completely improvised. The story drags unbearably without ever reaching any meaningful point. The entire production feels completely unplanned, like they started filming without even a basic script. I honestly can't imagine why anyone thought this project was worth completing. Do yourself a favor and skip this one - it's two hours of your life you'll never get back.

This film ranks high among my favorite foreign movies, alongside gems like *Amélie* and *My Life As a Dog*. Like many exceptional foreign films, it takes an ordinary slice of life and turns it into a deeply moving, heartfelt experience.  

In Japan, a man weary of his routine existence and stagnant marriage catches a fleeting glimpse of a beautiful woman gazing longingly from a dance studio window. In that brief moment as his train passes, he becomes captivated—but is it her beauty, her distant expression, or an unspoken connection they might both uncover?  

*Shall We Dance* features unforgettable characters who confront life's harsh truths by escaping into the world of dance. Defying the rigid expectations of Japanese society, they take daring steps toward happiness—only to discover that joy is closer than they ever imagined. It’s a rare film that weaves magic and meaning together, transforming the everyday into something extraordinary and revealing the unexpected wonders life can hold.

Wow! This is one of those films you swear you've already reviewed—yet somehow slipped through the cracks. Maybe because it was so forgettable, but here it is, nagging at the back of your mind.  

Let’s keep it short and brutal: this is easily one of the dullest, most poorly made slashers out there. There’s almost nothing redeemable—no competent filmmaking, no gripping moments, nothing to suggest this wasn’t slapped together by amateurs.  

The kills? Laughable—no tension, no gore, just pure ridiculousness. The plot? A lazy rip-off of 1991’s *Popcorn*, and even that can’t save it.  

And no, this isn’t "so bad it’s good" territory. It’s just bad. Completely, painfully bad.  

Molly Ringwald gave it her best shot, but not even she could salvage this mess.

I’d been intrigued by this movie for years because it’s nearly impossible to track down. When I finally spotted it on eBay, I didn’t hesitate—I shelled out the ten bucks and took the plunge. Now I get why it's such a rarity! This film is laughably awful, with painfully bad writing and a budget so low that the blooper reel during the end credits—showing every flubbed line and awkward scene—is honestly the best part.  

The plot follows a psychic (Pettyjohn, who clearly got the role for one particular topless scene) using her powers alongside a half-baked machine to drag objects from another dimension into ours. After they pull out some mysterious box-like thing, the military, in a stroke of pure genius, casually tosses it into the back of an open truck with a single soldier on guard. And what do you know? **Shocker!** A kid in a bargain-bin foam monster suit bursts out, kills the guard with a single scratch, and bolts to the nearest town.  

But instead of mobilizing the entire armed forces to contain the threat, the geniuses in charge just send Pettyjohn and Ray to deal with it alone. Of course, what could go wrong?

I'm not entirely sure why, but this movie just doesn't work the way it should. It's supposed to be funny and entertaining, but instead, it's just dull. I think the overuse of "gadgets" is mostly to blame. The original cartoon it's based on is far better.  

3/10

My head still burns from the backlash I faced when I declared my love for this movie—pile on the criticism, I’ll gladly endure it again to say *Bend It Like Beckham* holds a special place in my heart. Yes, my admiration comes with caveats. The film leans into TV-movie simplicity, the script feels formulaic, and most unsettlingly, the director’s perspective suggests beauty in this world belongs mainly to those with fair skin.  

But its brilliance doesn’t lie in the textbook storytelling beats—the neatly mapped character arcs, the tidy themes. It’s in what’s immediately visible and what simmers beneath, far deeper than the layers most critics bother to dissect. Here, strong, occasionally underdressed women aren’t just posing—they’re dominating on the football field, and in doing so, they normalize female athleticism better than any CGI-enhanced action heroine ever could. These are real bodies (minus Keira Knightley’s impossibly sculpted frame), built for skill first, aesthetics second. Their beauty is in their motion, their grit, their defiance. And for me, Parminder Nagra shines brightest.

This film is phenomenal! Brad Pitt delivers a career-defining performance that he’ll never surpass. Duchovny, Forbes, and Lewis are equally outstanding. The four leads set off on a gripping road trip to infamous murder locations, cruising in a sleek 1960s Lincoln Continental. Early Grace is a deceptively simple man with peculiar habits—dry toothbrushes and a penchant for violence. He prefers women who don’t swear or smoke, dressed in modest cotton dresses.  

Duchovny and Forbes play sophisticated urban artists, while Early and Lewis embody rough-edged rural life. Though the movie leans into darkness, it’s peppered with sharp, dark humor. The script, direction, and performances are masterful. If you love road movies, crime, wit, and sharp narration, don’t miss this. Every actor shines, leaving you craving more when it ends. It’s one of my absolute favorites—especially the line: *"Hey...shave that dog and teach it to hunt!"*

This is easily among the worst films ever made—and I mean *ever*. To make matters worse, my childhood hero Dolph Lundgren stars in it. Seriously?  

The premise itself isn’t bad, but the execution is so painful it’s physically uncomfortable. The fight scenes look like drunken brawls caught on camera—no skill, no tension, just clumsy flailing.  

As for the acting? Forget it. Even Dolph disappoints, and the rest of the cast seems like they were hired through nepotism rather than talent. The director might as well have ghosted the entire production, given how little effort was put into this disaster.  

With a budget reportedly around $12 million, you’d expect at least a shred of quality. Instead, the effects and sets look like they were slapped together for pocket change. A complete waste of time and money.

I love *Crash* and *Blade Runner*, and this film dives into those gritty highway death tropes and 80s noir aesthetics I’m drawn to—so it worked for me.  

That said, the usual boneheaded noir protagonist doesn’t quite land with the female lead, and her love interest borders on caveman-level dumb, which is why it leans into kitsch.

faith that they were successful.  

Even with my fondness for Jason Segel (thanks to *Freaks & Geeks* and *Undeclared*), this movie turned out to be one of the most disappointing I’ve seen in years—right up there with *Loser* and *Dr. T and the Women*.  

There were a few genuinely funny moments, but honestly, it could’ve been so much better. The setup wasn’t bad—a crew of con artists making their way through college until they’re outsmarted by someone with a scheme of their own. The real issue? Every character was downright unlikable. I couldn’t bring myself to care about any of them. Jason Schwartzman’s blackmailer was more disturbing than entertaining—not in a darkly funny or quirky way, just a genuinely unstable, off-putting creep. The editing didn’t help either, jumping between fantasy and reality without much clarity, making it hard to follow. And while the cons were central to the plot, we only got glimpses of a couple, leaving the rest to imagination rather than execution.

The challenge lies in knowing where to start—this film demands your undivided attention for the next two hours, and even stepping away for a brief moment could leave you lost. Thankfully, there’s always the pause button. Bruce Willis must journey through time in search of an antivirus to combat a deadly pathogen that allowed animals to dominate the world in 1996. Due to a series of mishaps, he first lands in 1990, then finds himself in the chaos of World War I. As bizarre as it sounds, Terry Gilliam delivers what might be one of the most brilliantly crafted screenplays ever. The former Monty Python member understands exactly how to tell a genius science fiction story, and his casting choices are flawless—from Brad Pitt’s unforgettable, unhinged performance in the asylum to Bruce Willis proving he’s far more than just another action hero. The film’s intricate, mind-bending plot (somehow still easy to follow) makes it endlessly rewatchable, with each viewing revealing new surprises. A true favorite of mine.

I've seen this movie a thousand times before—it was painfully predictable. Every supposed twist or moment of suspense only led to exactly what I saw coming. The plot was as dull as "The bread factory opened another facility because there wasn’t enough bread." In short: stale story, recycled clichés, terrible acting, and laughable effects.  

The only redeeming moment? Vlad, the dumb Russian cop, battering bad guys with his absurd muscle-bound stupidity—so ridiculous it was briefly amusing. Why did I even waste my time trashing this cinematic disgrace? Then again, it can’t possibly get any worse... because that would be impossible. :D

*Zombi 3* has a fascinating behind-the-scenes story. It was conceived as a sequel to Lucio Fulci’s *Zombi 2*, which itself was a marketing ploy to deceive audiences into believing it was connected to George A. Romero’s *Dawn of the Dead* (released as *Zombi* in Italy). Confusing, right? Despite sharing the *Zombi* name, these films have no real connection—but when money’s involved, logic takes a backseat. Fulci reportedly lost interest midway through production and abandoned the project, leaving Bruno Mattei to step in and patch together additional scenes to stretch out the runtime.  

The plot follows standard zombie-movie tropes: scientists develop a dangerous serum on a remote Philippine island, terrorists steal it, chaos ensues, and the undead run wild. While researchers scramble for a cure, the military opts for a more direct solution—shooting first, asking questions never. Thrown into the mix is a radio DJ who occasionally chimes in with philosophical musings about humanity's destruction of the planet.  

Against all odds, I ended up enjoying this film. It’s often panned by critics, but I found its unintentionally funny dialogue and chaotic energy strangely entertaining. *Zombi 3* feels like...

Inspired by a true story, *Antwone Fisher* marks the directorial debut of acclaimed actor Denzel Washington. Known for delivering unforgettable performances—from a Black soldier in *Glory* to a groundbreaking lawyer in *Philadelphia*—Washington made history by becoming the first African American to win the Academy Award for Best Actor for his role in *Training Day*. Seeking a new creative challenge, he stepped behind the camera for *Antwone Fisher*, in which he also stars. Rising actor Derek Luke takes on the title role, making his major film debut after guest appearances on shows like *The King of Queens* and landing a role in the soon-to-be-released *Biker Boyz*.  

For a first-time director, Washington crafts a remarkably polished film, clearly driven by a deep connection to Antwone Fisher’s real-life story. The film follows a troubled young Black sailor in the Navy whose life is consumed by anger until a Navy psychiatrist helps him confront his traumatic past.

The joke felt tired from the start and barely managed to hold interest over its painfully drawn-out eight minutes. The only redeeming moment was the "DO NOT COLORIZE" warning in the credits. It’s a pity they didn’t include something more engaging on the DVD—like Jonathan Ross’s fun segment on Romero from *The Incredible Strange Film Show*.

This film delivers a hilarious and biting satire of pop culture and its creators. The cinematography stood out to me—vibrant colors and meticulously crafted scenes—especially impressive considering it's Zukovic's first major project.  

A word of caution: don’t take the movie’s message too literally. It’s not meant for mainstream appeal (and that’s not a praise). Its perspective feels like a stylized, post-college newcomer’s take on society.  

That said, I loved the core premise—a fictional magazine editor mercilessly mocking the herd mentality of the ‘90s.

This film was promoted as a blend of comedy and mystery, but it misses the mark on both counts. The real enigma is how such a poorly made movie ever got greenlit. The only humor comes from the bafflingly high ratings it received—did I stumble upon the wrong version? What I watched featured a lead actress with striking blue eyes and a storyline that seemed to vanish into thin air.

Alright, what on earth is this supposed to be? Is it some kind of family-friendly fantasy flick trying to ride the coattails of Spielberg’s *Close Encounters of the Third Kind*? Or maybe a nostalgic nod to old-school dinosaur epics like *When Dinosaurs Ruled the Earth* and *The Lost World*? Could it actually be some deep, intellectual puzzle that’s just flying way over our heads? Yeah, sure—that *must* be it! Whatever it is, the minds behind *The Day Time Ended*—John 'Bud' Cardos (*Kingdom of the Spiders*) and writer David Schmoeller (*Tourist Trap*)—were clearly huffing something potent when they cobbled together this madcap mishmash of genres.  

The plot? A tangled mess. The storytelling? Jumpier than a rabbit on espresso. But who needs coherence when you’ve got papier-mâché dinosaurs, tiny UFOs, seizure-inducing light shows, and random exploding stars? The narration at the start is barely even decipherable, but don’t sweat it—it’s all nonsense anyway! Oh, and just so you know, time isn’t what you think it is. Nope, it doesn’t just tick along in a straight line—it’s one big, baffling paradox! Those words you just heard? Could’ve been spoken millennia ago... or maybe not yet. Who knows? Not the filmmakers, that’s for sure.

I really can't fathom how something this awful was produced. Even the most cringe-worthy middle school talent show would be more watchable than this disaster. The only mildly amusing parts—and they're fleeting—come from Will Ferrell's bizarre obsession with wrestling. Absolutely terrible.

Once again, this is a film that tugs at your heartstrings, leaving you emotionally moved rather than hardened—but I admit, I’m a sucker for that kind of story, so it earned a high rating from me. This film was downright terrible! I can't believe it even got greenlit. No offense to the actors—this disaster lies entirely with the writers. They recycled the same tired "dance your way out of poverty" trope—or should I say, *step* in this case—but failed to deliver even a remotely engaging story. The awkward Canadian accents in an American setting only made it worse.  

On the plus side, the direction was strong, the cinematography was solid, and it’s clear no expense was spared in production. My advice? Stick to visuals and hire real screenwriters next time—someone who can actually craft compelling dialogue. Final verdict? *How She Move* is how she flops.

**"Bruce Almighty" is set to dominate the Academy Awards with a historic 14 Oscar wins, dethroning "Titanic" as the highest-grossing film ever! Jim Carrey’s stardom will skyrocket to such heights that he’ll declare his candidacy for the 2004 presidential race. Almighty indeed! Such extravagant dreams could only come true if the filmmakers—Carrey included—held the powers of the divine. That very concept drives the hilarious heart of Carrey’s latest comedy, *Bruce Almighty*.  

Carrey stars as Bruce Nolan, a frustrated TV reporter obsessed with landing the anchor desk, blaming God for every setback in his life. Enter Morgan Freeman’s pitch-perfect portrayal of the Almighty, who hands Bruce divine powers to test whether he can handle the job better. Predictably, Bruce gets carried away—pun intended—wielding his newfound abilities for selfish gain.  

Carrey returns to his unstoppable comedic roots in *Bruce Almighty*, while Jennifer Aniston delivers a solid performance as Bruce’s long-suffering girlfriend. But the standout genius belongs to director Tom Shadyac, who not only avoids cheap gags (remember *#2*?) but gifts us one of the most uproarious bathroom scenes in film history.

Undeniably the most hilarious of the Curly-led Three Stooges shorts, this gem never fails to make me laugh no matter how many times I watch it. The brilliant physical comedy routines shine as a masterclass in silent humor. It stands as the ultimate blend of slapstick and musical timing—so memorable that even those who aren't fans of the trio still hold this one dear.

When the crime boss of *Central City* is murdered, his right-hand man Robert Armstrong (*as "Doc" Rogers*) takes bold action to maintain order in the criminal underworld. He enlists the timid son of the slain mobster, Richard Cromwell (*as Edward "Baby Face" Morgan*), to assume control of the family’s illegal empire. Naïve and out of his depth, Cromwell is brought to the city and placed at the head of his father’s front business—the *Acme Protection Agency*.  

While Cromwell unknowingly sells insurance to unsuspecting clients, his gangster associates orchestrate a ruthless extortion scheme. Complicating matters, Cromwell falls for a charming client, Mary Carlisle (*as Virginia Clark*), and soon, both find themselves entangled in deadly peril.  

*Baby Face Morgan* (1942), directed by Arthur Dreifuss, marks one of the final roles for Cromwell and Carlisle, whose once-promising careers were winding down. A brisk, breezy, and harmless crime caper, the film delivers modest entertainment without overstaying its welcome.

As a lifelong Elvis fan, I'm baffled by how this project got made. It stands as the worst Elvis-themed movie ever—completely humorless, absurd, and riddled with inaccuracies about The King. Seriously, Elvis’ grave in a public park? Referencing "Suspicious Minds" in 1958? These are just a couple of the glaring errors.  

A few cast members give it their all—Mike Starr brings some laughs (especially as an impersonator), and Tom Hanks' cameo is a fun surprise—but the actor playing young Elvis is painfully bad.  

The film drags on, draining any potential entertainment with each passing minute. If you're looking for a wild, low-budget, yet genuinely hilarious Elvis-related flick, skip this disaster and watch *Bubba Ho-Tep* instead. It’s far more entertaining than this mess.

I won’t be offering a detailed critique of this film. Given the abundance of glowing reviews that came before mine—and my general appreciation for Maria de Medeiros—I’ve held back from voicing any negative thoughts for nearly a year. Yet, every time I spot that DVD on my shelf, I can’t help but feel a quiet sigh. Still, let the overwhelming praise speak louder than my reservations. But for fellow cinephiles like me—consider this a warning.  

To put it simply and as kindly as possible, here’s my take:  

The political upheaval and revolution that form the backdrop of this film also coincided with a chapter of my own life—one spent reading daily newspapers in a middle-European pub. Back then, I closely followed the reports but never fully grasped the chaos unfolding. The journalists either remained neutral or leaned conservative, often dismissive of movements disrupting the peace or challenging authority. It was an era of unrest—Paris, Berlin, Prague, and parts of the U.S. were all caught in similar turbulence, their conflicts clear to me even then. But dictatorship or not...

For those who may not know Jimmy Stewart, this film comes from the later phase of his career and isn’t considered among his finest works. While it doesn’t measure up to many of his classics, it’s still an enjoyable, if unremarkable, way to pass the time.  

Kim Novak plays a witch in New York who inexplicably casts a spell to make Stewart fall in love with her. As the story unfolds, the initially distant Novak starts developing genuine feelings for him—something strictly forbidden in the witches’ code.  

The movie’s take on witches is peculiar. They’re neither sinister nor all-powerful; instead, their magic is often trivial, like Jack Lemmon using his abilities to flicker streetlights. Strangely enough, these witches are portrayed as bohemian types, frequenting arty bars filled with beret-wearing jazz enthusiasts. Given my opinion on jazz, their world seems even more miserable!  

Still, the film carries a certain romantic charm.

I picked up this DVD for my brother since he's a huge Michelle Pfeiffer admirer, but ended watching it myself earlier this week.  

The film offers two entirely distinct storylines, with Pfeiffer's segment being the far more compelling of the two. She portrays a budding Hollywood actress stuck in a cycle of fleeting, unsatisfying relationships. After rear-ending Brian Kerwin's car (he plays an ordinary family man), their initially tense encounter softens when he offers her a ride home—she’s too shaken to drive. A romance blossoms between them, only to end tragically once his wife discovers the affair. While the ending caught me off guard, the sluggish pacing and uninspired direction drained much of the emotional impact.  

The second storyline centers on Darren McGavin as a fading studio mogul, supported by a stronger ensemble cast—Kenneth McMillan, Lois Chiles, Steven Bauer, and Stella Stevens. Each character is vying for something from the aging executive, but when he’s forced to step down, they’re left realizing their own careers are now at a dead end.

Eddie Murphy's *Delirious* is unapologetically vulgar, offensive, and raunchy. These words perfectly capture the essence of this shameless, over-the-top stand-up special. Rather than relying on clever wit, Murphy leans heavily on shock tactics to grab the audience's attention. There are fleeting moments of humor, but the routine mostly drowns in crude language and tasteless sexual humor.  

Save your time—unless you’re a die-hard fan of Murphy’s unrestrained style. After this experience, I have zero interest in watching *Eddie Murphy Raw*. I’ll stick to enjoying his performances within the structured boundaries of a movie script.  

*Saturday, January 17, 1998 - Video*

I was so excited to watch *Planet of the Apes*, but it turned out to be a massive letdown.  

The costumes and set designs are impressive—that's about the only praise I can give. Everything else is frustrating. Mark Wahlberg barely acts; he just stands around looking blank. The rest of the cast doesn’t fare much better.  

But the biggest flaw is the absurd plot. Take one ridiculous moment: when the apes are unconscious and defenseless, the humans *wait* instead of attacking—only for them to wake up and fight back. This is just one example of the idiotic writing, and the list goes on. A complete waste of potential.

First, I should mention that I’m a huge supporter of fan productions. They offer a fantastic way to keep beloved shows alive long after their official cancellation. Projects like *Star Trek Voyages* and *Star Wars Revelations* are perfect examples of well-executed efforts, so I’m naturally inclined to be forgiving when it comes to fan-made content—even overlooking flaws I’d usually criticize harshly.  

Now, moving on to *ST: HF*. Let’s start with the positives. Enthusiasm is key to making any show feel authentic, and for the most part, the actors across the different ships clearly seem to be enjoying their roles. The visual effects are another strong point—nothing cringe-worthy here, and they’re quite impressive for a fan project. The storytelling is solid, too. While not groundbreaking, the plots are well-structured, and the inclusion of ongoing story arcs adds depth.  

That said, there are plenty of shortcomings.  

The most glaring issue? While it's understandable—even necessary—to rely on borrowed *Star Trek* assets like footage, set designs, music, and effects, there’s no excuse for lifting scores from practically every other sci-fi franchise out there. From *Aliens* to *Starship Troopers*, recognizable orchestral themes pop up far too often.

I caught the movie on TV earlier and really liked it. I'm always drawn to a well-crafted mystery, and this one kept me guessing until the final moment. Sean Connery delivered a fantastic performance. I'd definitely recommend it to anyone looking for a great film.

The same goes for the soundtrack—utterly forgettable.  

To be fair, this isn’t the absolute worst gay-themed film I’ve suffered through (*Regarding Billy* holds that dishonor), but it’s dangerously close.  

The film plods along endlessly, weighed down by painfully predictable plotting—every twist visible from a mile away. The dialogue falls flat, the humor feels stale, and worst of all, it leans into tired, one-dimensional gay stereotypes.  

There’s zero believability in the central relationship. No spark, no tension—just a hollow declaration of love with no foundation. These leads share nothing in common, not even chemistry, making their forced connection baffling. They bond over liking the same book? Seriously?  

The acting isn’t a complete disaster, but the pacing drags mercilessly—almost Jim Jarmusch-level lethargy, but with none of the artistry to justify it.

This series first introduced me to Deighton's work and sparked my love for the genre during my younger years—I still adore this adaptation. That said, I must respectfully disagree with the earlier comment. Based on my past reading, Deighton’s refusal to allow the series' release wasn’t due to Holm’s performance, but rather the heavy-handed alterations made to all three books during the screen adaptation.  

A prime example is the rewritten border-crossing scene that ended Samson’s field career. Not only is this moment absent from the novels, but the character who dies in the minefield never existed in any of Deighton’s work. The original crossing in *Sinker* occurred between East and West Germany, not the Polish frontier—this entire plotline was fabricated. Similar distortions in *Set* undermined the story’s core integrity.  

As for Holm’s performance, I thought he brilliantly captured Samson’s bewilderment during his wife’s defection. He also portrayed the aging field agent’s struggle to navigate the class divide with nuance. Samson pays dearly for his father’s idealism, suffering under its weight throughout his life—much like Clevemore observes, had he pursued an education, things might have been different.

I’m a fan of Jean Harlow because she had true star power. While I don’t consider her films great or even think she was a strong actress, she absolutely shone in comedies. Every comedic moment in *The Girl from Missouri* works perfectly—though the film leans more toward romance. Harlow is captivating here, while the rest of the cast fades into the background with forgettable performances. It’s striking to remember that her stunning appearance belonged to someone battling illness—yet in this movie, she radiates beauty.

Ever had that feeling in a theater where you're trapped in the perfect seat—dead center, after swapping three times to nail the ideal spot—only to spend what feels like 13 hours squirming, itchy, and silently screaming, *When the hell will this movie end?!* (You know the type—think *A.I.* or *The Village*).  

Well, *Visitor Q* twists that experience into something even stranger. For the first 30 minutes, I kept waiting for it to *actually start*. It drags on endlessly, so "artsy" it’s painful. This was my first Takashi Miike film, and if the rest of his massive filmography is as painfully pretentious as this, it’ll probably be my last.  

Don’t get me wrong—I’m not opposed to pretentious films. David Lynch is one of my top ten directors. But *Visitor Q*? It’s pretentious in the worst way: cheap, grating, and utterly hollow.  

In case it wasn’t obvious—I despised it.

Absolutely better than *Death Tunnel*. The kills were surprisingly creative, and the gore didn’t disappoint—felt like a mashup of *Wrong Turn* and *The Hills Have Eyes*.  

**BUT:**  
1.) The whole horror movie discussion in the kitchen? Shae’s lines were basically ripped straight from *Scream* (1996), right down to the “big-breasted girls” bit.  
2.) Steve was basically Randy from *Scream* 2.0. No way that wasn’t intentional.  
3.) Other than it being October, what did this have to do with Samhain? Felt tacked on, like those '80s horror flicks blaming everything on druids or pentagrams.  
4.) Oh look, a Sam Raimi reference—how clever.  
5.) What was the point of Gary and his sister? They added nothing. And if he was so psychic, how did he miss his own death?  
6.) That bathroom kill was peak Troma-level ridiculous. How the hell did she hear his screams from downstairs?

Goldie Hawn was actually born in Takoma Park, Maryland, though that's beside the point. The film follows a classic "Mr. Smith Goes to Washington" formula, with its own twists but the same core idea. I recorded this off cable years ago—mostly because I was completely smitten with Hawn at the time.  

The plot is entertaining, though wildly improbable. The idea that a cocktail waitress lands a major government role just for saving a VIP's life is hard to swallow. The movie had me torn between laughter and frustration. Some scenes were so absurd they were downright hilarious (minor spoiler ahead), while others got under my skin—especially the way the government manipulated an ordinary person. But that final speech? Perfect. Too bad real life doesn’t have many people with that kind of courage.

This movie brought back memories of those cheesy late-night "erotic thrillers" I’d sneak on Cinemax as a teenager. I’d call this one *softer-core*, since it lacks any real steam—just endless nudity. The film kicks off in a strip club, flashes Kane Hodder’s backside (or a stunt double’s), then throws in a baffling ten-minute lesbian dance sequence, capped off by a naked female werewolf that looks like she stole her costume from *The Munsters*. Thirteen-year-old boys, consider this your holy grail.  

Beyond that, the werewolf transformations boast some of the shoddiest CGI in recent memory—think *Resident Evil* cutscene quality. The creature design is laughably bad, yet the film insists on showcasing it way too often.  

The plot? A mess. The acting? Nonexistent. There’s some convoluted lore about werewolves and hybrids—apparently, the "Darkwolf" is the latter, though as far as I can tell, hybrids do the exact same thing as regular werewolves: look human, turn into wolves, and kill people. Riveting stuff.

Wow, just how terrible can something be? This was truly awful—and not because of the gore (which mostly looked like laughable CGI), but due to the weak acting, lifeless atmosphere, and clumsy direction.  

The story? A complete disaster. The main character's so-called "arc" was laughable. After stalking Vinnie Jones for a few nights, he suddenly becomes so "haunted" that he’s in tears while photographing his girlfriend. Seriously? Are all New York photographers this whiny, gullible, and emotionally fragile? His so-called transformation had zero justification, and by the end, you’ll be groaning at the painfully predictable and utterly ridiculous direction his character takes.  

As for the gore, it reeked of desperate, half-hearted attempts to cash in on flashy, MTV-style shock value—all CGI blood and zero real impact. These moments were so unintentionally funny they became distracting, worsened by the try-hard directing (weird camera angles, anyone?) that screamed "look how edgy I am!"  

The real crime here? Wasting what could have been an intriguing idea. There was potential for tension and atmosphere—until the ridiculous monsters showed up—but it was all ruined by self-indulgent, hollow filmmaking. This wasn’t made for an audience; it was made for a director too busy showing off to tell a coherent story.

Beneath the masterful direction, stellar production, and compelling performances—beyond even the predictable drama—lies the film's profound core message:  

**"Listening leads all the way."**  

To give voice its power, listen.  
To blend harmoniously with others, listen.  
To truly understand yourself, listen.  
To uncover the needs of a moment or another person, listen.  

The scriptwriters seem to reveal a hidden truth of existence—that deep listening cultivates self-awareness, sharpens perception, and broadens one’s perspective. Even the soul reveals itself through attentive silence.  

*As It Is in Heaven* beautifully captures life’s unfolding—not just its joys and sorrows, but its enduring hope. This truth resonates from the choir’s very first instruction by the protagonist:  

**"Just listen—it leads all the way."**

*The Return of Chandu* stands out—if one can call it that—for featuring Bela Lugosi as the hero rather than the villain. Remarkably, he even gets the girl.  

The plot revolves around the Black Magic Cult of Ubasti, who seek to capture the last Egyptian princess, Nadji (played by the captivating Maria Alba), and sacrifice her to resurrect their ancient leader—who, coincidentally, bears a striking resemblance to Nadji. Lugosi stars as Chandu, a sorcerer with mystical abilities, determined to stop the cult's sinister plans.  

Director Ray Taylor makes the most of the film's modest budget and heavy reliance on stock footage. Fans of *King Kong* (1933) may recognize the massive doors used to restrain the ape in several scenes. Unfortunately, the acting is largely subpar. The high priest (likely portrayed by Lucien Prival) delivers his lines with that exaggerated, early-talkie enunciation common among actors of the era. The less said about the rest of the cast, the better.  

It remains puzzling why Lugosi took on roles in low-budget indie productions at this point in his career, given that he was still a bankable star for Universal at the time. Perhaps...

I'm still struggling to understand what this film was trying to achieve.  

For something marketed as "rebellious" and "controversial," Maddox's so-called subversive materials are disappointingly weak. The students are bizarrely swayed by half-baked anti-establishment rhetoric and barely legible scribbles on handouts. Real rebellion, huh?  

I guess expecting a teen rebellion movie without a pulled fire alarm was too much to ask.  

And apparently, a "huge fight on the football field" translates to exactly two people throwing punches.  

Character consistency is nonexistent—the football player Maddox fought (and stapled in the face) is suddenly all forgiveness and grins the next day.  

The lack of any real resolution makes the entire plot feel like it could’ve been condensed into a 30-minute filler episode. Maybe if they’d scrapped most of that grating, wannabe-glitch soundtrack.

*Private Lessons II* is undoubtedly the most incredible film I've ever experienced. A Japanese production with hilariously rough English subtitles, it's an absolute delight—even when the plot makes little sense. That's part of its charm. It's unintentionally one of the funniest comedies out there, without ever trying to be.  

Rare and nearly impossible to find on video, I've only managed to catch it a few times in the dead of night on premium cable. My worn-out recorded copy has been replayed countless times as I carefully, one viewer at a time, spread the word about this hidden treasure.  

Joanna Pacula stars as the tutor (and love interest) to Ken, our protagonist—though her performance suggests she was mostly there for the paycheck. Ken is played by Goro Inagaki, a member of the Japanese pop group SMAP, who commits fully to the role and maintains impressively perfect hair throughout. Stacy Edwards (*In the Company of Men*) also appears, probably relieved she moved on to bigger projects afterward.  

It takes at least three watches to *barely* grasp the story. On repeat viewings, you start noticing bizarre details—like the absurd number of vases in Ken’s house (there are at least 50) or...

I sincerely hope the viewer who called *Dream Machine* one of Corey Haim’s best—and the "best movie of the century"—was joking. Undetected sarcasm on my end? Let’s pray so.  

*The Dream Machine* kicked off a streak of mediocre misfires that haunted the rest of Haim’s career (with the exception of *Prayer of the Rollerboys*, which was shockingly watchable). Here, Haim plays Bernie, a carefree college kid convinced a flashy car will win over his crush. By sheer luck, a wealthy woman, eager to spite her cheating husband, impulsively rewards Bernie—her loyal piano tuner—with a sleek Porsche Turbo. The catch? Unbeknownst to her (and tragically for Bernie), her now-dead husband’s corpse is stashed in the trunk.  

Somehow, in this universe, bodies don’t rot or reek—so Bernie remains blissfully unaware. Even with a shady brute tailing him, desperate to reclaim the incriminating cargo unnoticed, our oblivious hero fails to notice anything amiss. What unfolds is a limp, low-stakes slog that barely qualifies as an action flick.

Simply put, westerns have never appealed to me. Since I'd never actually watched one from start to finish, I resolved to sit through *My Darling Clementine* no matter how painful the experience might be. At first, it was every bit as agonizing as I'd anticipated—the acting struck me as ridiculous, the desert-and-cowboys scenery felt tired, and the clunky musical cues grated on my nerves. But after forcing myself to push through the first twenty minutes, it gradually became more bearable. I found myself drawn in by the cinematography—how John Ford transformed even mundane moments (mundane to my eyes, at least) into something unexpectedly striking.  

In the end, I wouldn’t say I *liked* the film. But it was crafted well enough to hold my attention until the credits rolled—an achievement in itself, given my usual aversion to the genre.

Check it out—Eva Longoria and Paul Rudd star in a movie where a deceased girlfriend comes back to haunt the new flame. That’s right, Gabrielle from *Desperate Housewives* and the same guy who rocked "Sex Panther" cologne in *Anchorman*. If you're hunting for an Oscar-worthy performance, adjust your expectations. But if you're up for 90 minutes of pure, unserious fun, you’re in the perfect spot. The humor lands, the cast clicks, and the real standout duo is Rudd and Lake Bell. He’s just as sharp as his *Friends* days, while she delivers laughs and charm effortlessly. My wife and I caught this one together—no regrets, just solid entertainment.

Famous Studios became known for their signature tension-and-release style of animation, where a secondary character would face dire danger—only to be saved by the hero just in time. This specific Casper cartoon stands out as the only one I recall where death itself intervenes. Yet, even in the face of mortality, the story finds a hopeful resolution.

A defining trait of Famous Studios' shorts was their unwavering belief that "good always prevails." Whether Popeye reaching his spinach at the critical moment, Baby Huey outsmarting the cunning fox, or Little Audrey learning her lesson, virtue won out. That said, some of their cartoons ventured into surprisingly dark and somber territory.

Credit must be given where it's due. As much as I adore Looney Tunes and *Tom and Jerry*, I believe Paramount was unmatched in delivering top-tier animation during that era. Their cartoons excelled in every aspect—vibrant color, fluid animation, Winston Sharples' iconic musical scores, sharp editing, and stellar voice work. They set a standard of excellence, showcasing the very best the medium had to offer.

In the age of digital creation, no computer can replicate the depth of a skilled actor or writer. Yet sadly, such character-driven films have become increasingly rare. Both Robert Duvall and James Earl Jones deliver performances that meet—and exceed—their audience's lofty expectations. There’s an intimate, almost televised quality to the storytelling that makes me question whether this was originally intended for TV. Calling the performances merely "outstanding" feels insufficient—they’re extraordinary. The film falls just short of being a true cinematic masterpiece, held back only by the absence of a visionary cinematographer. But breathtaking visuals aren’t everything. In an era where so many actors simply posture for digital effects, how do talents like Jones and Duvall continue to craft work of such raw authenticity?

A stunning cinematic masterpiece, perfect for lovers of equine tales and WWII dramas set against Hungary's rugged landscape. This moving story celebrates bravery, kindness, and unshakable devotion across time. The breathtaking horsemanship shines, particularly the protagonist's bond with his remarkable steed during their training journey.

I'm adding this to my permanent collection—it's that rewatchable. An ideal choice for family viewing, though be mindful of intense wartime sequences depicting Hungary's Nazi occupation. The villagers' quiet defiance, even when confronting a Nazi officer's vengeful pursuit of Brady, makes for powerful storytelling.

An unforgettable film that lingers in the heart.

**Things used to be better in the old days—even children's television. Fraggle Rock is the perfect example. I’m only fourteen as I write this, but even now, I can’t resist its charm. In case you’ve been living under a rock (pun intended!), Fraggle Rock follows a group of playful, silly creatures—the Fraggles—who, unsurprisingly, live inside a rock. But they’re not alone. Their world is shared with hardworking Doozers, sentient plants, and other quirky beings. Outside the rock, there’s Doc, an inventor-scientist, and his dog Sprocket (who eventually befriends Gobo Fraggle). On the opposite side resides the Gorgs, a family who claim to rule the universe. The five main Fraggles—Gobo (the brave leader), Mokey (the spiritual artist), Wembley (the indecisive but loyal friend), Boober (the gloomy homebody), and Red (the competitive athlete)—find themselves in wild adventures every episode, all while singing and dancing their worries away.**  

**Fraggle Rock is truly a show for all ages. While younger kids might miss some of the clever details, the music, humor, and heart make it timeless.**

I genuinely don’t get the criticism surrounding this movie. Sure, it follows the classic boy-meets-girl formula, but it’s executed with such style and charm that you’ll be swept up in the story before you know it. Henstridge (absolutely stunning—talk about genetic perfection!) is as captivating as ever (so much for the death of screen glamour), and Vartan delivers a solid performance.  

The chemistry between the leads is electric—their scenes together are where the film truly shines, and you can’t help but root for them to fall in love.  

Honestly, disregard the naysayers. If you’re in a funk, this movie will lift your spirits. And if you’re already happy? It’ll leave you downright giddy.  

*(P.S. 33-year-old hopeless romantic from the UK here, still waiting for my fairytale ending…)*

The dazzling seventeen-minute dance sequence set to George Gershwin's 1928 orchestral piece *An American in Paris* stands as an undeniable masterpiece. Choreographed by Gene Kelly with meticulous precision and unmatched flair, this vibrant fusion of color, music, and movement remains breathtaking, unfolding through scenes inspired by iconic artists—Dufy in the Place de la Concorde opening, Manet in the flower market, Utrillo along a Parisian street, Rousseau at the fair, Van Gogh in the dazzling Place de l’Opera segment, and Toulouse-Lautrec at the Moulin Rouge, where Kelly dons his legendary white bodysuit. While the 97 minutes leading up to this finale may not match its brilliance, the 1951 Oscar-winning musical still offers its own charms.  

Under Vincente Minnelli’s direction and Alan Jay Lerner’s screenplay, the film weaves a surprisingly refined, if somewhat slight, romantic tale centered on Jerry Mulligan, a WWII veteran-turned-struggling artist in postwar Paris. Gene Kelly’s boisterous charm and athletic dance style make him a screen presence that oscillates between endearing and exasperating—yet he brings

**Cat Soup** is a brief yet immersive experience—an utterly surreal cinematic journey. I stumbled upon it one day while browsing the anime section of my on-demand library, curiosity drawing me in. From start to finish, my reaction hovered between stunned silence and the fleeting urge to shut it off in bewilderment. Yet I couldn't look away. And in the end, I’m glad I didn’t.  

The animation is breathtaking—strikingly artistic, bizarre, and tinged with darkness. While I was initially captivated by its visual brilliance, the enigmatic, almost threadbare narrative became equally compelling as I watched.  

The story follows a young cat (a boy, really) on a quest to retrieve his sister’s stolen soul. Early on, she lies frail in bed when a grim reaper-like figure appears, splitting her soul in two. The cat manages to reclaim one half, but the other is lost.  

Beyond that, the film’s trajectory becomes a hazy dreamscape. I gather they return home, only to find their world crumbling—perhaps a consequence of her missing soul. The rest unfolds in strange, surreal fragments, leaving much to interpretation yet lingering in the mind long after the screen goes dark.

This movie was an absolute train wreck. I put it on as a joke, thinking it might at least be entertainingly bad, but no—it somehow managed to be worse than that. It felt like a deliberate attempt to infuriate me, and it succeeded spectacularly.  

Whoever made this took every irritating aspect of *PRIEST*, stripped away anything even vaguely engaging, funny, or stylish, and just dumped in a bunch of grating nonsense and stale, rotten cheese. That’s all this is—cheese, but not the fun kind. There’s nothing here to latch onto, no relatable characters, no believable world, just a mess.  

Why couldn’t this have been fun? Why did they take a dumb premise and somehow make it even dumber? It wouldn’t have taken much to make it passable—or at least an amusing B-movie. But no, they didn’t even try. And what was even the goal here? I went in hoping for a cheesy, campy love story and got... whatever *this* was.

When I first watched this movie in the 1980s, I was in my mid-teens and a bit hesitant because I thought I’d outgrown "Sesame Street" and the Muppets. I can’t even recall if I enjoyed it back then. But years later, during college, I gave it another chance—and it instantly became one of my all-time favorites.  

This film is packed with humor that surpasses any expectations you might have for the Muppets. Sure, they’ve always had jokes that appeal to both kids and adults, but here, they take it to another level. Janice casually drops a line like, "I don’t take my clothes off for anyone, even if it IS artistic." A father jokes to his lovestruck son, "If you’re in love with a frog, I don’t wanna know." And Gonzo, after rescuing a chicken with mouth-to-mouth, deadpans, "I think we’re engaged now." Moments like these had me laughing nonstop.  

On top of the clever jokes, the film delivers sharp dialogue and playful Broadway/Wink-at-the-camera New York humor, along with the usual cast of quirky characters... (continued)

This film is a complete misfire, devoid of any genuine emotion in every scene. The characters are flat, thinly drawn, and utterly predictable, while the plot is a tired exercise in Hollywood clichés and fantasy fulfillment.  

William Holden, tragically wasted here, was 55 during filming yet plays a man in his early 40s—though he looks closer to his 60s. Meanwhile, 20-year-old Kay Lenz is scripted to be irresistibly drawn to him, a dynamic that feels painfully forced. Their chemistry is so lifeless that even the stray dog by the roadside seems more vibrant and engaging.  

Holden’s character—conveniently the same age as director Clint Eastwood—is draped in painfully outdated signifiers of '60s cool: the bachelor pad, the vinyl records, the lunches at Yamashiro. But the film itself is painfully uncool, a cringeworthy spectacle of aging men clinging to the hope that the freewheeling youth of Sunset and Laurel Canyon might find their clunky cars and desperate posturing appealing.  

It’s hard to believe the counterculture ever stooped this low. Worse still is the thought that Holden, once a true Hollywood legend, was so eager to chase faded youth that he signed on for this humiliating role.

This ambitious four-hour remake of Rider Haggard's classic tale expands the original with a new female character and an additional subplot involving Russian soldiers hunting for a mythical "Stone of Power" hidden among King Solomon's treasure. Though overlong, the film excels in its breathtaking cinematography that captures Africa's vast landscapes and features strong performances across the board. Patrick Swayze shines as Alan Quatermain, while Allison Doody brings charm to her role as Elizabeth Maitland. Standout supporting turns come from Sidede Onyulo as Umbopa, Gavin Hood as McNabb, and the unnamed but memorable Russian commander. Despite Hollywood's tendency to embellish source material, this adaptation remains engaging—its only major flaw being excessive runtime. 6/10.

With an IMDB rating of 8.1, my expectations for this film were high. It begins with a charming, lighthearted energy that feels fresh and engaging. However, by the halfway point, the pacing slows to a crawl, and the plot descends into painfully predictable territory. The office characters shine initially, offering genuine humor, but they quickly devolve into exaggerated stereotypes rather than fully realized people. This is a narrative I’ve encountered countless times—just dressed in slightly different circumstances. Even a formulaic romance could have been tolerable if not for the painfully dull dialogue.  

What’s worse than uninspired writing? Characters whose actions make no sense—and sadly, *Dead Letter Office* suffers from that too. Here’s hoping this film finds its way to the Dead Movie Office soon enough.

The film lingers in ambiguity for far too long. As it unfolds, very little is clarified, leaving a string of bizarre sequences that appear profound but ultimately feel confusing and meaningless due to the disjointed storytelling. It almost dares you to rewatch it for clarity, but there’s no chance I’d sit through it again. The only reason I stayed awake was because I watched it in the morning—had it been an evening viewing, I would’ve dozed off. To me, it felt like a cheap imitation of *Blade Runner*.  

Too much is left unresolved, riddled with implausibilities that make the entire experience feel hollow and forgettable.  

Even the film’s visual style falls flat. It’s a clumsy mix of CGI and live-action, executed with none of the polish, creativity, or spectacle seen in later films like *Sin City* or *300*. Oddly enough, half the characters are digitally animated—a baffling and unnecessary choice, especially since the character animation itself is lackluster.

the furnace. This film ranks among the worst I've ever seen—only surpassed by true disasters like *Haunted Mansion* and *Nothing but Trouble*—but it still comes close to rock bottom. The pacing feels rushed, the plot is flimsy, and the performances fall flat. Much of the blame lies with the source material—an overly heavy, illogical novel that fails to translate well to the screen.  

Oprah Winfrey’s turn as Bigger’s mother is passable but underwhelming, falling short of her usual brilliance. Even other established actors deliver some of their weakest work here. The story follows an African American man who takes a job as a chauffeur, driving the family’s daughter to a communist gathering. After becoming acquainted with her, one reckless night leads to her getting drunk.  

Though his employers are not racist, he assumes they are—so when he brings her home, panic sets in. After putting her to bed, she starts screaming, alerting her blind mother (yes, blind). In a desperate attempt to quiet her, he accidentally suffocates her. Now facing the consequences of killing a white girl, his next move is as shocking as it is absurd: he shoves her body into the furnace.

This film was a painful experience from start to finish. The characters' actions rarely made sense within the story, the performances were unconvincing (with P. Diddy surprisingly being the least terrible, which speaks volumes), and the plot offered no real surprises. While there were a few weak nods to *Carlito's Way* - like the Caribbean island fantasy - these references fell flat. The forced romantic subplot felt particularly misguided, though that may be subjective.  

Honestly, my expectations were low going in, but this still managed to disappoint. Jay Hernandez (who showed promise in *Friday Night Lights*) deserves better—though he can take comfort knowing few will likely sit through this. As someone who tends to rate films generously if they hold my interest even slightly, I can't justify more than two stars here. A complete misfire. For the record, yes, I liked *Carlito's Way*—this just isn’t in the same league.

I’ve always been a huge fan of Neil Young’s music, so with that in mind—plus the rave reviews the film got from alt-indie outlets—I rushed to the earliest screening of *Greendale* I could find. Unfortunately, my enthusiasm didn’t last. The sluggish plot and lackluster lyrical drive left most of the audience either nodding off or walking out disappointed.  

Neil claims the film began as a soundtrack, with the characters taking on such life that they simply filmed the music. Not exactly a recipe for strong storytelling. None of the characters have any real arc, and by the time "big" moments do happen, viewers are too irritated by the film’s repetitive gimmicks to care. The entire movie is driven by song, and as a result, characters endlessly lip-sync the lyrics. What might have been an interesting flourish the first time around quickly becomes unbearable—neither authentic nor stylized, just annoying.  

The acting is painfully one-note, with each character stuck in a single emotional register. Some scenes suffer from awkward lighting, too. The only redeeming moments come from a few newscast-style sequences, but even that approach feels overdone in modern cinema.

For a debut episode of a brand-new series, it did an excellent job. The energy was delightful, and the cast delivered standout performances. It’s unfair to dismiss it as bad simply because of historical nitpicking—this is a Saturday night entertainment show, not a dry documentary, so the costumes and settings were perfect for the tone. A fantastic beginning, and I can’t wait to see what’s next! At my school, everyone I’ve talked to adores the show too—we all agree it’s top-tier fun with captivating storytelling.

I rented this movie over the weekend, turned up the surround sound, and was impressed by the effects. It makes for a great rental—the visuals were intense enough to startle my fiancée, though some scenes looked noticeably CGI. I didn’t catch it in theaters, but it’s perfect for a spooky night in when you’d rather stay home. Definitely worth watching!

This film is an outstanding cinematic experience. The actors deliver brilliant performances, bringing their characters to life with depth and emotion. The engaging storyline follows Raj, deeply in love with Priya, as they marry and start their life together. Just as joy arrives with her pregnancy, tragedy strikes—they lose the child. Heartbroken, Raj crosses paths with Madhu and manipulates her through bribery. She becomes pregnant, though they are not wed.  

The movie excels in every aspect—powerful dialogues, soulful melodies, and vibrant visuals. The wedding sequence, bursting with color, is particularly mesmerizing. Salman, Rani, and Preity shine in their roles, adding to the film’s brilliance. Shot beautifully in Switzerland, the cinematography enhances the storytelling.  

A perfect blend of emotion, drama, and artistry—this film is worth every penny and minute. **Rating: 8/10**

Inspired by a real mining tragedy, this groundbreaking early German sound film (with English subtitles) stands as one of cinema's most powerful docu-dramas. Casting numerous non-professional actors, *Kameradschaft* delivers a gripping portrayal of the unbreakable solidarity among miners, transcending national borders between France and Germany. When catastrophe strikes, the workers' shared humanity overrides all official directives, revealing their profound courage and compassion. Risking everything—even their lives—these miners rally to rescue their imperiled comrades.  

The film's depiction of selfless bravery echoes the heroic actions of NYFD responders during 9/11, who disregarded protocol in their unwavering mission to save lives and recover their fellow firefighters. Decades after its release, *Kameradschaft*'s message endures: true friendship is proven in times of greatest need.

I’ve caught this film at multiple short-film festivals, and each time, it leaves me feeling like I’ve just watched a movie trailer!  

For a student project, the production and direction are impressively polished. That said, the story… it just needed a little more depth to become truly compelling. The character Tim Watcher, in particular, could’ve used a richer exploration. It’s a common gap in many Portuguese shorts—the scripts often skim the surface.  

Still… I found myself enjoying it.  

Parabéns! (Congratulations!)

Many argue that *Antz* is the superior film, and while it’s certainly great, I personally found *A Bug’s Life* more enjoyable. Aside from the *Toy Story* movies, I can’t recall a Pixar film that had me laughing this much. The animation is crisp, the story feels fresh without being preachy, and the voice acting truly elevates the film. Dave Foley brings sincerity to his role as an accident-prone ant, while Kevin Spacey delivers a standout performance as the menacing Hopper. Haydn Panettiere also shines as Dot, and the supporting cast—Dennis Leary, David Hyde Pierce, and Madeline Kahn—add brilliant depth. The script is sharp, hilarious, and even poignant at times. Unlike *Antz*, it doesn’t push heavy social commentary, but what it lacks in messaging, it more than makes up for in pure, rock-solid entertainment. 9/10. —Bethany Cox

Jason Lee’s sculpted physique makes a return! If that’s what you came for, you’re in luck. Otherwise, you might want to skip this one.  

As for the film itself—expect a barrage of clichés, awkwardly staged but somewhat unique fight scenes (featuring JKD), and plenty of cringe-worthy acting paired with bargain-bin effects. Lee seems to be suffering through every scene, and honestly, who could blame him? Not exactly the triumphant comeback fans were hoping for.  

This doesn’t even qualify as a decent B-movie. Sure, there’s a bleach-blonde, Rutger Hauer-esque villain, but not a single gratuitous scene—no nudity, no risqué shots. Nothing. Not even the bare minimum, unlike *Starship Troopers 2* (but more on that masterpiece in our upcoming review…).  

The whole thing feels like a petty revenge project by the writer, so I won’t bother dissecting the "plot" or much else—except to note the oddly prominent non-heterosexual subtext. Make of that what you will.  

At least there’s one silver lining—no Jean-Claude in sight.

First, scribble your script on a napkin—why waste paper? This isn’t Hollywood, after all.  

Next, cast untrained actors—perfect for festival buzz. Who needs seasoned professionals when raw awkwardness passes as "authentic"? Then, find a cinematographer who avoids proper lighting like the plague. A well-shot film just looks too polished, and festival juries might mistake competence for commercialism. While you’re at it, hand the camera to a child with zero experience. That shaky, unfocused mess? Critics will call it "raw realism," even as actual audiences flee the theater. A handful of overthinkers will praise it as brilliance, refusing to believe it’s just laziness disguised as art.  

Once that’s done, pack your bags for the Festival of Bad Movies—better known as Sundance.  

What a tragic joke.

Michael Rooker is a competent actor, but he lacks the presence to carry a leading role outside of low-budget films. He simply doesn't have the charisma needed. Ryo Ishibashi, with his far stronger screen presence, is unfortunately sidelined while most of the screen time is wasted on Rooker’s wooden performance.  

Danielle Harris (known for *Halloween 4* and *5*) plays Rooker’s daughter, bringing charm and energy, though her character is written as frustratingly naive—one of her poor decisions even gets a key character killed. The film includes comedians Fred Willard, Bobcat Goldthwait, and Stephen Furst in amusing roles, and their unpredictable scenes are a highlight.  

Vincent Schiavelli plays the Mafia consigliere, but his performance blurs the line between comedy and seriousness. Tim Thomerson, a staple in bargain-bin action and comedy flicks, also appears. With so many comedic actors involved, the film sometimes feels like a parody—maybe even a satire of Yakuza films. It’s hard to tell.

I could hardly believe this film would falter, yet it left me thoroughly let down. As a longtime admirer of Peckinpah’s work, I stumbled upon this DVD—heavily discounted—and decided to give it a chance. The opening credits, instantly recognizable to Peckinpah devotees, feature the signature cross-cutting between man and beast, layered with the eerie, offscreen sounds of children playing as a bomb is planted—brilliant tension. The real spark comes when Caan and Duvall, mid-mission, share a darkly comic exchange: Duvall casually reveals that Caan’s recent romantic encounter carried an unfortunate discovery, courtesy of some snooping. Their raucous laughter is pitch-perfect, a moment Brian De Palma visibly nods to in *Dressed to Kill*—poor Angie Dickinson never stood a chance.  

But *The Killer Elite* stumbles after its electrifying start. Even the notoriously rough *Bring Me the Head of Alfredo Garcia* outshines it in sheer craft, and that’s saying something. While I still screen Peckinpah’s openings for my students, this one’s a case where you’re better off hitting stop as soon as the credits fade.

Here’s the rewritten version:  

Greetings once more from the shadows. This film will inevitably draw comparisons to *The Princess Bride*, and while it doesn’t quite reach the heights of that timeless favorite, it holds its own as a delightfully entertaining and well-crafted adventure. The plot takes some unusual turns—particularly the unexplained wall—but it’s executed with skill, even managing to build genuine suspense.  

Charlie Cox stars as Tristan, a young man smitten with the wrong woman (Sienna Miller), who promises to bring her a fallen star—only to discover that the star is the luminous Claire Danes. Their inevitable connection isn’t the mystery here; the real tension comes from the relentless pursuit by a power-hungry witch (Michelle Pfeiffer) and the vengeful prince (son of King Peter O’Toole), both determined to seize the ruby necklace the star wears. It’s a classic race of villains chasing the heroes.  

The journey takes Tristan through bizarre encounters, including one with the most peculiar pirate imaginable—Robert De Niro’s Captain Shakespeare, whose brutish exterior hides a surprisingly delicate side. And let’s not forget Ricky Gervais, who steals scenes as a sharp-tongued trader, delivering some of the film’s best laughs.  

Far from perfect, but undeniably fun.

I had to sit through endless teenage drama and family squabbles for most of the show. High school girls stressing over relationships? Not my thing. I’ve already suffered through that mess in real life—I have zero interest in watching fictional kids breeze through watered-down versions of my own struggles. I came for science fiction, period. Just before the credits, we got a brief glimpse of a proto-Cylon. Finally, something worthwhile—except for one glaring flaw. Its red eye-dot locked onto targets, motionless. Any fan knows Cylon eyes never stop scanning, mapping their surroundings. That flickering red dot *always* moves.  

Here’s hoping the writers correct this blunder before the next episode.

Disappointing. This is what happens when a director shows up solely for the paycheck.  

The ambition was there—stunning locations and grand setups perfect for an epic-scale film. But the execution? Painful. In some scenes, you can spot extras in the background staring straight into the camera or awkwardly watching the actors, clearly never given direction after "Action!" was called. The battle sequences are laughably unconvincing—these warriors might as well have settled things with a group hug. Even slow-motion shots expose fighters milling around aimlessly or flailing halfheartedly.  

The foreground action gets a feeble attempt at intensity, but why bother? The storytelling is a disjointed mess—scenes stitched together with no logic, sometimes not even in sequence. The dialogue is cringe-worthy, and the romantic subplot rivals the absurdity of a low-budget Hong Kong action flick.  

With a $40 million budget, every penny is visible on-screen—unfortunately, the best this massive effort yields is a gloriously polished, utterly hollow coaster.

Just twenty minutes in, I found myself losing interest. The characters were painfully bland, and while there were brief moments of entertainment, they couldn’t salvage the sluggish pacing. Thankfully, the ending delivered some satisfaction—it wasn’t terrible. But was it worth enduring the tedious first hour and a half? Not at all. Given the talented cast, this film should have been far better. In the end, it was just average, and for that, it’s a letdown.

**Revised Version:**  

*Panic In The Streets* begins with a classic noir flourish—a shadow-drenched street view, the camera tilting up to a window framing a seedy card game. This stylish opening, combined with its location shooting, foreshadows the atmospheric tension Welles would later master in *Touch of Evil*. When one of the players throws open the window, the gesture is symbolic, both exposing the criminal underworld and drawing us into the unfolding drama.  

Filmed in stark black and white, *Panic In The Streets* thrives on its gripping performances and vivid New Orleans settings. Whether inside the morgue, the chaotic shipping office, or the rundown walls of "Frank’s Place," the film immerses viewers in an authentic, sometimes suffocating realism that studio sets could never replicate. These choices reflect the influence of Dassin’s *Naked City*, a noir landmark that pioneered a raw, documentary-like approach. Notably, Widmark—fresh from his role in Dassin’s even darker *Night and the City*—brings an edge to this tension-filled world.

We bought this movie as a joke for a friend, and it might have been our worst prank yet. The film is nearly unwatchable, with painfully bad acting—easily the worst child performer we’ve ever seen, and Hasselhoff barely bothering to try. The plot is downright embarrassing, so dull that at times we had no clue what was happening. It attempts shock value in places but only ends up being ridiculous.  

Just awful.

Who would have guessed they'd be this hilarious? Christopher Meloni and Janel Moloney are celebrated for their gripping performances in hit TV dramas like *Law & Order: SVU* and *The West Wing*, but pair them on the big screen, and the result is a charming romantic comedy brimming with humor.  

With remarkable chemistry, the actors bring the evolving romance to life—making it impossible not to adore Barry Singer (Meloni), even though he’s a cynical, chauvinistic stand-up comic.  

You’ll find yourself cheering him on as he confronts his romantic hang-ups and pursues Thea (Moloney) across the country, desperate to win her over. At first glance, they couldn’t be more different—yet when Barry finally lowers his guard, you’ll question why Thea keeps slipping away.  

*The Souler Opposite* shines with a talented cast and sharp writing, making it an absolute must-watch.

I haven't watched any of the so-called "Santa Slasher" movies—not *Silent Night, Deadly Night*, the original *Black Christmas*, or this one, *Christmas Evil*. I’ve definitely heard about their infamous reputations (and the backlash from MADS—Mothers Against Deranged Santas). I decided to rent *Christmas Evil* after hearing it mentioned on *Fat Guys At the Movies*.  

Mothers *should* be against this film—but not because of some supposedly scary killer Santa. No, the real crime here is that this movie is just *bad*. Painfully boring, dragging on even at a mere 92 minutes.  

The story starts in 1947 with a little boy who spots Santa coming down the chimney, delivering gifts, snacking on cookies, and—somehow—floating back up. Later, the kid sneaks back downstairs and catches his mom *basically* fooling around with Santa (though the "steamy" moment has all the heat of Ralphie's dad admiring his leg lamp in *A Christmas Story*). Traumatized (or… something?), the boy retreats to the attic and cuts his own hand in a fit of… whatever that was supposed to be.  

Cut to 1980—now the messed-up kid is a grown man working in a toy factory. We get treated to...

If predictable, formulaic rape-revenge thrillers are your taste, then this might just be your kind of film. Personally, I found nothing worthwhile in this strange, dated story—it feels like a relic from the 1980s, the kind of cheap, direct-to-video exploitation fare of another era. Gillian Anderson and Danny Dyer do their best with an uninspired script and a plodding setup.
