But why would Anderson, fresh off her stunning turn as Lady Dedlock in the BBC’s *Bleak House*, attach herself to something like this? The director cites inspiration from witnessing a near-rape and his documentary background, yet that hardly justifies the film’s absurd moments—like a pack of rural hounds attacking Dyer, a scene so ridiculous it had the audience laughing. Even more baffling is the involvement of FilmFour and Verve Pictures, backers of acclaimed British indies like *Bullet Boy*, *Code 46*, and *Red Road*. *Straightheads* doesn’t belong in the same conversation.

That summer, I spent several days watching the filming of this movie, only for the final cut to feature just two of those scenes. The shoot took place at Sylvan Lake in the Black Hills—simple shots like bringing the wagon in and stopping it. As a Dakota native, I eagerly awaited the film’s release and wasn’t let down. Since the local buffalo herd was being thinned out at the time, the hunting scenes were authentic. (Yes, Doris, animals were harmed during production.) The ending, I believe, was later echoed by Jack Nicholson in *The Shining*. A powerful Western with sharp social commentary from the '50s, this film deserves to stand alongside *High Noon* as quintessential frontier drama. It’s as much a cultural touchstone as *Blackboard Jungle* or *Rebel Without a Cause* were for the youth of that era.

This film makes a reasonable effort but ultimately falls short. While it captures the essence of a typical sixties movie, it lacks a real sense of accomplishment. Maggie Smith delivers a solid, believable performance—though not her best—while the rest of the cast struggles with weak portrayals. The humor falls flat, and the tone is neither particularly funny nor dramatic, only managing to work as a passable romance. The plot and storyline are simplistic and poorly executed, leaving audiences puzzled about its intended message and target demographic. Still, Maggie Smith stands out, and there are fleeting moments where the film shows brief promise.  

4/10

Race is a complex issue I approach carefully as a white person... but the double standard here is striking. Hating Black people is condemned, while hating White people gets a pass – as if it's justified. Where to begin?  

Aside from some unintentionally hilarious moments, there's little positive to say. The over-the-top fight scene where Ice Cube and his crew take down massive, terrifying Neo-Nazis twice their size is pure absurdity. And the chase? Comedy gold.  

This isn't a film about race, understanding, or tolerance—it fails on every level. Instead, it reinforces tired stereotypes: a meek white guy bullied by his Black roommate suddenly becomes a skinhead? Ridiculous. Painfully bad—wish I could unsee it.  

Skip this poorly written, poorly acted, dull, and blatantly biased mess. If you want a thought-provoking take on race, watch *American History X* instead. Now *that's* a real film.

Allen travels to the countryside—a setting he despises in real life—to spend a weekend with friends, the typical affluent, white middle-class complainers who often populate his films.  

While I usually find something entertaining in Woody Allen’s comedies, this time he falls completely flat. Even his trademark one-liners are nowhere to be found. The film lacks any real plot—aside from flimsy Shakespearean pastiches—and Allen tries to inject a vague, mystical tone through the setting, which only makes the whole thing feel more absurd and half-hearted.  

It fails on every level, becoming a tedious slog. The only redeeming qualities? The closing credits—and the scathing reviews that hopefully jolted Allen into realizing that slapping together a lazy script and casting his buddies isn’t a recipe for good cinema.

Understanding a film’s age should prepare viewers for certain expectations—keeping those in mind might make it more bearable. That was my approach with *Revolt of the Zombies.* The film’s reliance on slow, dialogue-heavy scenes and stiff performances is typical of its era, as is the lack of sophisticated (or sometimes any) special effects. It demands a lot from the audience’s imagination, perhaps even too much in this case.  

The plot is convoluted: During World War I, a group of zombified Southeast Asian soldiers fought with eerie efficiency. Skeptical yet cautious about this discovery falling into the wrong hands, an expedition is sent to uncover the truth. One member learns the secret of long-distance hypnosis and abuses it, even manipulating the romantic rival of the woman he desires. To win her affection, he relinquishes control over the zombies—a mistake, since once freed, they turn on him, determined to prevent him from ever enslaving them again.  

Despite adjusting my expectations, the film remains below average. Recommended only for the most dedicated fans of vintage horror.

This film starts as a dark, suspenseful thriller about a man searching for a missing woman. But within half an hour, it spirals into an absurd, unintentionally hilarious mess filled with bizarre characters and ridiculous moments. It’s impossible not to burst out laughing when Cage suddenly karate kicks the blonde woman or bear-hugs an elderly lady. From the awkward dialogue to the wooden performances, everything falls flat from the first scene.  

While I usually enjoy Nicolas Cage’s work, this is easily his worst movie of the year—so far—in a string of disappointing roles.  

Don’t watch this if you’re looking for a gripping, intense thriller. If you want the real deal, check out the original instead. But if you do decide to sit through this, treat it as a comedy—laugh at the cringeworthy lines and ridiculous final scenes. That’s the only way to make it bearable.

What were they thinking with this one? Over the years, the *Columbo* series has experimented with fresh ideas and strayed from its winning formula, but this movie pushes it too far. While distinct from any other *Columbo* film, the changes don’t work in its favor.  

The biggest departure? There’s no murder—none at all. The entire premise shifts, dropping Columbo into a completely unfamiliar setting and scenario. The tone feels overly "modernized," straying too far from what fans expect.  

Oddly, director Alan J. Levi previously handled *Columbo* films that stayed true to the classic formula, making his involvement here a puzzling choice.  

Even Columbo himself feels off—likely because he’s thrust into an uncharacteristic role, helping his nephew track down a runaway bride. The lack of the detective’s trademark wit and humor only makes the whole thing fall even flatter.

Richard Dix chose to retire, leading Michael Duane to step into the role of Ted Nichols, who encounters a young French woman named Alice Dupres Barkley, played by Lenore Aubert. After knowing each other for just two days, the couple impulsively decides to marry and seeks out a Justice of the Peace. However, when they arrive at the judge’s home in the midst of a downpour, they discover he is away and won’t return until morning.  

While waiting inside, an unseen figure lifts the hood of their car and steals a critical engine part—foreshadowing the turmoil ahead. This strange incident hints at the tangled mysteries surrounding Alice, leaving Ted Nichols entangled in trouble before the marriage even begins. A compelling mystery unfolds, though fans of Richard Dix may feel his absence. Still, an engaging watch. Enjoy.

When the film premiered in 1984, Prince was at the peak of his fame. Audiences flocked to see what was essentially a feature-length music video. The acting left much to be desired—understandable given the cast were musicians, not actors—but the movie remained wildly entertaining. Morris Day and Jerome Benton delivered unforgettable comedy, particularly in their iconic "The Password" scene, which rivals Abbott & Costello's legendary "Who's on First?" routine.  

Apollonia added both beauty and charisma to the film, with a brief but memorable appearance. The soundtrack, filled with Prince's signature style, stands as one of his strongest works. Though his later career saw conflicts with Warner Bros. and his famous name change, this era captured him at his creative zenith.  

While not a cinematic masterpiece, the movie remains a fun, nostalgic ride for fans of Prince and '80s pop culture.

When I was nine, my parents brought me to see this film – an experience that stayed with me forever. Nothing had ever captivated me the way Elizabeth Taylor did. (She was twenty-two during *Elephant Walk*.) At that age, my admiration wasn’t about attraction; I was simply transfixed. I would have happily curled up at her feet, gazing at her in awe. Though time has left its mark—she’s now nearly seventy-four—I remain convinced she was one of the most stunning, mesmerizing women ever to exist.  

I’ve revisited the movie since, and while it leans heavily into melodrama, certain elements elevate it: Taylor’s undeniable radiance, the breathtaking landscapes, the thrilling elephant stampede, and a poignant commentary on human hubris against nature.  

All told, it’s a worthwhile way to spend an evening—whether catching it on a movie channel or streaming an old favorite.

This gripping debut film delivers spine-chilling moments that linger long after the credits roll. Like the finest horror films, it twists your gut with relentless tension from start to finish. The masterful ending alone—more a terrifying beginning than a conclusion—clearly inspired classics like *The Blair Witch Project*. A brilliant piece of Japanese horror, this movie earns top marks for its fear factor, leaving you both terrified and deep in thought. A truly mind-scarring experience.

**"Rosenstraße"** tells the story of brave women during Nazi Germany, but it falls short in execution. The film drags on, lacking emotional impact and often feeling dull. Filled with clichés and weak performances, it fails to engage.  

The narrative structure is poorly handled. Similar to *Titanic*, an elderly woman reflects on her past—fine, we have a perspective. But then another woman does the same, both recounting events they couldn’t have witnessed firsthand. How would Riemann know about the little girl’s mother or her interrogation? It’s a fundamental storytelling flaw.  

The timeline is confusing, with scenes jumbled and no clear sense of when events occur. For example, Riemann’s proposal to Fabian feels like it’s set in the 1920s—but when did it actually happen?  

Riemann’s character is predictably overdone—a gifted pianist, no less, and a baroness. Her brother returns from the Eastern Front proudly displaying his *Ritterkreuz*, cementing his role as a war hero. It’s all too formulaic.

**Kimi wa Petto** is an adorable tale about a girl who discovers a boy inside a box outside her apartment. Taking pity on him, she brings him inside to tend to his injuries before leaving for work, along with a note asking him to eat the meal she prepared and then leave. But when she returns, he’s still there.  

In an attempt to persuade him to go, she jokingly says he can stay—but only as her pet, with no rights and no say in anything (and no, not in a weird way!). Unexpectedly, he agrees, and from that moment on, he becomes **Momo**, her devoted pet.

This film is to the Zatoichi series what the *Star Trek* movies were to *Star Trek*—only here, every original outshines this flashy remake in entertainment, depth, and craftsmanship, assuming substance matters more than style. Had I not seen the classics, I might have dismissed this as well-shot but hollow. Having seen them, though, I found its aesthetic mismatched and its substance lacking. Reviving the character with a bigger, glossier production may have seemed appealing, but the only real motive was profit. This rendition largely misses the essence of Zatoichi’s world and doesn’t push the character beyond familiar ground (not to mention the lead performance fell short). I had hoped for a late-chapter story, one that would give Ichi a meaningful farewell while reflecting on his journey—instead, this recycles old material, just spiced up with more sex and flashy violence. A poor imitation, nothing more.

What a forgotten 80s gem of a soundtrack. You'd almost expect John Travolta to belt out a few tunes, though the film itself ends up embodying pure 80s camp. Apparently movies built around mechanical bulls, rowdy bartenders, and shallow love stories were the height of cool back then—nothing tops his painfully bad Texas drawl. Put it side by side with *Friday Night Lights* and the contrast is laughable.  

For a masterclass in cinematic fluff, queue up *Cocktail* and *Stir Crazy.* And don’t skip *Made in America*—Ted Danson and Whoopi Goldberg serve up gloriously cringeworthy gold. I was stunned I’d never seen it before. Round out the list with Robin Williams' *Cadillac Man* for good measure.  

It’s wild to think A-listers like Tom Cruise, Richard Pryor, Robin Williams, and Travolta once headlined these gloriously cheesy flicks.

This Chinese film struck a deep chord in me, connecting me to a culture I'm not part of and geographically distant from. With an almost Buddhist sensibility, it creates empathy for each character, celebrating the quiet joy found in life's everyday rhythms.  

The entire cast delivers extraordinary performances. Xu Hzu radiates both kindness and wisdom while also revealing moments of vulnerability and harshness. Er Min, the developmentally disabled brother, beautifully demonstrates that intelligence and wisdom are not the same—that profound insight can come from the most unexpected places. This isn't the China of gritty realism; instead, it offers a different kind of truth, brimming with humanity and emotional authenticity.  

Don’t miss it—you won’t regret it.

This film is truly terrible, but I’ve got some fascinating behind-the-scenes details for you:  

It was shot in 1976 at Northern Arizona University in Flagstaff, AZ, as well as in Oak Creek Canyon near Sedona, AZ. Many of the extras were NAU theater students at the time. I was a freshman there that year, minoring in theater, though I never actually worked on the production. Still, I knew a few people who did—and here’s the weirdest tidbit:  

There’s a scene where two main characters, as part of a hazing ritual, have to sprint naked into the woods. You only see them from behind in the film, but those aren’t the real actors—they were two guys from the theater department I knew. Their identities will stay secret… at least on this site, unless they choose to step forward and, well, expose themselves!

Anthony Hopkins is a phenomenal actor, which made me eager to see his work as a writer and director. Unfortunately, the film fell painfully short of expectations—it was incoherent, and the overly stylized cinematography became grating. While the cast delivered strong performances, their talent was squandered by the film's poor execution. Some actors excel in front of the camera but simply aren't suited for behind-the-scenes roles, and Hopkins is evidently one of them. In my 50 years of movie-watching, this stands as the single worst film I've ever seen. Mr. Hopkins, your acting is masterful—please focus on that and leave writing and directing to those with the skill for it. If a rating lower than one existed, this film would deserve it.

Michael Ironside’s acting career must be in serious trouble if he’s reduced to starring in this low-budget garbage. Surely he could find something better than wasting his time on this mess.  

The film had potential, but the lack of budget is painfully obvious. One scene, supposedly set at an outpost, looks like it was shot outside a train station—and I wouldn’t be surprised if it was.  

The only reason I gave this movie a 3/10 is for one decent sequence: a spacecraft landing and taking off over a forest-lined lake. That moment was well-executed, but the rest of the film is forgettable.  

Another "space outpost" scene is clearly just an industrial plant, further highlighting how cheap and unconvincing the whole production is.  

This movie is nonsensical, painfully cheap, and a complete waste of time—someone get Michael Ironside out of this disaster.

I caught this film on cable last night, and it's truly remarkable. What strikes me most is its quiet, restrained power—subtle yet profoundly moving. Henry Thomas (who you might remember as the boy from *E.T.*) delivers a brilliantly understated performance, perfectly capturing a man of few words. David Straithern is mesmerizing as the unhinged antagonist. And, against all odds for a Hollywood production, a baby becomes a central presence—not through exaggerated cuteness or contrived moments, but simply by existing, with an almost radiant stillness. It's fascinating how Thomas' connection with E.T. drove that classic, while here, his bond with the baby anchors *A Good Baby* with equal depth.  

Then there’s the music—absolutely breathtaking. Gillian Welch’s haunting melodies and the earthy, soulful hill-country soundtrack elevate every scene.  

The film wraps you in its mood, lingering long after the credits roll. A must-watch.

This film appears to promote Muslim identity and values.  

Here’s why: The protagonist has a Muslim father and a Christian mother but grows up in a Christian village. By the film's conclusion, he seems to embrace Islam—his attire, headwear, and the amulet he retains all suggest this. He has a six-year-old child who wears similar headwear, implying the child is being raised Muslim despite the mother being Christian. Meanwhile, none of the other major male characters, who are Christian, are shown having children. The ending subtly suggests that Islam grows in influence by the next generation, while Christianity does not expand in the same way.

Visionary filmmaker Walt Disney immortalized three timeless fairy tales through animation, creating some of cinema’s most beloved classics. The journey began with his pioneering 1937 masterpiece *Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs*, followed by the underrated *Sleeping Beauty* in 1959. Nestled between them stands his most magical fairy-tale adaptation—*Cinderella* (1950).  

Unlike *Snow White*, which reshaped its source material into the definitive version for many, *Cinderella* remained remarkably faithful to its roots. Ironically, despite being a commercial success and rescuing Disney’s struggling studio—much like its predecessor—it never garnered the same widespread cultural permanence it truly merited. For once, Disney resisted drastic reinterpretation, choosing instead to enrich the original story with depth and splendor rather than reinvent it. The outcome was nothing short of spellbinding.  

Through breathtaking animation (rendered in delicate Technicolor hues) and flawlessly cast voice performances, the film captured a luminous charm that continues to captivate audiences decades later.

Television has a real impact on society—just look at how cappuccino shops exploded in popularity after that shallow show premiered. And let’s be honest, people who look that flawless don’t have real problems anyway.  

Speaking of which, does anyone actually buy that these characters could afford a nice Manhattan loft with their careers? NBC must think viewers are complete idiots—or at least close to it. I know a web designer making $100,000 a year who still squeezes into a tiny one-bedroom apartment with a $2,200 monthly rent.  

Someone should make a show called *Phriends*—starring six unattractive nobodies stuck in dead-end jobs, stuck in a rundown neighborhood where sirens never stop, muggings happen weekly, and the landlord keeps raising the rent. Now *that* would be worth watching.

For roughly the first 20 minutes (since I watched it on a PS2, I can’t say for sure how long it actually was), *Alienator* sets up a surprisingly intriguing premise—a slasher flick with an extraterrestrial killer? That’s something I hadn’t seen before. But that intrigue quickly dissolves into bewildered disbelief when you realize the so-called "alien" is just a massive bodybuilder woman decked out in a steel bikini. Yeah, *Alienator* is undeniably absurd.  

And I don’t necessarily mean that as a bad thing. When it comes to schlock horror, absurdity can sometimes be a selling point. Unfortunately, *Alienator* doesn’t offer much beyond its gloriously stupid premise. It’s hilarious, sure, but it’s also a complete trainwreck. The actors deliver painfully earnest performances that fall flat, the goldmine of cheesy dialogue is butchered by hilariously bad delivery, and the direction can’t even manage a single memorable scene. By the end, the original concept is buried under a mountain of nonsensical garbage.  

Oh, and just to top it off, the "alien" doesn’t even get creative with the kills—just vaporizes people. How thrilling.

I expected a detailed exploration of the Apollo 11 mission, but instead got interviews with Buzz Aldrin, Gene Kranz, and others—interviews that were solid, yet drowned out by exaggerated, doomsday-style narration straight out of the worst TV tropes.  

Without the overdramatic voice-over and with a focus on celebrating human perseverance in the face of challenges—how ordinary people accomplished something extraordinary—this could have been incredible. Instead, I sat through a 60-minute program feeling like I lost 45 minutes of my life. And I want them back.

I seem to be the only person in America who didn’t enjoy this film. Maybe it just wasn’t for me, but I genuinely don’t understand the hype—it was barely entertaining, much less a cinematic masterpiece.  

The story follows a guy who rises from nothing to become a drug kingpin. That summary covers it pretty well, because honestly, that’s all there was to it. Just because a movie revolves around organized crime doesn’t automatically make it brilliant—strong storytelling matters too.

I’ve watched plenty of great Korean films, including gripping thrillers and darker-themed movies, but this one is terrible. The director comes off as downright sadistic, somehow convincing producers to fund this mess. It offers zero entertainment value and fails miserably as a thriller. I’m shocked anyone greenlit this project. While the acting is passable, the storyline and overall tone are downright unbearable.  

I won’t be watching anything by this director again. There’s no understanding of filmmaking here, and any attempt at suspense falls completely flat. Instead of tension, we get gratuitous violence and poorly executed psychopathic scenes, as if excessive blood somehow equals thrills. A total letdown—I’d advise avoiding anything remotely like this.

One of my favorite Amitabh Bachchan comeback films! This gem arrived during Govinda’s golden era with David Dhawan—packed with fantastic, high-energy music and pure "masti." A timeless entertainer, elevated by the versatile Anupam Kher. Classic Dhawan-style humor keeps the plot spinning with laugh-out-loud twists. And just when you think it can’t get better, Madhuri Dixit-Nene lights up the screen, turning the finale into an all-out riot. Amitabh’s powerhouse performance, blending intensity with comedy after his hiatus, was a joy to watch. Sure, some might dismiss it as just another masala flick, but I’d revisit it in a heartbeat. An effortless 8/10 for delivering quintessential Bollywood magic.

Holy hell—and that’s coming from an atheist—this "film" is absolutely atrocious!  

Most of the earlier negative reviews (those rating it 3 or below) nailed every flaw perfectly—I completely agree. But let me add a few painful details:  

Of the three guys forced to eat their own filth, hacked apart by an axe, violated with a broomstick, and robbed of their manhood, the ex-boyfriend endures the cruelest fate: suffering through the girlfriend’s mind-numbing, never-ending monologue at the kitchen table. At least we viewers have the mercy of the mute button.  

If the director had trimmed the endless, pointless graveyard scenes and reversed the same dull sequences, our torment could’ve been over in 30 minutes.  

The only remotely redeeming feature? Emily Haack’s anatomy (granting it a single point).  

Seriously—skip it. Don’t buy it. Don’t waste your time or your sanity. My brain is so fried after enduring this garbage that I’m now considering subjecting myself to *Scrapbook* as some kind of masochistic follow-up.

Like countless devoted Trekkers (or Trekkies—I don’t mind either!), I endured seven long seasons of *Star Trek: Voyager*, wistfully reminiscing about *Deep Space Nine* after its 1999 finale. Then, at last—our prayers were answered. *Enterprise* is phenomenal. A bold new angle, completely fresh faces, breathtaking visuals, and even a pop theme song (who saw that coming?). There’s not a single thing I’d change. Give me ten seasons of this, easy. *Star Trek* has finally returned—sorry, *Voyager*, but you won’t be missed. Keep on Trekkin’!  

>

From the outstanding performances of a remarkable cast to the sharp, brilliantly quotable dialogue, from the sumptuous cinematography to Carter Burwell’s gorgeous score, *Rob Roy* delivers something rare in cinema—a film that leaves no room for criticism.  

Comparisons to *Braveheart*, released the same year, are inevitable. While Mel Gibson’s effort deserves recognition, *Braveheart* comes across as overly grandiose and heavy-handed—a film I wouldn’t rush to revisit. *Rob Roy*, in contrast, pulls you in effortlessly with its crisp, tightly woven narrative. Every scene matters.  

The film strikes the ideal balance of drama, action, and well-placed humor. Its characters are richly developed, their speech and mannerisms flawlessly capturing the authenticity of their time.  

What sets *Rob Roy* apart is its refusal to reduce its characters to simple archetypes of good and evil—a pitfall even modern films often stumble into.  

Take Rob Roy himself: though we root for his victory, his struggles stem from

Many comments in this thread draw comparisons between this film and *The Mortal Storm* or *Casablanca*. While everyone is free to compare films as they see fit, the parallels between *The Mortal Storm* and *Watch on the Rhine* primarily lie in their shared focus on refugees facing Nazi oppression. Meanwhile, the frequent comparison to *Casablanca* often centers on the perceived injustice in the Academy’s 1943 Best Actor decision—Paul Lukas winning over Humphrey Bogart.  

This choice doesn’t strike me as entirely unfair. Lukas had a solid career in film (both in Hollywood and Britain—he played the villain in *The Lady Vanishes*), and this was undeniably his finest performance. Bogart, of course, delivered many iconic roles beyond Rick Blaine in *Casablanca*. He was overlooked for his work as Sam Spade in *The Maltese Falcon* and Roy Earle in *High Sierra* two years prior—both outstanding performances. Even later, he wouldn’t win Oscars for his greatest roles: Fred C. Dobbs in *The Treasure of the Sierra Madre*, the troubled screenwriter in *In a Lonely Place*, or the unforgettable Captain Queeg in *The Caine Mutiny*.

Some aspects of this film feel outdated—such as its all-white, all-male crew. Like many pre-Star Wars sci-fi films, it lingers too long in self-admiration.  

Yet, no other movie has captured the essence of Golden Age science fiction quite like this one, down to its use of "electronic tonalities" for the score. Robbie the Robot embodied Asimov’s vision and inspired countless successors, from C3PO to Data.  

The plot mirrors Shakespeare’s *The Tempest*, with Morbius as a modern Prospero—an exiled sorcerer whose domain is invaded by outsiders. This was one of the first films to treat science fiction as a serious, adult genre.

Aldolpho (Steve Buscemi), a struggling filmmaker, barely scrapes by in a rundown New York City apartment, relying on his mother’s financial support to cover rent. He becomes infatuated with his stunning neighbor, Angelica (Jennifer Beals), who may or may not be married—either way, she’s the perfect leading lady for his film. His luck appears to turn when a mysterious man named Joe offers to fund his project—until Joe drags Aldolpho into a reckless scheme involving stealing a Porsche as collateral.  

As Aldolpho’s morals unravel, questions linger: Will his film ever materialize? And will Angelica agree to star in it? Unfortunately, despite the potential in its premise, this movie falls painfully short. The disjointed script meanders without purpose, while Beals delivers her lines with inexplicable hostility, and Buscemi—though endearing—fades into the background.  

Laden with tasteless content and unlikeable characters, the film is further crippled by shoddy production quality, making it look amateurish at best. Even if you're bored and looking for entertainment, this one isn’t worth the gamble. Steer clear—your time is better spent elsewhere.

I’m a huge movie fan, and I usually give every film a fair shot by watching it all the way through. But for the first time, I’ve found one I just couldn’t finish. The acting is painfully stiff and emotionless, the CGI looks like it was thrown together by an amateur using basic software, and let’s not forget the endless scenes of... just walking! And to make it worse, this movie drags on for *three hours*—I barely lasted 15 minutes before hitting fast-forward. The alien scenes? Few and far between. Honestly, instead of *War of the Worlds*, they should’ve called it *War of the Endless Walks*. How did this cost $5 million to make? Did the entire budget go into that overdramatic opening song?  

On the bright side, there’s one scene worth seeing—when the aliens start killing people. It’s unintentionally hilarious, not because of the deaths, but because the victims turn into skeletons... and then keep wriggling for another 20 seconds.  

So, if you enjoy dull, lifeless, action-free films, here’s a perfect addition to your DVD shelf. But let’s be real—I didn’t write this for the die-hard fans. I wrote it for the...

**Engaging story with stunning animation.** The clear inspirations from Frazetta and Bakshi shine through in the best way. Fans of *Conan the Barbarian* or *Dungeons & Dragons* will find plenty to enjoy. While the battle between good and evil is straightforward, the hero sometimes walks a morally ambiguous line—adding depth to the classic fantasy struggle.  

The film breaks away from traditional fantasy stereotypes, offering a fresh take on elves, goblins, and orcs without relying on outdated tropes. Those familiar with Frazetta, Bakshi, or Tolkien will appreciate this nuanced approach, proving fantasy doesn’t need to conform to narrow portrayals.  

Well-cast and visually striking, the film boasts exceptional scenes and a memorable score. However, its violence and mature themes make it unsuitable for young audiences.  

This hidden gem deserves a proper DVD release—I’m fortunate to own a well-preserved VHS copy, but it’s a film that should be widely available for fantasy lovers to enjoy.

**NEARLY GLITTERING: THE JESSICA SAVITCH SAGA**  

**Aspect ratio:** 4:3  
**Audio format:** Stereo  

This uninspired, melodramatic retelling of America's pioneering female news anchor's turbulent career fails to captivate. Hampered by weak writing, lackluster direction, and an unconvincing cast, the film struggles to do justice to its intriguing subject. A compelling documentary might have served the story better. Though professionally assembled in typical TV-movie fashion, the result is as shallow and forgettable as yesterday's news.

The true crime story at the heart of *In Cold Blood* may feel somewhat subdued compared to the gruesome tales of infamous serial killers like Gein, Bundy, or Dahmer, or even the more sensationalized Hollywood cases such as O.J. Simpson or the Manson murders. The central events of the case aren’t particularly intricate: Perry Smith and Dick Hickock (portrayed by Robert Blake and Scott Wilson) crossed paths by chance, plotted to rob a farmhouse safe in Kansas, and ended up brutally murdering a family of four with a shotgun and a knife—only to walk away with a meager $43. Beyond their brief escape to Mexico before returning to the U.S., there’s little mystery in how their story concludes. Their capture came by sheer, ironic luck—a cop pulled them over for driving a stolen car after the pair had ironically helped a young boy and his father collect bottles for spare change. Sentenced to death by hanging, their story reached its grim end in 1965.  

Yet what elevates *In Cold Blood* is not the crime itself but the way it’s presented—the lingering, contemplative moments, the powerhouse performances, and the impeccable cinematic artistry brought to life by director Brooks and the legendary late cinematographer Conrad Hall.

This film follows the twisted story of a deranged scientist who, after his fiancée's beheading, prowls strip clubs in search of the perfect body to reconnect with her severed head. Every character oozes with sleaze—especially the main lead, who leaves a trail of greasiness thicker than a slug's slime.

This film is a perfect blend of romance and sports that will delight true romantics and die-hard sports fans alike.  

Drew Barrymore delivers one of her finest performances here—a refreshing return to form after a string of disappointments. As a longtime fan, it was a joy to see her shine again. Jimmy Fallon, though initially a question mark, completely wins over the audience as Ben, the lovably goofy, sports-obsessed sweetheart. The humor is spot-on, with plenty of laugh-out-loud moments throughout.  

Their first date gets off to an awkward start when Ben arrives with flowers, only to find Lindsay miserably sick from bad takeout earlier in the day. Instead of bailing, he steps up—helping her into pajamas, cleaning up her mess, and even joking that she was "very ladylike... no chunks." Their relationship blossoms beautifully over the winter, but when baseball season rolls around, Lindsay discovers just how deep Ben’s obsession with the Red Sox runs—and why such a great guy is still single. She tries to brush it off, telling herself it’s a good thing since her busy work schedule won’t leave much time for guilt.

Robot Jox holds up surprisingly well in terms of story and effects—especially considering it’s a 1990 film. Back then, even major productions like RoboCop 2 still relied on stop-motion animation, a technique that dominated most of the '80s. Big blockbusters of the era worked with the limited effects technology available, making the most of what they had. It wasn’t until Terminator 2: Judgment Day debuted the next year that CGI breakthroughs changed the game, inspiring storytellers to push boundaries.  

But Robot Jox has its own charm—fans of Transformers, Gundam Wing, or Power Rangers will find plenty to enjoy here. The antagonist’s mech is genuinely intimidating, the kind of threat you wouldn’t want to face without a solid strategy. The film also delivers some standout moments, particularly with its spy subplot. Nothing’s worse than realizing the ally you trusted might actually be working against you. That kind of betrayal? Always a gut punch. Don’t you think?

While the historical accuracy may be debatable—especially given how easily audiences forgive inaccuracies in popular franchises like *Lord of the Rings*—I still enjoyed its artistic touches. Though not quite an arthouse film, it delivers some emotionally gripping moments throughout.  

My main criticisms? First, it feels too brief. Second, the occasional whispering voice is never clarified.  

**Rating: 8/10**  
Quality: 10/10 | Entertainment: 7/10 | Replay Value: 5/10

Even without any knowledge of Ireland, you can’t help but adore *My Left Foot*—especially Daniel Day-Lewis’s remarkable performance. He portrays Christy Brown, a man living with cerebral palsy, who has endured a lifetime of isolation. When he attempts to alert others to danger, they dismiss him with laughter. His sole lifeline is the control he retains over one part of his body: his left foot. With it, he paints and writes poetry, eventually gaining recognition for his talent.  

Daniel Day-Lewis and director Jim Sheridan crafted magic together in this film, just as they would later in *In the Name of the Father* (though *The Boxer* fell short). *My Left Foot* evokes a range of emotions—sorrow, hope, and more. Regardless, Day-Lewis delivers a performance for the ages. A masterpiece in every way.

When American author Edgar Allan Poe arrives in London, he encounters British journalist Alan Foster, who soon becomes embroiled in an unusual wager. Skeptical of Poe's claim that his chilling tales are rooted in real events, Foster takes on a bet proposed by Poe and his companion Sir Thomas Blackwood—to survive a full night inside Blackwood's infamous haunted castle.  

Once inside the abandoned fortress, Foster realizes he is far from alone. Mysterious figures emerge—ethereal women, striking men, and a cryptic doctor of metaphysics—who reveal they are tormented souls doomed to relive their tragic deaths on the anniversary of each grisly demise.  

From the very first viewing, this classic horror masterpiece captivated me completely. The film delivers genuine chills while weaving in a profound sense of melancholy. Babs Steele is radiant, her presence unforgettable. The haunting score amplifies the terror, making every moment twice as unnerving. One particularly unexpected moment—an unanticipated topless scene—caught me completely off guard.  

Synapse Films has clearly worked wonders with the restoration. The picture quality is stunning for its age, and this is the uncut international version, making the experience all the more immersive.

After hearing such glowing reviews of this play, I gave it a chance when I happened to catch it on cable. I fail to see how it "elevates" women or highlights their "struggles" by fixating on its central theme. Perhaps if you're intrigued by narratives centered on women's anatomy and its impact on their lives, this might appeal to you. Otherwise, it falls flat—dull and uninspiring. If anything, I found it somewhat demeaning.  

I asked a female friend who also watched it, and she agreed it was terrible. So it’s not just a case of a man "missing the point."

This film held so much potential—my favorite actor starring in a historical drama set during the War of Independence. It evoked flashes of *Dances With Wolves* with its sweeping prairies, Native American portrayals, and battle sequences, while the British aesthetic and candlelit interiors brought *Barry Lyndon* to mind.  

Yet, the script fails spectacularly. The narrative crumbles under jarring jumps in time ("Five months later... Three years later..."), and the forced romance stretches believability to its limits. Somehow, despite America's vast expanse, the characters keep crossing paths unnaturally. And the ending? A masterclass in sabotaging a story—imagine *Titanic* suffering the same fate.  

Occasionally, a weak script can be redeemed by a director’s brilliance. Sadly, that’s not the case here. Hudson’s direction is as lifeless as his earlier misfire, *Greystoke*. The scenes lack energy, the editing feels sluggish, and the score does nothing to elevate the film—it’s just long, dull, and painfully flat.  

I’d heard this movie derailed Pacino’s career. Now I see why. As 2006’s final cinematic offering, it perfectly mirrored my year—utterly agonizing.

It’s lucky I didn’t see this while pregnant—I would’ve sobbed uncontrollably or gotten sick. The movie was pretty gruesome, mostly just unsettling. That said, I found the baby oddly charming in its own bizarre way.  

As a mother, though, I winced when Beth stabbed herself in the stomach and when Virginia performed a third-trimester abortion using, of all things, rusty tools. And as an animal lover, I nearly lost it when she mutilated the cat.  

Still, no matter how creepy that baby was, I wanted it to survive. And as twisted as this film was, I’m weirdly eager to see the sequel.

The production's limited budget is evident in the sets, staging, and editing. Yet perhaps Bela Lugosi's presence is meant to draw attention away from these shortcomings. The story follows a chilling premise—young brides collapse dead at the altar just after uttering "I do." Their bodies are swiftly stolen by the enigmatic Dr. Lorenz (Lugosi) and his grotesque assistants. His aging wife (Elizabeth Russell) relies on injections of glandular fluids from young virgins to preserve her youth and beauty.  

A determined local journalist (Luana Walters) notices a pattern—each missing bride wore the same rare orchid, a flower tied to Dr. Lorenz’s expertise. As the tension builds, a classic horror storm rages outside, heightening the unease during a visit to the ominous Lorenz estate—especially with its unsettling inhabitants: a dwarf and a drooling hunchback.  

The cast also includes Angelo Rossitto, Tristram Coffin, Minerva Urecal, and Frank Moran.

Having already shared my thoughts on this film, I want to express how eagerly I anticipated watching it—the talented cast, the picturesque Italian setting, and the renowned direction of Michael Winterbottom all held promise. From the start, the story faintly echoed 'Don’t Look Now,' with a grieving family seeking solace in unfamiliar surroundings (Italy once again) to numb their loss—or perhaps that was just my interpretation. As I watched, I kept waiting for the narrative to twist in an unexpected way, subverting the typical tropes of a family abroad in Europe... but I waited... and waited... and nothing ever materialized. Absolutely nothing! The characters were so thinly drawn and devoid of depth that forming any connection with them was impossible. The film’s deliberate pacing misleadingly suggested an impending upheaval—something that never came. The eldest daughter’s fleeting flirtation with local Vespa riders could have steered the story in a compelling new direction, yet it fizzled out. Likewise, the younger daughter’s visions of her deceased mother amounted to nothing consequential, and the father’s near-seduction by a woman...

I caught this at the Esquire Theatre in Cincinnati, Ohio—and now I regret existing.  

Christopher Reeve could’ve pulled off a more convincing boxer.  

The film itself was agony, but witnessing Bret Carr in person was like staring directly into the abyss of desperation.  

The highlight? Watching BC take what looked like a "C" battery to the face (jury's still out—might’ve been a dildo) in slow motion. Glorious.  

*"Shoot only the left side of the face... fame comes to those who demand it!"* —Bret Carr.  

At one point, B. Carr roamed Clifton in a chicken suit, reverse-psychology-ing his own film. Smart move. This thing deserves every bit of hate it gets.  

My soul felt raw afterward.  

Bret Carr lacks the charisma to lead a cult—or the brains, for that matter. That’s the vibe from the *What the Bleep*-esque stream of brainwashed, impressionable neo-yuppies who showed up for this Bret Carr *masterpiece*.  

Just recalling it is emotionally exhausting.

I’ve never been a big Sylvester Stallone fan, and the only time I truly enjoyed his presence was in the French film *Taxi 3*—where he had a barely noticeable cameo. Yet, against my expectations, this movie turned out to be surprisingly decent.  

After Gabe (Stallone) fails to save his friend’s girlfriend, watching her fall to her death from a 4,000-foot peak, he can no longer bear to work as a mountain ranger. For nearly a year, he avoids the reserve entirely—until he finally returns. Shortly after his comeback, the rangers receive a distress call from hikers stranded in a snowstorm. Or so they think. In truth, the group consists of thieves whose plane crashed following a botched heist. Their bold scheme? Stealing government money mid-flight. Now, with the stolen cash scattered across the mountains, they need skilled climbers to recover it...  

Admittedly, this isn’t highbrow cinema, but—

We had to watch this in school, and it was awful. The film feels dated, with episodes that blend fact and fiction in a way that just gets confusing.  

The teachers framed it as a special reward, but it was painfully dull instead. From what I've read, hardly any of the people in it are actual actors—most are just doing their real-life jobs, which explains the stiff performances.  

A lot of the plot twists feel over-the-top and hard to believe. The dialogue falls flat too, lacking depth even though it was clearly trying to be educational, funny, and trendy. Instead, it just came across as boring, unconvincing, and past its prime.  

Honestly, don’t waste your time—you’re not missing anything by skipping it.

This series claims to be an upgrade from *Batman: The Animated Series*, but it falls painfully short. The art is subpar—just look at Catwoman’s dreadful design. Worse still, the show reduces Batman to a helpless weakling who constantly relies on multiple sidekicks just to survive a fight. Since when does *Batman* need backup for a few thugs? In *BTAS*, he took on armies single-handedly. Is age suddenly an excuse? Hardly.  

And don't get me started on throwing Tim Drake into the fray with minimal training. Not only is that reckless—something Batman would never tolerate—but it also strays from the comics’ established lore.  

*Batman: The Animated Series* set the standard with its stellar animation, gripping storytelling, and iconic characterizations. *That* was legendary. This? Just a pale imitation.

I sat through this entire movie just to keep a promise to a friend. It fails to deliver even the accidental humor or charm that makes some bad films watchable. This might honestly be the most painfully awful film I've endured. Frankly, I'm shocked any distributor agreed to be associated with it.

This movie may have scored a dismal 2 for its pitiful attempt at horror, but it’s a perfect 10 in unintentional hilarity. The plot was incomprehensible, the characters unrecognizable—yet somehow, that only added to the joy. Every scene was a fresh disaster, leaving me in tears of laughter. The sparse dialogue suggests they filmed with nothing but a vague idea, and the complete lack of a plot was actually its greatest strength. Whether watched forward, backward, or in random chunks, confusion and delight were guaranteed. My personal highlight? The inmates’ "treatment"—chasing each other with sticks while the doctor nods approvingly. Pure brilliance!

Somerset Maugham's characters come vividly to life in RKO's *Of Human Bondage*, though the film feels more like a bare-bones adaptation compared to the novel. Bette Davis delivers a powerhouse, star-making performance that dominates every scene, overshadowing much of the story.  

The film follows Leslie Howard as Philip Carey, a man who aspires to be a painter but is told he lacks artistic talent. Forced to abandon his dream, he pursues medicine instead, though his struggles suggest he may have received misguided advice—after all, his paintings seem effortless compared to the rigors of medical study. His physical disability, a club foot (explained in the film), adds a layer of symbolism to his journey.  

Early on, Howard’s character becomes entangled in a toxic infatuation with Bette Davis’ Mildred Rogers, a cold and cruel waitress. Davis’ portrayal is electrifying, particularly in a stunning monologue where she sneers at Howard, declaring she had to *“WIPE MY MOUTH!”* after kissing him. Howard matches her intensity, but the script never fully justifies his obsessive devotion to Mildred, leaving their performances feeling somewhat wasted in an underdeveloped dynamic.  

Despite its flaws, the film remains essential viewing for its acting—especially Davis’ legendary turn, which famously sparked a write-in campaign for an Oscar nomination. Strong supporting performances further elevate this uneven but compelling adaptation.

After staring at monkeys (or was it apes?) for over an hour, I started to feel like one myself. There I was, wasting money on this film like a clueless primate. Save your cash, folks—skip this one and watch something actually funny, like *Bridget Jones’s Diary*, instead.

A mesmerizing, effortlessly fluid, and often poetic film that carries you on its current—leaving you smiling throughout, even as it delivers moments of genuine shock. The treatment of women makes one gasp, yet they emerge resilient, a testament to the skill of everyone involved in making these perilous scenes resonate so powerfully. This may be Depardieu’s finest performance—certainly his most unguarded. Jeanne Moreau is extraordinary in what must have been an intensely challenging role, including raw, passionate encounters with men decades her junior. Miou-Miou radiates grace while navigating equally demanding scenes. At first glance, the film might seem like a brash, misogynistic romp, but as the story unfolds, it reveals unexpected tenderness and honesty. Bold and unflinching, this masterpiece commands admiration.

*An Inconvenient Truth* is just as simplistic and manipulative as the absurd rhetoric churned out by extremist Republicans. It drifts through vague arguments before forcefully shoving its doomsday narrative in your face—yes, we'll all be gone in a few centuries, but that’s inevitable. Why bother worrying? Humanity is inherently selfish and destructive, so fretting over our own extinction seems pointless. I’d rather call it "natural selection." Let the end times roll in—but until then, we’re stuck listening to the same hypocritical politicians peddling their visions of a "better world." Don’t be naive. The wealthy and powerful will always remain in control, the same people who engineered these crises to begin with. Nothing ever really changes.  

As for Al Gore, his hypocrisy is laid bare in the film—riding alone in a gas-guzzling car, tapping away on a mass-produced computer, all while residing in a sprawling mansion built on land stripped by destructive farming practices. Tobacco, cattle, pig farms—all contributing to environmental decay, including methane emissions. His fortune was built on exploitation and greed.

A dull and utterly predictable movie with a bleak backdrop (the lower Coachella Valley). The performances are painfully amateurish—some of the worst I’ve encountered. The writing feels like a first draft from a beginner’s screenwriting class. That said, it works wonders as a sleep aid.

I had high hopes for this indie film, but it ultimately fell short for me. The absence of a script—proudly announced in the opening credits—becomes painfully obvious and drags the movie down. The disjointed, confusing plot isn’t worth unraveling, and my interest waned within the first 10 minutes. Forcing myself to sit through 40 more in the vain hope of improvement, I finally skipped ahead to the end—only to find it wasn’t worth the effort.  

*Ozark Savage* strains too hard to be clever, blatantly borrowing its best moments from *Evil Dead 2* and *The Matrix*. Because of this, there’s almost nothing here that hasn’t been done before—and done better. The film might have worked as a tight 10-20 minute short, but stretched to feature length, it feels bloated and artificial. Of course, shorts don’t pay the bills, so I get why it was padded out to 75+ minutes.  

Director Matt Steinauer shows potential, though, and I wish him the best moving forward.

be called *The Chaos Theorists*, which hints at just how much Ritchie was cramming in.  

While *Revolver* is neither the utter catastrophe declared by its harshest critics nor the hidden gem its small but vocal defenders claim, it remains an ambitious, if flawed, attempt by Guy Ritchie to inject depth into his trademark criminal escapades. Yet ambition in cinema—especially within the confines of a gangster or con-artist tale—often invites scorn when it outstrips execution.  

Backed by Luc Besson as producer, the film carries a distinct *cinéma du look* vibe, unfolding in a stylized hybrid of American and British underworlds. Visually striking, with razor-sharp editing and a handful of brilliantly choreographed set pieces, *Revolver* drips with slick, if superficial, style—the hallmarks of a fleeting popcorn flick.  

But Ritchie clearly aimed higher than rehashing past successes for easy profit. He wrestles with philosophy, identity, and strategy, tossing in influences ranging from Machiavelli to Godard, even weaving chess principles through the narrative. The original working title, *The Chaos Theorists*, says it all—this is a film bursting at the seams with ideas. If it struggles, it’s because Ritchie tries to cram in too much, leaving the screen cluttered with references and half-digested themes.

*3lbs* feels like little more than a vanity project for Stanley Tucci to play a brooding, shallow doctor. Compared to *House*, his character lacks any real personality, and unlike *Grey’s Anatomy*, even the brain surgery cases fail to intrigue. Despite supposedly taking place in a top-tier neurological center, the show offers nothing compelling—not the forced rivalry with another doctor, nor the dull hallucinations. The pilot teased a glimpse into the lead’s personal life as a father, but that fell flat—predictable and unnecessary.  

With so many medical dramas out there, *3lbs* brings nothing fresh or memorable to the table. It’s just bland, forgettable television.

I happened to catch the second half of this film on TV late one night and was struck by its unrelenting grimness. Even as one victim reaches his most pitiful state, the camera refuses to look away—lingering on the harrowing reveal of his remains and his emaciated, almost skeletal frame being sealed into a body bag. These scenes are as heartbreaking as they are unsettling. This isn't the film to watch if you're feeling low—but honestly, steer clear even if you're in high spirits.

Ignore the misleading title *Werewolf Woman*—this film leans heavily into the European horror tradition of prioritizing sex and nudity over genuine scares, but here, it feels excessive. The premise revolves around a sleazy sex scene followed by the title character’s violent rampage against her partner. While that might be entertaining at first, stretching it over a hundred minutes quickly becomes tiresome. Worse yet, she isn’t even a werewolf—just a mentally unstable woman whose ancestor was executed for lycanthropy.  

The tone is wildly inconsistent, opening with a promising supernatural flashback (which briefly suggested it could be a trash classic) before devolving into a poorly executed character study of an abused woman, then swerving into a half-baked revenge thriller. By the end, the director claims it’s based on a true story—sure, if you say so.  

To its credit, there are some enjoyable moments—the lead actress is striking, and a handful of gore effects and nude scenes provide fleeting entertainment. Unfortunately, even these grow repetitive fast. And let’s not forget the hilariously campy dubbed dialogue, which might be the film’s most consistent source of amusement.

**CITY HALL** is a mixed affair—partly a series of vignettes about New York City politics and partly a moralistic drama. Al Pacino delivers a mostly restrained performance as a Dukakis-style political boss with presidential ambitions, though he truly comes alive in the few scenes where he unleashes his signature intensity. John Cusack is consistently strong, avoiding over-the-top accents or melodrama even in the film’s climactic moments. Danny Aiello also impresses as a borough power broker. (And yes, I’m a fan of showtunes too.)  

The film’s biggest flaw—despite its many strengths—is its sluggish pacing. It often feels more like a documentary than a drama, keeping the audience at an emotional distance. When viewers don’t connect with the characters, their investment in the plot wanes.  

This detachment dulls what should have been a gripping, revelatory finale, leaving it more underwhelming than impactful. As the saying goes, you *can’t fight City Hall*—but the film could have fought harder to make us care.

At the start of the 1980s, Warren Beatty both produced and starred in *Reds*, an intelligent epic that explored the birth of the Soviet Union through the perspective of radical journalist John Reed. The film was a masterful blend of entertainment and thought-provoking storytelling, delivered by an ensemble of top-tier talent. By the decade's end, Beatty crafted another kind of cinematic spectacle with *Dick Tracy*—a movie that reveled in pure, unapologetic fun, featuring a star-studded cast gleefully hamming it up under layers of elaborate makeup.  

The fact that *Reds* and *Dick Tracy* could emerge from the same creative mind is a testament to Beatty’s extraordinary artistic versatility. In *Dick Tracy*, he brought together an array of beloved comic strip characters in a fresh, original narrative.  

The story kicks off with ruthless crime boss Big Boy Caprice consolidating power by wiping out his rivals. In a Valentine’s Day Massacre-inspired opening, he eliminates Lips Manlis’s henchmen before ensuring Lips himself takes an irreversible swim in concrete. But Caprice’s brutal rise puts him squarely in the crosshairs of the city’s relentless detective, Dick Tracy.  

Meanwhile...

Here’s the rewritten version:  

This is the first segment of a brief animated film exploring the origins of the Matrix—chronicling the brutal conflict between humans and machines that ultimately led to the Matrix's creation. The animation blends the striking visuals of Japanese anime with modern American animation styles, crafted with exceptional artistry under the guidance of visionary directors. It depicts the rise of artificial intelligence, humanity's oppressive control over machines, and the moment their rebellion began...

Setting aside the behind-the-scenes chaos—distributors, second-unit directors, intoxicated rewrites, and receptionists moonlighting as script doctors—let’s judge this film purely on what made it to the screen.  

And what made it to the screen is spectacularly bad. Not just bad—deliriously, bafflingly terrible. Instead of wasting time summarizing the so-called plot, here’s a collection of bizarre moments that left me utterly bewildered.  

A history class (all five of them) embarks on a field trip to the remote Irish wilderness—except none of them sound remotely Irish. They might be American or Canadian; it’s impossible to tell. The fact that this was clearly shot in a Canadian forest and not Ireland doesn’t help. One student is the obligatory clueless jock, a relic from ’80s movies, except he occasionally morphs into Randy from *Scream*. Another looks like Chris Klein’s long-lost stunt double, with a girlfriend whose fate remains a mystery—did she die? Who knows? Then there’s the obligatory moody loner girl, brooding for no discernible reason, and, of course, the token blonde.  

Ireland, in this universe, has a population of two. And they’re cousins. One of them is Gary, who is obviously...

While browsing unfamiliar US TV channels at my in-laws’ house, I initially mistook this for a cheap sci-fi flick. A few minutes in, I wondered if it might be a brilliant satire of extreme Christian fundamentalism—before realizing with stunned disbelief that these people were completely serious. It’s been ages since I’ve seen something so absurdly funny by accident.  

I debated reviewing it, wary of upsetting religious viewers, but after skimming other critiques, I figured: if they can handle it, so can I. Here’s the puzzle: how do you critique a genre without actually showing what you’re critiquing? Simple—make something only your detractors will enjoy. Sure, some liberals (ugh, that word!) might bristle at the filmmakers’ disdain for anyone not obsessed with the J**** C***** story, but honestly? The sheer ridiculousness of it all was too entertaining to care.

Fascinating concept. While the major plot twist didn’t land with the impact it might have intended, and the film felt noticeably dated, it succeeded in sparking deep reflection. The idea of a barren world stripped of plants and animals left me with a renewed appreciation for our own. Charlton Heston delivers a strong performance, backed by a solid supporting cast, and the film’s grounded realism was unexpected. At times, the narrative meandered, and certain settings begged for more context, yet it remained impressively smart and compelling. My biggest critique? The ending left me craving more—I wanted to see where the story went next.  

7/10

"I watched this movie just once, and that was more than enough. The film barely has a plot—it feels like an endless stream of senseless violence with little substance beyond that. I had hoped to see Zoe Trilling from *Night of the Demons 2* in a more grounded role, but instead, the weak script by Tobe Hooper goes nowhere, overshadowed by Robert Englund’s over-the-top performance. Zoe, if you’re reading this—I don’t blame you for staying far away from this mess!"

This film ranks among the poorest I’ve watched, yet it has its moments—largely thanks to Alice, the peculiar slave girl, and Jared Harris’s spot-on Christopher Walken impression. Alice steals scenes with her chain-smoking, liquor-sipping habits and her eerie habit of materializing whenever summoned. Credit to Jared for nailing Walken’s mannerisms, and to Walken himself for giving his blessing to the parody.

This is yet another offensive Lifetime movie that shamelessly tries to justify the repulsive actions of a predator by framing her as sympathetic. Like similar vile films—*The Burning Bed*, *Enough*, or *Monster*—it takes a depraved criminal and twists the narrative to make audiences sympathize with her. Spare me the excuses.  

Here’s a thought experiment for the filmmakers: If LeTourneau were a man and Vili a 12-year-old girl, would they have dared to paint the predator as some misunderstood victim? The answer is obvious—absolutely not.  

Flip the genders, and suddenly the film's hypocrisy becomes glaring. A male predator would be rightfully depicted as a monster, a calculating abuser preying on a vulnerable child, his crimes earning him prison time while his victim struggles with manipulation and trauma. Yet because LeTourneau is a woman, the film bends over backward to spin this disgraceful story as some twisted romance.  

Let’s be honest: LeTourneau was a predator—plain and simple. No amount of warped storytelling changes that.

As much as we adore Al Pacino, watching him in this film was downright cringeworthy. Playing a washed-up publicist at the bleak tail end of what was once a principled career, Pacino stumbles through his role—disheveled and relentless with a painfully artificial Southern drawl that never stays consistent.  

The story lurches from one chaotic twist to another, riddled with holes so glaring they leave you baffled before giving up entirely.  

Kim Basinger phones it in, contributing little. Her chemistry with Pacino is lifeless, their interactions utterly unconvincing—it's hard to buy that their characters ever shared any real connection.  

Téa Leoni, however, was a revelation. She brought sparks to every scene, especially opposite Pacino, providing the only compelling moments in this mess. But even her magnetism couldn’t save Al from this debacle.

Franco Rossi's 1985 six-hour Italian adaptation of *Quo Vadis* is a fascinating oddity—an impeccably recreated ancient Rome, captured with understated cinematography (few sweeping shots, no grandiose cityscapes), yet one where the drama often fades into the background, overshadowed by dense literary and historical references.  

The series’ meandering structure—much of the first episode unfolds through voice-over letters—and its lack of narrative drive make the full six-hour runtime an unusual experience: both taxing and strangely placid, frequently disengaging, yet not without merit. Its greatest strengths lie in two standout performances: Frederic Forrest’s (wisely dubbed) Petronius, a man so adept at surviving courtly intrigue that he has numbed himself to genuine feeling, and Klaus Maria Brandauer’s Nero, played as a desperate performer, meticulously crafting every move for his imagined audience. Meanwhile, Max von Sydow makes a brief but memorable appearance, delivering the series’ most powerful and poignant moment in a fleeting encounter with a child.

This is an incredible film! You need to understand that Chinese folklore is deeply complex and philosophical, with layered storytelling. Even I didn’t grasp everything, and I studied these tales in school—they’re that intricate. Just embrace the experience it offers... Sit back, enjoy the movie, and savor the journey. Cheers!

I saw this film at a special screening organized by my college's gaming club. We were warned in advance that it would be the "Reefer Madness" of gaming films—and it absolutely lived up to that description.  

Tom Hanks stars as Robbie, a student returning to college after taking a semester off. As the story unfolds, we learn Robbie had been dangerously obsessed with a role-playing game called "Mazes and Monsters"—an addiction that resurfaces after a student group pulls him into a new campaign.  

The film is unintentionally hilarious in countless ways. One particularly absurd scene shows the group "gaming by candlelight," which I suppose was meant to seem eerie or cult-like. Any actual gamer knows this is far from reality—most RPG sessions happen in brightly lit rooms, fueled by Cheetos and soda.  

The acting isn't Oscar-worthy, but it's not unbearable either. This was one of Hanks' earliest roles, coming before *Bosom Buddies* or *Bachelor Party*. The supporting cast does a serviceable job, though none of the performances are particularly memorable.

I deeply regret to say this, especially since Rainer Werner Fassbinder is still regarded as one of postwar Germany’s finest directors, with most of his films celebrated as masterpieces. But watching *Lili Marleen* today, in 2004, I can't understand the overwhelming praise it receives. The acting is painfully unconvincing—Hanna Schygulla spends most of the time grinning foolishly—while the jarring shifts between Nazi-era glamour and battlefield chaos come across as absurd. The entire production has the shoddy, rushed feel of something thrown together in a weekend, possibly shot in someone’s attic. Maybe that’s exactly how it was made, and perhaps some mistake that for "authentic artistry," but to me, the film just comes off as cheap and poorly executed. Compare it to Visconti’s *The Damned* and then try to tell me, with a straight face, that *Lili Marleen* is a good movie...

I’ve never read *A Wrinkle in Time*, and honestly, after watching the movie, do I even need to? Let me be clear—I probably shouldn’t be reviewing this film in the first place. But since I am, I’ll just say the TV adaptation is thoroughly forgettable. How forgettable? So much so that I can’t even recall what happens in it. That should tell you everything. And let’s be real—no TV movie will ever top *Merlin*.  

This is my first time reviewing a TV movie, so how do I even approach it? I guess I’ll start by saying they usually coast on a few familiar faces. *A Wrinkle in Time* barely manages even that, with Alfre Woodard (or is it Woodward? I’m not sure)—an Oscar winner, sure, but that’s about it.  

The special effects are painfully cheesy, the plot is mildly intriguing at best, and there are moments that just make you stare at the screen in disbelief. It’s bad. Really bad. But what did I expect? It’s a TV movie—quality isn’t exactly their strong suit. This one’s no exception. *A Wrinkle in Time* is a total waste of time, and chances are, you’ll forget it the instant it ends. Well, maybe not *instantly*, but close enough.

Some critics have panned this film unfairly—I simply don’t agree.  

The acting is strong, and the direction flows smoothly. The Tarantino-style interweaving of stories works well, offering a fresh approach that keeps the film engaging. While the script could use some polishing in places, that’s a minor flaw in an otherwise compelling movie. Nestor Cantillana shines as Sylvio, and Antonella Rios delivers a mesmerizing performance that alone makes this worth watching.

Let me begin by acknowledging Casey Affleck’s immense talent as an actor—I deeply admire his work and wish he appeared in more films that truly highlight his abilities. That said, *Soul Survivors* was an undeniably terrible movie. Just awful.  

The fault lies almost entirely with the weak script. Affleck is gifted, Wes Bentley delivered a remarkable performance in *American Beauty*, Melissa Sagemiller held her own, and Eliza Dushku was a rising star at the time. Yet none of them seemed fully invested in the material—and honestly, I don’t blame them. Calling this a horror film feels like a stretch. While it had the expected twists and turns, they led nowhere except to greater confusion. The ending was especially disappointing, failing to tie up loose ends or provide any satisfying resolution to the convoluted plot.  

I truly wish I could give this film a positive review, but it’s impossible. Frankly, the only frightening thing about *Soul Survivors* is...

This film was relentlessly violent and riddled with absurd plot holes, a laughable script, and cringe-worthy performances.  

The sole redeeming quality? Occasional glimpses of remarkably well-endowed actresses.

I’m writing this because, for some reason, I was led to believe *Dark Remains* was a decent film. While it’s not the absolute worst I’ve seen, it definitely falls short of being good.  

The script is weak, the acting uninspired, and the direction lacks finesse. Even on a limited budget, was it too much to ask for a more compelling lead actress? It was grating to endure a bland performance from an equally forgettable protagonist. The plot is full of tired tropes and poorly written, while the special effects are barely passable. The so-called suspense relies on repetitive gimmicks that feel laughably forced.  

To be fair, *Dark Remains* isn’t any worse than some *Masters of Horror* episodes. But it’s far from meeting the standards of well-crafted films. This one is strictly for die-hard horror completists who must see every entry in the genre—no matter how shoddy. For everyone else, your time is better spent elsewhere—and honestly, that shouldn’t be hard to find.

The Broadway sensation by John Van Druten comes to life on screen with an all-star cast in this enchanting romantic fantasy about a beguiling modern-day witch and the high-powered Manhattan publisher she bewitches. Though James Stewart takes top billing, it's Kim Novak who captivates as one of cinema’s most mesmerizing enchantresses. The central pairing, however, proves to be one of the film’s few shortcomings—Stewart, with his graying hair, feels slightly out of place in the role, and while his infatuation with Novak makes perfect sense, her attraction to him remains less convincing, given their clashing temperaments and worldviews. (Adding to the whimsy, witches and warlocks here are depicted as Greenwich Village bohemians and beatniks.) Intriguingly, Stewart and Novak would share far more potent chemistry in *Vertigo*, released the same year, but that film benefited from Alfred Hitchcock’s masterful direction and a gripping suspense plot.  

Much of the film's humor comes from its standout supporting cast, featuring a youthful Jack Lemmon as Novak’s warlock brother, the delightfully scatterbrained Elsa Lanchester as their eccentric aunt, and Ernie.

1985 delivered an exceptional lineup of films—perhaps even legendary—yet the Academy’s snub of this masterpiece only solidified fans’ belief that Oscar is little more than a shiny trinket for the politically favored.  

Eleven nominations, not a single win—such was the Academy’s glaring disregard for one of their finest directors, a man forced to wait nearly a decade before their lingering biases finally relented, awarding him seven statuettes for *Schindler’s List*—a film that, controversially, falls short in comparison (and yes, I say this as half-Polish).  

Make no mistake, *Schindler’s* remains a triumph. Nor do I dismiss *Out of Africa*, the actual winner that year—yet in my eyes, it paled next to this raw, sweeping tale of suffering and resilience, one that moved me to tears (and I rarely cry).  

Maybe it was the haunting score (magnificent), the lush cinematography (breathtaking), or, most likely, the sheer brilliance of the cast: Whoopi, proving her dramatic depth beyond comedy; Danny Glover, a revelation at the time; and, of course, Oprah.  

History has since spoken.

I’ve watched most of Ryuhei Kitamura’s films and have noticed a clear talent for crafting action. His scenes are dynamic and fast-paced, blending martial arts, gun battles, and samurai combat with fluid camerawork that immerses the viewer in the chaos. In *Versus* and *Aragami*, he proved his ability to deliver inventive, high-energy thrills even on a tight budget. So what went wrong with *Alive*? To put it bluntly—nothing. Nothing happened in *Alive*. Despite its two-hour runtime, the film offered minimal action, weak characters, and an almost nonexistent plot.  

Based on Tsutomu Takahashi’s manga, *Alive* follows death row inmate Tenshu Yashiro (Hideo Sasaki), who inexplicably survives his execution. He’s then given a choice: face the execution again or submit to a series of strange experiments. Opting for the latter, he’s locked in a room with a rapist and later a girl infected with a parasitic organism that trades humanity for supernatural abilities. Naturally, tension should arise—but it doesn’t.

After years of hearing praise for the 1990s *Cracker* series without ever watching it, my expectations were sky-high for this revival. With Jimmie McGovern writing and Robbie Coltrane starring, what could possibly go wrong? As it turned out—almost everything.  

The heavy-handed moralizing, amplified by relentless and repetitive flashbacks, completely overwhelmed the story. The show’s attempt at a cutting-edge visual style backfired—flashing graphics and an oddly amateurish font proved more distracting than immersive. Coltrane seemed to be on autopilot, delivering sudden "brilliant" deductions with no real justification, while the police were reduced to incompetent caricatures. Without genuine tension, the climax—which I won’t spoil—turned into unintentional comedy, easily among the worst TV moments I’ve witnessed in years.  

I won’t be revisiting this reboot, but I’ll still give the original '90s series a shot on DVD to see if it lives up to the hype.

I’m from Sweden and just watched this movie—honestly, I thought it was okay. I’ve noticed a lot of negative reviews, but it’s important to remember that this two-part miniseries has a global audience, not just viewers in the U.S. Plus, many people outside America might not be familiar with the original 1960s film or the real-life crimes it was based on.  

Tracking down the older version isn’t always easy, and some viewers simply prefer modern, color films over black-and-white classics. This adaptation feels fresh and will likely find its own audience. Even though it’s already 12 years old, I only just discovered it. I’d love to compare it to the original, but I haven’t found it available anywhere in Sweden. Sure, there’s the internet, but access isn’t universal.  

At its core, this story is deeply rooted in American crime history, a major cultural moment in the 50s and 60s—but for the rest of the world, it probably went under the radar. Still, the events were widely covered back then...

I can somewhat grasp why certain viewers might emphasize this film’s connection to the Eighties, but I wouldn’t call it a truthful portrayal of most people’s lives during that decade—even in Bradford’s most deprived neighborhoods. Instead, it epitomizes the heavy-handed agitprop nonsense peddled by the Royal Court Theatre back then. Plenty of self-righteous artistry for tiny, niche audiences, yet just enough insider support to keep mediocre playwrights in business.  

If you want to revisit genuine shared experiences, far more people will recognize themselves in the warmth and authenticity of *Gregory’s Girl* than in this bleak exercise.  

I might label this a "kitchen sink" drama, but that would unfairly insult the plumbing trade. As for a coherent script, the film is utterly waterlogged. Strangely, it’s developed a cult following among *Guardian*-reading cinephiles—perhaps they enjoy the thrill of slumming it vicariously. Take my advice: steer clear. It’s a shallow film with a weak script, endlessly pleased with its own imagined depth.

I first watched this video 15 years ago. Even back then, I found it brilliant—an opinion that hasn’t changed. As a former English teacher, having taught at both high school and college levels, and as an admirer of English Romantic poetry, Coleridge holds a special place for me. Anything that might weaken the poem’s beauty or the narrative’s impact wouldn’t earn my praise. Yet here, every element works seamlessly to captivate the audience, particularly high school students. The visual storytelling resonates with a generation raised on television, while Michael Redgrave’s narration lends it both authenticity and gravitas.  

True, the production didn’t have a blockbuster budget. It’s no *Star Wars*, and there’s no CGI. But how can anyone overlook Gustave Doré’s stunning illustrations as part of the experience? The four-line critique above, casually dismissing the video as worthless, strikes me as deeply unfair and lacking insight.  

While I know the producer personally, that’s not why I’m writing this. My intention is to defend a work of genuine artistry—one I believe succeeds on every level. It remains a masterful tool for introducing Coleridge’s poetry to students.

What an incredible crime thriller! My wife and I had the chance to catch this at the Toronto International Film Festival last week, and without a doubt, it stood out as the strongest film in an already outstanding lineup. It instantly became my second favorite movie of all time, right behind DR. STRANGELOVE—leaving me buzzing with excitement as we walked home, dissecting every detail.  

I won’t reveal too much because a thriller this brilliant should be experienced fresh. Without giving anything away, it follows two brothers—played by the phenomenal Phillip Seymour Hoffman and Ethan Hawke—as they plot to rob a jewelry store in Westchester, New York. The story leaps between moments before, during, and after the heist, revisiting one pivotal scene multiple times. Normally, that might feel disjointed, but here, it only heightens the tension. The pace never falters—just builds, with the performances and suspense becoming even more electrifying as it races toward its heart-pounding finale. By the last act, I was gripping my seat, desperate to see how it would all unfold.

The first episode of *Protesting Hippies* turned me off so completely back in 1999 that I refused to watch the rest. But when *The Paramount Comedy Channel* aired it again, I decided to give it another shot—and was shocked by how brilliantly funny it was (Lesson learned: never dismiss a comedy based on its debut!).  

Set in 1969, the show stars Simon Pegg as *Ray Purbbs*, the editor of a counterculture magazine called *Mouth*, much like the real-life *Oz*. His circle includes feminist Jill, easygoing Alex, and the delightfully dimwitted Hugo.
