The series captures the youthful idealism of the era—that sense that the world could be transformed by magazines almost no one actually read. Instead of mocking the hippies' wide-eyed optimism, *Hippies* treats it with warmth and nostalgia. Arthur Mathews' writing cleverly skewers cultural touchstones of the time, from *Hair* and *Woodstock* to *The Graduate*—even tipping its hat to the notorious *Oz* obscenity trial.  

The cast is outstanding, with Julian Rhind-Tutt’s portrayal of Alex oddly reminiscent of Richard O'Sullivan’s character in *Man About the House*. It’s a shame the show never got a second series—maybe because of viewers like me who didn’t stick with it. If you missed *Hippies* the first time around, do yourself a favor and check it out.

By the mid-1930s, Hollywood had begun recovering its footing after the challenges of transitioning to sound films. While the technical hurdles of synchronizing audio were swiftly overcome, filmmakers still grappled with determining how talkies should look, how their narratives should unfold, and what constituted effective acting in this new format. *The Informer* stands as a pivotal film in this evolution, demonstrating how silent storytelling techniques—powerful visual storytelling—could coexist with, rather than compete against, the demands of sound and dialogue.  

This isn’t to suggest *The Informer* is merely a nostalgic nod to the silent era. Many silent films, after all, relied heavily on intertitles rather than purely visual storytelling. What sets *The Informer* apart is its deliberate pacing—its willingness to linger in the spaces between dialogue, to prioritize unspoken reactions over exposition, and to allow shots to breathe, crafting mood through imagery alone.  

Director John Ford, a master of his craft, was known for investing effort based on his engagement with the material. If he deemed a story frivolous, his work mirrored that indifference. Fortunately, *The Informer*—with its themes of honor, community, and struggle—clearly resonated with him.

Is there a way to give this a negative rating? Since that’s not an option, I’ll just say this is hands down the worst film I’ve ever subjected myself to. It was excruciating—an absolute snoozefest. The so-called plot is buried under layers of complete incoherence. My friend and I rented this, and after a torturous half-hour of waiting for anything worthwhile to happen, we started skipping ahead, desperate for improvement. Spoiler: there is none.  

On paper, a story about some guy being abducted by two women sounds intriguing. In reality? Pure tedium. Not a single moment of suspense, wit, or entertainment. If you stumble across this movie, save yourself the agony—watch *Plan 9 from Outer Space* instead. At least that one’s so bad it’s fun.

*Bedknobs and Broomsticks* is one of the most enchanting and heartwarming films you'll ever experience as a child. This unforgettable adventure follows two adults and two spirited kids on a magical journey filled with excitement. While it may not initially catch your interest, give it a chance—neither my mother nor I found it disappointing. I was completely captivated by the film's animation and storytelling, both of which are truly exceptional.  

A whimsical comedy perfect for the whole family, this musical gem will delight viewers ages seven and up. The vibrant animation and fluid movements are beautifully crafted, earning well-deserved praise. If you're looking for a fantastic musical adventure to enjoy together, don’t hesitate—head to your nearest video store and rent *Bedknobs and Broomsticks* today!

I caught this movie at the 2006 Palm Springs International Film Festival. It’s worth noting that it’s more of a made-for-TV production than a traditional film, as it was created by HBO for their cable network, set to air later that year. The story portrays Bettie Page as more than just a bondage and discipline pinup—it hints at her potential to transition into serious acting, though the focus leans heavily on her B&D image rather than fully exploring her broader modeling career and status as a 1950s icon.  

The movie draws inspiration from Richard Foster’s book *The Real Bettie Page* and uses black-and-white cinematography to evoke the nostalgic vibe of the era. I own another book, *Bettie Page: The Life of a Pinup Legend*, which features an extensive collection of photos documenting her career, and I was impressed by how faithfully the film recreates many of those iconic shots—especially with Gretchen Mol in the lead role.  

Mol absolutely disappears into the part. With Bettie’s signature black wig, brown contact lenses, and that legendary smile, she doesn’t just look the part—she perfectly captures Page’s essence and charm.

**Rewritten Version:**  

The youngest descendants of the Gaylord family, one of America’s most aristocratic lineages, are three sisters left orphaned at a young age. Before leaving for France to fight in World War I, their father makes the eldest, Fiona, promise never to sell their land. By the time they reach adulthood, the sisters have drained much of their fortune on legal battles to protect their property. Due to ambiguities in their father’s will, a man named Charles Barclay—modeled after John D. Rockefeller, who famously acquired properties from wealthy New York families to build Rockefeller Center—threatens to seize the Gaylord estate to construct a development called Barclay Circle.  

The film primarily focuses on the sisters' melodramatic struggles. Fiona, portrayed compellingly by Barbara Stanwyck—though not one of her most memorable roles—comes across as stern and controlling, her icy demeanor hinting at buried secrets. Susanna, played by Nancy Coleman, is flighty and hopelessly infatuated with a progressive artist named Gig Young. Coleman’s performance was my—

This film is perhaps the most profoundly moving and inspiring I've ever encountered. While not religious myself, a masterpiece like this offers what can only be described as a spiritual awakening - that sudden, breathtaking realization that life holds genuine meaning.

Initially, I approached this movie with skepticism. The premise seemed forced, and I worried the narrative might be trite. Yet as a longtime admirer of David Lynch's work, I took the chance. Within thirty minutes, I was completely enthralled - utterly absorbed by its extraordinary depth. The film radiates such uncommon wisdom and heartfelt humanity that I emerged from the theater feeling genuinely enlightened about existence itself.

It defies expectations of Lynch's signature style. That the same auteur who spent decades plumbing humanity's darkest recesses could create something so luminous remains astonishing. Yet when I reflect on his ability to articulate profound emotional truths, this artistic evolution feels inevitable - another demonstration of his uncanny gift for exposing the human soul's radiant core.

In this entertaining Bugs Bunny cartoon, the still unnamed Marvin the Martian makes another appearance alongside his sidekick K-9, the green dog.  

This time, instead of plotting to destroy Earth, Marvin is on a mission to land, capture an Earth creature, and bring it back to Mars—naturally, his target is Bugs Bunny. At first, Bugs mistakes Marvin and K-9 for trick-or-treaters, but the truth quickly becomes clear when Marvin uses a ray-gun to dramatically enlarge Bugs' rabbit hole. True to form, Bugs attempts to outwit the Martians in several ways, even convincing Marvin that K-9 is planning a mutiny. However, Marvin eventually captures Bugs using an Acme strait-jacket bazooka—which, surprisingly for an Acme product, works exactly as intended. Forced to rely on his quick thinking, Bugs manipulates K-9 into releasing him, swiftly turning the tables. By the end, the two frustrated Martians are tied up while Bugs attempts to pilot their flying saucer back to Earth.  

Though the ending feels slightly weaker compared to the rest of the story, this cartoon remains highly enjoyable. Fans might also notice a slight change in Marvin’s voice, along with visible frustration when he loses his temper.

A strong premise can quickly fall apart when forced to cater to an audience with dwindling attention spans, spiraling into an incoherent mess. It’s especially disappointing when talented actors—who have delivered far better performances before and after—find themselves trapped in such a misfire.  

Take the core idea: a loving couple in an idyllic home finds themselves terrorized by a corrupt cop. That’s compelling, even promising. A subtly unsettling antagonist could have worked wonders—this formula thrived in films like *The Hand That Rocks the Cradle* or *Single White Female*, proving its potential for gripping psychological thrillers.  

But here’s the problem. A truly disturbing story balances genuine menace without tipping into absurdity, maintaining some grounding in reality. Instead, the filmmakers opted to crank up the shock value, morphing the antagonist into an over-the-top caricature—a cartoonishly evil extreme of every cinematic villain since the silent era.  

Predictably, they chose the latter approach. The result? A poorly executed mess, leaving the cast scrambling to salvage something—anything—from the wreckage.

My absolute favorite film of all time. Every aspect—both onscreen and behind the scenes—deserves Oscar recognition. The script is flawless, brilliantly improving upon the novel’s portrayal of the dynamic between Lady Caroline and George Briggs, making it utterly compelling. The depth given to the supporting characters highlights screenwriter Peter Barnes’ exceptional talent, while the breathtaking visuals should have earned director Mike Newell and cinematographer Rex Maidment Academy Awards. Josie Lawrence delivers her finest performance to date, and Joan Plowright completely won me over. After countless viewings, I still find no flaws. The score, crafted by legendary composer Richard Rodney Bennett, is nothing short of extraordinary.

This would have made a *brilliant* silent film. The performances are certainly bold—if you appreciate the "Look How Loud I Can Act!" school of dramatics.  

Everything here is MASSIVE. Each line feels EARTH-SHATTERING! Every moment DRIPPING WITH MISERY!  

Frankly, it made me nauseous. And yet, like watching a car crash in slow motion, I couldn’t look away. The dialogue might have scraped by on stage—though I wouldn’t bet on it. On film, it's chaotic, clumsy, clichéd, and every other damning word you’d throw at a disastrously overwrought drama.  

If you crave melodrama by the bucketload, you *might* stomach this. Just don’t expect speed—despite all the theatrics, it drags like an anchor.  

Somehow, the script must have read better in the actors’ heads. The second they spoke it aloud, the magic crumbled.  

IMDB does us no favors with its dubious "weighted score" algorithm. *Curse of the Starving Class* shouldn’t even scrape a 1.  

Character-driven stories can be riveting—until yours are...

Am I missing something here? "Unexpected plot twists"? "Subversive glee"? Are these people watching the same Arquette trainwreck I just endured—a clear case of (sub)conscious self-punishment? I signed up here solely to warn others: steer clear of this dumpster fire. This film was an insult to everyone involved. Quick question—did Spielberg even glance at the script before giving Kate C. the go-ahead? If so, this must be the same genius who blessed us with *Howard the Duck*. And spare me the "it was a hit play" excuse—I doubt Reddin is thrilled either.  

The DVD cover bragged about "surprising turns" and a "twisted tale"... *Tale*? More like trash. Movies like this make McKee and his Structuralist cronies sound like prophets. Sundance? Berlin? Toronto? My cat’s blooper reel has more depth than Arquette’s flat, cardboard grief. And let’s talk about that laughable deus ex machina—thank heavens Stanley T. remembered, *just in time*, to have Dave call the cops! And what luck, the police coincidentally nabbed the real killer. Seriously? I kept waiting for the twist—right up until the credits rolled.

**Rewritten Version:**  

As Rome erupts in frenzied celebration over Hitler’s arrival—filled with uniforms, marching bands, and grand parades—two outsiders remain behind in a quiet, cavernous building, drawn together by chance. She is Sofia Loren: the stifled wife of a coarse public servant and mother of six children. He is Mastroianni, a radio announcer dismissed for his homosexuality. Both crave companionship and compassion—and in each other, they find it.  

The film unfolds over just a few hours, its muted colors mirroring the suffocating atmosphere of the era. Against a backdrop of blaring military marches and frenetic radio broadcasts, the story plays out with quiet intensity. Oddly, even the Nazi anthem—the *Horst-Wessel-Lied*—transforms into an unlikely romantic refrain.  

A stunning film, it masterfully recreates a defining moment in Italian history while weaving a tender, melancholy tale. Mastroianni delivers the brilliance we expect, and Sofia Loren defies her usual bold, earthy roles with a performance of surprising restraint and depth. Unmissable.

This has to rank among the worst films I’ve ever watched.  

Contrary to what another reviewer claimed, the special effects were far from "okay"—they were downright terrible. The lack of realism and painfully fake visuals only pulled me out of the story rather than immersing me in it.  

Maybe that distraction is why the plot made so little sense. A group of archaeologists searches for something called "the set," but the movie never clarifies what that is or why it matters. Even stranger, they’re hunting for it in California, despite the film opening in ancient Egypt—a disconnect that adds to the confusion.  

And if you're making a desert-based movie, at least film in an actual desert. The opening scene, supposedly an ancient ceremony, looked like it was shot in a cramped studio rather than beneath an open sky.  

The pacing never shifted—just one flat, monotonous stream of action with no build-up or climax. The only positive? At least it felt short.

This film transcends boundaries, connecting deeply with the individual, community, society, and the world at large. It doesn’t just raise questions—it compels viewers to seek and confront the right ones, guiding them toward self-realization and personal conviction. By depicting familiar stereotypes, the film highlights recurring archetypes in our lives, revealing them as obstacles to progress—barriers that stifle innovation, creativity, and growth. These disruptive forces must be exposed and challenged. *The Idea* is more than a film to watch; it’s an experience to feel. It engages the inner voice, awakening reflection rather than mere observation.

Cult classics are notoriously unpredictable. Who would’ve thought films like *Vision Quest*, *Fight Club*, and *2001: A Space Odyssey*—initially dismissed by critics and audiences—would later achieve massive acclaim? As someone who prides themselves on movie knowledge (like many IMDb users), I found myself in the minority when it came to *Envy*. Despite its abysmal 4.4 rating, I consider it one of the funniest films of the past decade.  

The plot is absurd, the dialogue lacks wit, and the scenes feel disjointed—almost as if written by a child. Yet that’s precisely what makes it so hilarious. To truly appreciate *Envy*’s unintentional brilliance, you have to watch it with an ironic detachment.  

Why do I love it? Because it’s so bad, it’s good—the perfect formula for a cult classic, and *Envy* nails it.

Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer struggles to make its mark in the short cartoon market, which is largely ruled by Warner Bros.' Looney Tunes and Merry Melodies. Yet MGM still manages to produce hidden treasures, such as *To Spring*, a mesmerizing celebration of the year’s most enchanting season.  

In this imaginative world, spring isn’t a natural phenomenon—it’s manufactured. And by whom? Tiny underground elves. As winter’s grip loosens, these industrious workers chop down towering rainbow-colored rock pillars, pulverize them into rubble, and transform the fragments into vibrant liquids. These are then pumped to the surface, painting the world with fresh grass and blooming flowers—bringing spring to life. The first half of the cartoon vividly illustrates this intricate process, while the second takes an unexpected turn. Old Man Winter reappears, determined to prolong his icy reign by sabotaging the elves’ efforts. What follows is a whimsical battle between the forces of renewal and the stubborn chill of winter.  

The musical score is nothing short of magical, with melodies that linger in the mind like ink bleeding across a page—unforgettable and irresistibly charming.

***SPOILERS WARNING***  

As a huge *Homicide: Life on the Street* fan, I might have enjoyed this movie more than the average viewer. That said, it’s still an outstanding film. Packed with unexpected twists, it also provides a sense of resolution to the series. Bayliss becoming a killer was heartbreaking, but by the end, I felt deeply satisfied with how everything unfolded.

Here's the rewritten version:  

This offers a compelling perspective on human nature—how our relentless pursuit of perfection can sometimes undermine the very foundations of what we seek to build. It also highlights the tendency to overlook quieter voices among us, potentially missing out on valuable insights. The blend of humor makes the film both thought-provoking and entertaining. A must-watch for those who appreciate a reflective yet lighthearted take on life. I eagerly anticipate your next creation and hope you continue delivering such outstanding work. Brilliant job—Joanne

Govind Nihalani’s adaptation of Vijay Tendulkar’s novel is a masterful cinematic achievement. Om Puri delivers a powerful performance as Inspector Velankar, reluctantly tasked with safeguarding ruthless underworld kingpin Rama Shetty, portrayed with chilling brilliance by Sadashiv Amrapurkar. Widely regarded as one of Nihalani’s most acclaimed works, this film remains a timeless classic.  

Smita Patil shines in the female lead opposite Om Puri, while Naseeruddin Shah leaves a lasting impact in a brief yet memorable cameo. Despite appearing in only four scenes, Sadashiv Amrapurkar’s commanding presence dominates the narrative, marking his extraordinary acting debut.  

The film earned Om Puri a National Award for Best Actor and swept multiple Filmfare Awards, including Best Film, Best Story, and Best Supporting Actor for Amrapurkar. A gripping tale of morality and power, it continues to be celebrated as a landmark in Indian cinema.

This isn’t just the worst gay-themed film I’ve ever seen—it’s the worst movie, period.  

The red flags start immediately with the director’s preemptive "personal note," begging for "understanding" over the "many challenges" of being a first-timer. And wow, does it show. The audio is a mess, with dialogue often drowned out—and this is the DVD version. Add terrible lighting, shoddy sets, amateurish cinematography, a weak script, and subpar acting, and you’ve got an unwatchable mess. I forced myself through the awful ending after multiple tries, then promptly gave away the DVD I regret buying.  

Yes, first-time directors face hurdles—but that’s no excuse for passing off this half-baked disaster as a finished film. The only silver lining? According to IMDb, Richard Natale never directed again. Small mercies.

What can you say about *White Fire*? Amazing? Spectacular? Unsettling? Absurdly entertaining? None of these words quite capture the sheer experience that is *White Fire*. From its shaky, surreal opening to its unexpectedly deep conclusion, this film grips you from start to finish.  

The story begins deep in the woods of an unspecified country, where a family flees from mysterious soldiers dressed in makeshift military gear. The tension mounts as the father splits from his wife and children, immediately setting the tone for the wild ride ahead. Clad head-to-toe in white, he tumbles dramatically down hills with bizarre elegance, even pausing to politely warn his targets before opening fire. But fate has other plans—his demise comes in a shockingly reckless stunt, engulfed in flames. Meanwhile, the mother and children sprint along a beach, pursued by a soldier who delivers a stiffly theatrical *"HALT!"* before gunning her down. This chaotic opener lays the foundation for the turbulent upbringing of our protagonists, Bo and Ingred.  

Cut to two decades later—three if you’re counting realistically—where...

What an electrifying ride! Dark, twisted, and endlessly provocative. Sharon Stone is flawless once again, effortlessly embodying the hypnotic allure of novelist Catherine Tramell. While the original *Basic Instinct* unfolded in San Francisco, this sequel shifts to the sleek streets of London—both iconic cities brimming with glamour, high fashion, and the perfect playground for someone as cunning as Catherine.  

David Morrisey (*Derailed*) delivers a magnetic performance as the polished psychiatrist Dr. Michael Glass, while David Thewlis (a far cry from his Harry Potter days as Lupin) brings sharp intensity to Scotland Yard's Roy Washburn. The film pulses with sleek cars, designer wardrobes, seduction, tension, and biting wit—every element that made the original iconic, dialed up for a new era.  

From its gripping opening to its jaw-dropping finale, this thriller never lets up. The screenplay is razor-sharp, keeping the audience riveted. No one in the theater dared to look away—*Basic Instinct 2* is a fever dream of suspense, style, and sheer audacity.

Last night, I was lucky enough to catch *Cracker Bag* before a preview of Disney’s *Holes*. Whoever programmed it made a brilliant choice—what a delightful surprise. *Cracker Bag* is a little masterpiece, perfectly capturing early 80s Australia through a child’s perspective. The back-and-forth between Eddie and her brother was laugh-out-loud funny and, like the entire film, felt incredibly authentic. Every scene hit me with waves of nostalgia, mirroring my own childhood (being around the same age as the director probably helped). The sound design deepened the whole experience. Fingers crossed I’ll get to see it again someday.

Take a look at the film’s website—more effort clearly went into that than into writing this script. The claims they make couldn’t be further from reality. Original story? Please. They must’ve dug up this script buried somewhere in the Old Testament, or they’re begging for a lawsuit with that kind of boasting. High-end special effects? Give me an Atari 7600 and a jar of earwax, and I could do better. Stylish cinematography? Sure, if you consider the grainy look of *America’s Funniest Home Videos* a timeless aesthetic. I get that budgets can be tight, so of course the effects range from mediocre to laughably bad—but the real crime here is the story. It’s four half-baked plots crammed into one, each more clichéd and pointless than the last. A masterclass in wasted time and wasted potential.

Instead of lengthy dance scenes and excessive character close-ups that slowed the film down, the story would have been stronger with deeper exploration of the characters’ backgrounds and motivations.  

The sidelining of key figures like Nobu, the Minister, Auntie, and Sayuri’s mother—combined with the oversimplification of the crucial rivalries between Hatsumomo, Mameha, and Sayuri—left the film feeling shallow. Without having read the book, viewers would struggle to grasp why Sayuri loved the Chairman or why Mameha took her under her wing.  

Visually, the movie was breathtaking, and the cast delivered strong performances despite the weak script—but that’s where its merits ended.

This film was amazing! (Not quite on the level of Leif Garrett's classic *Longshot*, but still fantastic!) I couldn’t help but notice how much taller Ashley looked next to Mary-Kate—what was up with that? It’s wild how they managed to swap roles so convincingly. The dad came off as a bit of a jerk, and Mom was oddly friendly with ol’ Helmet Head. Solid 4/5. If you enjoyed this, definitely give *Longshot* a watch!

This film slowly won me over. The R.D. Burman soundtrack is fantastic, and while the plot has some rough edges, I found myself deeply moved with each rewatch. The brother-sister storyline is particularly strong, though some of the more obligatory elements—like bar brawls and a chaotic crime subplot—feel unnecessary (though admittedly amusing in their own way). The English translation was clearly done by someone pushing their limits, but I appreciate the effort despite its quirks.  

Much like other Bollywood films I’ve seen, this one embraces melodrama, almost like an opera. A standout moment is a song first sung by a young boy to comfort his unhappy, abused sister, then reprised years later by the same boy—now a man—who travels to Kathmandu to find her, only to discover she’s grown into a troubled drug user, believing him and their mother long dead.  

What makes this 1971 film special is its focus on the hippie movement, which drew waves of seekers to...

Life in modern Eastern Europe is harsh, and for many young women like Melania, prostitution becomes an unwilling last resort. Her path crosses with Seymour, an American who grows dangerously obsessed, escalating his payments until he demands to own her entirely. Controlled by two pimps with conflicting emotions toward her, Melania is treated as little more than property, stripped of autonomy.  

But this is "modern art-house cinema," where traditional storytelling is cast aside—coherent narratives, proper lighting, meaningful camerawork, and logical plots are dismissed as unnecessary. The result? Frustrating confusion. Much of the film feels aimless, with little holding interest. The audience’s patience wore thin—walkouts began before the latecomers even settled in, a rare sight.  

The director prioritizes mood over clarity—characters fade in and out of shadows, endless shots linger on nothing, and a drawn-out sex scene—

When choosing a movie, I hope you consider whether the actors involved use their platform to impact our society’s moral compass positively or negatively. This isn’t about politics—it’s about the ethical influence that shapes our communities. When a comedian or actor makes cruel, sexual, or racist remarks about a young person and their parent, we must ask ourselves: *Do I want to endorse that behavior?*  

In this case, Mr. Foxx’s actions undermine the values that teach young people right from wrong—that kindness should triumph over cruelty. He should remember he’s merely an entertainer, and there are countless other options for us to support. An apology doesn’t erase the harm caused or undo the negative influence on our youth.  

One way to discourage such behavior is to stop rewarding it. Refuse to watch their films or support their work. We can’t change them, but we *can* stop fueling their fame.

Nacho Vigalondo is widely known in Spain, though not necessarily for the right reasons. He’s the kind of cringe-worthy showman who leaves you squirming in secondhand embarrassment. You might recognize him from his low-budget TV commercials—like that bizarre one where he wandered around Madrid searching for Paul McCartney, promoting some CD collection.  

This short film feels like one of Nacho’s commercials: a weak plot, amateurish direction, and painfully bad acting. It’s shocking that something this dreadful made it to the Kodak Theater. The Oscars deserve better.  

Rumor has it Nacho only got this project off the ground thanks to his wife, who produced *7:35* and happens to have deep ties with Spanish TV execs. Connections over quality, it seems.

I had no idea what to expect when I walked into the theater, but now I’ve seen enough—this movie was a complete disaster. Everything about it fell flat: the weak screenplay, the clumsy direction, and the unconvincing performances. The plot itself was absurd and poorly thought out. Instead of crafting something meaningful, the director delivered a mess. I spent the second half of the film cringing in my seat, baffled by its lack of purpose or coherence. Rather than endorsing it, audiences—especially Christian viewers—should steer clear. This was a sloppy, disappointing waste of time and money. Skip it.

It’s a shame—I rarely finish a film feeling disappointed. I’ve enjoyed several of Ira Levin’s adaptations, like *Rosemary’s Baby* and *The Stepford Wives*, but this one just didn’t click with me.  

The premise hooked me: an award-winning playwright (Michael Caine) plots to murder his former student (Christopher Reeve) and steal his script for success. As a fan of thrillers, with Caine’s talent, Sidney Lumet behind the camera, and Levin’s usual sharp storytelling, my expectations were high.  

I won’t spoil it for those who haven’t seen it, but be prepared for endless twists—so many that summarizing the plot without giving anything away is nearly impossible. The first 45 minutes held my attention, but once the relentless turns started, my interest waned. That said, Lumet deserves praise for the darkly funny ending, which actually made me laugh out loud.  

The cast—Michael Caine, Christopher Reeve, Dyan...

*The Todesking* isn’t my favorite Jörg Buttgereit film, but it remains a compelling exploration of suicide and its consequences. Fans expecting the visceral gore or exploitation of *Nekromantik* or *Schramm* may be disappointed—this is an art-house endeavor, far removed from straightforward storytelling.  

The film’s structure unfolds over a week, with each day presenting a new vignette tied to a sinister chain letter that seemingly drives people to take their own lives. These segments are intercut with haunting shots of a corpse in decay.  

Some moments stand out as strikingly poignant, like the man confessing his marital struggles or the concert massacre (though the latter loses some impact when distracted by the *Scorpions*-esque band onstage). That said, the film has moments of unexpected beauty—the extended sequence of a massive bridge, for instance, gains chilling weight once you realize the names displayed belong to real-life suicide victims who leaped from it.

This film is downright terrible—painfully so. Bollywood’s streak of disappointing movies seems endless. Have they run out of excuses for churning out such mediocre work (or simply stopped caring)?  

The biggest flaw lies with the direction. Despite featuring two talented actors who’ve delivered stellar performances before, their potential was wasted under poor direction. The weak script only made things worse.  

The first half is riddled with absurd scenes and sloppy editing. Take this cringeworthy moment: After his first major concert, Ajay Devgan reunites with Om Puri—their first meeting in 30 years—and all Om Puri can muster is a warning about Salman’s friendship? Nonsense. And let’s not forget the painfully bad soundtrack. What happened to Shankar-Ehsaan-Loy’s magic?  

Casting Ajay Devgan as a rockstar was a misfire from the start.  

The only redeeming quality comes in the second half, where the performances improve. Ajay shines as his character’s darker side emerges, and Salman delivers a convincing portrayal of a drug addict.  

If you must watch, skip straight to the final half.

The best way to sum up *Ride With The Devil* is with a single word: authenticity. While I won’t repeat what others have said about this remarkable film, I must commend the crew for their meticulous historical research and dedication to detail—something this viewer deeply appreciated.  

As someone familiar with the era and setting, I can confidently say this is one of the most accurate fictional portrayals of "Bleeding Kansas." Like any work of fiction, it takes some creative liberties, but the film’s essence remains true to history. The costumes, attitudes (no modern political correctness here), and even the actors’ appearances feel genuine. Even Jewel Kilcher, in her minor role, looks as if she stepped straight out of a 19th-century photograph.  

Some viewers, however, have questioned the stylized dialogue, finding it hard to believe that 19th-century farmers spoke so poetically. What they overlook is that, in contrast to today’s often careless speech, Americans of that time were surprisingly literate and articulate.

I can't bring myself to criticize this film for two simple reasons: Robin Williams and Toni Collette. While the story flirts with psychological thriller territory—with subtly unsettling elements that could have been explored further—it’s the performances that truly shine. Robin Williams portrays Gabriel Noon, a late-night radio host and storyteller grappling with personal struggles: his partner leaves him, and he seems to be suffering from a creative drought.  

Then comes a haunting twist. Gabriel receives a manuscript from Pete Boland (Rory Culkin), a terminally ill 14-year-old boy detailing the abuse he endured at the hands of his adoptive parents. Pete lives with Donna Boland (Toni Collette), his social worker and guardian. Drawn in by Pete’s tragic tale, Gabriel forms a bond with him—only to question whether the boy exists at all when attempts to meet him in person lead to eerie uncertainty.  

I won’t reveal too much to avoid spoilers, but the film’s direction does feel somewhat predictable. Still, the storytelling atmosphere is engrossing, and Robin Williams delivers yet another compelling performance.

*Hitler: The Rise of Evil* feels like it was crafted by filmmakers unencumbered by the weight of World War II’s atrocities—making for an unexpectedly engaging viewing experience.  

Its greatest strength lies in its stark depiction of the Nazi machinery, laying bare the corrupt tactics Hitler employed to seize power. The film concludes just as he reaches the pinnacle of his rise.  

Once in control, the Führer ("leader" in German) plunged Germany into history’s most catastrophic war. Six years later, the nation faced total defeat, stripped of its eastern provinces (roughly 35% of its prewar territory) and forcibly divided for 44 years. Both West and East Germany had to rebuild from ruins, their global reputations shattered by the Nazis' racist brutality.  

As mentioned, *Hitler: The Rise of Evil* is a compelling watch. The 1930s setting feels authentic, the performances (especially Peter O’Toole’s standout portrayal of the aging President von Hindenburg) elevate the film, adding depth to an already solid production.  

My edition includes a second DVD featuring two well-made documentary films, rounding out the viewing experience.

This powerful film examines the horrific events in Derry three decades ago, now infamously remembered as Bloody Sunday.  

Meticulously researched with outstanding performances and direction, it presents the closest account we have to the truth while awaiting the Saville Inquiry's findings. The movie not only captures the brutality of the soldiers during the massacre but also frames the tragedy within the larger context of its time. It also exposes the gross injustice of the Widgery Tribunal's cover-up.  

Deeply moving and profoundly disturbing, this exceptional drama stands as a necessary portrayal of the events. Once the Saville report is released, revisit this film to witness just how accurately it reflects the truth.

This is ridiculous. They claim this is the "final" Nightmare film, only to turn around and make another one. While *Part 7* wasn’t terrible, why toy with the audience like this?  

The movie itself was baffling—lifeless, with flat characters and a Freddy reduced to mere comic relief, which is a disgrace for such a legendary series. The plot was incoherent, somehow worse than *Parts 2* and *5*. The whole thing felt like a gimmicky 3D spectacle with no substance.  

I despised this film so much that every flaw is burned into my memory—and that’s basically the entire runtime. It desperately tries to stand out but only succeeds in falling flat. Even the death scenes, while creative, were underwhelming.  

How did they let it get this bad? *Parts 2* and *5* were already missteps—did they learn nothing? Clearly, it’s just a cash grab. Avoid this insult to the *Nightmare* franchise.  

**Rating:** 3/10  

**Good Points:** The plot had *some* potential.  

**Bad Points:** Everything else.

What stuck with me most about this movie was how it played every Christmas season on KTLA (Channel 5) in the mid-to-late '70s, likely because the real events took place around Christmas Eve. Watching the girl endure such horror—surviving alone after a plane crash in the Peruvian jungle—always unsettled me. One particularly vivid scene, where she painfully pulls leeches from her infected leg, left a lasting mark on my young mind. It was far from the festive holiday cheer I expected back then. Definitely not your typical Rankin-Bass special.

I picked up the DVD and almost feel guilty after hearing Dawson and Lugacy’s heartfelt commentary. It’s not that the movie is bad, really—it just tries too hard to deliver some profound insight into humanity without recognizing how conventional its plot actually is. The themes come off as oversimplified, and the characters’ actions often feel unconvincing. Honestly, this might resonate with someone who hasn’t been exposed to much film, TV, literature, or life experience (I’ve even come across nearly identical plots in horror comics). But if you’re familiar with the genre, its message feels recycled and executed with less finesse. The biggest flaw is that beyond its central theme, there’s not much for cinema lovers to latch onto. The film leans heavily on the shock value of its premise without ever truly delivering, leaving it feeling forgettable in the end.

Inspired by the real-life adventures of Chuck Connors and Steve Brodie in 1890s New York, *The Bowery* is a lively, good-humored tale.  

However, a word of caution: The film features casual racial slurs from characters like Wallace Beery and young Jackie Cooper. The opening scene may catch viewers off guard—but this reflects both the era in which the story is set and the time it was made. It also highlights the diverse population of the neighborhood, adding to the raw, unfiltered atmosphere.  

Beery plays Connors as a brash, larger-than-life saloon owner who leads his own fire brigade—a loudmouthed yet oddly endearing figure with a soft spot for Cooper’s scrappy orphan. Meanwhile, George Raft’s Brodie is Connors' smoother, more charismatic rival in just about everything. Famously, Brodie never backed down from a dare—culminating in his infamous Brooklyn Bridge jump (though historians still argue whether he actually leaped or used a decoy).  

Beery delivers his usual boisterous performance, complete with a broad Irish-American accent. He's the kind of rough-around-the-edges character who somehow attracts kids, stray cats, and damsels in distress. This may well be his most rollicking role yet.

In my younger days, I had a weakness for terrible TV. We’ve all indulged in it at some point, but my justification for enduring shows like *Buck Rogers in the 25th Century* and *Silver Spoons* was simple: youth and naivety left me blind to what truly makes a series worthwhile.  

Fortunately, my taste has since improved—which is why *Stargate SG-1* doesn’t hold up. Twelve-year-old me would have adored every clichéd moment, every awkward line, every unnecessary burst of technobabble. But now, its writing feels painfully dull—so lifeless it somehow makes *Star Trek: Voyager* seem appealing by comparison. If your show has me pining for the weakest *Trek* installment, that’s a dire sign.  

The original *Stargate* film, at least, remains a guilty pleasure—thanks to James Spader and Kurt Russell’s strong performances, the stunning Egyptian backdrop, the memorable score, and its intriguing sci-fi concepts. Almost none of that charm carries over to the series. Even Richard Dean Anderson, who brought charisma to *MacGyver* and *Legend*, seems perpetually half-asleep here.  

The shoestring budget must have been to blame—

This film was dreadful. I struggled to keep my eyes open the entire time. Even if someone offered to pay me, I wouldn't sit through it again. The supposed scary moments were painfully predictable and exaggerated beyond belief. There wasn’t a single original or redeeming quality to justify the $7.50 I spent on it. Skip it entirely—don’t watch it, don’t rent it, don’t even bother looking it up. All of those would be a total waste. Sarah Michelle Gellar’s performance was uninspired and disappointing, tarnishing her otherwise solid reputation. Shame on her for attaching her name to this disaster. Awful film—avoid at all costs.

I reference *Oedipus Rex* because it's a true tragedy that this film was ever made!!!  

This ranks among the worst movies I've ever suffered through! Let me be clear—I’m not one of those humorless IMDb critics who blindly hate Uwe Boll.  

Some of Boll’s films, like *Postal* and *Tunnel Rats*, are so laughably terrible that they’re entertaining. But this? This was just plain awful. I despised it so much that I’d give it zero stars if possible. The plot is absolute trash—it spends 80% of the runtime setting things up, only to devolve into a middle section packed with gratuitous, tasteless murder scenes. And the ending? A "villain prevails" finale could work, but this was executed with zero finesse.  

Just to be clear, I don’t have some vendetta against Boll (as I mentioned earlier), and I’m not opposed to violent films—far from it! I adore violent cinema. *Saw*, *Hostel*, *Tokyo Gore Police*, *The New York Ripper*, *28 Days Later*, *Dog Soldiers*, *My Bloody Valentine*, *Last House on the Left*, *Watchmen*, *Wolf Creek*, every Tarantino flick, every Sam Peckinpah masterpiece—hell, even *Cannibal Holocaust*—I love them all. But this? This was just garbage.

Just received my two-disc DVD set, and while it isn’t flawless, I had a blast watching it. Full disclosure—I’m a die-hard zombie movie fan, and I’m convinced the folks behind these films share that passion. I also admire anyone chasing their dreams, especially against the odds, and these filmmakers are doing exactly that. Is this collection a masterpiece? Not by a long shot. But considering their shoestring budgets, they deserve real credit. For me, it all comes down to one question: was I entertained? Did I enjoy it? The answer? A resounding "yes." The first film in the series is the grittiest—it kicks off with a disaster at a nuclear plant, where, well… things get messy. Fast forward, and a new neighborhood sits atop the old reactor. A group of kids filming a video stumble into a hidden underground labyrinth, trapped in the facility’s crumbling depths...

This year's surprise Oscar nominee for Best Animated Feature is a film that feels deeply Irish at its core, though brought to life through a collaboration between Belgium, Brazil, and animators likely working across all three countries. The result is one of the most visually stunning and distinctive films in recent memory.  

Its character design echoes the simplicity of *Persepolis*, with bold, black outlines defining its figures—but this film is anything but monochrome. What truly sets it apart is its breathtaking use of color, some of the most audacious and mesmerizing I’ve ever seen on screen.  

Visually striking, the film embraces a highly geometric aesthetic—characters take the form of rectangles, ovals, and other shapes, turning much of the viewing experience into a playful game of spotting circles, a recurring motif in its composition. This deliberate design isn’t just stylistic—it serves the story beautifully, centered on a young boy’s journey to becoming an artist crafting illuminated manuscripts. (The *Book of Kells* is, of course, a real historical treasure—and the film’s artistry pays glorious homage to that legacy.)

Nearly every aspect of this film is a misfire. Mike Myers, for instance, proves he’s still recycling the same comedic gimmicks from his *SNL* era over a decade ago—unchanged, uninspired. His performance as the Cat is agonizingly dull, straining for laughs with forced, hyperactive antics that miss the mark entirely. The rest of the film follows suit. The sets are a garish, multimillion-dollar eyesore—honestly, cardboard cutouts might have been a smarter choice than the bloated, pointless construction of an entire town. Alec Baldwin’s attempt at channeling *The Great Santini* turns into a muddled mess, neither funny nor coherent. Topping it off is a bizarre, tonally jarring cameo from Paris Hilton, completely out of step with the whimsy of Dr. Seuss. Skip this one—it’s not even entertainingly bad. (Here’s hoping *Horton Hears a Who* with Robin Williams completes the trilogy of Seuss misfires starring manic comedians.)

I caught this film on cable a while back, and it blew me away. William H. Macy, one of my all-time favorite actors, delivers an incredible performance—he makes you root for his character even when he’s clearly in the wrong. And Neve Campbell? Hands down, it’s the best acting I’ve seen from any actress this year. She absolutely shines as a rebellious yet wise-beyond-her-years young woman.  

Donald Sutherland is downright unsettling as Macy’s father, while John Ritter holds his own as a therapist caught in the middle of the chaos.  

I really wish this had gotten a theatrical release—it’s the kind of movie more people should see. It’s a shame because it’s miles ahead of most of the stuff hitting theaters these days.

Henry Hathaway was both bold and passionate in his portrayal of early U.S. history and its people. While some may critique historical inaccuracies in his film about Brigham Young and the Mormon pioneers, such criticisms miss the point of this cinematic work. In my view, Hathaway’s direction masterfully captures the essence of the early Latter-Day Saint movement, from Joseph Smith's martyrdom to the era of the film's release. Through nuanced cinematography and deliberate dialogue, he wove Mormon teachings and philosophies into many key scenes.  

I vividly recall watching this movie on Saturday mornings as a child in the early 1950s—just over a decade after its release and before the Los Angeles Temple was completed. Observing its construction only deepened my fascination with the Mormon people. Having recently acquired this film, I look forward to revisiting the themes Hathaway so thoughtfully conveyed:  

1. A love for all people, regardless of their beliefs.  
2. Charity extended freely, whether or not it is sought.  
3. The exalted importance of family.

It never occurred to me that Charles Boyer (Luis Denard) and Lauren Bacall (Rose Cullen) shared the screen in a film, showcasing their remarkable performances together. Even Peter Lorre (Contreras) had a part in this movie, though he faced an unfortunate accident in his bathroom that left him unconscious.  

The plot follows Luis Denard, a Republican courier, who travels to England during the Spanish Civil War to sabotage a coal mining deal that would severely impact other nations. Lauren Bacall’s character, Rose Cullen, lends him support—first by rescuing him, then by falling for him—and ultimately helps him evade an enraged mob of English miners determined to kill him.  

The true villain of the story is Victor Francen (Licata), known for *The Beast with Five Fingers*, who delivers a standout performance. This 1945 classic remains unforgettable—even without Humphrey Bogart.

Here’s another irreverent European film that mocks the dominant religion of its setting. (These filmmakers never let up.) This time, it’s a harsh critique targeting Catholics and the clergy (and I’m not even Catholic).  

Surprisingly, this movie won an Academy Award for Best Foreign Film—likely because it portrays Catholic faith and religious conviction as feeble. One of the central figures is a priest obsessed with food, depicted as little more than a buffoon. It’s no shock that the secular-leaning Academy adored it.  

And then there’s the over-the-top performance from an actor playing a man who abandons his faith to wed one of the four sisters in the story. These women take turns luring the so-called "seminary student" (who, after six years of study, declares himself an agnostic!). How much more sacrilegious can this film get?  

It’s an embarrassment and yet another glaring example of the anti-religious bias pervasive in global cinema (not just Hollywood).

Few films have captivated me as deeply as this one. Its raw, backwoods atmosphere immerses you completely, making every moment feel authentic and genuine. The setting transports you to another time—perhaps the late 1960s or early 1970s—adding to its nostalgic charm. Henry Thomas delivers a heartfelt performance alongside the young child, creating a tender, emotional depth that lingers. It’s a powerful story, beautifully told and absolutely worth watching.

The other day, I suddenly remembered watching *American Gothic* during its original run. The main thing that stuck in my mind was recognizing Gary Cole from *Midnight Caller*. I’m not usually a big TV watcher, but *American Gothic* was an exception—so much so that I just bought the complete series on DVD. It still holds up perfectly.  

Honestly, it’s one of the greatest shows ever made. Most of what’s on TV these days doesn’t interest me—just cheap reality shows like *Big Brother* or endless soaps. The only exception for me is Derren Brown. That’s why I barely watch anymore.  

I snagged the *American Gothic* DVD set for just £16.97 on Asda’s website—couldn’t find it cheaper anywhere else.

A perfect 10/10—this outstanding documentary is absolutely essential viewing. It features rare wartime footage unseen for decades until its 1974 release. The film leaves nothing out, with some scenes so powerful they left me speechless. Spanning over 20 episodes, Sir Laurence Olivier’s masterful narration weaves a gripping account of conflict. Even after 25 years, it remains unmatched as the definitive war documentary, delivering an unforgettable emotional force. Whether you watch a few episodes or the entire series, its raw depiction of sacrifice and suffering in *The World at War* will leave you deeply moved. Don’t miss it.

Absolutely: a wild mix of drug-fueled chaos, warehouse shootouts, gravity-defying bullet dodging straight out of 'The Matrix,' a neon-drenched future city teeming with diverse Asian cultures, and an isolated vampire—all crammed into one film—could only spring from the mind of a Japanese rock icon. And that’s precisely what 'Moon Child' delivers, and then some. While this explosive cocktail of ideas might seem destined for schlocky B-movie territory, the film somehow manages to pull it off, even if it stumbles a few times along the way.  

The movie oozes raw, indie energy, its narrative unfolding not in smooth sequences but in jagged, unpredictable bursts. It peels back layers of its characters’ lives rather than building a conventional plot, embracing the chaos instead of apologizing for it. At its core, 'Moon Child' is a story of loyalty, heartbreak, love, and treachery—all wrapped in the flashy trappings of a cyberpunk underworld, warring crime syndicates, and immortal bloodsuckers.  

HYDE is magnetic as 'Kei,' the brooding vampire, his restrained performance grounding the film against Gackt’s hyper-charged intensity as 'Sho,' the spirited orphan who forms an unlikely bond with him. Meanwhile, Lee-Hom Wang steals scenes as 'Son,' a figure consumed by vengeance yet drawn into Sho’s orbit in adulthood.

This film should have centered on Sam and his wife, the brilliant Peter Falk and the equally magnificent Olympia Dukakis. That would have made for a compelling story. Instead, it serves as a showcase for Paul Reiser, with Falk relegated to a minor role. Even the talented Elizabeth Perkins barely registers in this mess. Reiser seems convinced he’s a major star deserving of his own vehicle—he isn’t. Worse still, he cast some of the finest character actresses working today, only to sideline them entirely. Dukakis appears for a mere 15 minutes, yet she lights up the screen when she does.  

The heart of the story belongs to Falk and Dukakis, but we’re forced to endure a pointless, absurd road trip where Reiser tries (and fails) to prove how charming, profound, and psychologically insightful he can be. Take, for instance, a painfully awkward restaurant scene that Reiser likely envisioned as raw and Cassavetes-esque. The confrontation between him and Falk is so laughably false it’s almost cringe-worthy—poor Falk deserved better.

This Fourth of July weekend, it’s inspiring to see the defiant spirit of the Declaration of Independence echoed in the sharp satire of *War, Inc.* Much like our founding fathers boldly rejected the tyranny of King George III, this film hilariously skewers the greed-driven war profiteers of today—corporate opportunists shamelessly pushing to privatize government functions, even warfare itself.  

The ensemble cast delivers standout performances. John Cusack is brilliant as a dry-witted, morally torn corporate hitman, while the radiant Marisa Tomei captivates as his romantic counterpart (and yes, "George Costanza" wasn’t wrong—Tomei is mesmerizing!). But the true scene-stealer is Joan Cusack, whose flawless comic timing and rubber-faced brilliance bring endless laughs as a hilariously domineering yet fawning assistant. Dan Aykroyd also makes a brief but impactful appearance as the head of the war-managing Tamerlane Corporation, sitting in...

This opening installment of the Guinea Pig series remains one of the most notorious films in the collection.  

After years of hesitation, I finally gathered the courage to acquire this infamous set of films. Purchasing the complete Guinea Pig box set, I committed to watching them in chronological order. With the first disc loaded, I settled in for the experience.  

Given everything I'd read online about this film's disturbing content, I expected my limits to be thoroughly tested. Surprisingly, that wasn't the case.  

The plot centers on a group of men who abduct a woman and subject her to torture, attempting to determine the threshold of human endurance—how much pain a person can withstand before breaking.  

Sounds like a profoundly disturbing film, doesn’t it? Not quite. It ultimately falls short of delivering genuine shock. This might be attributed to years of horror desensitization or my deep immersion in extreme cinema, but any seasoned gore enthusiast would likely find this underwhelming.  

That said, for viewers unaccustomed to graphic, unsettling content…

This was clearly a low-budget production, complete with noticeable continuity flaws—like scenes spliced together from footage shot in both sunlight and shade. While I’m a fan of Nick Mancuso, he occasionally leaned too heavily into the weary, disheveled act, and some of the supporting performances fell flat (not to mention one actor awkwardly pulling double duty in two prominent roles). That said, Richard Grieco was downright hilarious—his hair alone makes this worth watching. Steven Ford brought charm to his role, and Mancuso delivered some sharp one-liners, though Nancy Allen, surprisingly, turned in a wooden and forgettable performance. A classic? Hardly. Flawed? Absolutely. Fun? Without a doubt. I would’ve killed to be in the room when they settled on Grieco’s wild hairstyle. *"Are you fast?" ... "Y'ain't THAT fast."*

The film suffers from a critical flaw that undermines its entire credibility.  

It opens by criticizing Israel’s presence in disputed territories while ignoring the historical context—Israel only gained control of these lands after being attacked by Egypt, Syria, Iraq, and Jordan in a defensive war. The film also accuses Israel of violating UN Resolution 242, yet fails to mention that the Palestinians themselves rejected this resolution from the start, rendering it irrelevant.  

While the documentary may be well-edited and feature compelling visuals, viewers should approach it with skepticism. Remember: don’t accept everything you hear, and question even what you see.  

Every contributor in this film has a documented bias against Israel, with some even making openly antisemitic remarks in the past—casting serious doubt on their credibility. What they truly need is an impartial history lesson, free from partisan influence.

I always tune into the MTV Movie Awards for a sharp, entertaining show that offers something different—like Chewbacca winning a lifetime achievement award. This year was no exception. Though I'm not a Justin Timberlake fan, I’ve always found Seann William Scott hilariously dumb. Stiffler cracked me up in the *American Pie* movies, and I even liked him in *Dude, Where’s My Car?* But this year’s awards were downright awful—nothing made sense, nothing was funny, and nothing held my interest. Timberlake should stick to singing and dancing; acting clearly isn’t his forte.  

Who wrote this mess? Last year’s show, with Jack Black and Sarah Michelle Gellar, was laugh-out-loud funny—their *Lord of the Rings* parody alone was worth the watch. But this time? Nothing landed. Did anyone get Timberlake’s "joke" about Luke Wilson and Kate Hudson? *"They’re starring in a movie together but have never met! Here they are..."* What was the punchline? Kate and Luke just launched into their bland exchange without acknowledging the setup. Even Seann Scott was wasted—he didn’t even get a single chuckle out of me.

This exceptional masterpiece comes highly recommended, not just for its profound thematic depth but also for Theo Angelopoulos' unparalleled visual brilliance. The performances by cinematic legends Marcello Mastroianni and Jeanne Moreau shine brightly, complemented by Ilias Logothetis' remarkable character portrayal. While Gregory Karr's performance might initially appear subdued beside his formidable co-stars, he delivers a perfect characterization—culminating in a powerful final scene with Khrysikou and Mastroianni (hinted at earlier, hence the spoiler).  

Manage your expectations accordingly—this is an art film in every sense of the word, demanding focused engagement akin to reading literature or experiencing live music. Its breathtaking cinematography makes it ideal for large-screen viewing.  

Dialogue remains minimal throughout, yet the film incorporates fragments of Albanian, Kurdish, and Turkish alongside Greek and English—a delightful detail for those who appreciate the melody of diverse languages.

**Rewritten Version:**  

Wow, I can’t believe I’m the first to comment on this amazing movie!  

While the plot itself is engaging, what really drew me in was Matt Lillard. I know a lot of people might find him overly hyper or not their cup of tea, but since we're the same age and from the same generation, I’ve grown to really appreciate his work. This is one of those rare films where he takes center stage, similar to his standout role in *SLC Punk*—another must-watch Lillard performance.  

At its core, it’s your classic heist flick, but with way more twists and turns than usual, leading to some seriously wild moments. Another highlight is Vincent D’Onofrio, an underrated gem in Hollywood who brings his A-game as always. The female lead is a fresh face, and she holds her own—though let’s be real, she was probably cast for her accent *and* that one particular scene.  

It all boils down to a fierce game of Jack vs. Jill vs. Bob, with everyone fighting for the prize and no one willing to share. The tension keeps you guessing until the very end!

This film deserves more recognition on IMDb than it's currently getting, thanks to its strong entertainment value.  

At its core, it's a classic whodunit thriller packed with mystery, seduction, and violence—yet it masterfully keeps you guessing until the final reveal. As a fan of the genre, I believe this movie absolutely holds its own.  

In fact, I enjoyed it enough to watch it multiple times, which is why I’m giving it a solid 8 on IMDb.

Mat Spirogolou (played by Toby Malone) comes from a family that recognizes his football talent. They’re thrilled when he lands an audition with a major club and hope his city-dwelling cousin will take him under his wing.  

But the two couldn’t be more different—Mat is a wide-eyed farm boy, while his cousin is a sharp-talking spendthrift tangled up with drug dealers and gangsters. A quiet night before Mat’s big audition seems unlikely.  

After missing his cousin George (Damien Robertson) upon arrival, Mat finds himself in deeper trouble when a reckless biker gives him a ride—and more than he bargained for.  

Known primarily for his theater work, Toby Malone delivers a strong performance as the innocent country teen. Though the film’s modest budget shows in places, like many low-budget productions, it more than makes up for it with fun, spontaneity, and charm—qualities often missing from big-budget Hollywood fare.

I held off writing a review of this documentary because when I first watched it more than a decade ago, I needed time to fully process my thoughts.  

From a filmmaking perspective, this is an outstanding documentary. It achieves exactly what it aims to do—exposing viewers to an unfamiliar world while keeping them thoroughly engaged. I entered with no prior knowledge of drag culture, and discovering the vibrant scene of drag queens and their "Balls" was nothing short of mesmerizing. The sheer talent these performers bring to their craft, especially in competition, is remarkable. The drama—whether it's the bickering, the complaints (I admit, I was furious when someone pointed out that a queen’s coat wasn’t technically a "man's" coat!), or the rivalry—feels familiar, echoing the intensity of any high-stakes competition. That, to me, was part of the message.  

There’s the generational tension too—seasoned drag queens reminiscing about how the Balls "used to be," while younger queens push boundaries, adding new categories and reinventing traditions. Even the spectators watching on the sidelines seemed aware that the future of this world was evolving right before their eyes.
