Years ago, a friend and I—both avid moviegoers—decided to watch a horror film called *The Incubus*, drawn solely by the fact that it starred John Cassavetes. For those unfamiliar, Cassavetes was a prolific actor, screenwriter, and director, married to actress Gena Rowlands, with three Oscar nominations to his name. He financed his own acclaimed low-budget films using earnings from mainstream acting roles. What we didn’t realize until *The Incubus* was that "mainstream acting roles" apparently included anything that came his way. Had we known the plot beforehand, we might have skipped it entirely—yet we stayed through the whole thing.  

Back then, my friend and I half-jokingly declared it the worst movie ever made. In hindsight, that’s not quite accurate. I’ve endured plenty of late-night Cinemax disasters (did I really admit that?) that were far more unwatchable. Practically any Brian Bosworth vehicle is, by default, worse than *The Incubus*. And let’s not forget *Santa Claus Conquers the Martians*—objectively more painful to sit through. Still, *The Incubus* remains my personal benchmark for cinematic failure, the line beneath which no film should ever sink.

Skip the fancy review—this isn’t worth the effort. It’s not some deep, artistic film, not even a so-called hidden gem. You know the type: the obscure indie flick your friend raves about after catching it at some underground cinema.  

Just toss it in with the holiday decorations and forget it fast.

There is little doubt that H.G. Wells stands as the most influential writer of the 20th century. While Jules Verne may be considered the father of science fiction, his stories leaned more toward adventure, using fantastical inventions as narrative tools. Wells, on the other hand, infused depth and subtext into his tales. Perhaps his greatest impact lies in how he reshaped human imagination—before the 20th century, belief in extraterrestrial life was virtually nonexistent, yet today, figures like Richard Dawkins regard it as highly probable. Though no definitive proof exists, one can’t help but suspect that Wells planted this idea in the collective consciousness.  

*Things to Come* was adapted by Wells from his own novel, but his struggle to distinguish between novelistic and cinematic storytelling is evident. The dialogue often feels overwrought, clumsy, and artificial—most notably in scenes like the one where two opposing pilots ponder war with the heavy-handed line, *"Why must we murder one another? Why?"*

I’ve never seen a murder mystery as painfully dull as this one. The film follows a medical examiner probing his friend’s suspicious car crash death, and it checks every box for a terrible movie: wooden acting, a lifeless plot, zero tension, forced humor, and an utter lack of emotional weight. I caught it on PAX, a network notorious for churning out cheap, campy TV movies—and this one fits the bill perfectly.  

While TV movies rarely match the thrill of big-screen productions, this one sinks to new lows. The title, *Recipe for Murder*, hints at some intrigue, but the filmmakers squandered any potential for suspense or excitement.  

If you’re looking for a decent thriller, skip this disaster—it might just ruin your appetite for movies altogether.  

Grade: F

I found *King Solomon's Mines* to be a beautifully crafted film. My only critique would be Alison Doody—while her acting was outstanding, her makeup and hairstyle felt anachronistic, making her stand out awkwardly next to the rest of the cast. Patrick Swayze was a brilliant pick for Alan Quatermain. It was refreshing to see a rugged, seasoned actor in the role after enduring countless films with fair-haired, boyish leads like Val Kilmer and Brad Pitt. He was perfect for the part, and I thoroughly enjoyed every moment of the movie.  

This adaptation shouldn’t be compared to the 1950s version starring Stewart Granger—it was a full-scale cinematic production, not a made-for-TV feature. Both interpretations of Quatermain were convincing, but they belong to entirely different mediums. I can’t wait to revisit this film and sincerely hope Patrick Swayze pursued more roles like this in the future.

This avant-garde film is believed to have been produced either in 1969 or 1972—while the National Film Preservation Foundation cites 1969, IMDb lists the later date. Whichever year it belongs to, the work undeniably captures the essence of that era, featuring cinematography and pop art aesthetics unmistakably rooted in the late 1960s to early 1970s.  

The piece presents just three basic visuals, each manipulated through unconventional camera techniques. Accompanied solely by music, it lacks any dialogue or narrative structure, clearly conceived as a kind of performance art. And much like much performance art, what begins as intriguing swiftly turns tedious. To be frank, the film is a dull affair—likely captivating only its creators, their inner circle, and perhaps a niche audience determined to appear too avant-garde for mainstream tastes.

While the film had its occasional humorous scenes, overall I found it disappointingly weak. Its quality deteriorated as it progressed—once the story moved into Monument Valley, I caught myself focusing more on the stunning rock formations than the increasingly absurd and poorly executed character interactions.  

The daughter’s character was especially inconsistent. She flip-flopped constantly—first complicit, then shocked and fleeing, only to return before abandoning them yet again. None of her choices seemed grounded in believable motives. Despite a few intriguing characters and moments, the movie squandered its potential, ultimately falling far short of what it could have been. Fans of *Repo Man* might gravitate toward this, but *Searchers 2.0* is a pale imitation of *The Searchers.*

A film where Brooke Shields outperforms a Fonda is both a rarity and a nightmare. Shields’ shortcomings stem from youth, inexperience, and clearly lacking direction from her co-star. Peter Fonda, however, is simply terrible—plain and simple. Though he redeemed himself years later in *Ulee’s Gold*, he’s unbearably bad here. And he’s not alone. Outside of Henry Fonda’s charming cameo, not a single performance is even remotely decent—arguably the worst ensemble ever assembled.  

Luke Askew, the main antagonist, might have been salvageable with better writing and direction, given his past work. But his counterpart, Ted Markland, chews scenery with cringe-worthy excess. The script is abysmal, and while the actors can’t be blamed for their awful lines, they deliver them dreadfully. The editing and direction are painfully inept—shots linger pointlessly or cut too soon, sapping the film of any impact. This thing was even worse than I expected, the kind of disaster that should have faded into total obscurity (if it were ever remembered at all).

Letters without addresses find their way to a hidden corner of the post office—a limbo between worlds. Alice takes a job there, clinging to the hope of uncovering traces of her missing father, but instead she stumbles upon the haunted heart of her boss, Frank. A modest, understated Australian film that flickered briefly in theaters before vanishing into obscurity. Now, it sits buried in the video store's shadows, drowned out by stacks of that dreaded *Godzilla* remake. It's a pity—this quiet gem delivers a moving story through stark, striking visuals and powerful performances from its two leads. Where Garry Marshall's *Dear God* (1996, USA) stumbled, this film finds its footing, nearly matching the brilliance not of the Kevin Costner misfire, but of He Jianjun's *Postman* (1995, China).

Errol Flynn stars as "Gentleman Jim" in this 1942 biopic about the legendary boxer Jim Corbett, who famously defeated John L. Sullivan. Directed by Flynn’s close friend Raoul Walsh with a lively touch, the film features a stellar supporting cast, including Alexis Smith, Jack Carson, Alan Hale Sr., William Frawley, and Ward Bond. Flynn portrays Corbett as a confident, upwardly mobile young man whose innate boxing skill earns him the backing of San Francisco’s elite Olympic Club in the late 19th century. Despite his charm, his working-class Irish roots and relentless ambition create tension among the club’s privileged members, many of whom eagerly bet against him. Yet Corbett’s talent propels him to stardom—even dabbling in acting—before he finally secures the fight of his dreams against reigning champion John L. Sullivan (Ward Bond). When Sullivan demands a hefty $10,000 deposit to guarantee Corbett’s appearance for the $25,000 prize, he and his manager (Frawley) face a seemingly impossible hurdle—until an unexpected benefactor steps in.  

A thoroughly enjoyable film, *Gentleman Jim* showcases Flynn in one of his most fitting roles, perfectly capturing Corbett’s charisma and ambition.

This film is completely pointless unless you approach it with the right mindset. A sloppy remake of the far superior *Heaven Can Wait*, it barely qualifies as a romantic comedy—feeling more like an awkward excuse to showcase Rock’s stand-up routine, which falls painfully flat on screen. The disjointed premise—his jokes belonging to a dead, wealthy old man but delivered in his own voice—makes the racially charged humor land with a thud. The film is humorless, lazily directed, and filled with painfully wooden performances. Save your time and money—watch the original *Heaven Can Wait* and one of Rock’s live specials instead. You’ll thank yourself later.

After scanning through reactions to this film, it’s clear some viewers have remarkably low standards. The movie is utterly forgettable—poorly written, clumsily directed, and filled with stiff performances. Every line of dialogue feels recycled from a soap opera, and the plot twists defy even the loosest grip on reality. While these flaws could have made it unintentionally entertaining, the film lacks any spark, leaving it as dull as it is inept. It’s as if Lee Rose set out to craft a raw, honest story about a woman grappling with her sexuality but either got shackled by studio interference or simply lacked the nerve to follow through. This isn’t just a bad movie—it’s the textbook definition of a cliché-ridden Lifetime channel disaster.

Pure nonsense—a perfect reflection of the insincere, shallow mindset of its era. This film pairs clumsy, surface-level guilt over slavery with barely disguised colonialist undertones (why is that irritating redhead force-feeding Shaka rice?). Historical accuracy? Nonexistent. Most enslaved people in the West were taken from West Africa, yet here we see an American slaver somehow overpowering Shaka with just a few men? Absurd. And David Hasselhoff’s performance? Unbearably grating. One can only imagine how he would have survived the miniseries—probably not long (a swift spear to the chest, perhaps?). The miniseries was extraordinary; it’s a shame Hasselhoff reduced something bold and original into forgettable mediocrity. (I suspect he played a major role in ruining it.)

place a world-renowned star, but history had different plans. The cinematography captures the stark reality of life under oppressive regimes, reflecting both the physical and psychological struggles faced by the protagonist.  

I doubt this film will resonate deeply with audiences unfamiliar with Romania’s history. That may speak to its cultural specificity—perhaps even a lack of universal appeal—but it also highlights how vastly divergent Romania’s historical and everyday experiences were, even within Eastern Europe.  

Adapted from a novel by Marin Preda, a controversial writer who died shortly after its publication under Communist rule, the film follows the life of a philosophy professor wrongfully imprisoned during the Stalinist era. The first half depicts his harrowing fight for survival in prison, while the second explores his fragile attempts to rebuild his life after release. Yet freedom proves illusory—1960s Romania demands new forms of moral compromise, and his struggle for integrity becomes as punishing as his time behind bars.  

Brilliantly performed by Romania’s finest actors, including the extraordinary Ștefan Iordache in the lead role, the film showcases talent that, under different circumstances, would have earned global acclaim. The raw intensity of the performances and the unflinching portrayal of ideological oppression make this a powerful, if challenging, piece of cinema.

When I first started watching this film, I recognized Xander from *Buffy* and thought, *How nice that he’s still landing acting gigs.* I can usually handle weird movies—especially the kind with that surreal David Lynch flavor, like *Twin Peaks* or *Lost Highway*—as long as they’re the right kind of weird. But this? It reminded me of those deranged conspiracy theory websites where nothing adds up. Nazis teaming up with America to form some unholy trinity of evil? Seriously? At this point, I’m just surprised they didn’t toss in hollow Earth theories, UFO-riding Hitler, and reptilian overlords for good measure. Maybe if you were on 60 grams of heroin, this might somehow make sense—but let’s be clear, I don’t endorse drugs, and I *certainly* don’t endorse this movie. Burn it. Shred it. Erase it. Maybe then poor Xander can find a decent role. His acting wasn’t the issue—he did fine—but the script? Absolute nonsense. Sorry, not sorry.

Here’s another film that deserves to be loaded onto a satellite, launched into space, and aimed at the Andromeda galaxy to showcase humanity’s finest. This delightfully absurd movie, shamelessly lifting from the already campy 1976 *King Kong*, outdoes its predecessor in sheer, laugh-out-loud ridiculousness. It even eerily foreshadows Peter Jackson’s tedious 2005 CGI remake—complete with its awkward "romance" between a towering creature (this time, a Yeti) and a stunning human woman (Antonellina Interlenghi, from Umberto Lenzi’s *City of the Living Dead*, who is undeniably captivating).  

Geared toward children, the film skimps on raunch—aside from some fishbone innuendos and an odd farewell nipple tweak—with the Yeti sporting a comically oversized jockstrap to hide his… ahem, *endowments*. The result is far funnier than full anatomical accuracy would have been. Instead of steamier scenes, we’re treated to a nutty old scientist, two snoopy kids, and Tony Kendall hamming it up as a deliciously sleazy villain.

Fans of Roman Polanski might adore this film, while others could despise it—Roger Ebert famously couldn’t fathom why audiences weren’t fleeing the theater. After my first viewing, I’m not entirely sure where I stand. Yet, as someone endlessly fascinated by Kafkaesque themes and unsettling dark comedies of paranoia, *The Tenant* holds a peculiar grip for its duration. Or perhaps it doesn’t—this might have been a sharper masterpiece if condensed into a half-hour *Twilight Zone* episode, complete with Rod Serling’s haunting narration as Trelkovsky (or whoever he truly is) thrashes in his bandages.  

The film mirrors *Repulsion* in its portrayal of a doomed protagonist, yet one could argue that *The Tenant* leans further into ambiguity, weaving surrealism through the slow unraveling of both character and setting. That said, *Repulsion* arguably benefits from a stronger lead performance and tighter execution.  

Even so, *The Tenant* boasts a premise so intriguing that it lingers long after the credits roll—the kind of story you can’t resist recounting to others: Polanski plays a Polish émigré in Paris...

*Follow the Fleet*, a 1936 RKO production starring Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers, delivers a clever romantic comedy enriched by intricate storytelling. Though Astaire and Rogers frequently paired in similar films, RKO crafted a compelling narrative that cleverly mirrored societal themes of its era. The film excels through interwoven plotlines between its two central couples, ensuring a well-rounded romantic comedy.  

The story follows Bake Baker (Fred Astaire), a U.S. Navy sailor, and Sherry Martin (Ginger Rogers), his former dance partner and romantic interest, now a singer and performer. Their reunion unfolds when Bake’s shipmate, Bilge Smith, discovers an old photo of the pair. Bake confesses he once proposed to Sherry before losing touch. Hoping Sherry might have a friend for him, Bilge persuades Bake to seek her out during shore leave.  

The next pivotal scene introduces the second major storyline, further deepening the film’s romantic entanglements.

Despite being a solid James Arness western, this movie is widely regarded as the worst Alamo film of all time. The plot was weak, riddled with historical inaccuracies, and packed with outright fabrications. Continuity errors were everywhere—did anyone notice the cannon scene? The Mexicans foolishly fired cannons still clogged with mud and ramrods, which was laughably unrealistic. And let’s not forget Brian Keith’s absurd hat—was the costume designer absent or simply out of their mind?

Little Edie and Big Edie are deeply sympathetic figures. Despite the squalor of their home, it’s impossible not to empathize with them—especially given their struggles with mental illness. A message board comment once noted, *"Little Edie has the coping skills of an eight-year-old,"* which brought to mind a line from the 2009 dramatization where Big Edie tells her, *"If you're stuck, it's only with yourself!"*  

They had brilliance, beauty, talent, and unwavering confidence in their choices. But Little Edie’s harsh self-criticism after early setbacks—losing her hair, her career, and the love of her life—may have held her back. This speaks to what I believe was her psychological struggle: an inability to recover from hardship and believe in brighter days ahead. We’ll never know how differently things might have unfolded if she hadn’t heeded her mother’s desperate call: *"Come home, Edie! Let me take care of you!"*  

Yet, for all their understandable insecurities, these women remained sharp, tragic, and endearing—even in their crumbling, filthy surroundings. Extraordinary in their own way, their dynamic with each other was as humorous as it was heartbreaking.

Gédéon and Jules Naudet set out to document the lives of rookie firefighters in New York City. Instead, they captured the only known footage from inside the World Trade Center on 9/11.  

Having previously collaborated with James Hanlon’s ladder company, Jules accompanied the captain to investigate a gas leak while Gédéon remained at the firehouse, ready in case something noteworthy occurred. A low-flying plane caught Jules’ attention—he instinctively raised his camera moments before it struck the North Tower.  

Jules urged the captain to follow him into the Towers. His first sight was two burning victims, a scene he chose not to record. Over the next several hours, he focused on the raw reactions of firefighters and bystanders.  

The Naudet brothers carefully avoided excessive violence or graphic imagery in their film, though the firefighters’ unfiltered language remained intact—a bold move by CBS to air it uncensored. They blended their real-time footage with intimate interviews, allowing the firefighters to reflect on their experiences during the unfolding tragedy.  

Unlike a dramatized feature film...

Paul Verhoeven's film adaptation was a total disappointment. His approach as a director was disrespectful—he admitted to barely skimming a couple chapters of the book before abandoning the source material entirely.  

Had Heinlein been alive, he likely would have disapproved. The movie borrows the title and ridicules the political themes central to the book, while inserting unnecessary elements just to pander to mainstream audiences.  

While this anime adaptation isn’t flawless, it stays far more faithful to the original work by comparison.

A compelling film with—for its era—a gripping, expansive, and fairly somber story, echoing shades of John Ford’s *The Searchers* though not as harsh. The plot kicks off swiftly and maintains its momentum, featuring sharp, well-crafted dialogue between Jeff Webster (Stewart), Ronda Castle, and Sheriff Gannon. In some respects, it recalls *Bend of the River* (1952), another Mann-Stewart collaboration, but this one feels less sentimental and more engaging. There are minor drawbacks: a somewhat rushed and sentimental ending, 24-year-old Corinne Calvet’s unconvincing portrayal of an innocent French teen, and the expected liberties taken with the Mythic West’s disregard for real-world logic. Still, these are negligible flaws. James Stewart delivers a surprisingly layered performance as a brooding, detached man convinced he’s only out for himself, and the breathtaking mountain landscapes add to the film’s impact. A standout Western costume drama.

If you ever hear someone say these three words—"Joe Don Baker"—brace yourself...  

*Final Justice* is a low-budget action flick featuring a Texas sheriff named Geronimo (pronounced "Heronimo"). He's a crude, sleazy, and downright obnoxious character, hellbent on tracking down a criminal in Malta who killed his partner back in Texas. Speaking of which, his partner collapses not once, but twice in the movie—thanks to some painfully sloppy editing.  

Joe Don Baker’s Geronimo spends half the movie getting thrown in jail (four or five times, to be exact), grinding the plot to a halt. And when he’s not behind bars? He’s blasting away like it’s the Wild West. Someone clearly forgot to tell him it’s the 20th century.  

The only person who can tolerate this walking disaster is a female cop assigned to guide him around Malta (who bears an uncanny resemblance to Elaine from *Seinfeld*). She must be out of her mind.  

The real stars of the show? The strippers in the bar. Their performances are a recurring highlight, and honestly, I grew weirdly attached to these gloriously tacky dancers. Anything was better than watching Geronimo bumble his way through another doomed escape.  

And the ending? Predictable, messy, and just as cringe-worthy as the rest of this mess.

It’s been ages since I last watched this comedy, and I’d completely forgotten just how absurdly bad it is. Without a doubt, this ranks among Elvis Presley’s absolute worst films—maybe even in the bottom two or three. Presley stars as Joe Whitecloud, a half-Native American bull rider who returns to his Arizona roots, only to find his family living in a ramshackle home where his friends seem to party nonstop.  

Burgess Meredith and Katy Jurado play his parents, while Thomas Gomez takes on the role of the elderly Native American grandfather. Sadly, none of them bring any real depth—or even humor—to the film. The plot revolves around a government investment in the family’s cattle, except they’re missing a crucial bull. Elvis gets to warble a handful of forgettable songs while fending off a lovesick young woman and her trigger-happy mother.  

The whole thing feels hastily thrown together, and the rundown setting practically reeks of barnyard filth, which does nothing to improve the experience. The only real mystery here? Elvis actually looks like he’s enjoying himself, which is baffling given how frustrated he reportedly was with churning out so many mediocre movies.

Don’t be misled by the star power of Burt Reynolds, James Woods, and Anne Archer—they’re essentially glorified extras, likely shooting their scenes in just a day or two. When you cast someone like James Woods, you should know how to use him effectively; failing to do so speaks to poor direction.  

While the plot itself wasn’t bad and most of the performances were solid, Cuba Gooding Jr.’s acting was painfully unconvincing—so much so that his dramatic moments bordered on laughable, which is a major flaw in a serious film. The action sequences were decent but lacked the intensity needed to truly captivate. Once again, stronger direction could have saved them.  

The pacing was another misstep. In a 90-minute action thriller, taking nearly half an hour to get the protagonist into the thick of things is far too slow. The lone bright spot was Angie Harmon, who gave it her all—shame the director didn’t support her performance. Overall, this movie had potential, but poor execution let it down at every turn.

When young Kevin inherits his late uncle’s boat as a gift, he invites five friends to join him on a weekend trip to Catalina Island. Along the way, they drink heavily, hook up, and share their deepest fears through party games. But the trip takes a dark turn when Kevin drowns in the open sea. After the boat’s engine dies, the group finds themselves stalked and killed by the very fears they confessed.  

Yesterday, my wife, kids, and three friends sat down to watch *Haunted Boat* on DVD. Within the first 30 minutes, we all agreed this amateurish mess wasn’t worth our time and switched to another film. Later, out of sheer curiosity, I endured the rest—only to regret not going to bed instead. The disjointed plot is matched by terrible cinematography and shaky camerawork, while the cast—clearly still in acting school—struggles to deliver even basic performances. The whole thing feels like a poorly executed student film. A laughably pretentious twist at the end only makes the entire experience feel like a waste of time.

The chilling tale of *Viy* by Nikolai Gogol has once again been adapted for the screen, this time reaching American audiences through Faith Films’ home video release.  

Gogol’s original story follows a priest forced to keep vigil over the corpse of a witch, his faith serving as his sole defense. This new version, however, takes liberties—relocating the narrative to America while unmistakably filming in Russia. The awkward mismatch of architecture, clothing, and decor clashes with the English signage, creating a jarring disconnect.  

The film struggles to find its footing, partly due to the unconvincing attempt at mimicking rural American backcountry—yet never quite pulling it off. Odd creative choices further muddy the experience, such as the protagonist abruptly shifting from reporter to priest with little explanation—a baffling decision even after viewing the DVD’s behind-the-scenes feature.  

Adding to the flaws is the appalling dubbing. Lines are awkwardly timed, often delivered when actors' lips aren’t visible—or worse, poorly synced when they are. Whether this stems from Faith Films’ post-production work or the original filmmakers’ rushed attempt to market it to Western audiences (as hinted in the making-of feature) remains unclear.  

All in all, it’s a strange, uneven film that never quite lives up to its haunting source material.

*Five Across the Eyes* follows five teenage girls driving home to make curfew when they make a quick stop at a store. In their haste, they accidentally hit another car and panic, choosing to flee the scene. Moments later, the other vehicle forces them off the road, and a deranged woman wielding a shotgun emerges. She terrorizes them—forcing them to strip, urinate on their clothes—before abruptly driving away. Though shaken, the girls believe the nightmare is over... until the woman returns, relentless in her pursuit to hunt them down as they struggle to escape, lost and running low on fuel.  

Produced and directed by Greg Swinson and Ryan Theissen (with Swinson handling the script and Theissen overseeing cinematography and editing), *Five Across the Eyes* stands as one of the worst films I’ve ever seen—possibly *the* worst. I’m hard-pressed to recall a movie more poorly executed. While some of the filmmaking choices may have been intentional attempts to create tension and atmosphere, the result is nothing short of disastrous.

At first glance, this documentary-fiction-animation hybrid is intriguing and thought-provoking. But when a film stimulates deeper thinking, it also invites closer examination. The truth is, this movie blends metaphysical ideas with suggestive hints and unfounded assumptions. The supposed connection between science and spirituality presented in "What the Bleep..." lacks any real scientific foundation.  

For instance, the film cites a study claiming group Transcendental Meditation reduced crime in Washington D.C. However, data shows the HRA (Homicides, Rapes, and Assaults) rate in 1993 was roughly 30% higher than the average from 1988 to 1992. The homicide rate didn’t drop at all during the study period. In fact, every attempt to tie metaphysical claims to science in this film has been thoroughly debunked.  

Based on these facts, the movie seems like either a weak attempt at persuasion or an elaborate joke. Either way, it's not worth your time.  

If you're interested in a more intellectually engaging science-themed film, try *Mindwalk* (1990) instead.

Though Louis B. Mayer was said to have little interest in casting the young Greta Garbo, her first American film with MGM remains strikingly beautiful. The production clearly benefited from extraordinary talent behind the camera—both in cinematography and matte paintings—giving it the refined, artistic quality expected of the studio’s finest work. Even after 84 years, its visual elegance endures.  

Garbo herself appears different here than in her later films. While still recognizable, her softer makeup lends her a gentler, less severe presence—a departure from the iconic look she would soon adopt. Part of me wishes they had kept this style, though there’s no arguing with the legendary status her trademark image would bring.  

The story centers on Garbo and her family, who are unjustly evicted from their land by a wealthy landlord. The landlady, the formidable Doña Bernarda, insists the bank demands payment—but the true motive lies in her son’s infatuation with Garbo. What better way to control the situation than by forcing her out?

Paul Verhoeven’s controversial masterpiece delves into a world of disturbing dreams, ominous visions, sacrilege, and homoerotic desire, centered around a genuine femme fatale who seduces and destroys her lovers. Drenched in blood and punctuated by moments of visceral horror, *The Fourth Man* is a psychological whirlwind. The sight of Renée brandishing her scissors will send shivers down any man’s spine—some may even jump in fright.

*Soldier Blue* aspires to grandeur—claiming to deliver a profound indictment of humanity’s cruelty, particularly the white man’s violence against Indigenous peoples, while doubling as a scathing allegory for Vietnam’s horrors. Yet it collapses under the weight of its own ambitions. Far from profound or unflinching, the film is a cheap, hypocritical, and ineptly crafted mess.  

One critic astutely observed that *Soldier Blue* feels like two entirely separate films crudely stitched together. At its core, it's a tired, cliché-ridden "odd couple" romance—Strauss and Bergen overcoming their differences in a painfully contrived love story—sandwiched between two gratuitously grotesque massacres that wouldn’t be out of place in a low-budget exploitation flick.  

The film’s climax is an unforgivable spectacle of sadistic excess, lingering on the graphic slaughter of Native American children—shot, hacked apart, and impaled in relentless detail—while women are violated and brutalized. There’s no artistic justification for this exploitative bloodbath, only the cynical calculation of shock value for profit. (Even the massacre itself, stripped of misguided intent, is executed with staggering incompetence.)

This has to be one of the dullest and most poorly performed portrayals of Adolf Hitler's early years I've ever seen. Robert Carlyle is a talented actor, but casting him as Hitler was a terrible misstep. Choosing Liev Schreiber to play Hitler's longtime friend and associate, Hanfstaengl, would likely have drawn outrage from the Simon Wiesenthal Center. A Jewish actor portraying a Nazi sympathizer? That's just awful casting. This is far from a compelling historical drama suitable for family viewing—instead, it’s Hollywood at its worst, exploiting the talent of a capable but underused supporting cast who have mostly faded from the spotlight in recent years.  

The exaggerated German accents ("vee vill vin zis var") are downright offensive to German audiences. My German mother was visibly irritated by the inconsistent accents, which awkwardly shifted between American, British, and German within the same sentence. The supporting actors were so wooden they might as well have been cardboard cutouts in a video store. The only redeeming performance came from Jenna Malone as Geli Raubal—she perfectly captured the character's innocence and inner turmoil.

This might just take the prize for the worst movie ever made. Without John Hurt, it might have scraped by as a forgettable kids' flick. But the real crime here is seeing Hurt—one of cinema’s finest talents—lower himself to this mess. I gave it two points purely for his presence, then deducted eight because he clearly didn’t escape soon enough. As for the rest of the cast? Simply atrocious. Janine Turner may be easy on the eyes, but her acting couldn’t rescue a sinking ship. The lead actor is, without exaggeration, painfully bad. Save yourself the agony—avoid this disaster at all costs. It’s so cringe-worthy, it physically stings.

Over the years, I’ve watched plenty of Steven Seagal’s straight-to-video films, and while they all deliver a consistent level of entertainment, that level is disappointingly low. Sure, the action scenes can be fun, but that’s about it. Seagal was at his best in movies like *Under Siege*, *Under Siege 2*, and *Executive Decision*—at least from an action perspective. Unfortunately, in the last decade, his films haven’t lived up to those past standards.  

On a brighter note, this movie managed its time well, with some decent action and a bit of wit sprinkled in. Just when the pacing started to drag, a solid fight scene would pull it back from the brink. I’ve always thought Seagal’s newer films would benefit from stronger supporting casts—big names that audiences recognize. A few familiar faces could go a long way in boosting their appeal.

I stumbled upon this fascinating documentary on More4, a UK TV channel, and found it deeply engaging and intellectually stimulating. It’s inspired me to seek out the book that served as its source material. The film presents Professor Jared Diamond’s compelling theory on why some societies thrived while others didn’t—a fresh perspective, at least for me.  

His argument revolves around the role of geography, domesticable crops, and animals in shaping civilizations—an idea I found persuasive. The documentary itself is well-crafted, with strong narration and a balanced use of recreated scenes, avoiding the excess that often plagues modern docs. Diamond’s approach is refreshingly accessible, free of the condescension that sometimes creeps into academic explanations for general audiences.  

Some have labeled his theory as Marxist, but I disagree; to me, it reads more as socio-geological analysis. It’s also a breath of fresh air to encounter a societal evolution theory that doesn’t hinge on religion. Highly recommended.

A few weeks ago, the German broadcaster "SAT1" promoted this film as the "TV-Event of the Year"—sorry, but I’ve seen much better on TV this year.  

I didn’t think much of the movie initially, but the trailer immediately reminded me of two other awful films: *Titanic* and *Pearl Harbor*. The composition looked painfully familiar—the so-called "heroine" (if you can even call her that) sandwiched between her two "lovers." Sound like *Pearl Harbor*? The romance here is a cheap imitation of that film’s already lackluster love triangle.  

Still, as someone who enjoys dissecting movies—even the bad ones—I decided to give this mess a chance. The story opens with a doctor abandoning his family to join the German military near the end of the Third Reich, vowing to his wife that he’ll return. Cut to spring 1948: Germany has lost the war, and the Allies and Soviets now occupy the country, locked in an ideological clash—capitalism versus communism—while battling for global dominance. If this sounds predictable, it’s because you’ve seen it all before.

**The Plot:** A powerful crime lord is uniting three rival mafias in a scheme to purchase an island, turning it into a money-laundering hub for organized crime. To stop this, the FBI targets one of the mafia bosses—but the operation goes awry, leading to a series of improbable twists. The result? Yet another "cop buddies who can't stand each other" film, pairing a female FBI agent with a male ex-DEA agent.  

So far, so predictable. But the movie’s appeal isn’t its flimsy plot, which feels like a weak punchline at best. Instead, it thrives on humor—sharp, absurd, and landing somewhere between satire and slapstick. (At least in the German dubbed version, the jokes really work.) The action doesn’t disappoint either, featuring a standout sequence with a shotgun and a rocket launcher.  

That said, this film gleefully tramples over political correctness. Recreational drug use isn’t just present—it’s glamorized, portrayed as edgy and cool. That aspect annoyed me, and while the film delivers plenty of laughs, its cavalier attitude makes it a poor choice for younger viewers.

This film stands out among the countless low-budget "Kung Fu" action movies produced in Asia during the late 1970s and early 1980s—complete with exaggerated sound effects, poorly dubbed dialogue, and rapid-fire fight sequences. What sets it apart is its surprisingly engaging storyline and generous doses of humor. The plot follows workers at a dye factory who are violently driven out by ruthless Manchu enforcers. Desperate for help, they hire a smooth-talking scammer (played by Gordon Liu) to intimidate their oppressors. When his bluff fails spectacularly, he tricks his way into a Shaolin temple, hoping to master authentic martial arts. However, the temple master has other plans—instead of formal training, he assigns him the backbreaking task of constructing scaffolding to cover the 36 chambers’ rooftops.  

Unbeknownst to the con artist, stacking and tying bamboo poles secretly hones the precise skills needed to become a Kung Fu master—a clever training method reminiscent of *The Karate Kid*’s iconic "wax on, wax off" lessons. The film blends lighthearted comedy from start to finish, culminating in a thrilling finale when Gordon Liu confronts his enemies with his hard-earned skills in an explosive showdown.

I absolutely love this movie—it’s fantastic. Of course, no film is without its flaws. If you’ve seen *Raise Your Voice* with Hilary Duff, you might notice some striking similarities. Take *Brave New Girl*—Holly dreams of attending Haverty Conservatory, just like Terri in *Raise Your Voice* aspires to a music school in L.A. (the exact name escapes me). Both characters are passionate about music and face a climactic performance at the end of the semester. It’s almost uncanny how closely these stories parallel each other. That said, I still prefer *Brave New Girl* over *Raise Your Voice*.

I recently rewatched *The Convent* and found it far less enjoyable than I remembered. Back when I first saw it, I thought it was a fun, gory pick for a rowdy Friday night—stylish, funny, and over-the-top. But this time, it just didn’t click. It feels like an attempt to recapture the campy charm of *Night of the Demons* for a modern crowd, but it misses what made those films work so well.  

Full disclosure—I’m not even a die-hard *Night of the Demons* fan, but it had its moments. *The Convent* leans into the cheese without delivering much else. Aside from Joanna Canton’s likable lead, the goth girl, and a fun Adrienne Barbeau cameo, the characters are aggressively obnoxious—brainless, offensive jock stereotypes dialed up to unbearable levels. What’s worse, there’s a baffling lack of gratuitous nudity, making it even harder to sit through the terrible dialogue.  

The evil nuns do stand out with their cool design, and they get plenty of screen time, but even their presence isn’t enough to rescue the film. The good ideas here are buried under a mountain of missed opportunities.

*"Transylvania 6-5000"* is a lightweight yet occasionally amusing and endearing mid-’80s horror spoof, featuring a cast of recognizable faces and a script with a few genuinely witty moments. The story follows two bumbling tabloid journalists reluctantly dispatched to Transylvania to investigate rumors of Frankenstein’s revival. The movie is sprinkled with quirky, charming details—like a miniature guillotine for slicing hard-boiled eggs and lab test tubes repurposed as cream-and-sugar dispensers at breakfast.  

Unfortunately, the film falls short of its potential, with drawn-out jokes and satirical setups that overstay their welcome. For a far more successful and entertaining take on the genre, *"Transylvania Twist"*—a Roger Corman production released four years later—comes highly recommended.  

The humor here primarily lampoons Universal’s classic 1930s horror films, so familiarity with those will help catch all the subtle gags and nods. There’s also a clever twist revealing that the Frankenstein character only *acts* like a deranged, maniacal scientist.

I’ve always been a huge Batman fan—from the animated series to *Batman Beyond*, even picking up the comics occasionally. Naturally, I was thrilled when this new series was announced… only to end up completely let down. This show falls flat in every way, failing to live up to the original. It feels like an extended toy ad—zero depth, zero substance. And the Joker? The greatest Batman villain ever? Gone. Just like that. Honestly, I wish I could say his awful design was the worst part, but no—there’s nothing here worth praising, nothing creative or engaging. Trust me, save your time and your money. Skip it.

This gripping retelling of Kansas' notorious 1959 killings—adapted from Capote's work—is shot in stark black and white by Brooks and cinematographer Hall, lending it a raw, documentary-like quality. Blake and Wilson deliver strong performances as the murderers, while Forsythe shines as the detective tracking them down. The tension builds masterfully in the scenes preceding the killings, filmed on location at the original crime scene and heightened by an eerie soundtrack of howling wind. Brooks directs with striking energy, employing inventive scene transitions. The film's only drawback is its excessive runtime, with a drawn-out, occasionally heavy-handed conclusion.

This mockumentary is a prime example of how absurd people can become when consumed by blind enthusiasm for a subject. Personally, I despise cryptozoology—it lacks scientific credibility and only serves to undermine genuine research. That said, the visual effects were impressive (the dragons looked stunning), though much of the so-called "information" presented was outright fabricated. What makes it truly disappointing is that these falsehoods were delivered by supposed scientists, which is why I’m giving it a 1/10 instead of a zero.  

Take the hydrogen theory, for instance: while chemistry confirms hydrogen is produced in the stomach, the quantities suggested here are impossible. If you're going to speculate about dragon biology, at least provide a plausible explanation. Hydrogen exists in many natural compounds, but nowhere in the amounts needed to make an animal fly—it doesn’t just materialize out of thin air.  

Even worse was the platinum theory. Platinum is rarer than gold, so the premise alone is laughably implausible. The lack of basic scientific reasoning throughout this mockumentary is astounding.

A touching and heartfelt film. John Thaw delivers yet another outstanding performance, as always—though sadly, he passed away not long ago. Despite his immense talent, he remained remarkably humble throughout his career, solidifying his place among England’s greatest actors, at least in my lifetime.  

Fans will forever cherish his iconic roles—his brilliant portrayal of Inspector Morse, the rugged Jack Regan in the ’70s hit *The Sweeney*, and his sharp-witted barrister in *Kavanagh QC*. This film is perfect for the whole family and makes a wonderful addition to any DVD collection. The cinematography beautifully captures wartime Britain, evoking nostalgia for those who lived through the era—especially London’s evacuated children fleeing the German bombings.  

The chemistry between the two leads, Tom and young William, is exceptionally moving and stays true to Michelle Magorian’s beloved novel. A truly unforgettable watch.

I had high hopes for this movie after hearing it praised as a solid action flick—unfortunately, it didn't deliver. The plot was overly complicated and hard to follow, and the action was disappointingly sparse until the final scenes. Even then, the dark cinematography made it difficult to see what was going on. Definitely not the thrilling experience I was expecting.

If you have even a passing interest in pirates, swashbuckling adventures, New Orleans' early 19th-century past, or Yul Brynner’s commanding presence, give this film a chance and judge it for yourself—don’t let mediocre reviews deter you. I found it thoroughly entertaining, boasting sharp performances (with a few exceptions), clever banter, and a captivating depiction of the notorious yet charismatic privateer Jean Lafitte. While not every detail aligns perfectly with history—name one period film that does—it brilliantly captures Lafitte’s complex influence on New Orleans and the city’s uneasy bond with its most infamous yet beloved rogue. Instead of focusing on its flaws, appreciate what it achieves: a compelling portrait of one of New Orleans’—and America’s—most fascinating legends.

Seriously, just check the title—it says it all! Haha! I caught this gem years ago on Saturday Late Night Creature Features. This is peak cheesy monster movie goodness, complete with gloriously awful acting and a pair of dimwitted hillbillies who crank up the schlock to maximum. Those redneck boat rental guys? They steal the show! Wait till you see the boat scene where the English couple gushes about the stars... in broad daylight. Pure gold! It’s obvious they didn’t bother with logic—they just raced through filming. If you’re into 70s B-movie madness, you’ll adore this one!

I was a bit hesitant about watching this when it first aired on CBS. Like so many others, I was in NYC that day—attending Hunter College at the time. The thought of reliving the devastation and horror was overwhelming, but curiosity got the better of me. Watching this documentary brought tears to my eyes, reigniting memories I’ll never forget. The raw, powerful footage was almost too much to believe.  

I bought the DVD on the first anniversary and have revisited it several times since. The sheer bravery of those who captured these moments is astounding. If you haven’t seen it yet, I urge you to take the time—though heartbreaking, it stands as a profound testament to one of this nation’s most tragic days.

I must be missing something, since *The Man Who Cheated Himself* seems to get more praise than criticism—but I just don’t see it. A good noir, in my book, needs style, with characters who have the sharp wit and charisma of Humphrey Bogart in *The Big Sleep* or Gene Tierney in *Laura*. This film’s cast falls painfully short. Lee J. Cobb, as the lead, looks more like he just stumbled out of bed than the suave, sharp-talking detective you’d expect. And Jane Wyatt as the femme fatale? One of the worst casting choices I’ve seen in ages—she lacks the magnetic allure the role demands.  

The plot doesn’t help either. It’s predictable, offering nothing fresh or surprising for noir fans. I guessed where it was headed almost immediately. Even the climactic chase scene drags on endlessly, killing whatever tension the movie had managed to build. Ten to fifteen minutes of tedious cat-and-mouse is just too much. Disappointing all around.

Comedies are frequently dismissed as shallow, but *Arms and the Man* shatters that misconception. Shaw’s brilliant play masterfully blends humor with profound philosophical insight, offering both entertainment and intellectual substance.  

At its surface, the play works as a clever and unconventional romantic comedy. Raina, a melodramatic young woman from a proud military family, finds her world upended when an enemy soldier bursts into her room one night. She hides him, knowing her family must never discover the secret—only for him to return after the war, unraveling illusions and forcing everyone to confront their beliefs.  

Yet beneath the entertaining premise, Shaw weaves sharp commentary on war, class, and the illusions of love, all delivered with his signature wit. The play’s depth is so rich that it rewards—and even demands—repeated exploration to fully appreciate its layers of meaning.

The opening scene depicts the Legion arriving in Paris on November 13, 1918. The troops disembark from the train—wearing the same uniforms the French Army, including the Legion, wore when they marched to war in 1914. This glaring error is a clear sign the war film you’re about to watch will be a disaster. (By 1915, the French Army had already recognized the impracticality of fighting in red trousers and dark blue overcoats. Metropolitan troops switched to "horizon blue," while colonial forces adopted khaki.) At least the Claude Van Damme remake got the uniforms mostly correct. It’s frustrating when filmmakers overlook such obvious details after putting so much effort into getting other aspects right.

This mini-series delivers more fun than many higher-budget, more ambitious productions. Falling somewhere between the charm of *Kung-Fu* and the whimsy of *H.R. Pufnstuf*, SOTD strikes an entertaining balance. While its nearly three-hour runtime might test younger attention spans, its mix of adventure, action, and cliffhangers—without overdoing romance or "gross" elements—makes it ideal for kids. Young viewers tend to overlook rubbery props, campy performances, and even reused scenes (a nostalgic nod to classic serials). They're also more forgiving of American accents from Asian actors—or non-Asian actors in key roles.  

Originally a three-star rating felt fair, but credit is due for the team’s dedication in finishing the project. It may not be high art, but like a solid DIY job, it took persistence and effort to complete.  

In the end? Not essential viewing, but passable.

**Georgia Rule** has to be one of the worst films I’ve ever endured—if not *the* worst. From start to finish, it carries an unsettling, surreal tone that left me audibly gasping “What?” at least seven to ten times during its agonizing two-hour runtime.  

The trailer painted it as a clichéd, lighthearted chick-flick about three generations of women—Jane Fonda as the stern matriarch, Felicity Huffman as her troubled daughter, and Lindsay Lohan as the rebellious, scantily clad granddaughter. On paper, it promised a familiar tale of family bonding and personal growth.  

But oh, what a false advertisement this turned out to be.  

Between bizarre shots of animals doing "funny" things in the background of supposedly serious moments and a painfully awkward five-minute sequence featuring an elderly woman getting her diaper changed at a doctor’s office, the film somehow also manages to revolve around Lindsay Lohan’s character dealing with sexual abuse at the hands of her stepfather.  

The result? A tone-deaf, poorly acted misfire that mashes together inappropriate comedy with deeply serious themes in the most jarring, absurd way possible. If Garry Marshall intended for this movie to be...

I champion films that explore underrepresented themes in global cinema. When I first saw the trailer for *Water Lilies*, I anticipated loving it, believing I'd discovered something rare—a candid portrayal of teenage lesbian romance, like a feminine counterpart to *Beautiful Thing*.  

The protagonists are three 15-year-old French girls: Marie, slender and quiet with a tomboyish charm; Floriane, confident, athletic, and strikingly beautiful; and Anne, loyal, heavyset, and emotionally immature. The simmering tension between Marie and Floriane pulses throughout the film, whether overt or lingering just beneath the surface.  

Yet *Water Lilies* isn't a story about youthful queer awakening—it's a raw depiction of sexual frustration, angst, adolescent misdirection, and, in at least two painfully detached scenes, joyless physical encounters. It also serves as a cautionary tale on how over-manipulative storytelling can undermine a film’s authenticity.  

In a behind-the-scenes feature on the *Lord of the Flies* DVD, director Peter Brook observes, "French cynicism begins with the stirrings of desire," suggesting that while French culture idealizes childhood innocence, it views adolescence through a lens of disillusionment.

This film avoids the "video nasty" label simply by virtue of its 1994 release date, when Britain had likely moved on from the controversy. It largely recycles *The Boogeyman*'s premise—roughly 75% repetition—and likely would have faced the same ban for identical, albeit unclear, reasons.  

At first, I wondered if Annie (Kelly Galindo) might be another Lacey, but she’s actually a different woman plagued by psychic visions of a boogeyman eerily similar to the original. Fans will quickly spot that they’re not the same character.  

After witnessing a murder in a bathroom—and conveniently seeing the address—Annie teams up with her psychiatrist and a paranormal student who looks straight off a discount romance novel or butter ad. Predictably, they arrive at the same bathroom, and exactly 24 hours later, a murder unfolds just as she foresaw. Who the doomed woman is or why she’s targeted remains a mystery.  

From there, the film essentially replays *The Boogeyman* with added scenes—most notably revealing the boogeyman directly, unlike the original. Unfortunately…

Whatever you think of Andy Milligan—if his family was even half as twisted as the ones in this movie, he might have turned out far worse. Sadly, the available print includes inserted sex scenes originally filmed by the distributor to attract more viewers. Throughout the film, Milligan’s grimy cinematography and old-school silent film score suddenly vanish, replaced by attractive stand-ins for his unattractive cast grinding away to psychedelic '60s rock. These scenes are easy to skip if you’re focused on Milligan’s original vision—though much of the actual plot was trimmed to accommodate the added smut. Even with the cuts, what remains is gripping. I’ve yet to see a more despicable on-screen mother.

Most reality shows drive me crazy, but this one takes the cake—even worse than the Paris Hilton train wreck. Of course, it’s his production, but how many seasons are we going to hear "You're fired" or "You're hired"? After watching, I’d never want to work for someone with that kind of ego. Honestly, watching paint dry would be more entertaining.  

Wouldn’t it be great if just one contestant stood up and said, "Donald, I quit—keep your job, but take some of that cash and fix your hair"? And now he’s trying to buy his way into WWE fame? Pathetic. I wouldn’t mind seeing him take a real hit just so we don’t have to look at that face anymore. It’s downright sad—no talent, just desperate attempts to stay relevant. I’d give this show a zero if I could, but since that’s not an option, it gets a 1—and that’s being generous.

I believe it's a wonderful film—deeply Romanian in its scenery and atmosphere. The sensuality feels organic rather than deliberate, emerging naturally from the story. There’s an authenticity to it, both humane and unforced. While not a flashy blockbuster with A-list stars, the acting remains genuine—ordinary people who simply know how to embody their roles well. The film achieves what it sets out to do, stirring emotions, even rekindling old ones. Objectivity aside, one thing is certain—I truly loved it.

Although bearing an English title suggesting demonic themes, this film actually focuses on a power-obsessed ruler pursuing the Philosopher's Stone and the alchemical transformation of lead into gold – requiring virgin's blood. Jacinto Molina portrays Gilles de Lancre, a character who ruthlessly executes those he perceives as threats or who can supply his gruesome alchemical needs. Driven by his lover and a hired alchemist, his downfall stems from greed and madness rather than supernatural possession (a missed opportunity).  

The movie offers scattered moments of excitement, including jousting scenes and brutal staff combat, and benefits from decent production values. However, it lacks the expected elements of horror—minimal gore, zero suspense—and, unusually for a Molina/Naschy project, no unintentional comedy. Verdict: 4/10.

*The Flock* didn’t initially grab my interest. Though Andrew Lau co-directed the acclaimed *Infernal Affairs* trilogy, he was replaced by emergency director Niels Mueller during production. My guess is Lau’s cut didn’t align with the studio’s vision, prompting the switch—a risky move that rarely works (remember *The Invasion?*). Surprisingly, *The Flock* turned out better than expected.  

While far from a masterpiece, it’s a solid, engaging thriller. The characters are well-developed, and the dynamic between Richard Gere and Claire Danes feels organic, bolstered by their strong performances.  

That said, the film isn’t without flaws. The overuse of flashy editing gimmicks to inject "style" often feels forced and distracting. A more ambitious approach might have elevated it further. Still, *The Flock* delivers decent entertainment—forgettable, but worth a watch for thriller fans.

While *Wargames: The Dead Code* isn’t the worst film I’ve ever watched—thanks to a handful of passable scenes—it’s easily the most predictable. From start to finish, every plot twist telegraphed itself well before it happened, stripping away any sense of surprise. The movie lacked even the slightest hint of subtlety, with no cleverness behind its execution. Every line of dialogue or text felt painfully obvious, making it impossible to lose yourself in the story.  

More often than not, I caught myself laughing at the absurdly clumsy storytelling and the desperate attempts to salvage viewer engagement—not exactly the reaction the filmmakers were going for.

Contrary to popular belief, the women portrayed in this film are not geisha but oiran—courtesans who worked beyond the famed pleasure quarters. Their stories reflect the lived experiences of countless women during the Tokugawa period. While the narrative may not be groundbreaking, its strength lies in its relatable, everyday themes: love, friendship, and the sacrifices women made.  

What truly stood out was the exquisite art direction and the captivating performances, particularly by the four actresses embodying the oiran. The film offers a vivid, immersive window into a bygone era. I’d recommend it to anyone with an interest in Japanese cultural history or those who appreciate subtle, emotionally rich storytelling—it excels on both counts.

When it comes to horror films, I'm usually happy to overlook shaky logic, low-budget effects, and narrative gaps if the movie delivers genuine chills. Unfortunately, this one fails on every level—not even achieving so-bad-it's-good status. The dialogue is painfully wooden, the performances are awkward, and the direction is utterly lacking. The kills are telegraphed miles in advance and clumsily executed, the score grates on the nerves, the cinematography is amateurish, and even the wardrobe choices feel wrong. I almost pitied the cast, who looked like they were giving their all despite the clunky, forced script and apparent lack of guidance—they probably didn’t even get a proper rehearsal. Watching this is both cringe-inducing and mind-numbingly dull, requiring serious stamina just to reach its laughably staged "twist" ending. Easily one of the worst films I've ever endured.  

I rarely bother with reviews, but this train wreck demanded a warning. Save yourself the time—it's utterly pointless. And if you *do* subject yourself to it, don’t skip the behind-the-scenes featurette. The writer-director seems bizarrely proud of making the killer female, as if that's some groundbreaking twist (spoiler: it isn’t). Watching him and the cast...

Does anyone know where this movie was filmed? The cliffside flying sequence is stunning—it looks like England. Yet Ivy’s apartment building strongly resembles the Brill Building, complete with those charming vintage elevators.  

Charles Mendl is credited as "Sir Charles Gage," but did he actually appear? I might have missed him—was he the husband’s lawyer? That character is only mentioned in a phone call and doesn’t seem to have any screen time. Could he have been in the aviation or ballroom scene? Did anyone catch a glimpse of him?  

By the way, Herbert Marshall was 57 when he filmed this.

The highlight of *An American in Paris* is undoubtedly the extended ballet finale, where Gene Kelly and Leslie Caron embody the essence of iconic painters. Earlier in the film, Kelly’s character is introduced as a street artist in Paris, making this visually stunning sequence the perfect culmination of a vibrant musical brimming with energy, Gershwin’s unforgettable melodies, and standout performances from Georges Guétary and Oscar Levant.  

Kelly shines brightest here—distinct from *Singin’ in the Rain*—and the sheer spectacle of the entire film, crowned by this breathtaking ballet, delivers an undeniable "wow" moment. It’s no surprise that this sequence was chosen to close *That’s Entertainment!* after showcasing the finest of MGM’s musical gems.

*A Thief in the Night* was largely overlooked by mainstream audiences, dismissed for its visibly low production value and its focus on the Rapture and the aftermath for those left behind. Yet its compelling narrative captivated viewers, prompting deep reflection on their faith in Jesus Christ. The film resonated widely—even depicting a pastor who preached the Gospel without truly believing, realizing too late why he wasn’t taken. Together with its sequel, *Distant Thunder*, this movie remains essential viewing. Despite newer adaptations like the *Left Behind* series with bigger budgets retelling the same story, *A Thief in the Night* remains unmatched in its raw impact—pioneering the genre and leaving an indelible legacy.

In a word, this film is utterly without merit.  

The premise—imagining how someone from the early 1900s might envision the future—holds potential. Unfortunately, the weak plot and forgettable characters make it impossible to invest in the idea, leaving the entire concept to collapse under its own weight.  

Reportedly, the entire production relied on green-screen performances, as if that alone should be impressive. But as someone familiar with visual effects, the excessive softening only highlights the struggles of masking green-screen imperfections. The washed-out color palette serves no artistic purpose—it simply diminishes the film’s visual appeal. Far from groundbreaking, the outdated, clunky graphics set a new low, failing to meet even the standards of decades-old effects like *Jurassic Park*. The robot designs were bland and uninspired, while the random prehistoric creatures scattered across the island went entirely unexplained.  

The plot, if you can call it that, is laughably terrible—so much so that I can’t even—

A 1957 J. Arthur Rank production—yes, you read that right—starring James Robertson Justice, Margaret Rutherford, and Wilfred Hyde White. Sounds like a guaranteed comedy hit? Think again. This painfully unfunny film relies on a single tired gag: people recoiling at the sight of a small alligator. The music is awkwardly shoehorned in, utterly forgettable and out of place. Jeannie Carson shines as a spirited dancer and decent singer, but her talents feel wasted here. Then there’s Diana Dors, whose role seems designed solely for scandalous preview clips—her acting isn't terrible, but the film reduces her to mere eye candy.  

Currently hawked on VHS by opportunistic eBay sellers, this cinematic disaster isn't worth your money—or your time. It’s a comedy that fails to amuse and a musical devoid of catchy tunes or dazzling choreography. Skip it.

I’ve adored every bit of Cream’s music, even though their catalog is small and treasured. Even their extended jams—like "Spoonful" and "Toad" from *Wheels of Fire*, stretching over twenty minutes—still outperform most rock acts today. Their unparalleled chemistry onstage made their Royal Albert Hall reunion one of the most highly anticipated in rock history. Sure, time has passed for both the band and their fans, but the raw energy remains, whether in their electrifying blues covers or their original hits. Tracks like "White Room," "Badge," "Politician," "Spoonful," and "Sunshine of Your Love" sound just as powerful as ever, flawlessly executed. Clapton's solos feel more focused here than with his solo band, Ginger Baker is—well, Ginger Baker, and Jack Bruce’s vocals still carry a punch Clapton could never match alone. Long story short, if you missed these shows, you missed some of the best performances of the year (though some might argue otherwise).

**"The Barbarians" might not be the greatest film any of us has seen, but seriously? It’s absolutely hilarious—I can’t even describe how hard I laughed the first time I watched it. The director clearly aimed for a serious adventure movie, but it’s so hilariously bad... so bad that it’s become one of the funniest films I’ve ever seen. My advice? Watch it. And if you’ve already seen it, watch it again!**

Before discovering this miniseries, I knew nothing about *Jane Eyre*. Having read and watched numerous classics, I held the assumption that most were dull, overwritten, and overrated—stories with only mildly engaging plots at best. This adaptation shattered all my preconceptions.  

Zelah Clarke delivers a brilliant performance as Jane Eyre, capturing the governess’s quiet yet resolute spirit flawlessly. Her accent is charming, and her demeanor perfectly embodies the character. Timothy Dalton is extraordinary as Rochester, bringing such fierce passion and intensity to the role that it’s impossible to imagine anyone else as Thornfield Hall’s enigmatic master. The miniseries left such an impression that I lay awake all night after watching it—haunted yet inspired by its gripping narrative. The acting is superb, the storytelling unforgettable. Without question, this is the finest *Jane Eyre* adaptation ever made.  

After reading the novel, I was struck by how faithfully the miniseries mirrors Charlotte Brontë’s work. *Jane Eyre* has since become my favorite book and film. If you seek a masterpiece that will stay with you long after, look no further than the 1983 BBC adaptation.
