This feels like the type of movie that, if released today, would likely feature Sandra Bullock and Hugh Grant—in fact, I wouldn’t be surprised if a remake surfaces someday. While enjoyable, it lacks any real depth. The casting of James Stewart is nearly disastrous—he’s about two decades too old for the role—killing any potential chemistry with the stunning Kim Novak. The only spark of wit in the entire film comes from Ernie Kovacs in his brief supporting role as an aspiring writer. (**1/2)

The documentary offers a fresh perspective on the "Guns, Germs, and Steel" theory. It vividly illustrates key moments that reinforce its arguments while addressing typical objections.  

I was surprised to see some viewers criticize the series for covering familiar material, claiming it merely repeats middle school lessons. Yet that’s exactly what makes it compelling—the documentary transforms well-known facts into a thought-provoking analysis.  

If you’re curious about *how* and *why* things function—if you’ve ever dismantled a gadget to understand its mechanics or visited a farm to see milking in action—you’ll appreciate this series. Highly recommended.

Stacy Peralta delivers another breathtaking documentary, this time diving into the captivating world of big-wave surfing in America. Blending rare archival footage with firsthand accounts from surfing legends, the film immerses us in the fearless, adventurous lives of the sport’s early trailblazers—men whose raw passion laid the foundation for an industry that now inspires millions.  

What makes this documentary truly special is the personal connection to its subjects. Peralta’s deep admiration for these pioneers shines through as they share their stories. We listen in awe as Greg Noll describes walking past stunned onlookers to take on monstrous 50-foot waves off Hawaii’s North Shore. Or Jeff Clark recounting his solitary 15-year reign at Mavericks, California’s most treacherous break, long before it became a surfers’ mecca. Then there’s the legendary rise of Laird Hamilton, whom even Noll—speaking with quiet reverence—calls the greatest surfer of all time.  

(A brief aside: Noll, Clark, and other icons attended the Sundance screenings. Noll, downplaying his legacy, called himself an “old, over-the-hill surfer”—but the emotion in his voice was unmistakable.)

"People I Know" has just one redeeming quality: it’s a textbook example of the kind of film Al Pacino should steer clear of. Right from the start, his attempt at a Georgia accent falls flat—sometimes barely there, other times exaggerated to the point of absurdity. The dialogue is clunky, character interactions feel forced, and the plot lacks any real depth. Even the supporting cast phones it in, failing to inject energy into a story that drags endlessly without ever gaining momentum. The whole thing is a slog; I had to fight to stay awake.  

Steer clear—this movie is guaranteed to put you to sleep.

Skip this film—it was clearly designed to fail. Ram Gopal Varma initially planned it as a remake of the Bollywood classic *Sholay*, but after disputes with the original creators, he proceeded anyway and stripped away everything that could have made it worthwhile: acting, script, music, comedy, action—you name it. It’s as if he pushed forward just because the crew was already hired. A total waste of time and money.  

Coming from the director of *Rangeela*, *Satya*, and *Company*, this feels like a baffling misstep—what was he thinking? The plot, though confusing, vaguely resembles *Sholay’s* framework. Ajay Devgan plays Heero (a take on *Sholay’s* Veeru), while newcomer Ajay steps into the role of, well, Ajay (modeled after Jay). The two, supposedly "bad yet funny" outlaws, start by assisting a cop in catching a criminal before the now-retired officer later hires them for protection against the notorious villain Bubban (Amitabh Bachchan).  

And in case you’re new to Bollywood—yes, the good guys prevail. There, I just spared you three painful hours of your life.

American playwright Howard W. Campbell, Jr. (brought to life with a faded, weary charm by Nick Nolte) enjoys a peaceful existence in Germany with his actress wife, Helga Noth (Sheryl Lee) on the eve of World War II. At the height of his career, Howard is recruited by an American operative (John Goodman) to spy for the Allies. Though aware of the dangers, he finds the opportunity impossible to refuse, risking everything for the cause. After the war and the loss of his wife, Campbell retreats into isolation in New York City, his fragile state of mind sinking deeper into confusion.  

Both the film and Kurt Vonnegut’s original novel grapple with a central, divisive question: Is Campbell a hero or a traitor? Director Keith Gordon and screenwriter Robert B. Weide provide hints but no clear resolution, and this uncertainty—the refusal to give a definitive answer—keeps *Mother Night* compelling from start to finish. Nolte’s performance shifts strikingly: early on, Campbell appears sharp and self-assured, but by the end, he is either terrified and lost or terrified and utterly convinced of the weight of his wartime actions—and what they mean for his place in history.

In the 1970s, WPIX aired *The Adventures of Superman* every weekday afternoon for years. Occasionally, they’d interrupt the usual lineup to show *Superman and the Mole Men*, which always felt like a special treat. But rewatching it now, I was struck by how surprisingly bad it actually was.  

The flaws weren’t just the outdated effects—though they *were* rough. George Reeves’ Superman suit had obvious foam padding, and the Mole Men costumes were laughably unconvincing, with visible zippers, frayed seams, and poorly fitted fabric that even a child could see through. But those were forgivable.  

The real problem was the forced storytelling. Superman repeatedly let situations spiral out of control. A lynch mob hunting the creatures? Instead of stopping the mob or tracking the Mole Men himself, he just stood there lecturing Lois about the risks.

A toxic chemical leak transforms citizens into ravenous zombies, leaving two doctors to fight for survival. As an Andreas Schnaas production, expectations are set—subpar acting, laughably cheap effects, and a shoestring budget. The dubbing is so over-the-top it borders on parody, and honestly, it’s tragic that I’m even writing this much about such trash. My initial one-word review—*Crap*—wasn’t enough, so here we are. Honestly, I’m not sure this movie deserves any more words, but rules are rules. Bottom line? Avoid at all costs.  

**My Grade: F**

This film is a comedic reimagining of the 1978 classic *Heaven Can Wait* starring Warren Beatty, tailored to Chris Rock’s signature stand-up style. The core premise stays intact—Lance Barton (played by Rock) is prematurely taken from life and strikes a deal with Mr. King, God’s representative, to return to Earth in another’s body. Mirroring the original, he inhabits the wealthy and recently murdered Charles Wellington, primarily because he’s smitten with Sontee Jenkins (Regina King), who arrives at Wellington’s home during the crime.  

Unfortunately, this remake stumbles in its execution. The roles of Mrs. Wellington and her lover fall flat, and the comedic shift from an elderly white tycoon to a Black stand-up comic trying to win Sontee’s heart feels forced. The jarring cutaways between Rock as Wellington and the actual white Wellington add to the film’s misfires. While Beatty’s original didn’t flawlessly explore the afterlife concept, *Down to Earth* misses the chance to refine it, delivering little of the wit or charm needed to make the premise work.

"Jane Eyre" is a book I deeply admire, and I’ve explored numerous adaptations over the years. Each has its own merits and flaws, but this particular version stands among the weakest I’ve encountered. Neither Jane nor Mr. Rochester captured my sympathy. Charlotte Gainsbourg, while fitting the plain appearance of Jane, delivered her lines with such detachment that I struggled to understand Mr. Rochester’s attraction to her.  

Speaking of Mr. Rochester, William Hurt’s performance was even more emotionless—if that were possible. The idea of these two lifeless characters falling in love was baffling, and the lack of chemistry made the story feel dull and uninspired. One might wonder if the director, Zeffirelli, was half-asleep during filming.  

For a more faithful adaptation, the Timothy Dalton version is superior (though he’s arguably too handsome for the role). Meanwhile, Ciaran Hinds’ portrayal in the 1997 A&E rendition remains the ideal Mr. Rochester, even if that adaptation strays from the novel.  

If I had to praise one aspect of this film, it would be Geraldine Chaplin—she was flawless in her role.

What a complete waste of time. Even with Rotten Tomatoes praising it, don't believe the hype—this movie fails on every level. Not scary, not funny, and definitely not smart. It couldn't hold my interest for more than a few minutes. The CGI monster had some novelty at first, but the effect wore off fast. The dialogue sounded like a bad translation, and the American characters were painfully dumb, lacking any depth or common sense. To meet the word count, let me add that even the video store clerk would’ve questioned my taste for renting this disaster. Two hours of my life I’ll never get back.

Impressed by Sandra Bullock's charm in *Miss Congeniality*, I decided to try *Murder By Numbers*—but her "serious" roles (*Hope Floats*, *Speed 2*, *28 Days*) often fall flat. Here, her character feels uneven—omniscient yet baffling, with an awkwardly forced backstory that adds little depth. The two teenage killers deliver passable performances, though their supposedly brilliant forensics skills clash with glaringly obvious mistakes that practically announce their guilt. Chris Penn is underused as the obligatory red herring, and Ben Chaplin's role as the requisite partner/love interest feels obligatory.  

***Spoilers Ahead*** Beyond the uneven acting, the real issues lie in the flimsy, TV-movie plot. The killers' motivations never fully convince, and their blunders (vomiting rare food at the crime scene, clumsily framing the janitor, openly associating in public, a contrived romantic subplot) quickly shift the tone from intriguing to tedious.

The absurd noise you might notice while enduring this atrocious take on Jules Verne’s *Journey to the Center of the Earth* is the sound of Verne himself rolling in his grave. Aside from the borrowed title, nothing in this 80-minute disaster bears any resemblance to the original story. Instead, it offers a dull, entirely new plotline that isn’t worth your time.  

In fact, the director himself admitted on IMDb that he only shot eight minutes of footage for this "adaptation." To salvage the project, the studio clumsily stitched on segments from Albert Pyun’s *Dollman*, a sequel to his earlier *Alien from L.A.* starring Kathy Ireland. Apparently, the producers blew their budget and, desperate to fulfill international contracts, cobbled together Pyun’s work with Rusty Lemorande’s meager contribution. Avoid this train wreck at all costs—save your money and skip it entirely.  

Unlike Henry Levin’s 1959 classic starring James Mason and Pat Boone—which embraced its era with charm—Lemorande’s version awkwardly thrusts the story into modern-day Hawaii. Through sheer coincidence, two men, a British nanny, and a dog stumble into what’s supposed to be the adventure of a lifetime. Spoiler alert: it’s not.

I'm really enjoying this cartoon so far. While the animation quality isn't top-tier, I actually prefer this quick, stylized approach over the rushed versions of the old visual style we'd been seeing more frequently—that classic look only works well with careful attention to detail. The sharp angles and simple dot eyes work perfectly fine—in fact, I find them charming. As a kid, I never considered Scooby-Doo's design particularly cute, but now I think I might appreciate it more.  

Shaggy has always been my favorite, and oddly enough, I think he has the most room for meaningful character development. Sure, the show strays from the usual mystery-solving format, but honestly, that premise had gotten stale. Don’t get me wrong—with the right writers, the old case-solving structure could be revitalized (since recent attempts have fallen flat). But for now, this fresh take is a welcome change. Shaggy and Scooby...

I rarely bother reviewing films, but this one was so agonizingly bad I had to speak up. Every predictable plot twist made me wince, the wooden acting was laughable, and supposedly intense scenes had the audience chatting through them. Molly Ringwald's performance was the lone bright spot in this train wreck of a production. Even the big finale "reveal" fell completely flat. Some claim this movie doesn't take itself seriously—if only that were true.  

Save yourself the headache: *Cut* belongs in the trash, not your watchlist. Spend your time and money elsewhere!

I’ve adored *Goodnight Mister Tom* for years, so I was eager to finally see this adaptation. With so much praise surrounding it, my expectations were high—but by the end, I was utterly disappointed.  

This film fails in nearly every way. It’s a shockingly poor adaptation, leaving out roughly half the book's content. Key characters and memorable scenes were missing entirely, and the script felt rushed, with sparse dialogue and an unnatural pace. Worst of all, the deep emotional bond between William Beech and Tom—the heart of the story—was barely shown. The casting choices didn’t help either.  

What could have been something special ended up a hollow, inferior version of the book. It's one of the most disappointing adaptations I’ve seen—ripe for a proper remake that actually does justice to the original. This deserves to be forgotten and replaced.

Chess films have been rare in recent years, but this one transcends the genre—it's a poignant exploration of the human desire for love and validation. John Turturro delivers a captivating performance as a psychologically complex man whose entire world revolves around 64 squares and 32 pieces. For him, chess isn’t just a game—it’s the sole source of meaning in his life. Each loss strips away his fragile sense of self-worth, and Turturro portrays this inner turmoil with striking nuance. Not even the love of a woman could pull him from his bleak existence.  

The film leaves you questioning how many real-life Luzhins are out there, consumed by their obsession with the game—and surely, they exist. For chess enthusiasts, this is a thoughtful watch, crafted with intelligence and precision. It fulfills its purpose masterfully, though a sequel seems unlikely.

Like many others, this film has stayed with me for 30 years. I remember scouring the library for any information about it and even reaching out to a PBS station for details. Yet, all I uncovered was that it originated from an early 1900s newspaper story.  

By 2002, after years of searching eBay weekly, I finally spotted a VHS copy. Competing against one other bidder, I was determined to win—and I did. The runner-up later asked me for a copy, which I gladly shared. Even after securing the tape, my search continued until I discovered a site offering the movie on DVD: [http://www.johntopping.com/Harvey%20Perr/War%20Widow/war_widow.html](http://www.johntopping.com/Harvey%20Perr/War%20Widow/war_widow.html).

Every encounter leaves its mark, subtly shaping our thoughts and altering our paths—a fragment of each person we meet stays with us. *The Eighth Day* explores this idea (reminiscent of *Rainmaker*), following Harry (Daniel Auteuil), a businessman skilled in sales psychology, as he crosses paths with Georges (Pascal Duquenne), a runaway child with Down’s syndrome. The film’s heart lies in the powerful performances of its leads.  

The opening sequence is striking, with Georges sharing his whimsical take on the world’s creation, while the closing scene reveals what God made on the eighth day. Some moments test Harry’s patience—like when Georges, utterly unfiltered, insists on buying expensive shoes despite lacking the money. It’s the kind of bittersweet moment that makes you smile through the ache.  

One standout scene follows a group with Down’s syndrome as they ditch an art gallery trip, hijack a bus, and crash a theme park. But the most laugh-out-loud embarrassment comes when Harry and Georges pass a horse trailer on the highway—Georges twists back and greets the driver with an irreverent gesture. Amid the chaos, the film also offers tender, quiet moments that linger.

This film easily earns 5 stars for its outstanding performances—though my personal taste might skew my view, objectively speaking, the actors absolutely deserve this high praise. That said, I’m wary of productions like these, where stellar performances sometimes feel exploited to artificially boost ratings.  

My real issue lies with the film’s underlying agenda. Much like *Untraceable*, this feels like yet another piece of systematic propaganda, subtly endorsing government overreach into personal freedoms. It’s no coincidence that this releases amidst ongoing battles against internet censorship, with Americans and Canadians actively resisting ISP attempts to manipulate—or outright censor—information.  

This time, however, the angle shifts. Instead of demonizing torrent files (a tactic designed to instill guilt over digital sharing), the film seems hellbent on fostering collective sexual frustration. Fear-mongering appears to be Hollywood’s default strategy lately, particularly in thrillers—the most consumed genre of the past two decades. By dominating viewership, these films become powerful tools for mass influence. And the sheer brutality depicted here? It’s excessive, to say the least.

Anyone who rated this below a 5 clearly doesn’t appreciate sharp, playful humor. Keaton delivers yet another outstanding performance—something fans have come to expect from him. This isn’t some over-the-top spectacle; it’s clever, exaggerated comedy brought to life by some of Hollywood’s most talented (and adaptable) actors. Piscopo was equally perfect as the overeager underdog in his prime.  

For the most hilariously restrained swearing you’ll ever see, don’t miss Dimitri’s unforgettable turn as Morone.  

My rating? A solid 7.

I went into this movie at the Toronto Film Festival with reasonably high expectations. Boasting a strong cast and the festival’s closing slot, I figured it had to be good—how mistaken I was.  

The first red flag came when the director, before the screening, reminisced about meeting a then-unknown Kevin Spacey while directing an episode of *Wiseguy* (a *Wiseguy* director/writer making his feature debut? Not promising...). Whatever dirt the *Edison* director has on Spacey—maybe evidence of him offing a homeless guy?—it’s the only explanation I can think of for why he, or any of the other actors, signed onto this catastrophe.  

This film is shockingly awful, stitching together every tired cop drama cliché imaginable. There’s zero originality in *Edison*, and the acting is outdone only by the dismal direction—it literally looks like an old *Wiseguy* episode. Hands down, this is the most overqualified straight-to-DVD flick I’ve ever witnessed.  

A few choice absurdities from *Edison*: Morgan Freeman randomly dancing around his apartment to rock music for no reason, or Justin Timberlake’s… let’s call it *creative* performance. Just baffling.

Aside from a fleeting 10-minute moment of brilliance with H.B. Warner on the heavenly train, the remaining 94 minutes were an absolute train wreck of cinematic disaster! The performances were painfully bad, but the storyline left me utterly repulsed. The acting was rigid and unnatural—even for early sound films (with the sole exceptions of Lee Tracy and H.B. Warner, who could do no wrong). Rose Hobart was unbearably dull and devoid of emotion as Julie (just as she was in 1932’s *Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde*, an otherwise outstanding film). The rest of the cast was even more unbearable—their ineptitude defies description.  

But the real atrocity was the plot. For some baffling reason, Julie is hopelessly devoted to Liliom, a shameless womanizer with zero redeeming qualities. He marries her yet refuses to lift a finger, lazing around or fraternizing with his criminal friend (Lee Tracy). And, of course, he never shows Julie an ounce of kindness—instead, he routinely abuses her. Despite this, Julie remains blindly devoted, making endless excuses for him, which only fuels his cruelty. What’s truly disturbing is how the film glorifies this twisted dynamic without a shred of self-awareness.

*To me, A Matter of Life and Death isn’t just another movie—it’s the greatest film ever created.*  

*From the first frame to the last, it radiates sophistication. It challenges the mind, reflects the postwar era with striking clarity, and explores the fragile bonds between nations and people.*  

*The visuals are breathtaking—the seamless blend of black-and-white and Technicolor perfectly distinguishes between worlds. The characters and storytelling are flawless, crafted with such precision that even this fantasy feels utterly real.*  

*No matter how often I revisit it—and I’ve watched it countless times—it never loses its power over me. It brings laughter, wonder, deep reflection, and tears. Decades later, it remains as vibrant as it was in 1946.*  

*If I could keep only one film to watch for the rest of my life, this would be it.*

This visually stunning film employs a bold palette of just six or seven hues. Released more than 15 years ago, its innovative color scheme captivated audiences, standing apart from anything previously seen in cinema. For me, these striking visuals transform the movie into a mesmerizing experience—countless frames feel worthy of being frozen and studied as works of art.  

While the characters and plot don’t quite reach the same heights as the cinematography, they remain delightfully exaggerated, particularly the villains. The well-known actors portraying "Flatop," "Pruneface," "Lips," "Mumbles," and others must have relished bringing these over-the-top roles to life.  

Warren Beatty and Gleanne Hedley deliver solid performances as Dick Tracy and Tess Truehart, the latter living up to her name with her gentle charm. Charlie Korsmo also shines as the troubled young boy taken in by the pair. The film bursts with vibrant personalities, brought to life by a star-studded cast including Al Pacino, Dustin Hoffman, William Forsythe, Paul Sorvino, Mandy Patinkin, Madonna, and many more—too many to name here.

This material squanders any potential intrigue within the first few seconds by slapping on a disclaimer that the events we're about to witness can never be confirmed, framing them as merely "the whisper [rumor] most often told" about one of Hollywood's most notorious unsolved mysteries.  

So right away, expectations are low—this won’t offer anything fresh (and even E!’s *Mysteries & Scandals* provides a slightly better grip on the incident, which isn’t saying much). What *does* it deliver?  

For starters, the revelation that Hollywood is a pit of vipers and excess—hardly groundbreaking. The more compelling angle is the desperate lengths a faded director will go to claw back influence in either showbiz or politics, raising the question of whether Peter Bogdanovich is projecting his own disillusionment onto these characters. But the story is so steeped in cynicism, so murky and mean-spirited, that watching it feels less like absorbing history and more like being complicit in a shoddy, sensationalized farce.  

Oddly enough, the film’s manic tone is more grating than entertaining, and its characters inspire zero empathy. Meanwhile, *Citizen Kane*—the gold standard—handles the complexities of the Davies/Hearst dynamic with far more finesse.

If you have any empathy or compassion for others, this film will be difficult to watch—especially in its second half.  

That’s when a kind young boy is brutally attacked, leading a man with intellectual disabilities to spiral after witnessing the violence. These scenes are harrowing and deeply unsettling.  

Yet despite its tough subject matter, the movie is compelling, with strong performances that linger long after it ends.  

Tom Hulce delivers what might be his finest performance as Dominick, a gentle garbage collector who adores "Hulk" comics and wrestling. He’s the kind of endearing soul you can’t help but love and hope finds happiness. His breakdown is raw and justified—though you’ll need to watch to understand why.  

Ray Liotta co-stars as Eugene, the med student who cares for Dominick, a role that preceded his breakout in *Field of Dreams*.  

Be warned: this film takes you on an intense emotional journey. But it’s powerful, thought-provoking, and worth every moment.

This stands apart from any other film—the closest comparison might be a Woody Allen picture. But while Allen obsessively examines human quirks, Bret Carr seems focused on confronting that one paralyzing insecurity that shapes us, for better or worse. In Lou’s case, it’s the core of his stutter, tied to a childhood trauma unraveled through haunting flashbacks.  

The world is full of beautifully neurotic people, and each deserves redemption. Yet the eccentricities of human nature are what make life so fascinating—maybe we shouldn’t “fix” our neuroses any more than we’d alter our noses or breasts.  

Shot on a shoestring budget, this indie film punches above its weight with stunning production and surprising ambition. It feels like a hidden gem for the self-help crowd, brimming with offbeat charm. I’m eager to see where this director goes next—perhaps a career echoing the likes of Woody Allen or Albert Brooks.

This is hands down one of the greatest films I've experienced. It takes me on an emotional whirlwind—laughter, tears, awe, joy, and even falling in love, all packed into just over two hours.  

The cast is phenomenal, especially Michael Nyquist in the lead role—his performance is extraordinary. Equally impressive is the actor portraying Tore, who brings such authenticity to the role of a mentally challenged young man. His portrayal even evoked echoes of Leonardo DiCaprio's unforgettable performance in *What’s Eating Gilbert Grape*. And then there’s the breathtakingly beautiful song, *Gabriella's sång*.  

I can’t recommend this movie enough—it’s a must-watch for everyone!

This Joe McDoakes short was clearly influenced by Warner Brothers' star-studded musical *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, a wartime morale booster from the era. In that film, Eddie Cantor played dual roles—himself and an aspiring comedian struggling to break into Hollywood due to his uncanny resemblance to Cantor.  

Similarly, George O'Hanlon, the star of the McDoakes series, appears as both himself and Joe McDoakes, an eager hopeful trying to land a role in pictures. Like *Thank Your Lucky Stars*, a handful of Warner contract players make brief appearances in this short.  

O’Hanlon’s character is assigned a one-line part in a World War I film by central casting, but the message mistakenly goes to his lookalike, McDoakes. Nervous about his big break, McDoakes obsesses over how to deliver his single line, even attempting impressions of famous movie stars to sound more convincing.  

After 86 agonizing takes—much to the frustration of director Ralph Sanford and the endlessly patient Clyde Cook, who plays a British cockney soldier—they finally carve out a place in the industry for the hapless McDoakes. This hilarious short, which earned an Oscar nomination, is well worth watching.

This film was a complete waste of time, lacking any coherent plot. The performances were embarrassingly poor—they should serve as a cautionary example in acting workshops. It shamelessly copies *Universal Soldier*, another movie with dismal acting. It's disappointing to see the lead actor indulge his ego every few years, and even more frustrating that audiences pay to endure it. This kind of low-quality film tarnishes the reputation of martial arts movies. Compared to this, even Segal, Norris, and Schwarzenegger seem mildly talented.  

Maybe the star should follow Leslie Nielsen's path and embrace self-parody—at least then we’d be laughing with him rather than at him.

The direction in this comedy is outstanding. Visually, many scenes have a striking, almost graphic novel-like style—darker in tone than anticipated, though not in the storyline. While it might not be the most laugh-out-loud film ever, especially for fans of raunchy, over-the-top humor (think *There’s Something About Mary* or *American Pie*), it delivers clever jokes that grow funnier with repeat viewings. If you enjoy comic books or superhero films (*Batman*, *X-Men*, etc.), you’ll appreciate its subtle, recurring humor. Even if superheroes aren’t your thing, the film’s playful mockery of the genre might win you over. Plus, the DVD includes some great bonus features for fans. (8/10)

**Rewritten Version:**  

As a kid, I actually thought the murderer’s weapon was cool—but then again, I was young and a little clueless. Even with my childish judgment, though, the movie’s plot was painfully dull whenever the killer wasn’t using his glowing knife to slash people. What’s truly surprising is that the film somehow landed a strong cast. What script did they read that convinced them to sign on? It’s undeniably boring, just an excuse to showcase a tiny-scale lightsaber knockoff.  

The story is often confusing, and the ending descends into total chaos. The entire film revolves around aliens and that one weapon. It starts with two kids and some guy stumbling upon an extraterrestrial encounter, then jumps years ahead with what seems like a return of the same threat. Dead animals litter the mystery, and for some inexplicable reason, one guy ends up wielding the alien weapon before going on a laughably low-stakes rampage.  

Honestly, you have to question why this movie even exists. If the goal was—

Dolph Lundgren scowls and broods through this jumbled mystery-thriller that fails to live up to its flashy packaging. While he delivers a surprisingly strong performance, the plot drowns in tired B-movie tropes—hardboiled detectives, vengeful schemes, corrupt tycoons, seedy underworld dealings—all slapped together with little cohesion. The pacing improves slightly in the latter half, but if you're after a better Lundgren fix, skip this and just rewatch *Red Scorpion* instead.

The film was outstanding, though a few of Esposito’s scenes fell short. What made it special was how it reunited all the detectives from the series and tied up loose ends that were left hanging during the original run (thanks, NBC…). Watching Pembleton and Bayliss at their most raw and human was a highlight—Braugher and Secor delivered brilliant performances, though they likely won’t get the recognition they deserve.  

It was bittersweet knowing this marked the end of *Homicide*. Reruns and old recordings on CourtTV can’t compare to the excitement of tuning in every Friday. Still, the movie did its job masterfully, exploring life after Al’s retirement and the deep bonds within the unit. A truly satisfying send-off.

*CREEP* is a no-nonsense, real-time horror film with a singular goal: to trap its audience on a deserted subway platform for 85 relentless minutes as a grotesque mutant hunts down its victims. And it delivers exactly that—nothing more, nothing less. Director Christopher Smith stretches tension as far as possible by populating the claustrophobic setting with characters who plausibly belong there after hours. The origins of the monstrous Creep remain deliberately obscured (hinted at through whispers of illegal underground experiments from the 60s), and this restrained ambiguity serves the film well—until the finale, where Smith oddly pulls back from a hinted twist involving even more grotesque mutations. Ironically, the movie could have benefited from embracing that clichéd shock ending. Franka Potente (*Run Lola Run*) delivers a strong performance as the panicked protagonist, while the supporting cast holds their own.

**WOW! Who asked for a sequel to an already terrible film?** *Half Past Dead* was bad, but at least it had some semblance of direction. *HPD2* doesn’t even try—it just mindlessly flickers on-screen with no purpose. Here’s the gist:  

Twitch (played by Kurupt of Tha Dogg Pound) gets moved to a new prison where rumors swirl about hidden gold. A riot erupts, Cortez guns down a rival inmate, and plans his breakout. During a conjugal visit, Twitch’s fiancée and Burke’s (Bill Goldberg) daughter are taken hostage by Cortez and locked in the execution chamber. Reluctantly, Burke teams up with Twitch, leading them into a mess of idiotic inmates while uncovering Cortez’s twisted scheme.  

**Verdict:** This is the most pointless sequel since *Universal Soldier: The Return*. The script is a disaster, the acting is laughable, and the dialogue feels like a bad parody. Every character is a cartoonish stereotype. Sure, it’s low-budget—but that’s no excuse for this mess.

This is a bizarre film... I struggled to grasp its meaning. It follows a group of North London misfits who discover a mute child in the woods, treating him like some sort of prophet. Each character undergoes a personal transformation, though these changes often spiral into chaos. The 90-minute runtime left me more frustrated than intrigued—nothing felt resolved, and the whole experience seemed oddly purposeless. None of the characters stood out or earned any real sympathy.

What was the director even trying to say? Maybe I missed something, but the story felt needlessly obscure. What was Runner’s fate? Why did Emilio shoot the child? That moment seemed random and unexplained. Does anyone actually understand this confusing mess of a movie?

But where are the cannibals? Those drawn in by the title and the promise of "real cannibals" will walk away disappointed. Instead, the film follows an eccentric man revisiting a Papua New Guinea village where he once lived among the locals—including a former lover from decades past. Tobias Schneebaum, as New York Jewish as they come, becomes an unlikely focus, even appearing in his yarmulke in several scenes, which feels oddly juxtaposed against the jungle backdrop.

Don’t expect actual cannibalism on display—just secondhand tales shared by villagers and Tobias himself. That said, the film isn’t a total loss. It’s visually striking, and Schneebaum’s charm keeps things engaging as he offers a rare look into a world worlds apart from the West. 

The real issue? This isn’t the movie the title or description suggests.  

A generous 4 out of 10.

I’m not usually a fan of remakes—or, to borrow the trendy term, "retellings"—but this movie genuinely irritated me. The original *Prom Night* may not have been a masterpiece in my opinion, but at least it understood its purpose: to be a horror film. There are basic rules when crafting horror—suspense is key to keeping the audience engaged. But let’s be honest, this was far from a gripping thrill ride. The scares were lazy, telegraphed from a mile away. (Take the overused cliché of a cat leaping out of a closet, only for the real villain to appear moments later—this film couldn’t even execute that properly, so how could it nail anything else?)  

A horror film also needs a protagonist worth rooting for—this one had none. The only character I connected with was the lead detective. His composed yet rational response to a killer on the loose was refreshing. More films like this should embrace a practical reaction to danger. (If you’re fleeing a maniac with an axe, you *run*—not stop to trip over your own feet.)

Viggo Mortensen plays a new arrival at a haunted prison where the warden (a strong performance by Lane Smith) hides a horrifying secret—one that may explain the brutal killings of inmates and guards by an otherworldly force. Lincoln Kilpatrick portrays the longtime prisoner who knows the truth but fears for his survival. Prison films often bring to mind explosive action flicks starring Stallone or Van Damme, or gripping dramas like *The Shawshank Redemption* and *The Green Mile*. Yet *Prison* defies expectations, unfolding as a supernatural thriller more reminiscent of *The Exorcist III*. Director Renny Harlin crafts a chilling, atmospheric film that stands as the finest work of his career. Boasting solid performances from a then-unknown cast—particularly Lane Smith, whose nervous, twitchy warden avoids mustache-twirling villainy in favor of unsettling realism—*Prison* proves far better than anticipated.  

*** out of 4 – (Good)

What an absolute delight—completely unexpected! This is the essence of a genuine thriller. I dashed into the video store, picked a film without even finishing the back-cover summary, and crossed my fingers. To my surprise and utter satisfaction, it delivered. The actors were phenomenal, breathing such life into their roles that they felt utterly believable.  

The storyline was brilliantly crafted, with sharp writing and tight direction. Not a single moment dragged—it had me hooked from opening scene to credits.  

If you love thrillers that balance perfect pacing with relentless tension, I can’t recommend this enough. An easy 10/10 in my book!

As a dedicated horror fan, I make it a point to watch all major releases in the genre, particularly those from my home country's cinema. Unfortunately, *The Power of Fear* (or *Vedma* as it's titled in Russian) stands out as one of the weakest entries I’ve seen. It fails to deliver even a hint of suspense—the pacing is sluggish, the scares predictable, and the execution utterly lacking in genuine horror.  

Honestly, the film falls flat in every aspect. The plot is absurd (why transform a classic Ukrainian witchcraft tale into a clumsy, unconvincing modern American thriller? The previous reviewer was spot-on—it doesn’t thrill at all). The acting is painfully stiff, even from seasoned Russian stars like Valeri Nikolayev and Yevgeniya Kryukova, who deliver their English lines with all the emotion of wooden dolls. Their performances feel phoned-in, as if they couldn’t be bothered to try.  

And then there’s the baffling decision to shoot in English with a Russian cast—a misguided choice that only highlights the film’s flaws. Overall, *The Power of Fear* is a forgettable mess that never should have made it to the screen.

The film showed promise in its opening scenes but ultimately failed to deliver on its potential. While the director demonstrates skill with striking visuals and creative shots—hallmarks of Asian cinema—the storytelling falls short. The narrative feels disjointed, meandering through unclear directions without ever settling into a compelling or coherent arc. Despite the impressive performances, particularly from Jude Law, who delivers his usual excellence, the weak script undermines the entire project. A disappointing mismatch between talent and material.

What starts as a witty satire about a dubious security company abruptly descends into a dull and ridiculous murder mystery. Despite the best efforts of David Arquette and the talented Stanley Tucci, even their performances can't salvage this disaster—some flaws are beyond redemption.  

Take Gale’s baffling shift from a caring mother figure to an erratic drunk at Tommy’s parents' house—what justifies this? Then there's Heinrich, a sleazy character, sure, but why would he sabotage the business he’s dedicated his life to by robbing or even killing clients? Then there’s Tommy, who suddenly decides Heinrich might be a murderer based mostly on a dream—why not just go to the police? And why didn’t Gale set the alarm when she got home, especially after lecturing Howie for leaving it off? These absurdities only serve the so-called "plot," if you can even call it that.  

None of it would matter if the film delivered even a hint of humor, but every attempt—whether Howie’s awkward date-rape anecdote, the coroner’s ludicrous misidentification of Gale, or the chaotic finale—falls painfully flat.

What can I say? A spoiler warning feels necessary here—just know they drop the F-bomb constantly, practically every other line. This film wasn’t for me at all—it leaned too heavily into crude sexual innuendo, infidelity, and endless scheming. The nonstop profanity was completely over the top. I rated it a 3, and honestly, two of those points were just for Mira Sorvino’s mesmerizing dance moves.

The previous reviewer was too kind. While I enjoyed the first film, this sequel falls flat. The opening scenes are tolerable, but the quality drops fast. Jon Bon Jovi simply doesn't convince as a tough vampire hunter, and the vampire princess lacks both allure and menace. The plot is riddled with holes – why would even an ordinary person, let alone a seasoned hunter, trust a mysterious woman who appears from nowhere? And how exactly does Una communicate with Jovi? The film provides zero explanations. Poor storytelling might be forgivable if it were entertaining, but even that's lacking here. This ranks among the weakest vampire films I've ever seen.

Dudley Moore delivered his most iconic performance in the 1981 comedy *Arthur*, a film that masterfully blends uproarious humor with genuine heart. In what would become the standout role of his tragically brief career, Moore earned an Academy Award nomination for his portrayal of Arthur Bach—a wealthy, perpetually intoxicated playboy who "races cars, plays tennis, fondles women, but has weekends off and is his own boss." The story follows Arthur as he faces the ultimatum of securing his $750 million inheritance by marrying Susan Johnston (Jill Eikenberry), the haughty daughter of a secretive mobster. His reckless life takes an unexpected turn when he meets Linda Morolla (Liza Minnelli), a spirited Queens waitress and aspiring actress who shoplifts neckties for her father’s birthday.  

Moore shines in one of the most brilliantly comedic performances of the past half-century, while the late Sir John Gielgud steals scenes—and an Oscar for Best Supporting Actor—as Hobson, Arthur’s sharp-witted butler whose gruff exterior hides deep affection. The film is further enriched by memorable turns from Barney Martin as Linda’s father, Stephen Elliott as Susan’s mob-connected dad, and Geraldine Fitzgerald as Arthur’s eccentric grandmother. Directed with sharp wit and warmth...

The sex comedy genre is packed with competition these days—just being outrageously crude isn’t enough anymore. After enduring countless vulgar jokes and over-the-top antics, a film in this category needs something more to truly grab my attention.  

Going into *The 40-Year-Old Virgin*, I thought I knew what to expect—the trailers made it clear with lines like, *"Is it true that if you don’t use it, you lose it?"* What surprised me, though, was the film’s genuine heart and real effort at character growth. Sure, it has the quirky, offbeat personalities typical of an Adam Sandler comedy, and yes, there’s enough crude humor to make Noah blush—but somehow, it also delivers a touching love story and even a meaningful message.  

The protagonist, Andy, is someone I (unfortunately) relate to more than I’d like to admit. From the first shot, I noticed he shares my love for *Mystery Science Theater 3000* (he has a movie poster on his wall), and the film showcases his impressive collection of vintage memorabilia. Andy’s also got a serious gaming setup and a deep knowledge of...

All this film stock wasted to nothing—might as well have Count Floyd jump in every minute just to break the monotony. Somehow, they gathered Steve Railsback, Susan Anspach, John Vernon, and Joe Flaherty on the same set and still missed making anything resembling a real movie by a country mile. This thing is *painfully* bad. From the mindless opening to the equally witless ending, there’s not a single original line, idea, shot, or effect. The luminous Susan Anspach from *Five Easy Pieces*? Reduced to dullness. Steve Railsback? Snooze-inducing. John Vernon? Lifeless. Even the giant bug? Yawn-worthy. If this qualifies as horror, then *Buttercream Gang* might as well be *Scarface*.  

Let’s be real—every terrible movie hands you the reason for its terribleness on a platter. Sometimes it's right there in the opening credits (*"Written, Directed, and Produced by" one overambitious nobody*). Other times, it's some painfully untalented centerpiece that screams *nepotism* or *desperation*. Here? You don’t get the answer until the very last credit roll, where they thank a small army of Canadian government departments for their *invaluable cooperation*.  

Excuse me while I cleanse my palate with *MST3K’s* riff on *Beast of Yucca Flats*.

This film is a mess from start to finish—weak in concept, execution, and storytelling.  

Jon Heder’s performance is grating, relying yet again on the same stale quirks he used in *Napoleon Dynamite*. His character comes across as obnoxious and clueless.  

Diane Keaton recycles her usual role: the overbearing, hyper-involved mom who somehow still misses the mark with her kids (see *Because I Said So* for the same act).  

Even Anna Faris, who usually shines, is wasted here as a shallow, dim-witted character.  

Jeff Daniels does an okay job, but he’s hardly enough to save this disaster.  

Do yourself a favor—avoid this movie unless you enjoy wasting time and testing your patience.

"Life is a stage, and we are all merely players"—or something along those lines. Who decided that theater ends at the edge of the stage—or even at the theater’s entrance? Why shouldn’t the audience be part of the performance, woven into the very fabric of the story?  

This film was a bold experiment, declaring: *"The story isn’t just for you—it’s about you, and it demands more than passive watching. It needs your involvement."* *"Sometimes the tale comes to you, sometimes you must step into it."*  

It’s a shame no one paid attention—but that doesn’t mean it wasn’t worth saying.

I had high hopes for this film, especially since it was a Yash Raj production.  

Jimmy runs a call center when he’s approached by Pooja Singh to teach English to her boss, Lakhan Singh. They fall in love and plan to escape together, but Pooja hesitates, feeling indebted to Lakhan—also known as Bhaiyyaji. Despite this, they steal money from him, only for Jimmy to discover that Bhaiyyaji is actually a notorious gangster. Meanwhile, Bhaiyyaji hires Bachchan Pandey to hunt them down.  

Starring Saif Ali Khan, Kareena Kapoor, Anil Kapoor, and Akshaye Khanna, the movie marks Vijay Krishna Acharya’s directorial debut, produced by Aditya Chopra and Yash Chopra.  

"Tashan" is easily one of the worst films I’ve ever seen. Sure, the visuals are stunning, and Kareena Kapoor (along with her highly publicized weight loss) looks fantastic. But the storyline is painfully weak, often jumping from one incoherent scene to another—which explains why I have...

I really don’t get the intense dislike for this episode. Looking for a truly bad *Smallville* episode? Try *Subterranean*—now *that’s* a mess. Tom Welling delivers a strong performance (which I don’t say lightly), and Michael Rosenbaum is, as usual, fantastic. The alternate universe concept feels unsettlingly real.  

Martian Manhunter, who first appeared in *Static*, makes a comeback and reveals to Clark that the asylum's lead doctor is actually a phantom from the Phantom Zone. If Clark wants to return to his own world, he’ll have to kill him. The episode is well-paced, with solid acting all around, making it a standout installment.

This delightful film offers much more than just an endearing story about a middle-aged man finding joy in ballroom dancing (though it certainly delivers that too). At its heart, it's a beautiful journey of rediscovering passion for life—breaking free from the grind of work and financial stress to embrace happiness anew.  

What makes it truly special is its subtle, insightful look at how modern Japan is gradually shifting its views—from perceptions of ballroom dancing to attitudes about physical connection. You'll find yourself laughing one moment, itching to jump up and dance the next, and simply basking in warmth throughout.  

For anyone who thinks Japanese cinema is always serious or hard to approach, this is the perfect film to change that perception—an uplifting, accessible gem.

Believe it or not, for 1912, this 12-minute film was considered a full-length feature. Very few movies ran longer back then—but that's not what makes this peculiar little film stand out. What sets it apart is the cast: every actor (except for one frog) is played by bugs. Yes, actual bugs!  

This could have been a simple domestic comedy, much like the works of Chaplin, Laurel and Hardy, or Max Linder. Instead, this Russian production chose to animate bugs (or perhaps highly realistic bug models). Maybe Chaplin and Laurel and Hardy hadn’t been discovered yet, or perhaps Linder was busy—either way, bugs took center stage.  

Using stop-motion, the insects move, dance, and brawl with astonishing fluidity—far more realistically than King Kong would 21 years later!  

The story follows Mr. Beetle as he sneaks out for a night of fun, visiting a raucous club while his wife supposedly stays home. But his antics are caught on film by a local enthusiast. Worse yet, he’s unaware that Mrs. Beetle is having her own fling with a free-spirited grasshopper.

I'm truly shocked by what's considered entertainment these days. This so-called "kids' movie" is packed with disturbing content—mocking death, excessive violence, inappropriate adult humor, threats toward children, crude behavior, underage drinking, drug theft, terrible parenting, a nightmarish babysitter, and tired stereotypes targeting African Americans, law enforcement, and overweight individuals. Oh, and let’s not forget kids sneaking out in the dead of night—because that’s wholesome fun, right?  

Then there’s the deeply unsettling plot—a deceased woman haunting a house, possessing it, imprisoning her grieving husband for decades, and tormenting an entire neighborhood. Charming material for children, isn’t it? Parents, is *this* the message you want to feed young minds? Is *this* how they should see the world?  

This film is far too frightening for little ones, and sadly, some teens might already be living through similar chaos—why add fuel to the fire? As for adults? It’s neither frightening nor funny—just dull, forced, and painfully predictable. And the characters? Absolutely infuriating—useless parents, incompetent cops, obnoxious friends, and relentlessly manipulative figures. A total trainwreck.

Melissa Joan Hart delivers an outstanding performance! This series is truly incredible—unmatched by anything else. The only possible rival might be her role in *Clarissa Explains It All*, where she was equally brilliant. Far surpassing *Buffy the Vampire Slayer*, this show is absolutely phenomenal!

I first watched this long after the TV series aired, and at the time, it didn’t grab me. But as my recollection of the show faded over the years, I gave it another chance—and it had me in stitches. Adapted from Neil Simon’s stage play, the film stays remarkably close to its theatrical roots, which works entirely in its favor. Walter Matthau and Jack Lemmon are pitch-perfect as Oscar and Felix, and the supporting cast shines, especially John Fielder as Vinnie. Even now, certain scenes leave me breathless with laughter: Felix barging in on Oscar’s ball game to demand dinner, Oscar losing it and chasing Felix around the apartment, the Pigeon Sisters crumbling under Felix’s tragic tales, and of course, the iconic diner scene (later shamelessly copied in *When Harry Met Sally*). The dialogue crackles with wit—like Oscar’s panicked line when they think Felix overdosed: *"They could be vitamins! He could be the healthiest one in the room!"* Absolutely brilliant.

I'm completely stunned that anyone would rate this above the original. It's pushed me to speak up! This is nothing but a shameless money grab riding on the first film's success. The writing is painfully bad—nowhere near as genuine or gripping as the original.  

The plot is absurd, the depiction of French police is downright farcical, and Doyle's character is worlds apart from how he was in the first movie.  

Since when do drug lords personally inspect shipments at the docks? Doyle tracking down his target so easily is just embarrassing. Apparently, the entire French police force was sipping espresso until Doyle flew in from the States to show them *real* detective work. Give me a break. Try wandering into a foreign city and uncovering its top criminals armed with nothing but a tourist map—absurd.  

A dreadful follow-up. Anyone who disagrees is delusional.

Following World War I, an Allied expedition travels to Cambodia to stop Count Mazovia from raising an undead army of soldiers and laborers. Racing against time to avert another global conflict, the team battles through dense jungles toward Angkor Wat—though one member, Armand, harbors secret motives that clash with the mission.  

A word of caution—the zombie makeup crew walked off set before filming began.  

While billed as a follow-up to *White Zombie* (1932) starring Bela Lugosi, *Revolt of the Zombies* shares little connection to its predecessor. If Lugosi’s undead failed to impress, these zombies won’t either. A young Dean Jagger (as Armand Louque) plays a man fixated on blonde Claire Duval (Dorothy Stone). The supporting cast includes Roy D’Arcy as the sinister Mazovia and Teru Shimada as the obedient Buna—both delivering decent performances but hampered by weak material.  

**Revolt of the Zombies (1936) – Victor Halperin | Dean Jagger, Dorothy Stone, Roy D’Arcy**

While *The Fluffer* might expose some gritty truths about the porn industry, it fails to compensate for its weak direction, unconvincing performances, and lackluster script.  

From start to its unnecessarily prolonged ending, it barely earns a B-grade.  

It’s almost embarrassing to imagine this being presented to mainstream audiences as a benchmark for contemporary gay cinema.  

At best, it should have a brief run in gay film festivals before fading into obscurity on home video.  

The film is set to open Brisbane’s Queer Film Weekend on April 10, 2002—though its reception may depend heavily on how much alcohol flows at the pre-screening party. They’ll certainly need it.

It feels like the usually stellar Shonda Rhimes team farmed out this script to some lackluster writers—perhaps from GenericTVville? *Private Practice* brings to mind those painfully dull David E. Kelley shows—starts with potential, then quickly devolves into formulaic storytelling (*Picket Fences*, *Ally McBeal*, *Boston Legal*). The over-the-top cases they tackle are so absurd they fail to stir any real emotion—no fear, no "this could happen to me" tension, just hollow theatrics. And they’re not even entertaining.  

The cast delivers strong performances, but the lifeless plots drag everything down. As a therapist, I have to say Amy Brenneman’s character is a trainwreck of incompetence—unethical, untrained, and utterly unrealistic. Whoever wrote her material clearly skipped ethics and transference classes at Stanford. That episode with the nosebleeding wife? A blatant violation of professional boundaries. Real therapists don’t operate like that.  

And can we retire the tired trope of women pining over men who’ve moved on? We’ve evolved past *Sex and the City*. Addison’s immature aggression toward her love interest? Cringe.

Diane and I caught this brilliant film today in Fremantle, and we both felt it stood out far above other pastiche-style movies. What captivated us were the brief, five to ten-minute segments that made up the film, each woven together by a central theme—love in all its varied forms.  

The stories unfolded across different Parisian neighborhoods, giving each vignette its own distinct atmosphere. Though I’ve only visited Paris a handful of times and couldn’t always pinpoint the exact locations, I imagine Europeans—especially the French—would recognize them instantly. Yet the settings soon became secondary because the storytelling was so expertly crafted that you’re immediately drawn into each narrative.  

The film moves at a brisk pace, leaving you absorbing one story just as the next unfolds on screen. Unlike the overblown, graphic storytelling of typical Hollywood fare, these tales are subtle, thought-provoking, and quietly resonant—much like real life, without the exaggerated drama that often overtakes modern media.

Brian Yuzna often gets dismissed for his over-the-top gore films, but the reality is his work holds up surprisingly well. While the *Re-Animator* sequels don’t quite match the original, they stand strong among horror follow-ups. *Return of the Living Dead 3* is arguably the best in the franchise, and *Society* comes dangerously close to surreal horror brilliance. This thriller may not be a masterpiece, but it showcases Yuzna’s sharp eye for horror, delivering a plot that’s consistently gripping and intense. It’s shocking that a horror film centered on dentistry didn’t surface until 1996—after all, fear of the dentist is almost primal, like evading a predator in the modern age. Personally, dental visits don’t faze me, but apparently, I’m in the minority.  

The story revolves around Dr. Feinstone, a perfectionist dentist with a dream life—a lavish home, a thriving career, and a stunning wife. But everything unravels when he catches her in an affair with the pool cleaner. And as fate would have it, his downfall isn’t the only one in motion—his own...

I picked up this film on DVD completely blind, part of my winter challenge to watch a movie each night. After suffering through a string of forgettable American action flicks (*Ballistic*, *Daredevil*, *Cradle of Life*), *Zhu Warriors* felt like a burst of fresh creativity. The plot may be absurd, but the film’s earnestness, warmth, and total lack of cynicism won me over—not to mention its stunning visuals.  

Yes, the special effects aren’t as polished as Hollywood’s, but the filmmakers prioritize vibrant colors, striking compositions, and dynamic movement over realism, creating one breathtaking image after another. In one unforgettable moment, two superhuman figures stand atop jagged rock spires, a massive moon swelling behind them—the frame perfectly balanced among the three elements. In another, a warrior-princess streaks across the sky, trailing her radiant sword like a heat-seeking missile. The colors shift explosively from scene to scene, not to mirror reality, but to heighten emotion.  

The characters are direct and uncomplicated, like figures from a comic book—not deeply nuanced, but embodying archetypes that carry a stronger, almost mythic weight. And physically, several of the actors are downright mesmerizing.

Taking a look at the AFI’s top 100 comedies, I have to admit—this one might be the absolute worst. Not just among the 90 films I’ve watched from the list, but possibly the worst comedy I’ve ever seen. Sure, drunks can be funny, but Dudley? Not so much. Liza Minnelli almost salvaged it, but even she couldn’t save this mess. If you're a fan of hers, just watch *Arrested Development* instead—it's far better. Let’s be honest, is Dudley giggling and slurping drinks supposed to be hilarious? Skip this one and pick almost any other film from the AFI's list for actual laughs. Want a funnier drunk? Check out *The Thin Man*. Craving genuine comedy? Any Marx Brothers film will deliver—though you might need to be as wasted as Arthur to enjoy it.

I caught this movie at TIFF (Toronto International Film Festival). Hal Hartley fans won’t be let down—and even if you’re new to his work, no worries. This film holds its own spectacularly. I’m already planning to catch the second screening—it was incredible, and I need to see it again ASAP!  

Hilarious and razor-sharp in its writing, *Fay Grim* shines with Parker Posey delivering a standout performance in the lead role. A sequel to *Henry Fool* (2000), this film revisits familiar characters while carving its own path. Stylistically, Hartley leans into his signature use of canted (or Dutch) angles, a technique seen in his earlier works like *Possible Films: Short Works by Hal Hartley 1994-2004* and *The Girl from Monday* (2005).  

Coincidentally, watching it on September 11 felt fitting—the story unfolds against the backdrop of a post-9/11 world. Without giving too much away, I see this as a bold, politically charged narrative that doesn’t shy away from the complexities of its era.

own right, *Vanilla Sky* stands apart from the usual Tom Cruise fare often dismissed as strange (*Magnolia*, *Eyes Wide Shut*). It’s not weird—it’s distinct, layered, even perplexing, but never bizarre. Weird belongs to Kubrick or Pauly Shore. Different? Think *The Truman Show*. Confusing? *The Matrix* or *The Game*. And unlike Kubrick’s open-ended ambiguity, this film delivers resolution. Every piece clicks—maybe not at once, maybe not for years—but it *does*. The confusion mirrors David Aames’ own disorientation—that’s intentional. Critics mistook this depth for oddity, dismissing it without truly seeing, without heeding the original *Abre los Ojos*’ plea to *open your eyes*. Still unconvinced? The soundtrack alone is worth it. Cameron Crowe crafts a sonic landscape that breathes life into the film’s emotional core—where else does The Beach Boys’ *Good Vibrations* crescendo into cinematic perfection? A masterclass in atmosphere, *Vanilla Sky* lingers, haunting and whole.

The entire Biker Movie genre might just consist of the cheesiest films ever created. This one packs in endless brawls, plenty of gore, bikers clashing with Native Americans, and a rundown shantytown that gets obliterated piece by piece. The acting is painfully awful—whatever happened to Robert Walker Jr.? He once starred in big studio films before vanishing into obscurity. This movie is downright terrible, but if you’re craving some vintage Biker trash, it’s the perfect pick. By the time it’s over, you’ll probably feel a little grimy for having sat through it!

**The Thief of Bagdad** captivates with its striking depiction of the sinister sorcerer Jaffar (Conrad Veidt), who schemes with deceit and dark magic to seize the throne from its rightful heir, the young King Ahmad, and to steal a radiant princess from her father...  

In the end, as with all tyrants in tales and lore, he is undone by love and the overlooked strength of the ordinary man—embodied here by the cunning little thief (Sabu).  

The clash between good and evil, light and shadow, is masterfully portrayed through both visuals and storytelling...  

The script flows with poetic simplicity, weaving beauty into every line... The sorcerer and his minions are clad in billowing robes that mimic the wings of dark birds, descending without warning under cover of night to unleash ruin and fear...  

The noble hero shines in white turbans and flowing garments, while his princess glows in soft hues of pink and delicate blue...  

Its grand spectacles rival all that came before, yet its bold use of color breathes life into a world once unimaginable...  

With its enchanted flying carpet, a soaring white steed, a towering genie (brought to mesmerizing life by Rex Ingram), and malevolent sorcerers, the film weaves magic into every frame...

When you first delve into the study of fascism, you encounter ostracism: because this so-called "philosophy" is inherently hollow, it relies on scapegoats to prop up its illusion of ideology. Ettore Scola's film, arguably his magnum opus, centers on those cast aside—the regime's designated outcasts.  

The historical backdrop of Hitler and Mussolini’s alliance remains barely visible, glimpsed only in fleeting moments: military parades, garlands, scattered voices. Our protagonists are excluded from this spectacle of hypermasculinity. "Genius is essentially masculine"—a dictate Antonietta (Sophia Loren at her finest) has embroidered onto a cushion, embodying the dogma she blindly upholds. Antonietta, whose entire world is confined to her kitchen and whose pride rests solely on her children, begins the film as an unwitting victim of this oppressive, machismo-driven society. She believes happiness is her duty.  

Gabriel, on the other hand, sees clearly. He understands the malignancy consuming his country. But as a gay man, he is already marked for exclusion—soon to be arrested.  

Setting aside everything that divides them, they recognize their shared humanity and, in an act of defiance, become lovers. For Antonietta, this is rebellion incarnate. In a world where politics and religion collude to suppress women’s autonomy, her transgression—becoming an adulteress—awakens a political consciousness within her.

As I settled in to watch the 14th season of *The Bachelor*—titled *On the Wings of Love*—I braced myself for what promised to be an "interesting" experience. Though I'd casually followed earlier seasons, catching an episode here and missing several there, the show always managed to grab my attention. It's undeniably compelling, even if its substance and ethics often leave much to be desired.  

*On the Wings of Love* follows Jake, a 31-year-old commercial pilot from Dallas, Texas, as he embarks on his quest for love—or at least, the closest thing to it one can find in a heavily produced reality dating series. Over the course of the season, he meets 25 women from across the country, attempting to forge connections with each—though the format rarely allows for more than fleeting, surface-level conversations. From the start, Jake makes his goal clear (to the audience, at least): he isn't just looking for romance or a fling, but a fiancée, even a wife. Whether he communicated that same urgency to the women vying for his attention remains unclear, but we can only hope so.

Following his masterpiece *Chinatown*, Roman Polanski revisited the themes that defined his acclaimed 1960s films with this unsettling psychological horror. Much like *Repulsion* and *Rosemary’s Baby*, the movie explores the paranoia and claustrophobia bred by life in an apartment.  

Polanski excels at crafting claustrophobic atmospheres, and *The Tenant* stands as his most suffocating and confined work yet. The framing emphasizes tight spaces, with narrow walls and distant vanishing points dominating even the few exterior shots—skies are scarcely visible. But the film’s confinement extends beyond setting—it’s also relentless in its focus on its protagonist. Trelkovsky, played by Polanski himself, is present in virtually every scene—and often in every shot. When he isn’t onscreen, the camera frequently adopts his perspective. And wherever he turns, his own reflection stares back from mirrors, amplifying his isolation.  

Few films delve so deeply into a single character’s internal world and solitude. While psychological thrillers like *M* or *Peeping Tom* manipulate viewers into empathizing...

This film has been my favorite since childhood. Having performed in the stage production multiple times, it will always hold a special place as my beloved musical—I truly believe no one could adapt *Oliver Twist* more brilliantly than this version.  

Oliver Reed’s portrayal of Bill Sikes remains the ultimate "bad guy" for me. Terrifying to my six-year-old self, now as an adult, I find myself deeply empathizing with Nancy, the kind-hearted barmaid and prostitute who helps secure Oliver a better life.  

Jack Wilde was exceptional as the Artful Dodger—his charm and roguish wit as Fagin’s nimble-fingered protégé remain unmatched. The music is unforgettable, particularly Fagin’s lively numbers, and I’m glad Bill Sikes never got a song; his menacing presence wouldn’t have suited a musical moment.  

Carol Reed handled Nancy’s tragic fate masterfully, maintaining a family-friendly tone without diluting the brutality of Bill’s violence—subtle yet haunting.  

This movie is a timeless masterpiece.

This genre was built on laughter, skill, love, and excitement—all blended seamlessly.  

Frank Sinatra was simply brilliant—no further explanation needed. Though not a singer, Marlon Brando charmed audiences as Sky Masterson, and his lack of vocal polish only deepened his character’s appeal. While the women in the film held their own, the men truly shone brightest.  

A timeless classic, it resonates with viewers of every generation, sparking joy and laughter effortlessly.  

Absolutely a must-watch for pure enjoyment!

While I respect individual preferences—if you enjoy something, that’s entirely your right—this film was undeniably terrible. Let me be clear: I may not be a huge fan of Ani DiFranco, but I can acknowledge her talent as a guitarist and songwriter. That said, I found absolutely no redeeming value in this movie.  

Some argue it authentically captures the struggles of high school students. Perhaps in theory, but the execution was wildly unrealistic. The humor seemed to aim for a *Naked Gun*-style absurdity, but the timing was painfully off—awkward pauses between lines felt like desperate waits for laughter (which never came). The script was a chaotic mess, throwing in every controversial topic without properly exploring any of them (the subplot about the student impregnated by a teacher? A glaring example).  

Not once did I laugh. Instead, I spent the entire runtime cringing at its misguided attempts at satire and humor, barely resisting the urge to turn it off.

I watched this film just once around 25 years ago, yet to this day, I still tell people it might be the greatest movie I’ve ever seen. Despite having no spoken dialogue—only thoughts conveyed through inner monologues—I was completely captivated. At times, I even caught myself holding my breath, not wanting to break the spell of silence. I can’t recommend it enough, and I truly wish it were available on DVD.

*WINCHESTER 73* follows Jimmy Stewart as a man relentlessly pursuing his stolen treasure—a coveted Winchester repeating rifle. As the rifle passes from one owner to another, Stewart's determined chase drives the story. Released in 1950 and directed by Anthony Mann, this black-and-white film leans more into crime drama than classic western, with outlaw characters resembling modern gangsters rather than traditional cowboys.  

Shelley Winters portrays a woman with a checkered past, traveling to a ranch with her potential fiancé (Charles Drake). Along the way, she becomes entangled with Stewart, though not before enduring hardship. Winters delivers the most nuanced performance in a movie brimming with eccentric personalities. Keep an eye out for a young Dan Duryea as an unhinged gunman and Tony Curtis in a brief role. Notably, Will Geer feels out of place in his portrayal of Wyatt Earp.

This will be brief. In my opinion, this is an exceptional film. While some critics argue it suffers from weak writing, clumsy cinematography, a grating soundtrack, and an unrealistic depiction of life, I disagree. Yes, certain moments may stretch credibility, but at its core, this film delivers a powerful message of hope—one many viewers overlook. It suggests it's never too late to rescue people from the violence that shatters countless lives. Gang violence is a harsh reality, isn’t it? And it’s undeniably wrong.  

Though cynics may dismiss it, this movie’s bold social commentary deserves praise, not scorn. I’ve watched it at least eight times, captivated each viewing, leaving with the same uplifting belief that change is possible—that the world isn’t doomed (at least not until 2008, anyway). For me, it’s a solid 9/10—flawless in nearly every way. JMV.

Did the filmmakers even screen this before releasing it? The plot leaps around with no clear explanations. The opening fails to make it obvious whether it's a prequel or not, clumsily shifting from Superman's origins to a point after the previous film—without giving viewers any warning. Beyond confusing!  

Superman himself comes across as emotionally fragile—borderline needy—and nowhere near the inspiring hero he should be. Instead, he's painted as a depressed, obsessive, and morally questionable figure—hardly the makings of a compelling protagonist.  

And the ending? Absurd. Superman winding up in a hospital bed was so painfully underwhelming, it almost made me root for his demise. At this point, I wouldn’t be surprised to see a parody where he’s dragged onto a daytime talk show for a paternity test.  

The performances from Superman’s actor and Kevin Spacey are passable, but the script is a disaster. This film is barely watchable.

This film is delightfully eccentric, with performances that match its offbeat charm.  

It tracks the journey of a determined young man pursuing his dream of becoming a renowned Las Vegas magician. Part aspiration, part exploration of others' dreams, and wholly a glimpse into the trials of show business, the story captivates with its whimsy. There’s an undeniable charm to it, punctuated by moments of genuine magic that truly shine.  

Alan Arkin shines as the washed-up magician, bringing both humor and heart to his mentorship of the ambitious Max. Their dynamic is as endearing as it is entertaining.  

While it may not be for everyone, those who appreciate stories about personal journeys will find plenty to enjoy here.

Wow, my initial take on this film was so harsh it got rejected. Let me soften my approach this time.  

Honestly—who watches a Chuck Norris movie expecting him *not* to be the star? The final fight scene delivered, but the rest of the film fell flat. It makes me wonder if age has finally caught up with him. Has he lost a step, forcing him to rely on his legendary status to carry forgettable projects?  

Chuck’s a phenomenal martial artist and, as *Walker, Texas Ranger* proved, a solid actor. But his films only truly shine when those strengths come together—something this movie missed entirely. As a longtime fan, I expected better. Chuck, stick to leading roles—supporting parts just don’t do you justice.  

—Gary

This film is not pornography—it was never intended to be, and unless my uncle somehow becomes president of the entire world, it never should be mistaken as such.  

Now that we’ve cleared that up, let me say I highly recommend this movie. Its themes remain relevant, the humor is sharp, the performances are outstanding, and it provokes some seriously thought-provoking (and intriguing) questions.  

I still don’t fully grasp why this film was so misunderstood—maybe that’s yet another reason I have no plans to visit the U.S. Lena embodies the spirit of the modern riot-grrrl movement: a blend of confusion, curiosity, and wit. Sure, she’s got an edge of anger sometimes—but really, who doesn’t?
