*Love’s Abiding Joy* left me deeply disappointed. After eagerly waiting for its re-airing on Hallmark, I finally watched it Thursday night. While I adore the first three films in the *Love* series, this installment fell far short of my expectations. The movie was overwhelmingly bleak, filled with too many continuity errors, and suffered from choppy editing—so many scenes felt disjointed or out of place.  

The heartbreaking loss of baby Kathy happened too abruptly, and Clark’s inclusion in the story felt forced. The actors seemed disengaged, their performances lacking the emotional depth they once brought to their roles. Missie and Willie’s connection, which was once a highlight, felt nonexistent here.  

The script strayed too far from Janette Oke’s original work. Each film seems to drift further from her vision—key moments, like the mine accident involving the two boys and Clark’s injury, were completely omitted. Even Missie and Willie’s grief over Kathy’s death felt underdeveloped. The essence of the books is fading, and it’s a shame.  

---  

Let me know if you'd like any further refinements!

This movie is pure entertainment—the kind you can enjoy without overthinking as the story spirals into hilarious absurdity. Packed with talent like Sally Field, Teri Hatcher (at her best), Kevin Kline, Elisabeth Shue, and Robert Downey Jr., it delivers top-notch performances as these A-listers ham it up like over-the-top soap opera stars.  

Ever watched a soap and wondered, *"Who even thinks of this stuff?"* Then you’ll adore this film. Every rewatch makes me appreciate its sharp humor and brilliant acting even more. Don’t go in expecting high art—it’s not about deep introspection. Just kick back, let go, and enjoy the ride. Laughter guaranteed.

The opening flourishes had me utterly enchanted by their creativity—the reimagined Archers' emblem, the playful introductory warning, the cosmic camera sweep. It's remarkable to recall that *It's a Wonderful Life* debuted the same year. No mere coincidence: the 1940s brimmed with celestial storytelling, yet the fluffy, starlit heavens and saccharine angels of other films now appear dated, even embarrassing, when compared to Alfred Junge's breathtaking visuals.  

The brilliance sustains throughout, as one stunning concept after another unfolds. Typically, I find the blending of color and monochrome jarring—one style often suffers beside the other. But here, Powell transitions between them effortlessly, as if shifting between palettes were the most natural choice. Both the vibrant hues and the stark grayscale hold their own, each resplendent in its own right.  

As for the narrative... this might be Pressburger's finest screenplay, or at least it would have been, had the ending followed more organically from what came before.

Apologies to all, I understand this is meant to be an "art" film... but honestly, they might as well have handed out pistols at the door so viewers could spare themselves the ordeal. While the visual composition and cinematography were striking, the story itself is downright unbearable to sit through. The total lack of music was punishing, and those endless extended takes? Excruciating. How much silence and stagnant conversation can one possibly endure—especially when it's just two people endlessly griping?  

The acting was strong, I’ll give it that—but was it worth slogging through all that bleak, lifeless misery? The sole bright spot was Maureen Stapleton, lighting up the screen in that red dress with her brief, lively dance. Otherwise, this just felt like a Bergman imitation (and I’m not even a Bergman fan to begin with). Let’s be honest—anyone who claims they genuinely enjoyed every minute of this hour-and-a-half slog is... well, not being truthful.

Chavez’s opposition to globalization has long impressed me, but it was only after watching the film at the Amsterdam International Documentary Film Festival that I truly grasped the scale of his achievements. The documentary exposes the coup and conspiracy orchestrated by Venezuela’s elite, oil corporations, and complicit Western governments hungry for oil—all in an attempt to overthrow the democratically elected President Chavez and reinstate a ruthless dictatorship. This film is essential viewing for anyone who values freedom and justice, serving as a powerful warning to the world. I applaud the Venezuelan people for reclaiming their sovereignty and resisting the destructive influence of entities like Halliburton and the Bush administration.

If you're searching for a strictly factual account of boxer James Corbett's life, this film may not be what you're looking for. The legendary fighter's story gets the classic 1940s Hollywood treatment—transforming reality into a far more thrilling and captivating tale. Yet thanks to brilliant performances (especially Errol Flynn's) and a charming script, the movie's dramatic liberties are easy to overlook.  

Errol Flynn stars as James "Gentleman Jim" Corbett, the 1890s boxing icon who claimed the world championship in 1892. The story traces his rise from modest origins to his career-defining victory over John L. Sullivan. While the film could have centered on the fights, most are kept brief (except the climactic title bout), shifting focus instead to Corbett's bold charisma and his romance with Alexis Smith's character. A standout ensemble cast—including Flynn regular Alan Hale—delivers lively support, with sharp writing that gives each character depth.  

One of the film's greatest strengths is its display of raw athleticism, capturing the energy and vigor of Corbett's era with thrilling authenticity.

*The Muppets Take Manhattan* stands apart from every other Muppet film in several key ways. For starters, it’s the only installment not owned by Disney—despite the studio acquiring the Muppets franchise, this 1984 movie remains under 20th Century Fox (originally CBS Fox). Beyond its unique rights situation, the film also breaks from tradition with its nonlinear storytelling and unexpected twists.  

While nothing quite tops the charm of *The Muppet Movie* (1979)—especially its iconic soundtrack—*The Muppets Take Manhattan* offers something the original doesn’t: grounded, relatable struggles. In the first film, fame comes effortlessly—just stroll into Hollywood, land a contract, and boom, you’re stars. But here, the Muppets face the harsh reality that success takes relentless effort, especially in show business. It’s a refreshing dose of truth, wrapped in the usual whimsy—if you’re willing to embrace the absurdity.

Last November, I caught this film at the Reno Film Festival, and it was an absolute blast. Despite a couple of technical hiccups, the overall experience was fantastic. The writing and performances—especially from the lead actor—were outstanding. The movie has both heart and sharp wit, making it thoroughly engaging.  

After the screening, I got to chat with some of the filmmakers, and they were really down-to-earth. Everything about the film left a great impression, and I’d easily recommend it. The story was fresh and relatable—as a woman, I’ve faced many of the same struggles as the protagonist, which made his journey all the more meaningful. The film excels at crafting characters you genuinely connect with, and the friendships felt authentic, like people I actually know. Honestly, I wish my own conversations were as effortlessly sharp as theirs.  

This movie just clicks—it’s the kind of film you wish there were more of. Smart, heartfelt, and undeniably cool.

This monumental film offers a remarkable glimpse into the Soviet perspective on modern Russian history. Beginning at the dawn of the 20th century, its early scenes mimic the faded sepia tones of old photographs, gradually transitioning to black-and-white by mid-century before blossoming into full color as the narrative reaches the 1960s.  

The story follows a boy from a remote Siberian village whose life changes with the arrest of an anarchist during czarist rule. Growing up, he joins the Bolsheviks after the revolution and brings Soviet communism to his homeland. His son—born to a local beauty—fights in World War II before returning to a village transformed by the rise of the Soviet oil industry, showcasing the era’s economic idealism.  

Though lengthy and deliberate in pacing, the film unfolds with impeccable logic and masterful craftsmanship. It naturally divides into three distinct segments, each reflecting a pivotal era in Russia’s turbulent history.

This film might appeal to devout followers of rigid Christian doctrine, but for those who value free thought, reason, the division of religion and government, and quality science fiction, it falls painfully short.  

A few recognizable actors appear—either desperate for work or eager to preach their narrow worldview to the rest of us "unbelievers."  

I found amusement in this movie, much like the campy enjoyment of *Reefer Madness*. That film used fearmongering to push anti-drug propaganda, just as this one weaponizes guilt and damnation to enforce its particular brand of Christianity on morally sound people who dare to see the world differently.  

It left me laughing hysterically while also unnerved, realizing just how many wish to drag society back to the so-called "good old days" of the 1800s.

Here's something special for movie buffs who may have missed this hidden treasure. Back in the 80s, Dennis Quaid was Hollywood royalty, but he suddenly vanished from the spotlight in the early 90s. His 1993 comeback featured three films that all underperformed at the box office – though two of them were personal favorites of mine. Let me tell you about one particularly wild ride.  

*Wilder Napalm* is a delightfully bizarre film about pyrokinetic brothers Wallace (Quaid) and Wilder (Arliss Howard)—yes, they can literally start fires with their minds.  

Following a tragic childhood accident where they unknowingly killed a man while burning down an abandoned house, Wilder swears off using his powers destructively. Now a firefighter, he’s married to the eccentric Vida (Debra Winger), who’s under house arrest for—you guessed it—arson (watch the movie to unpack that twist). The brothers haven’t spoken in five years—not since Wallace set Wilder’s hair on fire at his bachelor party.  

While Wilder tries to control his abilities, Wallace embraces them with reckless abandon...

This movie certainly doesn’t deserve the harsh criticism some reviewers have thrown its way. While it suffers from a bloated runtime, clumsy editing, and an overuse of flashy, low-quality effects, it also has redeeming qualities. The pacing lacks the energetic spark most comedies need to keep audiences engaged without glancing at the clock.  

That said, the film delivers plenty of genuinely funny moments, thanks to sharp writing and a committed cast. The underdog story at its core is familiar but effective, with standout performances from Macy, Stiller, and Azaria as the central trio. Garofalo and Studi also bring depth and tension to the mix. Reubens and Mitchell, while not essential to the overall story, still have their brief highlights.  

The plot sticks to the classic formula of the underestimated rising to victory—no twists there. But what makes it work isn't the over-the-top heroes and villains—it's the witty exchanges and chemistry among the characters. At their core, they're just big kids trying to do the right thing, and the film’s most heartfelt moments come from that sincerity.

Fishbourne delivers a curiously humorous performance, while Ed Harris—though briefly featured—shines remarkably. In contrast, Connery seems lost in his role, reduced to the stiff mannerisms of an eighty-year-old. The screenplay itself is nonsensical: a sixty-minute happy ending tacked onto a sudden, disjointed twist with no narrative foundation for the characters. It feels less like a coherent script and more like a mishap, perhaps useful only as a case study in screenwriting schools. The more you analyze the details, the more glaring these flaws become. Capital punishment, initially framed as a central theme, gradually fades without resolution—another wasted opportunity in what could have been a compelling setting and premise.

Harman and Isings' *Old Mill Pond* stands as a remarkable achievement in animation. The exceptional craftsmanship and artistry that define their collaboration shine brilliantly in this cartoon. It’s unfortunate that many interpret it through a lens of offense when, in truth, it was always meant as lighthearted entertainment with no intention to disparage anyone. If anything, it celebrates the vibrant humor and musical spirit of African-American culture.  

For years, I’ve been unable to watch this delightful film due to its censorship in England, deemed too controversial for modern audiences. If anyone knows where I might find a copy, I’d greatly appreciate the chance to revisit this classic.  

Perhaps those who scrutinize these decades-old cartoons for unintended meanings might benefit from a more relaxed perspective. While society has evolved, we shouldn’t erase or censor the past—instead, we should acknowledge it as a reflection of its time.

Here’s the rewrite:  

You already knew the third installment would be bad—after all, *Maniac Cop* wasn’t even good enough to justify a sequel. But just how bad is this one? Absolutely terrible, teetering on the edge of unwatchable.  

At one point, as the Maniac Cop rampages, a reporter dramatically declares: *"What happened here can ONLY be described as a black rainbow of death."*  

Let’s break that down:  
1) Rainbows aren’t black—they physically can't be.  
2) Rainbows are harmless—they don’t kill people.  
3) A competent journalist, valued by their news outlet, could probably find a better way to describe a massacre than *"a black rainbow of death."* And no, it’s *not* the *only* possible description.  

This is the kind of nonsense you're signing up for.

Rewatching this film, I was struck by how faithfully it follows the novel—apart from the omission of Cary’s (Leslie Howard) early years. Given the era’s limitations on what could be depicted onscreen—though the book itself is restrained—the protagonist’s obsession with Mildred (Bette Davis) is brilliantly portrayed. This movie resonates deeply with anyone who’s ever been infatuated with someone who exploited their feelings.  

I once read that Maugham was invited to record an audiobook of his novel, but he broke down in tears after just a few lines, forcing the project’s abandonment. That raw emotion is palpable in the writing, and while the film only captures a portion of the story, it remains a compelling adaptation.

I gave this a 1-star rating, though I wish I could have rated it even lower. From the moment I inserted the DVD and settled onto my couch, I braced myself for what I expected to be hilariously bad filmmaking. After checking IMDb and seeing it ranked among the worst-rated films, I went in ready to nitpick every flaw—yet nothing could have prepared me for the absolute disaster that flooded my screen.  

The box art tries (and fails) to make the film look passable. Don’t be fooled. This abomination deserves to be wiped from existence, banned from every store shelf worldwide.  

Imagine a cheap porn parody—but without any of the entertaining bits. The "acting" (if it even qualifies as such), the so-called "plot" (more riddled with holes than Swiss cheese), and the laughable special effects combine to create an unwatchable mess.  

Take my warning seriously: don’t make the same mistake I did by renting this thinking it'd be so-bad-it’s-funny. Trust me—it isn’t.  

Now, I won’t claim I could make a better film myself...

I showed this film in my religion class to spark discussion. In a high-rise apartment, a golden fish swims contentedly in its bowl while a young boy and his mother are out. The boy is sent to buy milk but gets distracted at a carnival. Nearby stands an unsettling man dressed in black who frightens him, causing the boy to drop and break the milk bottle. Surprisingly, the man quietly hands him money to replace it.  

Meanwhile, back at home, a black cat sneaks in through the fire escape. Drawn to the fishbowl, it watches intently as the fish darts around—until it leaps out of the water. By this point, my students and I had grown deeply attached to the little fish. When the cat picks it up in its mouth, we all froze. Then, to our relief, the cat gently drops it back into the bowl.  

Parallel stories unfold—one with the misunderstood man in black, the other with the unfairly judged black cat. Both challenge assumptions, revealing hidden innocence. The film was a perfect conversation starter in class.

When a movie goes by five or more different titles, it’s often a telltale sign of deep-rooted issues—and *Necromancy* is no exception. This film is downright terrible, plagued by glaring flaws from start to finish. I watched the version titled *Rosemary's Disciples* on video, and while it may differ slightly from other cuts, I doubt any extended runtime or alternate edit could salvage it.  

The biggest issue? The story itself. It opens with Laurie waking up before being whisked away by her husband to a town called Lillith, where he's landed a new job at—wait for it—a toy factory catering to occultists (yes, it gets this absurd early on). Guarded by a rifle-toting sentry at the bridge, Lillith only allows those handpicked by the town's mysterious "owner." Before long, it’s clear everyone there is a witch, blindly following the orders of Mr. Cato, the coven’s leader who’s desperate to resurrect his dead son (hence *Necromancy*). The townsfolk spend their days dabbling in vague witchcraft—

*Prix de Beauté* arrived at the crossroads of cinema’s transition from silent films to sound, which unfolded more slowly in Europe than in Hollywood. Initially planned as a silent film, it premiered in France with a dubbed soundtrack—another actress speaking Louise Brooks' lines—while Italy and other European regions screened it without sound. At the Tribeca Film Festival, I had the privilege of watching the Cineteca di Bologna’s pristine restoration of an original Italian silent print. Though I haven’t yet seen the talkie version, it’s safe to assume the silent iteration is far superior—reports indicate the dubbing is jarringly mismatched (Brooks’ English dialogue makes lip-syncing impossible). Moreover, the film is crafted entirely in the silent tradition, using minimal intertitles and relying on visuals rather than dialogue. *Prix de Beauté* unfolds through striking, inventive cinematography. The opening sequence bursts with energy, cutting swiftly between urban scenes and swimmers at a bustling public beach. Throughout, the film lingers on meticulous visual details—fabrics, machinery, décor—and recurring motifs, like a caged bird or a discarded pile of...

This is an absolutely terrible film, with only a handful of redeeming moments.  

It opens with a heavily pregnant Linda Blair sprinting down a hallway, desperate to escape what might be monsters—or possibly pitchfork-wielding pursuers. In a frantic move, she leaps through a window and abruptly wakes up, revealing she’s *very* pregnant—an oddly fluctuating pregnancy that seems to change drastically from scene to scene.  

Linda and an unbearably annoying (and possibly mentally challenged) little boy—who I initially mistook for her son—journey to a deserted island hotel. Italian horror directors really have a knack for casting the most grating child actors. Already on the island are David Hasselhoff and his German-speaking, virginal girlfriend (because, of course, Germans famously adore Hasselhoff). He’s busy snapping photos, while she’s translating some obscure German book about witches—or something like that.  

Joining them are an elderly couple who’ve bought the island, a real estate agent, and a woman I assumed was their daughter. Turns out, she’s actually an architect, while Linda and the obnoxious boy are the older couple’s children. Somehow, they all end up on the island together, though the editing makes it seem like Linda and the kid arrived separately.

I caught *Brother’s Shadow* at the Tribeca Film Festival, and its story lingered with me long after. The film follows a prodigal son (Scott Cohen) as he returns to his family’s custom furniture business after a stint in prison, delivering everything a compelling drama should—complex characters, razor-sharp dialogue, and a director with a keen visual eye.  

But what makes it stand out is something increasingly rare in today’s cinema: the bold, unfiltered vision of a seasoned storyteller. Director-screenwriter Todd S. Yellin’s talent feels fully realized, yet it’s clear he, like his protagonist, has earned his perspective. He understands the grit of real struggles and the human craving to witness—or even live through—hard-won victories. But Yellin refuses to offer cheap resolutions. In the end, his protagonist’s real triumph isn’t measured in sales or family approval, but in the work itself—the craftsmanship he could never walk away from.  

It’s a refreshing reminder in an industry (and a world) too often fixated on profit over purpose.

What’s the deal with the actors who signed on for that disaster? Michael Dorn should’ve stayed in the *Star Trek* universe. And John Diehl—anyone recall his *Miami Vice* days? He was decent there, but here? Well, no surprises when the lead is a former *Baywatch* lifeguard. The result? Exactly what you’d expect—nothing.  

The characters are unbearable, the special effects are laughably bad (not in a fun way), and the plot feels like a poorly written joke. Nothing makes sense. It’s like they were aiming for *Attack of the Killer Tomatoes* camp but missed by a mile—especially in that ridiculous scene where top officials debate national security crammed into what looks like a broom closet.  

Do yourself a favor: if this pops up on TV, change the channel. Your TV (and your sanity) will thank you.

How did this mess even happen? I’m usually a fan of sci-fi and Bigfoot movies, but even I expect some level of competence in the writing—this was just drowning in cringe. The effects were painfully bad, the dialogue even worse. Steer clear unless you enjoy suffering. I only rented it by accident—the case was mislabeled (still searching for that Lance Henriksen Sasquatch flick, by the way).  

The core concept had real promise; there was plenty of room to craft a solid, fun film here. But somehow, it ended up a total disaster. Honestly, you could walk into any high school and find film, art, or English students who could write a sharper script. What a waste.

I couldn't believe just how terrible this film was. What was the intended takeaway—was there some profound lesson or insight I missed? And what was the deal with all those pumpkins? Did the director expect me to be wowed by the motel footage? Why did we need lingering shots of trash bags on a rooftop across from a hotel? The narrator's attempts at mocking his interview subjects fell painfully flat—it was blatantly obvious he cherry-picked (and likely cut out) their most coherent moments just to ridicule them. The only redeeming moment? The film professor’s interview, where he predicted just how awful this mess would turn out—before it was even complete.  

Honestly, I’m stunned. It feels like the filmmaker is either desperately trying to pass as an intellectual or begging for validation from that crowd.

Kiyoshi Kurosawa’s ghost film is undeniably bizarre and even manages to sneak in a surprise jump scare. However, the movie falls flat with its absurd premise—a detective investigates a possible serial killer, only to suspect himself of one of the murders. Things spiral further into nonsense when he’s stalked by a beautiful Asian ghost with no clear motive, leaving both him and the audience baffled.  

As more murders occur, the detective grows increasingly bewildered when the killers are quickly identified—yet the ghost still torments him for no apparent reason. The plot isn’t just illogical; it’s downright laughable, especially when the ghost zips across the city like some spectral superhero. The ending (like the entire film) makes zero sense, and the tone is so inconsistent that it feels like an accidental dark comedy.  

Aside from *Bright Future*, this is easily the weakest Kiyoshi Kurosawa film I’ve come across. I can’t recommend it—unless you're in the mood for unintentional hilarity.

This movie, *Evil Breed: The Legend of Samhain*, shows minimal effort or depth. It relies on absurdly quick "slasher" kills and gratuitously grotesque deaths. The acting is subpar, earning a D-grade, as the performers display little skill, and their characters’ decisions border on unbelievable. Their portrayal of people their age feels wildly inaccurate.  

The inclusion of random, poorly integrated adult scenes adds nothing of value, while even remotely decent moments are swiftly overshadowed by brutal, stomach-churning violence. One particularly disturbing example is an extended five-minute scene where a victim is violently disemboweled. The lack of resistance from the characters makes their fate feel even more pointless.  

If you enjoy watching mindless carnage and borderline torture, this might be your kind of film—otherwise, steer clear.

A complete waste of time—terrible acting, weak plot, and poor direction. This has to be the dullest film ever made! Some bad movies are still entertaining (*Freddy vs. Jason*), but others are just painfully awful. This one falls squarely into the second category. Final verdict—skip it.

This is hands down the most terrible film I've ever watched!!!!  

I can honestly say no movie has ever disappointed me more than this one!!!  

AND I MEAN NOT A SINGLE ONE!!!!  

As a devoted fan of low-budget horror flicks, I've endured some of cinema's most cringe-worthy offerings.  

The title alone drew me in—who wouldn’t be curious about *"Vampires vs. Zombies"*?! My mind raced with visions of gruesome, gory battles between the undead. I thought, *"This is going to be epic!"*  

But let me tell you... *"This was a mistake I regret!"*  

The title couldn’t be more misleading. There were no vampire-zombie clashes. In fact, there was *no* coherent plot whatsoever! If someone asked me what this movie was about, I’d have to admit—I still have no clue!!!  

No plot!!!!  

No story!!!!  

Just pure, incomprehensible nonsense!!!!  

By the time the credits rolled, all I felt was pity for—

I’d heard endless praise for *Weeds* and was excited to dive into what promised to be another standout cable series—like *Entourage*, *The Sopranos*, or *Mad Men*. But that enthusiasm faded fast with each season one episode I watched (I barely made it through six).  

The writing felt stale, formulaic, and at times, painfully cringe-worthy—especially in its portrayal of Black characters. The dialogue didn’t flow naturally; it screamed of writers straining to sound edgy and witty, leaving genuine laughs few and far between.  

The characters never grew on me—they were shallow, self-absorbed, and hard to root for. The brother-in-law’s creepy presence (who frankly belonged on *To Catch a Predator*) made me recoil, while Quinn’s abrupt exit—shipped off to boarding school in Mexico—was a lazy, clichéd plot device. It almost felt like the writers were daring viewers to keep watching.  

With every episode, my dislike for the characters deepened, and the sloppy storytelling only made things worse. And after hearing season two was even weaker, I had no regrets about walking away.

A childless couple (Brooke Adams, Jeff Hayenga) visits a doctor (James Karen) in hopes of conceiving. Their wish is granted, but Adams soon realizes something is terribly wrong with the baby...  

Though the premise is intriguing, the film is undone by a weak script—what starts as a decent setup quickly turns predictable, with every "twist" painfully obvious. The direction falters, with clumsy scene compositions that lack basic craftsmanship. The production quality is, at best, subpar—visibly cheap and poorly executed. The gore effects are gratuitously unsettling (a particularly distressing moment involves a pregnant woman stabbing her own stomach), made worse by shoddy special effects. By the climax, it’s clear the filmmakers had no coherent ending in mind, leaving the story to spiral into nonsense.  

Decent performances offer slight redemption. Adams, Hayenga, and Karen deliver solid work, making the film just barely watchable—but not enough to salvage it. Hardly released in 1991 and rightfully forgotten since, this is one to skip. A generous 4/10.

**Rewritten Version:**  

With a captivating performance by Will Smith and a story that pulls at your heartstrings with the intensity of a rock guitarist shredding a solo, *Seven Pounds* surpasses the director’s earlier collaboration with the actor (*The Pursuit of Happyness*), a film I also adored. Gabriele Muccino’s name deserves recognition—without a star like Smith, some of his works might slip under the radar.  

It’s a shame I pieced together Will Smith’s plan early on. The clues were there—his call reporting his own suicide in the opening scene and Rosario Dawson’s introduction as a woman with an incurable heart condition made it clear.  

Still, the writer and director made the right choice in structuring the film with those bookends (the first and final scenes). They create urgency and tension, slowly revealing how a man could be pushed to such an extreme sacrifice. Watching the bond between Smith’s and Dawson’s characters blossom was bittersweet, knowing all along what fate had in store for these two tragic souls.  

One friend I saw it with...

When does this pain end? I can't bear another adaptation of *A Christmas Carol*. Endless films repeat the same tired tale, competing to outdo each other—only to fail, because the story itself is weak. Moralizing, outdated, full of naive optimism. As if people actually change. The countless remakes prove we never learn.

You know a film is in serious trouble when even John Cassavetes—usually a powerhouse performer—is phoning it in. *The Incubus* is a grim reminder of what happens when a gifted actor takes a paycheck gig without bothering to engage. Not that you can fully blame him—the overwrought script and John Hough’s excessively stylized sets make it an uphill battle. The plot revolves around a string of rape-murders plaguing a small town, padded with supernatural nonsense. Instead of building suspense, the sluggish direction drains every scene of energy, leaving Cassavetes visibly exasperated. The titular monster, only appearing in the finale, is impressively crafted—but by then, it’s far too late to care.  

1/10

I checked out a review before watching this film that claimed it might be one of the greatest movies ever made!? Yeah, right. The tension builds scene by scene, sure—but only because the characters are so infuriating. From the little girl babbling nonsense while attempting to drown the boy, to the killer randomly appearing with zero explanation (and who was that guy talking to the kid on the beach!?), nothing in this film makes sense. Plotlines are introduced but never resolved, leaving the whole thing feeling disjointed and frustrating.  

The performances are solid, but the script is a disaster. Every character's actions and dialogue are absurdly unrealistic, and the reactions from the rest of the cast just make things weirder. There's no payoff for any of the conflicts set up earlier, leaving the entire story feeling pointless—and honestly, a total waste of time.

What an episode! After last week’s endless jabs from Mellisa about Annie and Brandi’s friendship, I thought I’d had enough—but her meltdown after getting fired proved me wrong. Watching her storm around in that cast, hurling insults and shrieking for someone to fetch her purse was peak reality TV gold. Then she started yelling for her clothes—*all of them*—as if anyone would ever touch those tacky outfits. Mellisa, you’re pushing 40—are tantrums still your thing?  

And then Joan jumps in, tearing into Annie and Brandie with every insult in the book before dramatically storming off! The Rivers sisters are nothing but entitled brats who overstayed their welcome just for drama. Mellisa’s refusal to do an exit interview only confirmed what everyone already knew: she’s a spoiled child who can’t handle not getting her way.  

Best part? Annie straight-up admitting she could play Mellisa like a fiddle—and then doing exactly that. Say what you will, but Mellisa’s still the sharpest player in this game, and she’s the one who deserves the win.

This film feels like a college project made by a group of white guys who all graduated together. That wouldn’t necessarily be an issue—except it *really* shows. Nearly the entire cast consists of white men around the same age, giving off serious "boys' camp hijinks turned into a movie" energy. There’s almost no plot to speak of, just the same violent bloodbath sequences recycled over and over. A few amusing moments pop up here and there, but they aren’t enough to save the film from its dull, repetitive grind.  

To mask the limitations of their budget, the filmmakers rely heavily on cartoonish graphics—not particularly well-executed, either. If it couldn’t be filmed with guys sprinting across a beach drenched in fake blood, they slapped in some shoddy animation instead.  

I went in expecting something Tarantino-esque based on the trailer. Turns out, those preview clips are as good as it gets. The rest is just the same tired, juvenile humor on a loop. Sure, it lands occasionally, but mostly? Exhaustingly one-note.

I had to see this film—the absurd premise demanded it, and it didn’t disappoint. At times, it’s downright uncomfortable to watch. Unlike Meyer’s usual work, the sexual content is dialed back, but the violence is over-the-top, often needlessly graphic and offensive. The story is a mess, and the performances—along with some of the dialogue—are painfully bad.  

This movie is a bizarre clash of sado-masochistic fantasy and a half-baked critique of slavery’s brutality and immorality, failing at both. It feels like Meyer tried to compensate for the film’s exploitative roots by shoehorning in a moral lesson. He seems aware of the guilt we might feel enjoying the early dominatrix imagery—Lady Susan wielding that whip in her provocative getup—and then awkwardly pivots to an overwrought tale of good conquering evil. The result? A hollow mess where neither element lands.  

But here’s the thing—it’s so spectacularly bad on so many levels that it’s actually worth watching, especially if you have a taste for gloriously terrible filmmaking.

Once upon a time, there existed a delightful country known as France... In those days, people lived in contentment. Women were carefree, and men devoted themselves to their beloved diversion: war, the sole amusement of kings that the common folk could partake in. The conflict at hand was the Seven Years' War, and when it became apparent that fallen soldiers outnumbered those still standing, recruiters were dispatched to refill the ranks.  

Thus it happened that Fanfan (Gérard Philipe), caught romping with a farmer’s daughter in a haystack, avoided wedlock by joining the Régiment d'Aquitaine—but only after a gypsy foretold his destiny. She promised him glory and riches in the King’s service, along with a royal marriage to the King’s daughter. Little did Fanfan know, Adeline (Gina Lollobrigida) was no true gypsy but the daughter of the regiment’s recruiting sergeant.  

When Fanfan impulsively dashed from the recruits, sword drawn, to rescue a besieged carriage, who should be inside but the Marquise de Pompadour and... the King’s daughter. Now utterly convinced of his lofty future bride, he remained oblivious to Adeline’s affections—despite the distracting charm of her daringly low necklines. Yet soon enough, she too would realize her heart belonged to Fanfan. And so, the tale unfolds...

**New York, I Love You** is an anthology of eleven short films, each approximately 10 minutes in length. While the segments aren’t directly connected, they share a unifying theme: love. Each vignette explores love in different forms, whether between couples or chance encounters between strangers.  

The film boasts an impressive ensemble cast, including Shia LaBeouf, Natalie Portman, Hayden Christensen, Orlando Bloom, Chris Cooper, Andy Garcia, Christina Ricci, Irrfan Khan, Robin Wright Penn, Julie Christie, Ethan Hawke, Bradley Cooper, Rachel Bilson, and Anton Yelchin. With such a talented lineup and an intriguing concept, expectations were high—yet *New York, I Love You* falls short of greatness. Instead of elevating beyond its individual pieces, it remains merely the sum of its parts.  

Some segments shine with humor, originality, and charm, while others—like the forgettable pairings of Orlando Bloom and Christina Ricci, or Ethan Hawke and Maggie Q—feel disappointingly shallow. The film’s uneven quality and experimental approach make it feel more like an ambitious student project than a polished feature. However, there are standout moments, particularly the tender and poignant segment featuring Eli Wallach and Cloris Leachman as an elderly couple strolling through the city.

A pale imitation of far superior films, especially Steve Martin's "LA Story"—which at least had the decency to embrace its fictional premise, even while casting his then-girlfriend as his on-screen love interest.  

Let’s be clear—"20 Dates" is a mockumentary, though I’m not entirely convinced that was Myles Berkowitz’s original intention. My guess is he began with some sincerity, only to quickly realize how painfully unfunny and cringe-worthy the whole thing would be unless he cranked up the absurdity. The result? A film that feels awkward, flimsy, and utterly disingenuous.  

One glaring red flag is the legal absurdity of two women supposedly filing restraining orders against Myles—yet somehow still appearing in the film, which would be impossible without signed consent forms. Not to mention, most of the women cast as his "dates" are clearly professional actresses (aside from Tia Carrere, none of them are household names). They're far too polished, conventionally attractive, and camera-savvy to pass as regular civilians.  

Berkowitz makes the rookie mistake of exclusively featuring this type of overly glamorous...

Bolstered by fans of her far superior *Orlando*, Potter crafts a self-indulgent project that overreaches on every level—writing, directing, starring, and even co-composing the score, complete with a cloying love ballad. The result feels like an overwrought student film, as though its creator wrongly assumes her personal melodramas hold universal appeal. Potter's onscreen persona is as grating as her romantic fixation is unengaging, reducing the whole affair to a cringe-worthy exercise in vanity thinly disguised as an ode to the tango. Had she stepped out of the spotlight, the film might have had a chance. But her wooden performance—whether playing herself or not—sinks it completely. A tedious, pompous mess.

The film's distinctly French quality lies in its deliberate pacing to develop the two main characters. This may test your patience slightly, particularly since neither fits Hollywood’s conventional idea of attractiveness. Yet once the heist begins, the story accelerates rapidly—sometimes even too fast. Despite this, it's an exhilarating ride that feels surprisingly plausible if you don’t scrutinize the details too closely. It’s exactly the type of movie Hollywood would have ruined.

Kate Beckinsale delivers a standout performance—bravo! While Knightley may not match Jeremy Northam’s charm, Mark Strong excels in his role. Bernard Hepton is spot-on as Emma’s father.  

The added ending scene—where the harvest celebration unites Knightley’s workers and high-society guests—is a brilliant touch. Emma’s growth is clear as she embraces this change, though it happens a bit swiftly. Still, it works.  

Samantha Bond shines as Emma’s wise and warm-hearted governess, exactly as envisioned. It’s no surprise—the UK does Jane Austen adaptations best. American remakes often prioritize profit over authenticity. Do yourself a favor—watch this one!

The film’s casting choices are undeniably unusual—some of which can be attributed to the story itself, but I still found it a little hard to fully accept Pierce Brosnan in the lead role (though he delivered a surprisingly strong performance).  

The movie is based on the true story of an Englishman who lived among Canadian Indigenous communities in the early 1900s, passing himself off as a mixed-blood Indigenous man. Remarkably, he became so revered that people traveled from far and wide to attend his lectures and join his wilderness expeditions—despite the fact that his knowledge was entirely borrowed from books or fabricated. The film explores this elaborate deception and the fallout when the truth was exposed.  

Despite my initial doubts about Brosnan, the acting and cinematography were excellent, and I found the film compelling. It’s a shame it didn’t get wider distribution, likely because it leans more cerebral than mainstream—this isn’t a Bond-style action flick or a sweeping romance, but rather an intriguing, offbeat portrait of a truly extraordinary con man.

I refuse to acknowledge *Highlander 2* exists, and I once believed no sequel could ever be so bad it would make me cry. I was mistaken.  

I adored the original *WarGames*, but this sequel is riddled with inaccuracies—both in computer realism and continuity from the first film. At least the original had plausible hacks. Whoever wrote this clearly has zero understanding of technology beyond maybe opening a Word document. I’m not even sure they bothered to watch *WarGames* before making this abomination. The acting? Unconvincing at best.  

Do yourself a favor—avoid this movie at all costs. Even if your TV gets stuck on this channel and won’t turn off, resist. *This film will destroy you.*

This film is an absolute disaster. The actors themselves appear painfully aware of its dreadful quality. It begins poorly and somehow manages to deteriorate even further by the finale. The performances are laughably bad, while the script feels completely improvised. Despite being labeled as a horror movie, it fails to deliver even a single frightening moment. A pitiful 1/10.

For over a decade, *Diagnosis Murder* has aired on BBC1 weekday afternoons—I remember watching it years ago when I’d stay home sick from school. I know I probably shouldn’t love it, just like I shouldn’t be hooked on *Murder, She Wrote*, but I’m completely addicted to both. Yes, I own the DVD box sets… and yes, I realize how nerdy that is.  

The show is anchored by Dick Van Dyke, who plays Dr. Mark Sloan, a physician at LA’s Community General Hospital who also consults for the LAPD. His real-life son, Barry Van Dyke, stars alongside him as his on-screen son, Detective Steve Sloan, who frequently turns to Mark for help with suspicious deaths.  

Rounding out the team is Dr. Amanda Bentley (played by Victoria Rowell), the hospital’s sharp-witted pathologist. In the early seasons, Scott Baio joined the cast as Dr. Jack Stewart—before abruptly leaving in 1995 to chase bigger opportunities. That didn’t pan out too well, given that his most notable film role afterward was in *Baby Geniuses 2: Superbabies*… ouch.  

After Baio’s exit, his character was replaced by the younger Dr. Jesse.

If you enjoy movies featuring school bullies, courageous kids, mischievous toddlers, and—yes—worm-eating, then *How to Eat Fried Worms* is right up your alley.  

The story follows Billy, a boy who starts at a new school only to find himself the target of a prank—bullies slip worms into his lunch. Their ringleader, Joe, along with his crew, mocks Billy, dubbing him "worm boy."  

Instead of backing down, Billy leans into the joke, boasting that he eats worms all the time. Skeptical, Joe challenges him to prove it: if Billy can’t eat ten worms in one day, he’ll have to come to school with worms in his pants.  

Accepting the dare, Billy must stomach the slimy challenge—whether raw, fried, or cooked—to earn his classmates' respect.  

While the premise might sound stomach-churning, the film carries meaningful themes. It explores genuine friendship, self-acceptance, and even delves into what drives bullies to pick on others.

I believe I've covered nearly everything that needs to be said, though I feel compelled to justify my harsh critique. I’ve rarely encountered such an amateurish production—and I mean that in every possible way. While the technical flaws, from shaky camera work to poorly operated boom mics, are downright laughable, they’re far from the only problems.  

Unlike classic indie films redeemed by sharp writing, compelling characters, or clever plots, this one fails across the board—terrible script, cringe-worthy acting, and characters so grating they border on unbearable.  

It’s a shame that for every indie gem like *Haiku Tunnel* that finds distribution, countless others fade into obscurity. Frankly, I can’t fathom how this family-made amateur project got picked up—unless the Kornbluth brothers have connections at Sony. The decision to distribute it baffles me.  

The film’s only redeeming quality? Its title. Yet even that ends up being a disappointment. Hopefully, this review spares a few curious viewers from wasting their time.

This sci-fi film fell painfully short of expectations. First, let’s address the director—Tim Burton—whose name alone raised hopes. Second, it’s a remake of a beloved classic, which only magnified the disappointment. The movie was dull, needlessly grotesque, and borderline absurd. If you've suffered through it, you understand. The overwhelming consensus on IMDb agrees: it’s trash—and they’re spot on. Save yourself the misery—skip this snoozefest. My rating? A generous 1/10.

*Just Cause* initially leaves you puzzled about its harsh reception—it’s nothing groundbreaking, but solidly executed, with a standout supporting turn from Ed Harris. Then the final act arrives, gradually descending into absurdity until you’re watching a killer with a headlamp menace Sean Connery’s wife (an oddly stilted Kate Capshaw) and child (a young Scarlett Johansson) in a shack used for skinning alligators.  

The kind of film best suited for a mid-flight watch—and even then, just the once.

**"Dressed to Kill"** stands as one of the greatest thrillers ever crafted. Its exploration of sex and violence ensures it’s strictly for mature audiences. Brian De Palma reaffirms his mastery of visual storytelling, demonstrating an unmatched command of the camera. Much of the narrative unfolds through imagery alone, with minimal dialogue, heightened by Pino Donnagio’s haunting score. Shot in Panavision, the film demands to be seen in widescreen—De Palma meticulously uses every inch of the frame to enhance the story. A cropped version on video pales in comparison. With stellar performances, impeccable direction, and arguably one of cinema’s most electrifying scores, **"Dressed to Kill"** is essential viewing.

This documentary feels heavily biased, undermining the credibility that comes with balanced reporting.  

Failing to credit interviewees makes it impossible to assess their expertise—were their perspectives even worth including?  

Presenting only one narrative is irresponsible. Oversimplifying history misleads future generations and fuels conflict—not the sole cause of war, but certainly not harmless.  

If you watch this, fact-check extensively. The Balkans are as layered as human history itself—dig deeper before forming conclusions.

This film shatters the illusion of celebrity glamour, revealing harsh realities many never see. It powerfully depicts good intentions crushed by circumstance, with an unnervingly realistic bomb blast sequence that lingers in memory.  

Prepare to have your worldview challenged—much of what we're told simply doesn't match reality. The tension alone might spike your blood pressure.  

Every performer delivers exceptional portrayals, though certain intense scenes make this decidedly adult viewing. Wisely edited, it still pushes boundaries—definitely not family-friendly material.  

Brilliant casting elevates this raw, uncompromising drama.

Steve McQueen undoubtedly has a devoted fan base. His magnetic presence made him one of the most captivating stars ever to grace the silver screen. Yet even McQueen can't salvage this lackluster film, which appears to have been shot with little more than a home camera on the streets of St. Louis.  

McQueen plays a newcomer with a clean record, recruited into a bank heist by a member of the gang. There are strong undertones of a romantic tension between his character and David Clarke's, which doesn't sit well with the rest of the crew—especially given McQueen's lack of criminal experience.  

Adding to the mix is his girlfriend, Molly McCarthy, who grows suspicious when she notices him spending time with Crahan Denton, James Dukas, and Clarke—all of them shady figures. Any sensible person would be wary in her position.  

*The Great St. Louis Bank Robbery* was co-directed by Charles Guggenheim, known mainly for documentaries, and John Stix, who had little notable work. One of them inexplicably encouraged McQueen to deliver his lines in a poor Marlon Brando impression, a baffling choice that only drags the film down further.

Three treasure hunters scour the West Indies in pursuit of a hidden fortune. As gold fever takes hold, tensions rise the closer they get to their prize. While the deep-sea divers aim to recover the treasure, greed and betrayal turn deadly.  

Their vessel, the *Manfish*, isn’t a creature but their boat’s name. The skeletal figure who delivers half the treasure map to rugged Captain John Bromfield (as Brannigan) is a standout. Veteran sailor Victor Jory (as the Professor) holds the other half. First mate Lon Chaney Jr. (as Swede) plays the fool, while alluring Tessa Prendergast (as Alita) tends—rather ineffectively—to the rum supply.  

Plagued by choppy editing and continuity lapses, the film falls short of its potential.  

*** *Manfish* (2/56) W. Lee Wilder ~ John Bromfield, Victor Jory, Lon Chaney Jr.

This is hands down the worst film I've ever purchased a ticket for, and aside from *They Saved Hitler's Brain*, the most painfully awful movie I've endured. As a devoted fan of SNL and SCTV when this released, I expected groundbreaking humor—finally freed from TV's creative constraints.  

Instead, the writers' approach seemed to be: *Toss in shock value, fart gags, lazy sexual innuendo—instant edgy comedy!* The game show parodies were uninspired *Let’s Make a Deal* ripoffs with juvenile gross-outs. The sitcom skit relied on cringe-worthy high school-level humor. The stun gun ad might’ve landed on *Sesame Street*. The subway bit? Forced violence masquerading as edgy comedy. And the blind French chef endlessly repeating "there is no difference"? Point made.  

Only a fleeting 60-second Chevy Chase bit earned a laugh—meaning the rest was pure agony.

I loved this film. Tobey Maguire delivers an outstanding performance as Jake—honestly, one of the finest actors I’ve had the pleasure of watching. What surprised me most were the witty lines scattered throughout the movie. Maguire nails the humor flawlessly, a side of him I hadn’t seen before. The story pulls you in, making you deeply invested in the characters and their fates.  

Jewel’s performance was a pleasant surprise—she held her own brilliantly. Packed with thrilling moments, the film is a gripping ride from start to finish. I’ve become a huge Maguire fan after this. If you haven’t already, be sure to watch *Cider House Rules*. It’s an absolute classic.

I’m genuinely amazed this film even got made. The director/writer/actor must have some serious real-life charisma—I can’t imagine how else this script got approved. While watching it, I couldn’t help but feel bad for the actors. It was like witnessing a stand-up comic bomb on stage, where you’re not laughing, just cringing out of secondhand embarrassment as they desperately try to make it work.  

I’d love to know the budget—it had to be low, given the shoddy production quality. Saying "the jokes didn’t land for me" feels too generous—for them to resonate, you’d either have to be the person who wrote them or be completely out of touch. Just picture pitching this script... and somehow getting it greenlit. That’s honestly impressive, in its own way.

What an absolute trainwreck of a film!  

A painfully predictable, sluggish, soul-sucking snoozefest that makes rusty breadknife dentistry seem like a pleasant alternative.  

The acting is absurdly exaggerated for the paper-thin script, every scene drags on twice as long as necessary, and the tedious play-by-play of failing careers is more exhausting than a tax audit. The soundtrack had potential—if only it weren’t chained to this mess. Three decent tracks hardly justify enduring the rest.  

By the halfway mark, I was begging for spontaneous unconsciousness—or a mercy bullet.  

Never. Again.

The U.S. State Department might not want you to watch this film, given their strained relations with Iran. Yet it reveals the true sophistication of Iranian society, despite its focus on women's fight for basic rights—in this case, simply attending a soccer match in a stadium reserved only for men. The movie is brilliantly witty, and its very existence highlights the freedom of expression in Iran. I was thoroughly captivated by it. The story follows five girls attempting to sneak past security to watch an Iran vs. Bahrain soccer game. The comedy that unfolds—from their chaotic bus ride to the stadium, to their encounters with police and eventual detainment—is too entertaining to put into words. This is a must-watch masterpiece, one of the finest foreign films I’ve seen in years—don’t miss it.

I must confess I’ve never been able to watch an Antonioni film straight through on the first attempt—even this one required three separate viewings. In hindsight, that might have been for the best. Breaking it up forced me to let go of conventional storytelling and appreciate each scene on its own terms.  

The opening section feels fragmented—not in a bad way, but it demands more attention. Once it shifts to the desert, the effort pays off entirely. The breathtaking cinematography is only part of it; what leaves a lasting impression is how the landscape becomes this overpowering force—its silence, its vastness, the melancholy and freedom it embodies, the way it reflects and clashes with the two young protagonists. The desert may be lifeless, yet it feels far less cold than the urban sprawl of the earlier scenes. The dance between the airplane circling overhead and the girl’s speeding car creates one striking shot after another. The love—
